en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the Samayaprakāśa, a section of the Vīramitrodaya.
[To the one] whose brow is terrifying with a frown, where the fierce mane dances in a fit of rage and the eyebrows move in a frightful manner;

May the unprecedented form of Nṛhari protect us— his Bhairava-like gaze wandering, his body like that of a serpent-king swelling with pride, and the vast shell of the cosmic egg shattered by the fierce expansion of his yawning jaws, which were like the extinguished forms of his enemies.
With the impetuous force of his heavy fury surging forth at the onset of the great Daityas— fury that rivals the falling drops of nectar from the moon’s rays caught in the tips of his mane—
he licks the circle of the quarters with his tongue, which is like the cresting flame of a fire.
May Nṛsiṃha, with his impetuous strides, subdue my intense pride that is so full of arrogance. // 2 //

May that flute-player, who desires to sport with Rādhā, bestow upon you abundant and lasting welfare—he who causes the fall of the tall palaces of the enemies of the gods, headed by Kaṃsa, the destroyer of *saṃsāra*;
and whose eyes are clearly revealed as moon-like by the guñjā berries he wears as a garland on his forehead, as he longs to behold the beauty of our own sweet lotus-face hidden within his topknot.

May that Dhūrjaṭi protect you—he whose garment spreads out through the playful delusion [of his dance], who has drawn the moon upon his forehead as he moves; beneath whose feet the serpent-king Śeṣa and the lord of tortoises bend, rise, and stretch their bodies as he places his steps; whose host of hoods rises and flashes with hissing sounds; and who makes the kettledrums filling the sky resound as they are blown by the striking of his dancing matted locks.

May Heramba bring you long-lasting auspiciousness—he who, having taken his stand upon the sky, has begun a great plunge into the vast ocean with his trunk submerged; he who is as if praised by serpents gliding through the air, frantic from the slapping of their trunks and the tumultuous, buzzing clamor of swarms of bees bewildered by the tossing of his jar-like head.
Beholding the three worlds simultaneously with her three eyes from all sides, protecting the ten directions even with her ten arms,
she places one foot upon the lion and the other upon the supreme state.
May she who has slain her enemies and who crushed the buffalo-demon destroy your delusion, which is like a buffalo.

There was a sovereign of the circle of kings named Medinīamalla, who resembled Bhīma; he shattered his enemies, brought happiness to the world through his nobility, fulfilled the desires of those in need,
possessed abundant strength, and had a fame as white as the lord of venomous serpents.
In the royal lineage of Sīkāśī, he was like the moon in the ocean, the sovereign of all the earth. // 7 //
Desiring the village of battle, he of incomparable majesty— the abode of rest for all beings— advanced against the circle of enemies with a stride of vast valor, like the sun dispelling darkness;
and by his wrestling with the earth, he became like another mountain, noble as the essence of Mount Meru.
There arose, renowned throughout the circle of the earth, a king named Medinīmalla. // 8 //
Filling the world with moon-like glories that seemed to mock the moon as they issued forth, Arjuna— whose valor was irresistible, who surpassed Arjuna (Kārtavīrya) by his distribution of arrows,
whose glory in acquiring sovereignty was vast, and whose long arms possessed immeasurable virtues— [remained].
From this King Medinīmalla, there arose an incomparable lord of men named Arjuna.

The intellect of King Arjuna was pure, his forbearance peerless, his learning faultless, and his mind the sole abode of profundity; he was a destroyer of the misery of the wretched in bestowing gifts, and a cause of the flight of his enemies in battle.
He was the protection of the earths, and his fame, arising from the qualities of its cause, was as white as the arjuna flower.
Therefore, from Bhūmipati Arjuna— [a son] who was a treasury of singular nobility, an ocean of beauty, and limitless in his virtues— a being of immense majesty manifested;
he who, by the rising of his mature valor, shattered the wicked and earned great fame.
Malakhāna by name, the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth, was difficult to overcome. // 11 //
While he governed this earth with statesmanship, the world was free from enmity; even the impetuous onset of lordly elephants was rendered possible alongside lions.

The curious hawk played with birds, and the fish sported with crocodiles; what more need be said? Even in the deep forest, there occurred the "sporting together" (*śārdūlavikrīḍitam*) of tigers with deer.
Adorned by fame as white as the Himalayas, his majesty eclipsing the power of the oceans, Pratāparudra was born from Malikhaṇa through his exploits like a second Rudra in the three worlds. (13)
By Pratāparudra, the mind— which is pure wealth toward the seeker, equal to fame in bestowing honor, and a virtue to the world— was bestowed upon his son Rudra as if it were the earth itself.

Born from Pratāparudra and protecting the earth together with its oceans, that lord of the earth shone resplendent during the reign of Madhukarasāha, having performed the burning of the forests of his enemies. 15.

King Madhukarasāha shone with mature vigor; he was broad through the enjoyment of merit, intent on the application of welfare, free from the association of the wicked, and heavy with the application of well-performed deeds. He appeared resplendent as the very earth rested upon his pillar-like arms.
Dispelling the suffering of the multitude of subjects, manifested by the great rise of his splendor,

he was like the full moon— substantial with its abundance of nectar and delighting the assembly; he was like the lord of the twice-born (Brahmā), who possesses a radiant garland of white lotuses and is the protector of the stars.
The king is victorious—he who possesses true compassion, who acts like a bee [for his subjects], and who has put shame upon his enemies. // 17 //
Having entrusted the burden of the earth to Vīrasiṃha, that lion among kings,
Madhukarasāha— whose impurities were consumed by the fire of knowledge— ascended to heaven.

King Vīrasiṃha, a lion among men, became a lord of the earth who, with his profound majesty, cast his hosts of enemies into darkness; he was a delighter in dance and song, and possessed noble elephants and horses. // 19 //
Upon his departure, not even a single enemy remained here as a survivor of the battle, despite the sudden arrival of numerous hosts of elephants;

rather, [the foe] stood there in a wretched state, even though staying within the depths of a thicket, casting his eyes high into the quarters all around with a startled gaze turned in every direction out of fear.

The generosity of King Vīrasimha, the lion among heroes who transcends all desires, surpasses the wish-fulfilling tree; his fame exceeds the ocean of milk; his wisdom outweighs the preceptor of Śakra; his great essence towers above Mount Meru; the weight of his majesty overcomes the forest fire; and his prosperity prevails over the god of love. What is there that does not surpass something else? (21)

While Vīrasiṃha— the Indra over the entire circle of the earth— was, by his gifts, instantly turning supplicants into those free from begging and making his adversaries his enemies, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) freely produced every desire in their hearts, the wish-granting tree (Kalpadruma) fulfilled whatever was requested, and the thought-gem (Cintāmaṇi), its very birth rendered purposeless, brought about anxiety-free repose for those who sought refuge in it.
Having wandered and wandered tirelessly through the three worlds for a long time, she traversed the path of Viṣṇu’s feet above the vessel of the universe;
now, having completely covered the cosmic egg as if it were her own small circle of ground, her swan-like radiant fame serves as an ornament for all the worlds. 23.
When the lion among kings, Vīrasiṃha, extends the impetus of his giving, he regards the ocean as a mere drop of water and the mountain of gold as a mere speck of dust. (24)
When the son of Pāṇḍu had drawn his great bow into a circle like a coil of a serpent and was conquering the Khāṇḍava forest with the dancing of his eyes,
and when that lion among heroes was eager to bestow his wealth upon the mind [of Arjuna], then indeed was Karṇa described by the people as noble-minded once again.

Having united within himself various virtues— heroism, magnanimity, profundity, fortitude, compassion, charity, and so forth— which rivaled the lord of serpents bearing the heavy burden of the earth, the meritorious Vīrasiṃha remained himself devoid of qualities, having immersed himself in Brahman, like the pre-eminent crest-jewel of the kings of the Juhāra dynasty.

While King Śrīdhīrajuhārasiṃha—by whose mere knitting of the brows his enemies were broken—ruled this earth like a father through royal policy free from calamity, the rivers possessed sweet waters, the trees bore excellent fruit, the land became fertile, and the worlds, their sins shaken off by the sound of the Vedas, shone free from sorrow. (27)

During the battle at the departure of the lion-like King Juhārasiṃha, whose lineage is born of the earth—who filled the slopes of the sky with fierce displays and whose soldiers were formidable in their intense, war-dance-like *tāṇḍava* and began their attacks with effortless ease, like the cows of the Milky Ocean fleeing from the cave of Mount Govardhana—whom indeed upon the circle of the earth did not strike with fear, even those who possessed the wealth of heroism and magnanimity? (28)

The deep *huṃ* sounds of heroes, the grandeur of elephants, the marvel of the galloping of lofty horses— these belong even to the armies only so long as King Siṃha of the Juhāras has not yet prepared his festival for battle against the enemies who hold fast to the fortresses of mountains, waters, forests, and difficult terrains.

If this high-minded one sets his mind upon giving, then the Mountain of Gold feels fear, Karṇa suffers shame, Dadhīci wastes away, and Bali assumes a false form; indeed, that tree of the world-aeon becomes utterly soiled.

By the prowess of his various austerities—such as the construction of palaces, step-wells, temples for the Nāgas, and the gifting of jewels—he has surpassed the realms of Mahendra, Candra, Varuṇa, Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu.
Having conquered the vast earth through his fierce valor with the strength of his bow-arms, where does the majesty of King Juhāra-siṃha not prevail? Indeed, it prevails everywhere.

Brahmā became four-faced, the destroyer of Smara five-faced, and Skanda six-faced, being exceedingly eager for the festival of song in honor of the fame of King Juhārasiṃha; and beholding the vast extent of that [fame], the earth consisting of seven continents, the mountains, the sky, the celestial river, the three worlds, and the directions were all brought forth by the wise Creator.
Because the celestial tree was so tall that they could not reach its flowers, all the goddesses together praised the equal generosity of the illustrious King Vīrajuhārasiṃha;
for while the divine tree remained bent with its neck weighed down by the unbearable burden of their shame.
The celestial women praised the abundant flowers that were being easily gathered.

He who is Bhīma, Sahadeva himself, whose flanks are invincible in battle, who shines with the abundant glory of the Niṣkuṭa clan, who possesses the great renown of Arjuna throughout the circle of the earth,
who possesses the splendor of Karṇa, who is as fierce as Kṛtavarman and Bhīṣma, and who is as difficult to conquer as Duryodhana.
If Yudhiṣṭhira were to become enraged, who could stand before him? // 34 //
He whose name was Vikramāditya, who adorned the world with the garland of his excellent fame and who shattered his enemies through the abundance of his splendor and the onset of his valor—
he was tall of stature, broad-shouldered, and possessed arms like massive iron bars; he was the ornament of his lineage.
He became a son who was praised by all, who caused joy to the hearts of the virtuous, and who brought delight. // 35 //
Fulfilling the hopes [of the world] by bestowing his rays, the friend of the lotuses,
possessing the splendor of a rising celestial garment, with the brilliance of the sun made manifest, forever destroying all defects,
shines here like the light of a beautiful dawn through the high ascent of the mountain of Indra's enemy.
The son of the king, the pure Vikramāditya himself, brings about a most auspicious day. // 36 //

He who rendered the celestial trees useless by making his own wealth meaningful for the multitude of supplicants; he who rendered the lords of the earth powerless by means of his own riches; he whose intellect increased in its growth, rivaling the preceptor of the gods;
and he who is praised in the assembly for his various virtues such as honor, vehicles, and other gifts.
O brother, he has been born once more as Vikramāditya himself for the delight of the multitude of great poets. // 37 //

His generosity was limited only by the desires of the needy; his initiation of war ended only with the destruction of his enemies; his anger ceased only at the end of his speech; his path toward valor and fame extended to the ends of the earth; his courtesy lasted as long as the protection of the world; and his devotion to Hari remained until the end of his life.
When the limit is completely removed by the roar of a hero’s prowess, supreme welfare increases. // 38 //
He creates the splendor of the Hemādri mountain in an entirely different manner; he fashioned a fair body [for Śiva] which shines upon Kailāsa and clearly illumines the circle of the quarters.
He did not place the Lord of Serpents upon his ear, yet he made the Gaṅgā hidden within his matted locks. This Lord of the worlds has manifested the sovereign power of this man’s fame.

In the lineage of the venerable Dūravāra, there was a lord among the twice-born, renowned as the scholar Haṃsapaṇḍita— the "Swan of the Rising Swan"— who was a jewel upon the crest of the circle of Śrīgopācala,
and whom Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī long served together, free from all rivalry.
He was an enjoyer who, with impetuosity, treated both equally—whether they were rich in food or rich in virtues.

The mass of smoke from his shimmering sacrifices was perceived by people here as the flowing tresses of the dancing-girls of his manifest fame, who perform their graceful dance with skill throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, like fire from the friction-sticks, there arose from the earth a sovereign of incomparable splendor, the crest-jewel upon the heads of kings,
the foremost gem among men, the protector of the name of Dharaṇī, a chariot-warrior, possessed of many virtues, wealthy, and a mine of fortune for those who beg on earth.
From Ramaramana Mishra, Parashurama Mishra was born. // 42 //

Having come from afar in former times to the city of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), and having obtained as her most venerable teacher the illustrious Caṇḍīśvara— the preeminent among Agnihotra-sacrificers— she acquired faultless knowledge; and being purified, she shines forth in many ways through great exertion, becoming steadfast.
Does she not still bear fruit, like a wish-fulfilling creeper, among her descendants even today? 43.
Having abandoned the service of the lotus-face of the Guru and having cast aside the dance performed before the mouths of the four-faced Brahmā, she now endures here—
adorned with ornaments, full of aesthetic flavor, and endowed with virtues.
He who performs the *tāṇḍava* dances upon the surface of his tongue. // 44 //
Upon her lap she is like a creeper of hair; at the boundary of her eyes, she is like a single line of collyrium;
on the surface of her forehead, she is like a musk-deer made of musk; upon her head, she is like a stream of tresses;
and rising upward, her braid is like a swarm of bees agitated by the desire for fragrance.
The continuous column of smoke from whose sacrifices became a deer-marked banner for the gazelle-eyed women of the quarters. // 45 //

From the illustrious Paraśurāma Miśra—treasury of radiant fame, treasury of irreproachable learning, treasury of exquisite poetry, treasury of memory, and treasury of the glory of the Vedas—was born in this world his son Mitramiśra, who possessed no less dignity due to the weight of his father’s meritorious deeds. (46)

By the command of the illustrious Vīrasiṃha, who swiftly brought about the accomplishment of hundreds of tasks, [this work] was composed: the *Śrīvīramitrodaya*, which is the sole abode of Dharma and Artha, consisting of sacred injunctions, the eye for observing ritual action, the great rising of the lotus of Smṛti, and composed of the Śruti.
Therefore, in this city for the delight of the world, the virtuous Śrīmitramiśra [composed this work] for the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva). 47.
Having taken to heart in his mind the entire meaning declared by the sages Hārīta, Gobhila, Parāśara, Nārada,
and others, Mitramiśra— the jewel among scholars— directed by King Śrī Vīrasiṃha, composes this *Samayaprakāśa*.
In that regard, concerning the illumination of time, this sequence is described:
first, the essential nature of eternal time is taught, and then the limiting adjuncts of time are set forth.
Now follows the determination of the years, solstices, and seasons in their proper order;
and then the description of the months, fortnights, and lunar days in their sequence.
Following the general determination of which lunar days (tithis) are to be accepted or rejected,
the ascertainment of the second day (dvitīyā) occurs after the ascertainment of the first day (pratipad).
At the conclusion of the determination of the third [lunar day], the determination of the fourth is recorded;
after the determination of the fifth, the determination of the sixth is proclaimed.
At the conclusion of the determination of the seventh lunar day (saptamī), there follows the general determination of the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī);
thereafter, the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī is described in detail.
Next, the determination of the ninth lunar day (Navamī) is presented, followed by the determination of Rāmanavamī,
and thereafter the determination of Mahānavamī is proclaimed.
First is the determination of the tenth lunar day (daśamī), followed by the determination of the eleventh (ekādaśī);
at the conclusion of the determination of the twelfth (dvādaśī) is the ascertainment of the thirteenth (trayodaśī).
The general determination of the fourteenth lunar day has thus been proclaimed;
now, the determination of the Narasimha-caturdaśī is proclaimed here.
Now, in this very context, as an incidental discussion, follows the determination of the Jayantī festivals and the decision regarding the fourteenth day of the months of Jyeṣṭha, Kārttika, and Māgha.
Then, Śivarātri and its concluding ritual (pāraṇā) are proclaimed therein; next, regarding the rites of the fifteenth day, is the determination of the rites of Śrāvaṇī;
and in connection with the Uṣākarma, the three times for the ritual disposal (utsarga) are set forth.
Following that is the determination of the fifteenth day of Kārttika;
after that, the determination of Holi; and after that, the determination of the festival days (parva).
The determination of the time for the *grahaṇa* (eclipse), the *ekabhakta* (single-meal fast), and the *nakta* (night-fast) follows;
after that, the determination regarding the occurrence of both the *nakta* and the *ekabhakta*.
Next is the determination of the Nakṣatra-fast (nakṣatropavāsa) which is not requested;
thereafter, following the determination of the Saṅkrānti, the intercalary month (malamāsa) is described.
Next, the determination of what rites are to be performed and what are not to be performed during an intercalary month;
and the discernment of what actions are to be done and what are not to be done when Jupiter, Venus, and other planets are in their infancy and so forth.
The times for the Śrāddha rites are the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the Aṣṭakās, the Anvaṣṭakās,
the day preceding the Aṣṭakā, the occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), and thereafter the dark fortnight (asitapakṣa).
The dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, as well as the asterism Bharaṇī,
and the thirteenth and fourteenth lunar days are specified here in their respective order.
Next are the times for miscellaneous śrāddhas, followed by the day for optional (kāmya) śrāddha;
then the beginnings and ends of the yugas, and thereafter the beginnings of the manvantaras.
The beginning of the eon (kalpādya), the Vyatipāta yoga, the Vaidhṛti yoga, the intercalary day (avamadinam),
the time for the first-fruit śrāddha (navānna-śrāddhakāla), the day of the new-moon śrāddha (navaśrāddhadina),
and the time for the funeral rice-ball (pretapiṇḍakāla) are proclaimed at the end of that [section].
The time for the *pātheya-śrāddha* (provision-shrāddha) is declared to be after the commencement of the journey.

The time for the collection of bones and for the offering of water to the deceased is ten days; within the first ten days, on the day of the new moon (darśa) or at its occurrence, the funeral rites for the deceased are then performed.
Immediately following that, the sixteen times for performing śrāddha are declared;
then, the determination regarding the Pārvaṇa and other types of śrāddha on the two lunar dates is explained.
Then follows the definition of the afternoon and other periods, the determination of the *kutapa* time,
the proper times for the *śrāddha*, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and the prohibited times.
Next are the miscellaneous times beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad) as meritorious dates;
then follow the meritorious lunar days determined by the influence of the constellations (nakṣatra), the days of the week (vāra), and so forth.
After this, during the night, there is the discernment of what should and should not be done,
followed immediately by the prohibition against frequenting crossroads.

The things to be avoided regarding specific lunar days and times have been stated, as well as the duties for the festival days (parvan), the characteristics of the ages (yuga-dharma), and furthermore, those things to be avoided during each age.
The characteristics of the Kali age and the things to be avoided in the Kali age have been stated in detail;
following that, the time for initiation and its exceptions have been proclaimed.
Then follows the time for naming, and after that, the times for the establishment of the sacred fires;
then the time for the animal sacrifice, and then the times for the four-monthly sacrifices and the Soma sacrifices.
Thus, in this matter, the venerable teacher Mitramiśra,
having thoroughly examined all the Smṛtis, has determined the proper rule here.
In that regard, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the actual existence of time are the Vedic scriptures and so forth.
For instance, there is the Ṛgveda scripture: "Therefore, one should give at the very time [prescribed]; one should not give at the wrong time."
In this context, regarding the word "time" (*kāla*), the terms "prescribed" and "prohibited" are to be supplied in their respective order.

Thus, there is the Yajurvedic mantra: "When that time has come, one should sacrifice at the proper time. Likewise, there is the statement: "When the time consisting of the year, months, and so forth has arrived, he was born."
“I am indeed Time; I am not of Time,” it is said.
“What is twilight, and what is the time of twilight? asks the Sāmaveda.
“Time and the divisions of time,” says the Manusmṛti.

"‘The times for ancestral rites (śrāddha) have been proclaimed,’ says Yājñavalkya. Likewise, according to the Yogaśāstra, perception is also stated to be a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), since yogis perceive past and future time directly through a specific form of restraint (saṃyama) consisting of the triad of concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). Furthermore, the followers of the Upaniṣads maintain that the direct perception of the witness-consciousness (sākṣipratyakṣa) is also a means of valid knowledge, as it is postulated by the principle of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for (anyathānupapatti) the memory of one who has just awakened from sleep: ‘I slept happily; I was not conscious of anything.’”
The followers of Jaimini maintain that it is perceivable by all the sense organs;
furthermore, the Purāṇa is also an authoritative source, stating: "This blessed Time is beginningless, infinite, undecaying, and supreme."
Therefore, time exists.
It is of two kinds: indivisible and divisible.
Logicians maintain that the former is distinct from God.
The Vedāntins and the modern logicians maintain that [the Lord] is non-different [from the individual soul].

Regarding the difference between the Lord and [the soul], there is scripture: "He is the maker of all, the knower of all, whose womb is the Self, the conscious one, the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the knower of all."
The Lord of the Guṇas is the cause of the dissolution of Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña, as well as the cause of the persistence of delusion, worldly existence, and bondage for those who remain.
Thus:
"The Time of Times" (*kālakāla*) is so called because he measures time that is produced in the form of years and so forth.
Also, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Time, which is without beginning or end, is known as Rudra and Saṅkarṣaṇa;
because of his reckoning of all beings, he is celebrated as Kāla (Time).
Because he draws forth all beings, he is remembered as Saṅkarṣaṇa;
and because he brings all beings to rest, he is proclaimed as Rudra.
"Because he is without beginning or end, he is the Great Supreme Lord. —
[Saṃvatsaranirṇaya]

By this, the argument that time is established as a distinct entity because there is no other determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for the inference of priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatva*) in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, is refuted; for scripture itself provides the determining factor. Let this matter stand as it may. However, since there is no utility for this time in ritual action other than its being remembered as something whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it is not further analyzed here.

However, that which consists of the year and so forth, delimited by the motion of the sun and other celestial bodies, is investigated because it is enjoined as a locus (adhikaraṇa) for ritual action by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "One should sacrifice on the full moon day with the Paurṇamāsī [offering]," and "In a place, at a time, and by means [of specific materials]. Furthermore, its being delimited by the motion of the sun and others has been stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O twice-born ones, the measurement and calculation of that [time], which is both extremely subtle and exceedingly vast, is to be known by the wise according to the motion of the planets."
Thus,
the determination of actions such as the blinking of an eye, which are perceived through direct observation, is stated in that very same place:
"A *mātrā* equal to the duration of a short syllable is proclaimed to be a *nimeṣa* (blinking)."
Therefore, O best of the Bhṛgus, no time more subtle than this can be perceived.
Just as a substance cannot be perceived when it is extremely subtle down to the level of an atom,
so too two *nimeṣas* (twinklings of an eye) are to be known as one *truṭi*, and ten *truṭis* are recorded as one *prāṇa*.
Six breaths constitute one *vināḍikā*, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā*; sixty of those *nāḍikās* are always proclaimed to be a day and night (*ahorātra*).
Likewise, thirty muhūrtas are proclaimed to constitute a day and night;
among them, O Rāma, fifteen are always said to be active during the day.
Likewise, O Rāma, fifteen night-rangers are said to be eternally present when the sun gradually traverses the northern quarter.
In that same manner, O mighty-armed one, there would be an increase of the day;
and as the day, O Rāma, attains its growth, [so too does the night].
"The increase of the muhūrtas dependent upon those [days] is likewise proclaimed," and so forth.

In that regard, since the Śruti declares time-units beginning with the *nimeṣa* to be constituent parts of the year, the year— which is the whole (*avayavin*)— is investigated here because of its primacy.

That which is called a *saṃvatsara* (year) is a specific period of time consisting of twelve months, according to the etymological derivation—"in this, the solstices (*ayana*), seasons (*ṛtu*), months (*māsa*), fortnights (*pakṣa*), lunar days (*tithi*), and so forth, dwell together correctly"—and in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "Twelve months are a year.
It is fivefold.
[Time] is divided into the solar, Bārhaspatya, Sāvana, Cāndra, and Nākṣatra types.
Thus it is stated in the Jyotiḥśāstra: "The solar, Bārhaspatya, Sāvana, lunar (Śaśadhara), and sidereal (Nākṣatrika) [measures] occur in sequence."
The Vatsaras are, in order, Mātula, Pātāla, Atula, Vimala, and Varāṅga.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is:
according to the convention of mathematicians, the letters *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya* represent the squares.
The pure vowel signifies emptiness (*śūnya*).
In this context, there is a collection of numerical figures according to the number of syllables in each group (*varga*).

Thus, in the word *mātula*, the number five is obtained by the letter *ma*, which is the fifth of the *pa*-group, and the number six is obtained by the letter *ta*, which is the sixth of the *ṭa*-group.
By the letter *la*, which is the third of the *ya*-group, the number three is indicated;
thus, according to the method that numbers proceed from left to right, when combined, three hundred and sixty-five solar days constitute a solar year (*saurasaṃvatsara*).
In this way, the word *pātāla* expresses the numerical value of three hundred and sixty-one.
A *bārhaspatya* year is measured by that many sunrises;
in this way, the word "incomparable" (*atula*) expresses the number three hundred and sixty.
A *sāvana* year is measured by that many sunrises.
Here, the word *vimala* denotes the number three hundred and fifty-four;
a lunar year is measured by that many sunrises.
Similarly, the word *varāṅga* expresses the number three hundred and twenty-four; a sidereal year (*nākṣatra-saṃvatsara*) is measured by that many sunrises.
If it is objected: "How can a year containing an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) consist of twelve months, given that there would be thirteen?"—we say no.
This is because of the statement: "A month is said by Bādarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days.
Since a single month is thus defined as consisting of sixty days, the count of twelve remains intact.
The scriptural statement, "There is a thirteenth month," is not a defect, as it refers to the presence of a thirteenth *darśānta* (lunar month ending in the new moon).
As for those sixty-year cycles beginning with Prabhava and so forth, they are indeed varieties of the Jupiter cycle (*bārhaspatya*).
Starting from the bright fortnight of Māgha, when the Moon and Jupiter are situated in the constellation of Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), [the cycle begins].
When both [the Sun and the Moon] are conjoined with Jupiter (Jīva), then it is known as the beginning of the sixty-year cycle (Ṣaṣṭyabda).
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharma: "And they are— Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, and Prajāpati."
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, and Dhāteśvara;
Bahudhānya, Pramāthin, Vikrama, Vṛṣa,
Citrabhānu, Subhānu, Tāraṇa, Pārthiva, and Vyaya.
Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛti, Khara,
Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, and Durmukha.
Hemalamba, Vilamba, Vikārī, Śārvarī, Plava, Śubhakṛt, Śobhana, Krodhī, Viśvāvasu, and Parābhava.
Plavaṅga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, Virodhakṛt, Paridhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, and Anala.
Piṅgala, Kālayukta, Siddhārtha, Raudra, Durmati,
Dundubhī, Rūdhirodgārī, Raktākṣī, Krodhana, and Kṣaya.
Thus [it is said].
Mādhava holds that these [periods], such as *prabhava* and the rest, belong to the lunar calendar as well.
The commencement of the solar year occurs when the sun is situated in Pisces (*mīna*) or Aries (*meṣa*).
The commencement of the Jupiter cycle (bārhaspatya) is by means of Jupiter’s transit through the middle sign (the zodiacal sign).
The commencement of the lunar (cāndra) cycle is from any given day or from any given tithi.
The commencement of the solar (sāvana) cycle is from any given nakṣatra and so forth.
Now follows their application.
Among them, the lunar [day] is used for the *tilaka-vrata*, the annual *śrāddha*, and so forth.
The *tilaka-vrata* has been described:
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "On the first lunar day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight in spring, when the season is beautified by *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees,
one should perform a ritual bath while established in religious observance (*niyama*)."
One should apply a tilaka mark made of sandalwood paste upon the forehead;
from that time forth, day after day, the face shall be adorned with the tilaka.
"It should be maintained for as long as a year, like the sky by the moon.
Here, because the commencement is prescribed on the first lunar day (pratipad), it is understood that this vow is to be accomplished within a lunar year (cāndra-saṃvatsara).
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*, however, regarding the annual śrāddha, it is stated: "The month for the annual śrāddha is traditionally held to be the lunar month."
Regarding the *sujanma* and other vows, the *Saura* [Purāṇa] states in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Blessed One, by what action is one not born into the womb of an animal?"
Having begun thus:
"At the time of the Sun's entry into Aries, the best of men, having observed a fast..."
Having thus described the nature of the vow with these words,
[the author] concludes: "By practicing this desired vow for a year, one does not take birth among Mlecchas or even among animals."

Thus, where actions are prescribed in relation to the transits [of the sun] and it is stated, "one should perform [the rite] for a year," the solar year (saura) is to be understood there. In cases such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), such as "the killer of a Brahmin shall perform penance for twelve years," the civil year (*sāvana*) is to be taken.
Likewise, the division of the lifespan (*āyurdāya*) and the performance of expiatory rites are determined by this same principle.
The service of enemies should also be performed by means of the sāvana rite alone.

Thus it is stated in the *Jyotir-garga*. However, regarding the offering of barley and so forth to Bṛhaspati, the *Bārhaspatya* states: "For those who give, the gift of sesame seeds during the year yields great fruit."
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, he gave a gift of barley preceded by the word "pari."
The gift of garments preceded by the word *idā*, and grains preceded by the word *anu*,
as well as silver preceded by the word *it*, is declared to yield great fruit.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharma.
Here, the word *vatsara* begins with *saṃparī* and so forth;
by this, the five names of the years—*saṃvatsara*, *parivatsara*, and so on—are indicated.
These five are designated as a "yuga. And so it is stated regarding Prabhava and the others in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
The first is the Saṃvatsara, the second is the Parivatsara,
the third is the Idāvatsara, and the fourth is the Anuvatsara.
"The fifth year is called *idvatsara*, and time is designated as a *yuga*.
Thus,
according to Bṛhaspati, a particular year is sometimes termed a *luptasaṃvatsara*.
And likewise, Vasiṣṭha says: "If Jupiter, having reached its natural motion, enters a state of retrogression (atīcāra)..."
The remaining portion of the previous heap will not come for consumption.
When the portion already consumed is included and the [lunar] month is thus made retrograde,
then, after twelve months, it is called a "lost year" (luptasaṃvatsara).
*Sahajām* means that which is distinct from the deviation caused by retrogression (*vakrātīcāra*).
Thus, the meaning is as follows:
if the planet has undergone retrogression and, for the purpose of traversing the remaining degrees of its previous sign, returns to its natural motion (*svābhāvikagati*), then [it is *sahajā*].

The meaning is that when [a planet] does not enter its sign— that is, from the degrees already traversed and the degrees traversed by accelerated motion (aticāra), inclusive— up until that day, it becomes a "lost year" (luptasaṃvatsara) for twelve months.
There is an exception to this in certain cases.
"If Jupiter is in excessive motion (atīcāra) in Aries, Pisces, Taurus, or Aquarius, there shall be no lapse of the [auspicious] time therein; so said the Blessed Yama."
Thus says Parāśara:
"When Jupiter, having traversed ten or eleven months of a zodiacal sign, enters another sign,"
The noble ones say that even if one does not eat before [the time] nor likewise afterwards, the year is not considered lost.

Regarding the prohibition of performing rituals during a *luptasaṃvatsara*, the *Rājamārtaṇḍa* states: "If Jupiter, having entered a state of retrogression (*atīcāra*), does not return to that same zodiacal sign,
it should be known as a *luptasaṃvatsara*, which is censured for all ritual acts."
Thus [it is said].
Vyāsa states an exception to this:
When Jupiter, the minister of the king of gods, commits an aticāra while situated in Taurus, Virgo, or Pisces—
even if he does not return to his former sign, they declare that taking a wife for the sake of auspiciousness is favorable.
Thus concludes the determination of the year.
Now, the *ayana* (solstice) is defined.
In this regard, although the word *ayana* generally denotes a path—as per the lexicon which states, "The *ayana* is a track, a way, or a road"—it is used here [to denote a specific period].
Nevertheless, in this context, three solar seasons (*ṛtu*) are called an *ayana*.

This is because of the *Taittirīya* Śruti: "Therefore, the Sun goes southward for six months and northward for six. Furthermore, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, having introduced the three solar seasons: [the text continues].
"And three seasons constitute an *ayana*.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*:
"In the six signs beginning with Cancer and Capricorn, those two *ayanās*, the southern and northern, occur respectively."
Thus,
because this [period] is prescribed by prioritizing the course of the sun, it is indeed solar (*saura*).

However, Mādhava notes that some say the six months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa constitute the northern course (*udagayana*) and the six months beginning with Jyeṣṭha constitute the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), and the source for that must be sought in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.

The application of these two—the northern and the southern—is as follows: during the northern course of the sun (udagayana), in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion (puṇyanakṣatra), [one performs] the tonsure ceremony (caulakarma), initiation (upanayana), the godāna rite, marriage, and so forth.
Likewise:
[the worship of] Mātṛs, Bhairava, Vārāha, Nṛsiṃha, and Trivikrama.
And the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura should indeed be installed during the southern course of the sun.
Such [details] as these should be understood as they are set forth in their respective contexts.
And it has been stated in general terms in the *Jyotiṣaratnamālā*:
"Prior to entering a house, the consecration of a temple, marriage, the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), and the initiation of vows..."
Auspicious rites should be performed during the northern course of the sun, whereas those that are censured should indeed be done during the southern course.
Thus ends the determination of the solstices.
Now, the determination of the seasons is undertaken.
And that consists of two months;
thus says the Taittirīya Śruti: "He lays them down in pairs;
therefore the seasons are in pairs."

A *dvandva* compound denotes a period of two months: Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons (*vāsantika-ṛtu*); Śukra and Śuci are the two summer seasons (*graiṣma-ṛtu*); Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two rainy seasons (*vārṣika-ṛtu*); Iṣa and Ūrja are the two autumn seasons (*śārada-ṛtu*); Sahas and Sahasya are the two early winter seasons (*haimantika-ṛtu*); and Tapas and Tapasya are the two late winter seasons.
According to the Vedic revelation, "the two seasons of the cool season" (*śaiśirāvṛtū*);

here, the dual number in the word *ṛtū* is intended to signify the two months that constitute those seasons. Furthermore, in this context, words such as *madhu* and so forth denote Caitra and the other months.
And so it is stated in the Mādhavīya:
"The month of Caitra is called Madhu, and Vaiśākha is Mādhava."
The month of Jyeṣṭha is Śukra, while Āṣāḍha is called Śuci.
The month of Śrāvaṇa is Nabhomāsa; Bhādra is called Nabhasya;
Āśvayuja is the month of Iṣa; and Kārttika is known by the name Urja.
The month of Mārgaśīrṣa is called Sahomāsa; Pauṣa is known as Sahasya; the month of Māgha is declared to be Tapaḥ; and Phālguna is remembered as Tapasya.
Thus,
these seasons are sixfold, as established by the previously cited scripture beginning with "Madhu and Mādhava," and also by the scriptural statement, "There are indeed six seasons."

As for the mention of "five seasons" in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*—specifically in the passage, "twelve months, five seasons"—that has been explained right there [in the same text]: "by the combination (*samāsena*) of winter and the cool season. "Combination" means unification; that is the meaning.
Furthermore, each of these, beginning with spring, is of two kinds: solar (*saura*) and lunar (*cāndra*).
In that context, because Caitra and the other months are lunar, those [days] comprised within them are also lunar.
The Śruti also states: "The Moon is the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ; he ordains the seasons.
And in the Bāṣkala-Śruti: "One [the Sun] looks upon all other worlds; the other (the Moon), ordaining the seasons, is born again."

In this context, because the Sun is mentioned from the verse beginning with "atrābhicaṣṭe" as the generator of activities such as the movement [of time], and because he is distinct from that [Sun] in the phrase "anya," it is the Moon alone who is stated to be the ordainer of the seasons (*ṛtu*).

Some, however, claim that the Moon's status as the creator of the seasons is due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the word "punarjjāyate" (is born again); but that is not correct, because the Sun's quality of being born again and again is also stated in the Śruti.
If it is asked, "When there is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), how can there be a season consisting of two months?",
[the answer is: because of the statement, "A month is said by Bādarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days," since a month comprising sixty days is considered a single unit.
Regarding the solar [reckoning], it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "O Rāma, two solar months are designated as a season (ṛtu)."
Thus it is said;
and in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* as well: "The two months of the Sun are the seasons.
Baudhāyana also stated: "Or, the spring [occurs] during Pisces and Aries."

Although the solar nature [of the seasons] is stated for the spring alone by the statement of Bodhāyana, it should nevertheless be understood that it applies to the subsequent seasons as well, upon a careful consideration of the statement from the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Their application, however, is to be seen in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth.
Among those, the Śruti says: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring; a Rājanya should establish them in summer; a Vaiśya should establish them in autumn," and so on.
Likewise, [it is said] regarding the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) during the rainy season.
Āśvalāyana states: "The *Aṣṭakā* occurs on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the winter and cool seasons.
Furthermore, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, specific distinctions for worship are described separately for each of the six forms (*ṣaṇmūrti*) during the six seasons beginning with spring.
In that very same [text], the giving of baths, ointments, and so forth is prescribed, as is the giving of cooling drinks during the summer.

However, in the *Devīpurāṇa*, Mādhava states: "The giving of sesame seeds in the rainy season, the giving of food in the autumn, and the giving of clothing during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira."
Likewise, the distinction between divine and non-divine [periods] has been stated in various places with reference to specific seasons; this should be observed there.
Thus concludes the determination of the seasons. Now, the month is determined.
And that [time] is fourfold, distinguished as lunar, solar, civil (sāvana), and sidereal (nākṣatra).
Thus it is said in the Jyotiḥśāstra:
The first month is called *sāvana*, the second is said to be *cāndra*,
the third would be *nākṣatra*, and the fourth is the *saura* month.
Thus it is said.
These characteristics are described in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"At the end of the full moon, the moon surpasses the sun."
Then, O Rāma, six zodiac signs [are traversed] in half a month; of this there is no doubt.
In this manner, by means of twelve parts, on each successive lunar day (tithi),
the moon gradually joins with the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.
Starting from one conjunction [of the moon with the sun] until the next conjunction,
that period of the moon and sun is designated by the wise as a lunar month (cāndra-māsa).
Likewise, it is traditionally held that there are thirty sunrises in a *sāvana* month;
a solar month is proclaimed by the Sun’s transit through a zodiacal sign.
"A lunar month is not said to consist of all the revolutions of the asterisms.
Thus, the lunar month is of two kinds: that beginning with the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇādi) and that beginning with the bright fortnight (śuklādi).
In that regard, the black [type] and others have been illustrated as shown in the Viṣṇudharmottara;
Hārīta speaks of the white type and others:
The beginning of the month is proclaimed as that time when Indra and Agni are invoked;
Agni and Soma are remembered at the midpoint, and Pitṛs and Soma at its conclusion.
Thus [it is said].

Here, by the words *indrāgni*, *agnīṣoma*, and *pitṛsoma*, the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the following first lunar day (*pratipad*), the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), and the new-moon day are indicated respectively.

This is because the sacrifice to Indra and Agni is prescribed for the first [day], the sacrifice to Agni and Soma for the full-moon day, and Soma accompanied by the ancestors (*pitṛmat*) in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña for the new-moon day.
By this, the month beginning with Śukla (the bright fortnight) is established; and the rule for these two has been stated by Nīlakaṇṭha Maṇḍana:

The lunar month is also of two kinds: beginning with the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) or beginning with the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa). Some do not accept a month that begins with the dark fortnight.
"Even those who desire [it], it is not desired by them to the south of the Vindhya.
Here, because Kṛṣṇa and others are prohibited to the south of the Vindhya, there is an option between the two [directions] to the north.

Even there, the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) and so forth are primary, while the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa) and so forth are secondary. On the first day of the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, when the sun had risen, Brahmā created the world at the very beginning.
Then he also set in motion the calculation of time:
the planets, the nāgas, the seasons, the months, the years, and the lords of the years.

Thus, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* regarding the commencement of the months, seasons, and years; for the year does not differ for those who follow the system beginning with the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇādi*), since the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is declared only in the system beginning with the bright fortnight (*śuklādi*), and its occurrence is impossible according to the *kṛṣṇādi* reckoning.

Although any collection of thirty lunar days (*tithi*) constitutes a lunar month because it is composed of *tithis*, nevertheless, due to the absence of the conventional designation "Caitra" and so forth therein, it is not mentioned anywhere in the *Dharmaśāstra* as a third type of month.
Likewise, the term "month" applied to solar months and the like is used in a figurative sense.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple powers (*śakti*). Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), for [the lunar digits] are called *kalās* because they are measured (*mīyante*) according to their own increase and decrease.
These months are traditionally defined as consisting of thirty lunar days (tithis).

Thus, because the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* demonstrates that the very basis for the application of the term "month" (*māsa*) is the calculation of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*) through their increase and decrease;
some, however, claim that among all months, only the solar or lunar month is the primary meaning of the word "month.
That is incorrect.

This is because it would contradict the statements in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*. Furthermore, the use of the term "month" (*māsa*) with respect to all four [types] is not contradictory, following the "umbrella-bearer" (*chatrinyāya*) principle—just as the term "son" (*putra*) is applied to the twelve kinds of sons.
Moreover, since there are scriptural statements regarding even the secondary (*gauṇa*) months, their inclusion in various contexts is not inconsistent.

According to the maxim that "there is no excessive burden for a word," and since there is no specific authoritative evidence [to the contrary], only the lunar month is to be understood. Likewise, words such as Caitra and others are also denotative of the lunar month alone.
Because it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings, because it denotes a specific month,

and by virtue of the grammatical rule established by Pāṇini— "The time joined with a lunar mansion" and "That full moon day occurs in this [month]"— which applies to technical designations (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, this conjunction is not possible even during the solar month of Caitra; for although there may occasionally be a conjunction with the full moon on a day joined with Citrā and so forth when the sun is situated in Pisces and the other signs, it is never possible for the full moons to be joined with Aśvinī, Puṣya, or Maghā while the sun is situated in Virgo, Sagittarius, or Capricorn. Nor should it be asked: "If there were no conjunction with a lunar mansion, how could it be Caitra?"
Because sometimes it is indeed due to the nature of the *yoga* itself;
and thus Cyavana says:
"The last two [months] and the second-to-last should be known as having three lunar mansions (*tribha*), and Phālguna is also considered to have three lunar mansions."
The remaining months should be known as divided into two parts according to the arrangement beginning with Kṛttikā.
Thus:
"the last and the penultimate" refers to Āśvina and Bhādra.

And this [calculation] of three lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and so forth occurs through the conjunction of two or three *nakṣatras*, such as the conjunction of either Kṛttikā or Rohiṇī on the full moon of Kārttika, or the conjunction of either Mṛgaśiras or Ārdrā on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, and so on.

Nor should it be argued that because the *Padma Purāṇa* states regarding the full moon of Kārttika—“when Bharaṇī occurs at any time on that [day]”—that there is also a conjunction with Bharaṇī, how then can it be said to consist of two asterisms (*dvibhatva*).
This is because what is intended is the conjunction with either Kṛttikā or Rohiṇī at the final moment of the full moon.
Furthermore, the lunar nature of Caitra and the other months is clearly stated.

In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): whichever lunar month, beginning with Caitra, is completed while the sun is situated in Aries or the subsequent signs, that is to be known as the [corresponding] month; when there is a double completion, the latter is the intercalary month (adhimāsa).
Brahmagupta also says:
"That month in which the sun's transition into Aries occurs during the lunar month is Caitra;
likewise, Vaiśākha and the others follow through their conjunction with the transitions into Taurus and so forth."
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, we shall explain how these two definitions do not fail to apply to the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) and so forth. As for the solar (*sāvana*) and sidereal (*nākṣatra*) months, since the terms "Caitra" and so on are never applied to them, it is not even to be suspected that they denote those [lunar months].
Now, the distinction between the primary and secondary months:
In the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, the month shall be defined by the new moon;
likewise, for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is defined by the solar ingress (*saṅkrānti*) and the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*)."
Jyotirgarga states: "The solar month is prescribed for marriage and similar rites; the sāvana month is remembered for sacrifices and the like;
and for annual ancestral rites, the lunar month is praised."
"Ābdike" means the annual rite;
"pitṛkārye" refers to the rites for the ancestors, such as those performed every six months and so forth.
Thus, he [the same author] says:
The division of the lifespan, the performance of expiatory rites,
and even the waging of war against enemies must be carried out according to the solar (sāvana) reckoning alone.
Uprāsana is the observance of the rules of conduct,
as the Grandfather [Bhīṣma] was toward the Kauravas by the Pāṇḍavas.
"In rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors, the lunar month is traditionally prescribed.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"One should perform the nakṣatra-sattras and the ayanas of the Moon by means of a month consisting of a full bhagaṇa. Thus it is stated in the Brāhma-purāṇa.
One should specify the lunar month beginning with the dark fortnight for rites related to the lunar days (tithi), that beginning with the bright fortnight for religious vows (vrata),
and that beginning with the solar reckoning for rites such as marriage.
Thus is the month; now,
the day is of four kinds.
As it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"In the lunar measurement, a day is proclaimed to consist of one lunar date (tithi)."
And by one day and night, a civil day (sāvana) is recorded.
A solar day is said to be by means of the Sun's passage through a zodiacal sign; a sidereal day is traditionally defined by the Moon's passage through a lunar mansion.
Thus:
"by the enjoyment of the zodiacal sign" means by the thirtieth part of the sign currently being enjoyed;
thus [is defined] the day.
Now,
the fortnight (pakṣa) is of two kinds, distinguished as bright (śukla) and dark (kṛṣṇa).
And so it is said:
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In that regard, there are two fortnights in a month, namely the bright and the dark in sequence.
The bright fortnight causes the increase of the moon, while the dark consists of its waning."
Thus [it is said].
Āśvalāyana states their application:

"The tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the godāna, and the marriage (*vivāha*) should be performed during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), in the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)."
Likewise, [it is said]: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira [seasons]," and so forth. This concludes the section on the fortnight (pakṣa).
Now, the lunar day (tithi) is determined in general.

In this context, a *tithi* is that duration of time during which, among the fifteen divisions known as the first (*pratipad*), second (*dvitīyā*), and so forth— which are distinct from the eternal digit (*kalā*) that is the pervasive essence of every month— there occurs either the transition from maximum proximity to the moon’s orb with the sun’s orb to maximum distance, or from maximum distance back to maximum proximity, for each individual digit.

Respectively belonging to the bright and dark fortnights, they are to be expressed by the terms *pratipad*, *dvitīyā*, and so forth, according to their established conventional meaning (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*).
Thus it is said in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* of the *Skānda*:
O Goddess, that which is called Mahākalā is said to be one-sixteenth part of the *amā*;
she is the supreme Māyā, established as the sustainer of the bodies of embodied beings.
The meaning of this is as follows:

That Great Māyā who exists as the foundational form, sustaining the bodies of embodied beings, is said to be the Great Kalā named Amā, measured by a sixteenth part of the lunar disc; she assumes the body of the Moon, is devoid of waning and waxing, eternal, and is designated as the lunar day (tithi) itself.

The other fifteen digits (*kalās*) as well, which are subject to waning and waxing and are utilized for the conventions of the day, constitute the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*); thus, the statement that there are exactly sixteen *tithis* is not contradictory.
"O fair-faced one, those very digits of the moon, beginning with the new moon (*amā*) and ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), are declared to be the sixteen *tithis*."
Thus it is said;
and also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"In that regard, there are two fortnights in a month, namely the bright and the dark, in their respective order."
The bright fortnight causes the increase of the moon, while the dark fortnight consists of its waning.
The lunar days (tithis) beginning with the first of the fortnight (pakṣati) are traditionally held to be fifteen in number;
they end with the new moon (darśa) in the dark fortnight, and with the full moon (pūrṇimā) in the bright fortnight.
Thus it is said.
And that lunar day (tithi) is of two kinds: full (pūrṇā) and incomplete (khaṇḍā).
Among these, the one beginning from sunrise and ending at sunrise is the full one.
"Starting from the time of sunrise, sixty *nāḍikās* are known as 'complete' (*sampūrṇā*)," according to the statement in the *Nāradīya*.
All [days] beginning with the *pratipad* (the first lunar day) from sunrise until sunrise are renowned as "complete" (*sampūrṇā*), with the exception of the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).
And because of the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Some, however, maintain that even for a lunar day (tithi) extending from sunrise to sunset, there is fullness when it is to be accomplished during the daytime alone.
But that lunar day which pervades the three junctions (trisandhya) is always to be honored."
Therein, no pair of days is observed, except for the day of Hari.
This is according to the statement of Parāśara:
"Pervading the three junctions" means pervading the morning, midday, and evening junctions;
it does not mean two morning junctions and an evening junction.

Because a number is applied to distinct entities, as in the case of "He offers three oblations," and because such usage is established in expressions like "He who recites [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day," they say that when an action is to be accomplished by a mere day, the term "complete" (*sampūrṇa*) refers even to that which extends only over that duration.
The *sampūrṇā* (complete) lunar day is not subject to determination; the *khaṇḍā* (defective) one, however, is.

Among these, the *sampūrṇā*—because the rite prescribed for that specific lunar day occurs on only one day and thus arises on no other day—is not to be determined, as there is no doubt [regarding its performance].

The *khaṇḍā*, on the other hand, because it exists across two days, gives rise to the doubt: "Where should the rite prescribed for it be performed? Since the repetition of a primary act (*pradhāna*) for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is improper, and since the rite prompted by it must be performed only once, it is therefore subject to determination.
It occurs thus;
however, in the case of a prohibition, even a fragmentary instance remains indeterminate.
The operation of both injunction and prohibition takes place by taking time as the occasion.
In that case, there is an injunction regarding the specific lunar day to be honored, but a prohibition regarding the time itself.
The venerability of lunar days consists in their fitness for the performance of rituals;
whereas a prohibition, being of the nature of abstention, depends merely upon time.
Thus it is stated by Vṛddhagārgya.

Here, the "causality" (nimittatva) of time means its non-prescriptibility (anupādeyatva), but not its actual causality, for that would result in every ritual action being considered occasional (naimittika). Nor is such an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) acceptable.

In such passages as "one should offer to the ancestors on the new moon day" (amāvāsyāyāṃ pitṛbhyo dadyāt), it is understood from the locative case (saptamī) and so forth that [the new moon day] is a subordinate factor (aṅga).

Nor should it be argued that this locative is merely a locative of occasion (nimitta-saptamī); for a case-ending expressing a grammatical relation (kāraka-vibhakti) is stronger than a case-ending used as a mere adjunct (upapada-vibhakti).

Nor does it follow that this would result in [the rite] being desired for all [times], because it is occasional (*naimittika*) due to scriptural injunctions regarding the sin of non-performance (*pratyavāya*) and so forth.

Furthermore, one should not argue that wherever there is merely the hearing of a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there it must refer exclusively to an occasion (*nimitta*) and not to time (*kāla*) in the case of a desired rite;
for some hold that even though time is heard as an occasion, since it is already present, there is no evidence to indicate it as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).

In reality, even though it is present, it is not included in the performance of a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*), as is the case with the *bārhadgira* verses and others; rather, it is some other [verse] whatsoever.
However, in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the attainment of spring occurs through another sentence that lacks a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.
"The prohibition concerns the time alone."
This meaning is not one explicitly stated by the words, but rather one obtained through logical necessity; thus he says, "But the prohibition... and so forth.
This is the meaning:
in prescriptive sentences (vidhi-vākya), the sentence-meaning is that the enjoined object is a means to the highest good (śreyas).
In prohibitions, however, it is the fact that a specific time renders an act—which is otherwise prompted by natural inclination—a cause of harm.

Thus, in cases such as "oil [massage] on the sixth day," since one understands that performing an oil massage on the sixth day leads to undesirable consequences, the prohibition applies to both halves of the sixth day.

Therefore, it is established that because the prohibition is determined by the sublation of the entire lunar day (*tithi*), the division of the day into segments (*khaṇḍa*) is not to be considered in the case of prohibitions.
And thus, when it is established by logic alone that all prohibitions are temporary—
[as stated]: "In the case of anointing the body, bathing in the ocean, cleaning the teeth,
sexual intercourse, birth, and death, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through that specific time [is the one to be observed]."
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. It should not be argued that the repeated mention [of the time] in the context of oil-baths and other rites is redundant; for it is said:

"On the first day of a month, at the beginning of a Yuga, during the eclipses of the moon and sun, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and during the Vaidhṛti yoga, the religious act must be performed as long as that specific time persists."

Thus, in the Skanda Purāṇa itself, that [definition] is cited as an illustration for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding the pervasion of the time starting from the beginning of Manu’s era.
The meaning of the phrase "the lunar day (tithi) that pervades that time" is this:
it should pervade the time of those [rites], such as the oil-bath (abhyaṅga) and so forth, by being their locus (adhikaraṇa).
Some, however, say that by this statement it is meant that for anointing the body and so forth, the lunar day (tithi) that extends throughout that specific time is prescribed;

but that is incorrect, because no injunction regarding the brushing of teeth or sexual intercourse on specific lunar days is observed, whereas prohibitions are indeed observed. In that regard, even when there is a conflict (khajḍā), [the same applies].
In rites prescribed for specific portions of a day, only that lunar day (tithi) which extends throughout that specific portion of the day should be accepted.
"Whatever the time of a rite may be, one should perform the rites during the lunar day that pervades that time; its waning or waxing is no cause [for rejection]."

Thus it is stated by Vṛddha-Gārgya. Furthermore, the time for ritual action (*karmakāla*), consisting of portions of the day, comprises three *muhūrtas* each in the form of morning (*prātaḥ*), forenoon (*saṅgava*), midday (*madhyāhna*), afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and late afternoon (*sāyāhna*). As it is said:
"From the first appearance of the sun's rays, there are indeed three *muhūrtas* [for the morning]."
But at dawn, the time that has passed is the fifth part of the day.
The Saṅgava period consists of three muhūrtas; then the midday (madhyāhna) is recorded as being equal to that.
Thereafter, three muhūrtas are prescribed as the afternoon (aparāhṇa).
Furthermore, that which is the fifth part of the day is known as the evening;
whatever is prescribed for these [periods], a wise person should perform that accordingly.

Thus it is stated by Parāśara. As for the twofold or threefold division, that which is prescribed in connection with a specific ritual act is to be adopted there; however, in its absence, experts in the Dharmaśāstras maintain that the fivefold division alone is to be used. And this is their intention:

For here, it is not the case that whatever is prescribed for those [other rites] should be performed here as well, because that would already be established by the injunctions of those original rites themselves.

Rather, whatever is prescribed as requiring a specific time is enjoined here with respect to these [days], just as in the rule “the Maitrāvaruṇa priest gives the directions and recites,” which is an injunction of a required element. Therefore, this is a general injunction;
furthermore, it will be explained later that this applies to occasions other than the fast-day, since that [fast] is accomplished over a full day and night.

Therefore, if on the previous day alone there is a complete occupation of the time for the rite (*karmakāla*) or a partial connection with it, the [rite] belongs to that previous day; for in the first case, one obtains the scriptural injunction regarding the time (*kālaśāstra*), and in the second, one obtains at least the time itself.
For this very reason, if the same conditions apply on the following day, it belongs to that following day.
When there is an unequal connection with both days, whichever [day] has the greater [connection] is the one [chosen].

However, when there is a partial connection through equality [of time], that action which is commenced in the morning and completed in the very same morning—therein, the time belonging to the commencement of the principal rite (*pradhāna*) is to be adopted.

"Whatever time is prescribed for a particular rite, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) is intended for its commencement, that very day should be observed; it must not be one from which the commencement has been excluded."
According to this statement by Baudhāyana, the rule regarding the pairing of days (*yugmavākya*) does not apply here;
as for the point that "having commenced the rite earlier, it is completed at midday or another such time."

In this regard, the application of the rules concerning even-numbered days (*yugma*) and so forth, which will be explained later, is the general rule (*utsarga*) for both cases where [the tithi] spans two days and where it is attained on one day.

However, the *Madanaratna* states: whether by equality or inequality, even if there is a partial connection with both days, if the time sufficient for the performance of the rite exists on only one side, then the rite should be performed on that side alone; if such time exists on both sides, then the determination is made according to the rules of the *yugma* and other such principles.

If it is not in both cases, but rather a connection with a portion of the rite, then in that case too, he says: "If it is from a statement concerning the commencement of the entire [rite], then [it applies] to all; if it is unequal, then by way of excess.
Now, if the determining factor is the statement regarding the pair (yugma), that is stated:
first, the statement regarding the pair is found in the Nigama—

The second, third, fourth, eighth, ninth, tenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days, when joined respectively with the first, third, fifth, seventh, eleventh, thirteenth, and fifteenth tithis, are auspicious.
Furthermore, the twelfth lunar day is auspicious when joined with the eleventh, and the full moon day when joined with the fourteenth.
Even when the new moon day (amāvāsyā) occurs, the pair of lunar days (tithi-yugma) yields great fruit;
this same pair, when reversed, causes great harm and destroys previously accumulated merit.
Thus:
the pair is the second [case],
Agni is the third.
Yuga is the fourth [case],
bhūta is the fifth,
and ṣaṣ is the sixth.
*Muni* is the seventh,
*vasu* is the eighth,
and *randhra* is the ninth.
*Rudra* refers to the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*).

Regarding the pairs of lunar days—the pair consisting of the second and third, the pair of the fourth and fifth, the pair of the sixth and seventh, the pair of the eighth and ninth, the pair of the eleventh and twelfth, and the pair of the fourteenth and the full moon, as well as the pair of the new moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight—there is mutual *vedha* (piercing) between them.

This is an injunction regarding a specific time inferred from praise, established on the grounds that when these days fall together in even numbers, they serve as the substratum for their respective rites and thus yield great fruit.
This pair has been explained.

Regarding the first lunar day (tithi) occurring within a pair, the "piercing" (*vedha*) of that first tithi by its predecessor and the "piercing" of the subsequent tithi by its own successor constitute a great defect; thus, according to the maxim of "indirect praise" (*na hi nindā nyāya*), this serves as a praise for the rule of being pierced by the predecessor (*pūrva-vidhi*), since it achieves syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
However, there is no assumption of an independent prohibition, as that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*),
because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) and complexity (*gaurava*) in the case of a prohibition (*niṣedha*).
This other statement regarding pairs found in the works of Āpastamba and others contradicts the aforementioned statement on pairs:

"The first lunar day (pratipad) should be joined with the second; the second should be joined with the first; and that third lunar day which is conjoined with the fourth is the one that bestows fruit."
And the fourth [day] on the third [lunar day] bestows the fruit of great merit.
And so forth.
Likewise, in the *Kharvadarpavākya* of Vyāghra and Uśanās:
"Dwarfness (*kharva*), pride (*darpa*), and likewise violence (*hiṃsā*)—this is the threefold characteristic of the lunar day (*tithi*)."
Avarice and pride are to be avoided; indeed, violence belongs to the past.
Thus:
*kharva* means equality;
*darpa* means increase.
Violence is destruction.
Likewise, there is also a statement regarding the white and black fortnights in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Vajra said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, when a lunar mansion and a tithi that has emerged halfway are seen together,
how should one who knows perform the fast, O Śaṅkara?
Īśvara said:

That lunar day (tithi) upon which the sun has risen constitutes that day and night; one should perform rites according to it, for the waning or waxing [of the moon] is not a cause [for determining the time].

That lunar day (tithi) on which the sun sets constitutes the full day and night; one should perform rituals according to that [tithi], for its increase or decrease is not a cause [for changing the timing].
In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken.
Thus [it is said].

Here, the statement regarding the bright and dark fortnights is for the purpose of establishing the determination of the lunar days (tithi) at sunrise and sunset as prescribed by the preceding sentence. However, some say:
For rites pertaining to the gods, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be known;
for rites pertaining to the ancestors, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be known.
Following this statement, some maintain that there is a fixed rule assigning the times of sunrise and sunset to the rites for the gods and the ancestors respectively;
but that is not correct,
because it would result in the subject matter of the opening and the conclusion being inconsistent.

Furthermore, because the upcoming statement regarding completeness prescribes that [the time] for the rite to the gods (*daiva*) must also extend until sunset, the intent of the stated rule is specifically to prescribe that [the time] for the rite to the ancestors (*pitrya*) extends until sunset. As for the mention that [the time] for the rite to the gods extends until sunrise, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), intended as praise, just as in the case of the statement: "For one milks for the gods while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*)."

Likewise, there is this statement of Devala concerning the totality [of a lunar day]: "The lunar day upon which the sun rises is to be known as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, vows, and so forth."
Whichever lunar day the sun reaches at its setting,
that lunar day is to be known as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, vows, and so forth.
In this matter, the following is the established rule:
the verses concerning even-numbered days pertain to rites for the gods (daiva),
while the verse regarding the "khārva" and "darpa" types of Brahmins pertains to rites for the ancestors (pitrya).
Regarding the pairs beginning with the second [lunar day], there are rules for their worshipability in rites such as ancestral offerings;
and regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites, there are injunctions concerning decrease and increase in the context of prosperity-rites (*vṛddhi*) and so forth.
Thus, according to the statement of Vyāsa and the Vedas (*nigama*).
Here, by the phrase "in matters such as the rules for worship" (*pūjyatāniyamādiṣu*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes all rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva-karma*).
By the phrase "the *ekoddiṣṭa* and others," the term "and others" (*ādi*) includes all ancestral rites (*pitrya*) other than the *abhyudayika-śrāddha*.

In the phrase "increase and so forth" (*vṛddhyādi*), by means of a *vātadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, there are rites such as *daiva-śrāddha* and others which possess divine attributes like the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), as well as *pitrya* rites; because these are not fixed in time due to occasions such as the birth of a son or prosperity (*putravṛddhi*), they cannot be determined [by the rules of increase and decrease].
By the phrase "decrease, increase, and so forth," the meaning is that the injunctions for those [rites] are merely words of vanity and pride (*kharvadarpavākya*).

As for the statements regarding the pairing of lunar days (*yugmavākya*), when there is mutual contradiction between them, or when the tithis do not fall within their scope—such as the tenth day (*daśamī*) and others—the arrangement is determined by the rule of the bright and dark fortnights (*śuklakṛṣṇavākya*), since it provides the necessary prescription.
Therefore, the mention of fasting at the beginning of the passages concerning the bright and dark fortnights is merely an illustration for all rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*).

Nor should it be argued that the restriction regarding fasting alone is established by the passages on the bright and dark fortnights, while for other matters, a mere option (*vikalpa*) should be accepted due to the contradiction between two conflicting statements regarding *yugma* (even-numbered days).

In that context, even though the procedure for the fast (*upavāsa*) is under discussion, the plural form in the phrase “one should perform the rites with it” (*tayā karmāṇi kurvīta*) indicates that this applies to ritual acts in general.

As for the statement of Devala, since the previous or subsequent day might otherwise be selected by the rule regarding paired days (*yugma-vākya*) and so forth, and because the lunar day (*tithi*) is the primary factor while the specific part of the day is secondary, the principle of "transgression of the subordinate for the sake of the principal" (*guṇa-mukhya-vyatikrama-nyāya*) applies. This means that when the specific lunar day is absent during its designated portion of the day, one should instead observe it on the day where the lunar day is present.
Since it would otherwise follow that the rite must be performed on any lunar day whatsoever, [the rule] is intended to ensure its performance specifically during the daytime portion.
Furthermore, this statement regarding the "entirety" (sākalya) applies with the exception of Manu and others,
because there is an exception made for Manu and the rest by the previously cited statement beginning with "tatra manvādau ca."
Regarding the first half [of the verse], there is no dispute among the Easterners concerning the pairs beginning with the second [day].

However, in the passage, “In the *ekoddiṣṭa* and in rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) etc., there is an injunction regarding decrease and increase,” the term refers to the midday *śrāddhas* by means of an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning that the *ekoddiṣṭa* is the primary archetype (*prakṛti*) of those midday *śrāddhas*.
This is because the principal *ekoddiṣṭa* itself cannot be determined as being performed on the very day the period of impurity (*aśauca*) ends.
By the phrase "in [the context of] increase and so forth," the *śrāddha* performed in the forenoon is meant.

"Decrease and increase of the moon" refers to the dark and bright fortnights (*kṛṣṇa* and *śukla-pakṣa*) as their basis; the "injunction connected with them" means the scriptural statement regarding the bright and dark fortnights.
Alternatively, "decrease and increase" refers to the dark and bright fortnights; the meaning is that the injunction or decision for which those two serve as the occasion or cause.
