This is the meaning:
regarding the *nirṇaya-śrāddha* other than the afternoon *śrāddha*, the determination is made according to the statements concerning the bright and dark fortnights;
however, in the case of the afternoon *śrāddha*, [the determination is as follows].
The Pitṛs worship that lunar day on which the Sun goes to its setting; for another [day] was assigned to them by the Self-born as the Aparāṅga.
From the supplementary statement joined with the reason "thus" (*itihetumat*), [the rule] applies to both sides [of the lunar fortnight] as extending up to the eighth day;

although the statement regarding the bright and dark fortnights (*śuklakṛṣṇavākya*) also applies to rites for the gods (*daiva*) on the tenth day and onwards, and thus does not have a scope restricted solely to rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), nevertheless, for the sake of establishing a systematic rule (*vyavasthā*), the statement regarding the bright and dark fortnights alone is the decisive authority for śrāddhas other than those performed in the afternoon (*āparāhṇika*).
Alternatively, the phrase "the injunction regarding decrease, increase, and so forth" refers to the [entire] statement; thus, there is no fault.

For this very reason, the mention of fasting in the statements concerning the bright and dark fortnights, as well as in the interrogative statement, is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for such ancestral rites (*pitrya*).
However, the statement beginning with "Kharva, Darpa, etc. is rootless (*nirmūla*), since it was not cited by the authors of the ancient compendiums (*prācyanibandhṛ*).
If, however, it is taken as including the root [of the fourteenth day], it refers exclusively to the new moon day:
"When the fourteenth day fills out its fourth watch and the new moon day is waning, at that very time the Śrāddha is prescribed."
Thus, because of its syntactic unity with the *Pariśiṣṭa*,

they say that even the mention of "decrease and increase" (*hrāsavṛddhi*) in the statement "for whatever action there is a specific time," namely in the phrase "decrease and increase are not the cause," refers exclusively to the bright and dark fortnights.
That is not so;

for while it is possible that the phrase "the decrease and increase" refers to the decrease and increase occurring within the lunar day (tithi) mentioned in the first half of the verse, it is improper to assume it refers to the decrease and increase of the moon— which is not at all present [in the context]—
and because, if it were taken to refer to sacrifices, it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

Furthermore, since in the first half [of the verse] there is a restrictive injunction that the statement regarding the "white and black" applies only to the *daiva* (celestial) rite, it is appropriate that—in accordance with the introductory context—the statement regarding the "white and black" in the second half also applies restrictively to the *pitrya* (ancestral) rite alone. To deviate from this and establish the restriction that the "white and black" statement applies only to the *pitrya* rite would result in a structural inconsistency (*vairūpya*). By this [argument], the inclusion of the *pārvaṇa* rite under the phrase "ekoddiṣṭa and so forth" in the *Viveka* and *Tithitattva*, as well as the inclusion of the "decrease and equality" under the phrase "increase, decrease, and so forth," and the inclusion of the "moon's waning and waxing" under the phrase "by which... [are thus explained].

The claim that, because of the inclusion of the phrase "itih" (thus), when a doubt arises regarding the increase, decrease, or equality of lunar days (*tithi*) in a *ekoddiṣṭa* or *pārvaṇa* rite, the determination is made respectively by the statements concerning the bright and dark fortnights and the statements concerning the setting [of the moon], has been refuted; for this would result in an inconsistency, as the principle is the same [in all cases].
Furthermore, the presentation of doubt by the phrase "in cases such as [the moon] increasing" (*vṛddhyādi*) is useless, because all definitive statements proceed only when there is indeed doubt.

Even when those [statements] exist, since there is no doubt when the [rite] is pervaded by the time of the action (*karmakāla*), they do not function to give rise to doubt; rather, it has been stated that they [serve only to determine] the fragmentation of the lunar day (*tithi*).
Moreover, the attempt to establish the rule that "that [day on which the moon sets]" and so forth refers specifically to the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], is also incorrect.
For although it is mentioned here in conjunction with the afternoon—
namely, "The rite for the gods is in the forenoon, but that for the ancestors is in the afternoon;
likewise, for the Śrāddha, the afternoon is superior to the forenoon"— [the term "forenoon" still applies].
By reflecting on such statements, there is no inconsistency whatsoever even if [the rule] pertains to all ancestral rites (pitrīya), because it concerns the afternoon of a day divided into two parts;
for even in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other rites, although they may begin in the first half of the *kutapa*, they must be completed precisely during such an afternoon.
And thus—
For rites pertaining to the gods, the lunar day (tithi) on which the sun has risen is to be known;
for rites pertaining to the ancestors, the lunar day on which the sun has set is to be known.
When the sun has risen, it is the time for offerings to the gods; when the sun has set, it is the time for offerings to the ancestors.
That lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas during the day and three muhūrtas at night is suitable for both the havya and kavya offerings.
Thus, general statements such as these are justified;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of restriction [of the rule] to the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha alone.
Furthermore, from the beginning until the conclusion, since the *pārvaṇa* alone is connected with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), [the rule] "at which the sun sets" [would apply].
It should not be argued that this statement refers exclusively to that [specific case],

because even the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha performed during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) begins precisely in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*); since it lacks any connection with the afternoon from its commencement until its conclusion,
the wise man should perform the śrāddha in the forenoon of the bright fortnight.
In the dark fortnight, during the afternoon, one must not cross the Rohiṇī constellation.

Thus, because it is stated with reference to the *pārvaṇa* as the archetype (*prakṛti*), the passage beginning with "yayāstam" (by which [the moon] sets) does not enjoin that the lunar day (*tithi*) must pervade the sunset in the *pārvaṇa*; rather, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that the lunar day pervades the sunset, as already established for all ancestral rites (*pitrya*) by the *kharvadarpa* statement.
By this—
When a rite for the gods has arrived, that lunar day on which the sun rises is to be known as complete; however, for a rite for the ancestors, it is the afternoon portion that is effective.
Thus, even the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya, despite its association with the afternoon (aparāhṇa), is explained as referring exclusively to all ancestral rites (pitrya).
Therefore, by the reasoning already stated, [the rule] regarding ancestral rites follows from the *kharva* statement,
and regarding divine rites (daiva) from the *yugma* statement.

It is established that when there is a conflict between the rules regarding the "pair" (yugma) and other statements, the determination is made by the specific rules for the bright and dark fortnights (*śukla-kṛṣṇa-vākya*) concerning those lunar days (*tithi*) not covered by the former. Where the status of being acceptable as "preceded by the previous day" (*pūrvaviddhā*) is understood from the "pair" and other statements—as, for example, in the case of the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*) overlapping with the second—there, that [third day] is not to be accepted only if the third day exists for three *muhūrtas* or more prior to sunset on the second day; otherwise, it is to be accepted.
But it is not [valid] when there is less than that duration of existence.
Thus, wherever the acceptability of an overlapping [tithi] (uttaraviddhā) is understood from statements such as those concerning "paired" days— for example, the second day overlapping with the third—
it is only when the second day exists for three muhūrtas or more after sunrise on the third day, or for even longer than that, and not when it is less than that.
In both fortnights, the lunar days (tithis) pierce the preceding and the succeeding day by three muhūrtas each; this is remembered as the general rule.
According to this statement of Paiṭhīnasi:
"When the sun has risen, the rite for the gods is performed; when the sun has set, the rite for the ancestors is performed.
That lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas during the day and three muhūrtas at night is [the one] for the offerings to the gods and the ancestors."
And because of this statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"When [the sun] has set," etc.; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action having begun. The meaning is: "having begun to go to its setting."
Because the day does not exist after sunset.
In this context, it is prescribed that [the time] must have a duration of two muhūrtas covering the sunrise and a duration of three muhūrtas covering the sunset.

However, it is not the case that [the rule applies] to that [time] which covers the sunrise for *havya* (offerings to gods) and covers the sunset for *kavya* (offerings to ancestors), because the qualifying attributes of the subject—the durations of two or three muhūrtas—are not intended to be significant here.
For this very reason:
"If that [day] upon which the sun sets were to last for three muhūrtas,
the wise know it to be complete for all religious duties."
Thus it is stated in the *Śivarahasya* regarding religious duties in general.
Furthermore, in the *Viṣṇudharma*, the mention of two *muhūrtas* should be understood as a secondary rule (*anukalpa*).
"A lunar day (*tithi*) that is waning should not be observed for three *muhūrtas*."
Even if it lasts for only two muhūrtas, that lunar day which is increasing in duration should be observed.

Because the word *api* (also/even) is heard in this statement of Dakṣa, and because the prohibition of the three-muhūrta period tending toward waning [the moon] in the first half-verse presupposes its prior applicability; furthermore, because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the three-muhūrta period is to be accepted for both increase and equality.

In reality, however, for the sake of making the first and second halves of the verse a single syntactical unit, it is more appropriate to understand the word *api* occurring in the second half as being supplied (*anuṣaṅga*) so as to serve the purpose of praising the two-muhūrta alternative, rather than being an independent prohibition.
Or else, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
By this [reasoning], the statement of Mādhava—that "this is an independent prohibition, and therefore the [tithi] touching the fourth *muhūrta* should be accepted"—is also refuted.

Likewise, in cases where either the *pūrvaviddhā* (the tithi overlapping with the previous day) or the *uttaraviddhā* (the tithi overlapping with the following day) is prohibited, if the preceding lunar day (*tithi*) is the one that determines the eligibility—as is the case when the first day (*pratipad*) is for the sake of the second day (*dvitīyā*)—then [the time] subsequent to the rise of the *pratipad*, lasting for three *muhūrtas*...
Furthermore, the subsequent lunar day is more [significant] as the piercer;
if the subsequent lunar day is the piercer—as when the second day pierces the first—then that second day must be three *muhūrtas* long before sunset, or even longer, but not less than that.
In both cases, the lunar days [affect] the preceding lunar day as well as the subsequent one.
They pierce [the targets] in three muhūrtas; this is remembered as the general rule.
This is because of the statement of Paiṭhīnasi:
"In the case of vows, fasts, gifts, and so forth, even a single ghaṭikā [of the auspicious time] may suffice."

Likewise, passages such as "Whatever lunar day (tithi) may exist, however small, at the time of sunrise," and so forth—which establish that even a [tithi] deficient by three muhūrtas is complete—are merely praises of the three-muhūrta overlap, according to the principle of the *āgneya-aṣṭākapāla* section; for this is clear from the inclusion of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "however small" (*stokāpi*). Enough of this.
And this determination applies to cases other than those rites such as fasting (*upavāsa*) that must be accomplished within a single day and night;

however, regarding fasting and similar acts, if the [tithi] is pure on the previous day but does not exist on the following day, or exists there for less than three *muhūrtas*, then even though it is odd-numbered, the previous one alone is taken because a [tithi] existing for less than three *muhūrtas* on the following day is not the subject matter of the *yugma* rule.
But if it is overlapped by three *muhūrtas* on the previous day and exists for three *muhūrtas* or more on the following day, then the determination is made according to the *yugma* statement.

Nor should it be argued that, although the latter [lunar day] is the subject of the rule regarding the pair (*yugma*), only the former should be observed because it pervades the entire period of a day and night (*ahorātra*) on the preceding day; for the status of being part of a pair and occurring at the time of commencement are more authoritative.

Furthermore, since fasting consists of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and according to the scriptural injunction, “The wise man should make his resolve in the morning,” that resolve must be made in the morning.

Some say that this is because the time of the subsequent lunar day (*tithi*) is the primary time for the performance according to the rule. However, Hemādri and Madanaratna state: "In the case of fasting (*upavāsa*), where the subsequent day is prohibited because it is overlapped by the preceding lunar day—as in the case of the second day (*dvitīyā*) overlapped by the first (*pratipad*)—if the second day is overlapped by the first even by less than three *muhūrtas*, yet exists on the following day even if by less than three *muhūrtas*, then the subsequent day alone [is to be taken]."
One should defile the tithi with a ghaṭikā, a third part of an argha, or even a very small amount,
just as a single drop of liquor defiles a full jar of *pañcagavya*.
Likewise:
"This piercing in every manner is a defiler of the fast.
Thus, with reference to the fast:
Even a penetration of only one ghaṭikā vitiates the subsequent lunar day.

Thus, because the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, the *Nigama*, and other *Smṛtis* state that the lunar day (*tithi*) is for fasting at its rising and for the *nakta* fast at its setting, it is said: "The lunar day belongs to the fast at sunrise and to the *nakta* at sunset. Furthermore:
In rites involving vows, fasts, and observances, that lunar day (tithi) which exists for even a single ghaṭikā at sunrise is to be accepted; however, the opposite is the case for ancestral rites.
Whatever lunar day (tithi) occurs even slightly at the time of sunrise should be considered full; one that has begun but lacks sunrise [is not].

Because statements such as those from Baudhāyana and others declare that even a very small [tithi] is to be accepted if it is rising [at dawn], when not even a small portion is obtainable on the following day, then—even if it is pierced by a prohibited previous tithi—it should be observed as a fast. For: "If days un-pierced by prohibited [tithis] are not obtained..."
If pierced for five muhūrtas, the Ekādaśī lunar day must indeed be accepted.
"A man should fast on other days pierced by half of that [period]," according to the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;
the syntactical connection is: "if those [days] not pierced by prohibited [times] are not obtained."

Regarding the acceptability of an Ekādaśī that is pierced by five muhūrtas: this should be understood to apply when the tenth day (Daśamī) lasts for five muhūrtas on the previous day, while the Ekādaśī on the following day lasts for only two muhūrtas and the Dvādaśī has undergone a decrease (kṣaya).

According to the *Madanaratna*, "piercing by five muhūrtas" refers to the period beginning from the dawn of the sun (aruṇodaya). However, the phrase "pierced by half of that" (tadardha-viddhā) is an indicative mark for any prohibited type of piercing.
This is in accordance with such statements as "half a *ghaṭikā* or a third [of a *muhūrta*]," and so forth.

However, where it is stated that the day overlapping the previous one (*pūrvaviddhā*) is to be accepted, it is logical to hold that the specific requirement there is an overlap of exactly three *muhūrtas*; this is the distinction.

Thus ends [the work of] the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Caturudadhivala, son of the illustrious Mahārāja Madhukara Sāha, grandson of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāparudra, whose lotus feet are illuminated by the clusters of rays from the crest-jewels of the entire circle of subordinate chieftains.

In the *Samayaprakāśa* (The Elucidation of Ritual Times), a section of the treatise titled *Śrīvīramitrodaya* composed by the illustrious Mitramiśra—who was commissioned by the glorious Vīrasiṃhadeva, who is like the sun causing the white lotuses of the earth’s grain to bloom; who is the son of Śrī Haṃsapāṇḍita and the grandson of Śrī Paraśurāmamiśra; who is the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the entire ocean of sciences; who is a lion to the great elephant of universal poverty; and who is the life-sustainer of learned men—this concludes the determination of general lunar days (*tithi*).
[The Determination of the First Day: Thus, when the lunar day (tithi) has been determined in general, it is now determined in its specific details.
Among those, the determination of the first day (pratipad) is set forth.
Because that [the first lunar day] is primary:
among the fasts observed on the *pratipad*, whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight, it is always the former [that is taken];
for "the *pratipad* and the fifth day should be fasted upon when conjoined with the preceding [day]."
Thus, from the words of Jābāli: "The first lunar day, the fifth, the fourteenth, the Sāvitrī [eighth], the Vaṭa-pūrṇimā [full moon of Āṣāḍha],
and likewise the ninth and tenth— these should not be observed as fast days when joined with the following tithi."
Thus, because of the prohibition against a [tithi] overlapped by another in the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*:
"The first lunar day (pratipad) may be joined with the second, and the second may be joined with the first."
This statement of Āpastamba refers to divine rites other than fasting;
furthermore, regarding fasting as well, it refers to the first lunar day (pratipad) when it does not fall in the afternoon, in accordance with the statements that will be cited later.
Moreover, this acceptance of the tithi overlapping with the following day for divine rites other than fasting applies specifically to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).

Because it is prescribed that even on the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), it must be one that is not overlapped by the previous [lunar day], such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*).
Nor should it be argued that this rule should be restricted to the fast (*upavāsa*) alone;

for if the statement regarding the "pairing" (*yugma*)—which concerns only the first day of the bright fortnight—were the specific subject (*viśeṣya*), it would be impossible to apply it as a restrictive rule (*upasaṃhāra*) to the general statements concerning fasting, which apply equally to both the bright and dark fortnights.
Nor should it be argued that the general statements themselves are restricted to a specific form by the "couple" (yugma) statement;

for according to that view, one must necessarily admit that the "couple" statement refers to divine rites other than fasting. Consequently, since fasting would already be established by that very statement, the general declarations would result in being purposeless.

However, Mādhavācārya, considering this to be a restrictive application (upasaṃhāra), states on the basis of the Āpastamba-sūtra that even for a fast on a dark lunar day, the subsequent [tithi] alone should be accepted.

Regarding other deities, however, it is beyond dispute that for Kṛṣṇa [tithis] the time is "pierced by the following" (uttaraviddhā), and for Śukla [tithis] it is "pierced by the preceding" (pūrvaviddhā).

Furthermore, this quality of being "pierced by the preceding" for Śukla tithis—both in the case of fasting and for other deities—does not apply when there is the presence of three muhūrttas at sunset; rather, it applies only to those [tithis] occurring in the afternoon (āparāhṇikī).
As it is said: "The first lunar day (pratipat) should be made 'facing' [the previous day] if it occurs in the afternoon."
Thus it is stated by Skanda.

As for the claim by the Gauḍas that this statement is rootless— or, even if it were rooted, that it refers to the ancestral rites performed in the afternoon because of the use of the word "yat" (which)— [that is incorrect].

It has been stated that this is because, with reference to the afternoon Śrāddha for the ancestors already established by another scriptural injunction, the rule regarding "facing the sun" (sammukhītvam) is prescribed as a matter of brevity.
That is not correct;
for if that were the case, the prescription of "facing the sun" with reference to the first lunar day (pratipad) would result in being rendered purposeless.
That very time which occurs in the afternoon is to be known as the *pratipad*;
by that [time], one should perform rites for the gods and for the ancestors—so Manu has declared.
This is also because it contradicts the statement of Vyāsa cited by Mādhava.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the afternoon [oblation] is the object of reference (*uddeśya*) due to its connection with the relative pronoun *yat*,
that too is incorrect.

By the reasoning already stated, it is understood that, with reference to the *sammukhī* [lunar day], only the status of being an *aparāhṇikī* is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Furthermore, the connection with the word *yat* (‘when’) is not defective even when there is a temporal separation, as in the case of the injunction: “When one offers into the *āhavanīya* fire.

However, when the *sammukhī aparāhṇikī* is not available, then the subsequent [lunar day] alone is to be taken, according to the general statement: “The *pratipad* should be accompanied by a second [day].”
Mādhava, however, states that even in that case, the time extending into the evening (sāyāhna) is to be accepted as the proper time because it serves as a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
The remainder [of the details] is to be understood from the general determination.

Furthermore, on the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of Caitra, for rites such as the oil massage (abhyaṅga) performed to mark the beginning of the year and so forth, the time occurring at sunrise (audayikī) is to be accepted.
In the month of Caitra, on the first day of the bright fortnight, when the sun had risen, Brahmā created the entire world.
According to this statement by Brahmā,
when the [lunar day] exists on both days or does not exist at all, the first [day] alone is taken.
The weekday that occurs at sunrise on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra is the lord of the year (*varṣeśa*).
In the pair of risings, the first [nakṣatra] would be the same; in the pair of non-risings, the first would also be the same.
Thus, according to the statement cited in the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"At the beginning of the year, at the beginning of spring, and likewise during the reign of Bali,
the first day (*pratipad*) must always be observed by the wise as joined with the preceding [lunar day]."
And because of the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"On the first day (pratipad) of the commencement of Navarātra— the pratipad for the worship of Caṇḍikā— it should not be performed if it is joined with the new moon (amāvāsyā)."
It should be performed for only a moment, endowed with the second and subsequent qualities.
Thus, from the statement in the Devīpurāṇa:
"O descendant of Kuru, O Bhārata, these three lunar days are declared to be supreme during the months of Kārttika, Āśvayuja, and Caitra."
Thus, having commenced with each successive step, [the number] should be made ten million according to the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
As for that which is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
Listen, O King, I shall explain the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍikā on the auspicious first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
Having begun thus:
"On a pure lunar day, the rite should be performed on the *pratipad* that moves upward;
having abandoned the first sixteen or even twelve *nāḍikās*."
"Those desiring continuity [of merit] should perform [the rite] in the afternoon when it is pure";
thus, the acceptability of the afternoon [time] has been stated, which is to be understood as applying when there is no *pratipad* on the following day.
However, that which is the white *pratipad* of Āśvina overlapping with the previous [day]...
One who desires auspiciousness should not perform the Navarātra vow on that day.
This is because of the prohibition of the *pūrvaviddhā* (the first lunar day overlapping with the previous tithi) found in both the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and the Devī Purāṇa.
A specific rule regarding the Navarātra will be stated hereafter.
However, the Pratipad for the Balyutsava is the *pūrvā* (the first tithi), according to the previously cited statement: "At the beginning of the year, at the beginning of spring," and so forth.
"Śivarātri should be observed on the day [of the lunar tithi] that is joined with the previous [lunar day], as is the day of Bali";
this is because of such a statement in the Padma Purāṇa.
Other specific details will be explained in the section on Dīpotsava.
The Holākā festival occurs on the first day of the lunar month coinciding with sunrise;
for it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "But when the month of Madhu has begun, on the first day as the sun rises..."

In both cases—whether it be the state of being "thus" (tathātva) or "not thus" (atathātva)—the former [lunar date] alone is to be taken, because of the scriptural statement: "at the beginning of the year, at the beginning of spring," and so forth.
This worship of Kāma is to be performed in the morning on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight once the winter season has passed.
And when the spring season has arrived at dawn,
O Pārtha, having truly consumed a mango blossom together with sandalwood paste— this is indeed the truth.
Then the person shall become level and happy.
Thus it is stated in the *Purāṇasamuccaya*.
Since the Mahattapa vow on the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada is a Rudra-vow, the preceding lunar day (tithi) should be taken;
for in all Rudra-vows, the tithi that is present at the commencement [of the day] should be observed.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.

Now, the second [tithi] is determined: in all rites pertaining to the gods, the bright fortnight (śukla) tithi is to be taken as the later one, whereas the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa) tithi is to be taken as the earlier one.
Regarding the Vedic statement establishing that the [first lunar day] is not to be accepted when pierced by the subsequent [second day]—
namely, "The first day (pratipad) should be accompanied by the second, and the second day joined with the first"—
this is according to the statement of Āpastamba.

And regarding the contradiction with the statement from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*: "O best of the twice-born, the first lunar day (pratipad) should be observed [on the day it begins], and the second [should be observed on the day it ends]," [the following applies]:
"In the bright fortnight, that lunar day (tithi) is to be accepted on which the sun has risen."
In the dark fortnight, that lunar day (tithi) is to be taken upon which the sun sets.
Thus, because a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*) is established by the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya;

however, some maintain that since the phrase "the fourteenth and the full moon" mentions the *paurṇamāsī* (full moon) in proximity, the entire sentence refers inherently to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and therefore the phrase "in the bright fortnight" does not function as a restrictive rule.

However, because it is impossible to restrict the scriptural injunction regarding the Yugādi (the start of the Yuga) to a general subject matter by virtue of its proximity (*sannidhi*) in the form of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), and because it is improper [to interpret] the *pratipad* as occurring on both sides of the new moon due to its co-utterance with the *pratipad*, the previously stated systematic arrangement is superior.
Now, if the sentences concerning the "pair" (*yugma*) and so forth thus refer to lunar days (*tithi*) suitable for all divine rites at all times—
The eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth,
thirteenth, and new moon days should be observed as fasts when they are conjoined with the following lunar day.

Otherwise, the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*—which teaches that [the Ekādaśī] should not be accepted when it is conjoined with another [tithi] and pertains solely to the fast (*upavāsa*)—would be rendered meaningless.
For in the absence of this specific declaration:
"The third, the eleventh, the sixth, and likewise the eighth lunar day... [would apply universally].
These lunar days (tithis) are to be abandoned for the fast, both at the piercing [of the sun] and below it.

Thus, since the statement of Nārada—by declaring that the third lunar day (tṛtīyā) does not invalidate the second (dvitīyā)—prohibits the use of a second day overlapped by the third for fasting, that prohibition must apply only to rites dedicated to the gods other than fasting.

Furthermore, when the Viṣṇudharmottara specifically prescribes the second day overlapped by the third for fasting itself, a conflict arises between the injunction and the prohibition; this conflict is resolved by the two sets of verses concerning the bright and dark fortnights.

Thus, since the mention of "undertaking a fast" here is intended merely as an illustration, it is established that this rule applies to all divine rites (daiva) performed on both the *paraviddhā* (overlapping with the next day) and *pūrvaviddhā* (overlapping with the previous day) tithis, according to the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights.
When a matter has been generally determined in this way, one should understand that the purpose of a specific injunction made despite a general prohibition is precisely this.

And as for the statement that the second lunar day (dvitīyā) of the dark fortnight should be taken when it is overlapped by the preceding day, that applies only when there is contact with the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*).
"O Lord, the first lunar day (*pratipad*) should be observed when it occurs in the afternoon;
likewise, the second lunar day should be performed when it occurs in the forenoon."
This is according to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but.
Such [a day] is one that is face-to-face (sammukhī), meaning it is joined with the previous [tithi].

Furthermore, since it would entail the fault of prolixity (gaurava) to interpret this sentence as enjoining both the morning-time (paurvāhṇikatva) and the quality of being overlapped by the previous day (pūrvaviddhatva), the injunction of morning-time applies only to those cases where the quality of being overlapped by the previous day is already established; thus, its scope is restricted solely to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
And although in this statement a twofold division appears due to the observation of the terms "forenoon" (pūrvāhṇa) and "afternoon" (aparāhṇa), [the meaning remains as stated].

Nevertheless, since "belonging to the afternoon" (*aparāhṇikatva*) cannot exist for something that occupies only the evening (*sāyānha*) under the view of a twofold division [of the day], the status of being in the afternoon must be established by adopting the fivefold division of the day;

and likewise, by association with that, "belonging to the forenoon" (*paurvāhṇikatva*) must also be explained according to the fivefold division alone, as its connection with the morning time is to be interpreted through the etymological derivation: "the former part of the day is the forenoon" (*pūrvo bhāgo 'hnah pūrvāhṇaḥ*).
[Objection: If it is explained in this way, then because this [lunar day] is pure (*śuddhā*) by its very nature, it follows that it must be accepted; thus, this statement would be purposeless.
[Response: Not so.

For in the absence of this statement, a lunar day which began on the previous day having passed the entire morning time, and lasts for three *muhūrtas* or more on the following day, would—due to being situated in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*)—be considered as the previous one alone.

It would have to be accepted [as the primary option]. However, since that [lunar day] lacks the quality of being "belonging to the forenoon" (*paurvāhṇika*) when this statement is present, and because on the following day the rules such as "the pair of days and the two fires" (*yugmāgni*) and so forth apply— stating that the subsequent [day] is to be pierced by the preceding— the purpose of this statement is established through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), namely that it establishes the acceptability of the subsequent [day] alone.

Now, an objection is raised: since the rules concerning the pairs of lunar days (*yugma*) and so forth have been established as pertaining specifically to the bright and dark fortnights by means of the statements regarding the bright and dark fortnights, how can they apply to the dark fortnight? It is replied:

the statements regarding the bright and dark fortnights serve as the basis for that establishment only when there is a conflict with the rules concerning the pairs of lunar days, such as "the second day joined with the first" (*dvitīyā pratipadyutā*).
However, when those [pair] rules are connected with the specific statement "occurring in the forenoon" (*paurvāhnikī*), then [the rule] "that which is joined with the first day" applies.

That [tithi] which occurs in the forenoon is to be accepted; for this reason, because there is a contradiction with such statements regarding the pairings of lunar days and fires (*yugmāgnivākya*), the rule is established as referring to the bright and dark fortnights.

However, in the case of a tithi that has commenced by abandoning the entire forenoon time and continues for three *muhūrtas* or more on the following day, since there is no statement prescribing it as one to be taken when overlapping with the previous day, the application of the rules concerning the pairings (*yugmavākya*) certainly applies.

However, that [day] which is less than three muhūrtas on the following day is to be accepted as the previous one alone, even in the absence of contact with the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), because there is no doubt [regarding its status] and because the statements concerning [the day] being overlapped by the next do not apply here.
The Easterners (*Prācya*), however, do not record this statement.
But in the opinion of Mādhava and Anantabhaṭṭa, all accusative cases are parā.
And likewise, Mādhava states: "If [the moonrise] occurs on the previous day, it is *asatī*; if it occurs in the morning on the following day, it lasts for three *muhūrtas*."
That second [lunar day] is to be observed when it is nourished by another; otherwise, it is the one joined with the preceding [day].
Thus,

on the second days of the dark fortnights of the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, for the vow known as Aśūnyaśayana, that [lunar day] which extends until moonrise is to be taken, because its performance is prescribed at moonrise;
and this constitutes its status as a "moonrise vow" (candrodayavrata).
"An arghya offering should be given to Candra with curd, unbroken grains, fruits, and so forth," according to the statement in another Purāṇa.
And the vow has been described as follows:
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
O descendant of Bharata, listen to the account of the second lunar day named Aśūnyaśayana,
by fasting on which, O lord of men, a woman does not fall into widowhood.
Thus it is said.
Here, by the word "upoṣya" (having fasted), worship is intended, not the mere cessation of eating.
Having bowed to Hari in the temple at night, one should eat while restraining one's speech.
Thus, because the practice of eating only at night (*naktabhojana*) is prescribed in another Purāṇa,
when the moonrise occurs on two days, the latter [of the two] is [the proper time], whether that [practice] exists or not.
[This applies] during the four dark fortnights of the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
One should perform the vow called Aśūnya, which yields even greater fruit when accompanied by the Jaya mudrā.
Thus, the *Madanaratna* states that because the procedure for the worship of Jayā is prescribed in another Purāṇa,

the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika should be taken as occurring in the afternoon (*aparāhṇika*) for the worship of Yama: "On the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship Yama in the afternoon."
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "The first [Ekādaśī] occurs in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the next in the month of Bhādrapada."
The third [lunar day] occurs in the month of Āśvayuja, and the fourth occurs in Kārttika.
In Śrāvaṇa, it is known as Kaluṣā; likewise, in Bhādra, it is considered Gīrmatā;
in Āśvina, Pretasañcārā; and in Kārttika, it is regarded as Yāmyakā.

Having thus described the vow on the first day, the worship of Sarasvatī on the second, and the Śrāddha on the third, that which is prescribed for the fourth is stated: "O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the second day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
Yama was formerly fed and honored in his own home by Yamunā."
Therefore, O Brahmin, this Yamadvitīyā is renowned throughout the three worlds;
on this day, men must not eat in their own homes.
With affection, one should eat from the hand of a sister; this increases nourishment.
And gifts should be bestowed upon the sisters according to the prescribed rule;
all sisters are to be honored, or, in their absence, those who have entered the path.
Hemādri states that those who have entered [the path] are considered to be sisters;
thus ends the determination of the second [category].
Now follows the determination of the third.
A third lunar day that is not the Rambhā-tṛtīyā should be joined with the fourth lunar day for all rites dedicated to the gods, such as fasting;
as it is said in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
O best of the twice-born, with the exception of the third lunar day known as Rambhā,
the [thirteenth] joined with a weekday (gaṇa) is recommended for all other rites.
Gaṇa = the fourth lunar day.
Āpastamba states:
"That third lunar day which is conjoined with the fourth bestows fruit."
It ensures that women do not suffer widowhood and bestows sons and grandsons.
In this context, by hearing the praise of the third case ending joined with the fourth, its status as that which is to be enjoined is understood;
and the prohibition of the third case ending joined with the second is also heard.
And thus:
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O dear one, the third [lunar day] which is ever pierced by the second should never be observed by those undertaking the vow."
by those devoted to the pursuit of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
"Except for one called Rambhā, the third [night] increases merit;
and regarding this, O son of the Kṛttikās, these words were spoken by the sages."
And in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "O Lord, the third [lunar day] must not be performed when it is defiled by the second;
that lowest of men who performs it joined with the second [day]..."
By means of the dharma performed here for one year, a man is liberated;
likewise,
O best of kings, he who performs [the rite] on the second lunar day conjoined with the Śeṣa constellation.
He goes to the terrible hell, the fearsome Kālasūtra.
The wise declare that she who, being ill-fated, performs the second marriage while the first remains undissolved, shall attain widowhood.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O Śikhidhvaja, the third lunar day must not be observed when joined with the second; if a foolish woman or man does so, [they incur sin]."
O dear one, when conjoined with the second lunar day,
one is deprived of the previously acquired merit.
Widowhood and misfortune shall certainly come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Even for that which is seen as a second [moon] for the duration of a *kalā* or a *kāṣṭhā*, [the same result follows].
O Śikhidhvaja, that third [observance] should not be performed alone; it should be performed together with a group by one who desires the supreme secret and is a practitioner of the vow.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "The third [lunar day] should never be performed together with the second."

In this regard, from the scriptural statements, “excluding the one called Rambhā” and “leaving aside the one named Rambhā,” it is understood that for the Rambhā-vow, the third lunar day joined with the second is to be taken, because of its direct injunction as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
“Likewise, Bṛhattapā, Rambhā, Sāvitrī, and Vaṭapaitṛkī.”
The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day should be observed as the face-to-face lunar days.
Likewise, O Brahmin: Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, Rambhā, the third [day] of the ancestors (Paṭapaitṛkī),
and Bṛhattapā.
The lunar day (tithi) should be observed as present (sammukhī).
And thus, even the statement regarding "the pair of two and three" (*yugmāgnīti-yugma-vākya*) refers exclusively to the *Rambhā-vrata*.

Furthermore, the prohibitions against a third lunar day conjoined with a second, and the injunctions for a third lunar day conjoined with a fourth, do not apply solely to the context of fasting (*upavāsa*). [This is evident from the verse:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, full moon, and fourteenth..."
The new moon day and the third lunar day should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following [lunar days].
It should not be argued that this is in accordance with the statement of Bṛhaspati,

because in such statements as "In all other matters, [the tithi] joined with a weekday (gaṇa) is praised," the quality of being "pierced by the next" (paraviddha) is mentioned even for activities other than fasting; however, the statement regarding the Ekādaśī and Aṣṭamī specifically establishes the status of being pierced by the next day only in relation to fasting on those particular lunar days.
However, it does not negate the fact that [the day] is already occupied by another ritual purpose,
because if it were intended for both purposes, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Some, however, maintain that the injunction of the third case-ending connected with the second case-ending refers specifically to the "white third" (*śukla-tṛtīyā*).

The prohibition, however, pertains to the third day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-tṛtīyā). Nor should it be argued that the statement regarding Rambhā would thus be rendered meaningless; for, by virtue of the previously cited verse beginning with "ekādaśī-aṣṭamī," one must resort to the practice of taking even a third day occurring in the bright fortnight as being "pierced" by the following day when it concerns fasting. Therefore, they say that the commencement of the Rambhā statement is justified as an exception (apavāda) to that general rule.
That is incorrect,
because the opposite could also be established.
The rule for the third lunar day joined with the second applies specifically to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa) third.
The prohibition, however, pertains to the third day of the bright fortnight (śukla-tṛtīyā).
Furthermore:
"In the bright fortnight, that lunar day (tithi) is to be accepted on which the sun has risen."
In the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken.
This statement conveys a meaning that is indeed contrary [to the rule].
For here, it is understood that the third lunar day (*tithi*) belonging to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), on which the sun sets, is to be taken as joined with the second day;
whereas for that same lunar day belonging to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), on which the sun rises, it is to be taken as joined with the fourth day.
In reality, however, it is not logical to establish the scope of injunctions and prohibitions based on the distinction between the "white" (śukla) and the "black" (kṛṣṇa).

For if that were the case, there would result a contraction of the many previously cited instances where the third case-ending joined with a second case-ending is prohibited, while the third case-ending joined with a fourth case-ending is enjoined.
In our position, however, there is no such contraction of the scriptural statements.

Because it is accepted that the prohibitions against the third lunar day joined with the second and the injunctions for the third lunar day joined with the fourth apply even during the bright fortnight due to the abandonment of the Rambhā-vow, the statement "in all other matters" is contradicted in your position.
The distinction, however, is that in our position, the rule regarding the pairings (yugma-vākya) alone is restricted to the subject matter of the Rambhā-vow.
And this second piercing (dvitīyāvedha), even if it is very slight, must not be rejected; it is not restricted to being only three muhūrtas in duration.
This is understood from such scriptural statements as, "joined with the remainder of the second [tithi]," and "even that which is a mere *kakalā* or *kāṣṭhā* [of the second].
For this very reason, the third [piercing] is also [to be accepted].
Even if it is joined with the fourth [lunar day] for only a very short time, it should be accepted; however, there is no concern for a ritual time (*karmakāla*) consisting of three *muhūrtas*.

This prohibition of even a slight contamination by the second [lunar day], as well as the acceptance of a slightly later third [lunar day], pertains exclusively to the vow dedicated to Gaurī, based on the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

However, in other types of vows, the requirement of three *muhūrtas* for the prohibited conjunction with the second lunar day (*dvitīyā-vedha*) must indeed be observed. But when not even a small portion of the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*) is available on the following day, then in all such vows, [the day] joined with the second lunar day is certainly to be accepted.
This applies to the eleventh, the third, the sixth, and the thirteenth [lunar days].
It should be observed even if it is overlapped by the previous day, provided it does not exist on the following day.
Thus, according to the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

"But when the third lunar day, being pure on the preceding day, increases on the following day, then even that pure [third] should be abandoned and only the one joined with the fourth should be accepted. This is because some hold that the excellence of the time joined with the fourth is understood from such statements as, "That joined with a *gaṇa* is praised."

Others, however, maintain that since prohibitive statements do not apply to such cases, and because no scriptural authority is found to establish that the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*) should be taken as necessarily joined with the following day even when it is pure and increased (*adhikā*), the statements regarding "being joined with [the previous] lunar day" (*gaṇayuktā*) and so forth refer to a situation where there is an overlap with the second lunar day (*dvitīyā-vedha*) or the fourth lunar day (*caturthī-vedha*); in such cases, one may take either the day overlapping with the preceding day or the day overlapping with the succeeding day.

When such a doubt arises as to which [day] should be accepted, they say that because this [third day] is the decisive factor in such a case— and since no doubt arises regarding the fullness of the lunar day (*tithi*), and thus rules concerning the conjunction with specific groups of planets do not apply— the third [lunar day] alone is to be accepted as the one to be taken. This, then, is the summary.

In all rites for the gods, such as the *upavāsa* (fast) on the days sacred to Rambhā and Vratārikā, the third lunar day (*tṛtīyā*) joined with the fourth (*caturthī*) is to be taken, not the third overlapped by the second (*dvitīyā*). In rites dedicated to Gaurī, even a very small overlap with the second is to be avoided; however, there is no requirement for the second to extend for three *muhūrtas*. Likewise, in the Gaurī-vrata specifically, the third joined with the fourth—even if it is only three *muhūrtas*—is to be accepted. In other rites, one must indeed rely upon the three-*muhūrta* duration of both the third and the second, respectively, as the "pierced" (*vedhya*) and the "piercer" (*vedhaka*).
But when even a very small portion [of the third lunar day] is not obtained on the following day, then even the second lunar day joined with the first (dvitīyā-viddhā) must be accepted for all vows;

however, in the case of the Rambhā-vow, only that joined with the second lunar day is to be accepted. In the absence of that, even one joined with the second lunar day is to be taken if it is pure (śuddhā);
furthermore, because of its fullness, the former [the one joined with the first] should be adopted.
Thus concludes the determination of the third lunar day.
Now follows the determination of the fourth lunar day:
the fourth lunar day should be taken as conjoined with the fifth, according to the scriptural statement, "Yugas and Bhūtas [conjoin]."

The eleventh, the sixth, the new moon day, and the fourth [lunar day] should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day; the subsequent days are preferred over those joined with the preceding day.
And because of this statement by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"In the vow of Vināyaka, however, the fourth lunar day joined with the third is to be accepted. Thus it has been said.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"The third lunar day conjoined with the fourth is the bestower of fruits;
and the fourth occurring on the third bestows the fruit of great merit."
"O child, this [hymn] which gratifies Gaṇanātha’s son must be performed by those observing the vow.
Thus it is said.
Here, by the force of the qualifying term "Gaṇanātha," it is understood that in the vow of Gaṇanātha, the fourth lunar day joined with the third is to be taken.
And thus:
"The third lunar day should be performed in conjunction with the fourth, and the fourth [should be performed] as the third."
One should never perform [the rite] joined with the third lunar day, nor ever with the fifth.
Thus is the statement found in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa,
and also the statement found in the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Lord, the fourth lunar day must indeed be observed as conjoined with the third."
Both of these pertain specifically to the Gaṇanātha-vrata;
furthermore, for the Siddhivināyaka-vrata, the fourth lunar day (caturthī) that extends through midday (madhyāhna) is to be accepted.
It is said: "For the Gaṇanātha, a fourth [tithi] joined with the mother [the third lunar day] is recommended."
If that [lunar day] extends across midday, it belongs to the following day if it occurs later.
Thus, according to the statement of Bṛhaspati,
the meaning of the phrase "on the following day" (*pare 'hani*) is as follows:
if the [lunar day] extends across the midday (*madhyāhna*) on the very next day, then it means that on that following day it is "pierced by the fifth" (*pañcamī-viddhā*).
On other lunar days, however, it should be understood that the rite must be performed at dawn, as it is stated in the *Gaṇapatikalpa*:
"O King, having bathed with white sesame seeds in the morning, one should perform the worship at midday";
thus, it is understood that midday is the time for the ritual action.

However, when the fourth lunar day is joined with the mother (the third) on the previous day and also extends across midday on the following day, then the Vināyaka vow must be performed on the latter day alone, due to its association with the quality of being "joined with the mother.
This is because the time for the ritual action (*karmakāla*) is fully pervaded by it on that very day.
Likewise, in the vow dedicated to the deity Nāga as well, the fourth lunar day that extends across midday is to be accepted.
Having fasted at whatever place the sun is at midday on the fifth lunar day, a self-controlled man should satiate the lords of serpents with milk and then break his fast;
for him, poisons perish and serpents do not harm him.
Thus, according to the procedure for the midday Nāga worship,
this much is the distinction:
when the midday [period] occurs on the preceding day alone, then it is indeed the former [day].
On other lunar fortnights, the fifth day alone must be taken;

for since the fifth day is the day of the Nāgas, its conjunction [with the moon] is highly commendable. However, some say that even in the vow dedicated to the deity Nāga, it should be taken as conjoined with the third day, just as in the vow of Vināyaka.
That is incorrect.
Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the two statements—one from the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa* and one from the *Skanda-purāṇa*, both cited previously—constitute valid evidence, we say no;
for those two operate only in a general sense.

For in that context, it is understood merely that "the fourth [lunar day] joined with the third is to be accepted," and not that "the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight joined with the third is to be accepted.

However, in accordance with the previously cited statement from the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*, we understand the essential meaning of these two statements to be that "the fourth lunar day joined with the third is to be accepted even when one desires a son of Gaṇeśa. Therefore, when there is doubt regarding the acceptance of the fourth lunar day—due to its overlapping with midday on both days during a vow dedicated to the Naga deities—the subsequent day alone is to be accepted based on the rule of the pair (*yugmavākya*).

But when the [lunar day] occupies the midday period on the preceding day alone, then the earlier [day] is to be taken, due to the superior authority of the scriptural rule regarding the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*).
As for the statement:
"The second [tithi], because of its overlap with the fifth; and the tenth and the thirteenth..."
On the fourteenth day, for the purpose of fasting, both the preceding and the following lunar days (tithis) should be rejected.
Thus, the statement prohibiting the fourth lunar day joined with the fifth applies specifically to the Vināyaka vow.
However, for the Gaurī vow, the fourth lunar day joined with the third should be taken, because the conjunction with the third is auspicious due to Gaurī being the presiding deity of that day.
Regarding the Gaurī vow on the fourth lunar day, it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
O descendant of Yadu, by worshipping Vināyaka on the fourth lunar day,
one becomes completely freed from all obstacles and attains the fulfillment of one's purpose.
Having said this, he immediately thereafter declared:
"On that very day, one should worship Nidrā, Rati, Śivā, Bhadrā, Kīrti, Medhā, Sarasvatī, Prajñā, Tuṣṭi, and likewise Kānti."
"One who desires knowledge should especially worship Sarasvatī.
Thus it is said.
Also in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
On the fourth day, however, by performing the worship of Gaṇeśa and Gaurī according to the prescribed rite, a man shall obtain success and good fortune in due order.
Thus it is said; and also in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, a wise man should worship Gaurī."
The fourth, named Varadā Gaurī, is well-worshipped there.
Thus:
"If Jayā is complete and the fourth [lunar day] is further diminished, that very Jayā must indeed be observed;
one should not perform it when it is pierced by the Nāga [day]."
This statement also establishes, by way of the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori), that the fourth lunar day joined with the third is to be accepted for the Gaurī-vrata.
For this is the meaning of the passage:
when, due to the decrease of the fourth day on the following day, it becomes overlapped (*viddhā*) by the fifth, whereas on the preceding day the Jayā [the third] extends over the entire day.
In that case, even a pure third day should be taken for the vow of the fourth day, and not a fourth day overlapped by the fifth which is full of defects.

However, this statement does not establish that a pure third day is to be taken for the vow of the fourth day, because its purpose is to prohibit a fourth day overlapped by the fifth; for if it were intended to convey both meanings, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
However, some, accepting that this statement concerns the *vināyaka-vrata*, explain it otherwise:

when on the previous day the *jayā* (the third lunar day) is complete at midday, but on the following day the fourth lunar day (*caturthī*) ends before midday due to its decrease, then— given that the *caturthī* is absent during the time for the ritual on both days— in response to the inquiry as to which day should be taken, this [text] states:
The statement begins: "And if Jayā is complete.
Even though Jayā extends into midday, the fourth lunar day (caturthī) joined with Jayā that occurs earlier must be taken, and not the subsequent fourth lunar day pierced by Nāga.
[This applies to] Gaurī-caturthī, the worship of the Vaṭa-dhenu, the worship of Durgā, Durmukha, and Holi.
The worship of Vatsa and Śivarātri—these, O King, utterly destroy a ruler along with his kingdom.
From this statement in the *Purāṇamuñcaya* as well, it is understood that on the occasion of the Gaurī-vrata, the fourth lunar day (caturthī) joined with the third is to be accepted.
"Gaurī’s fourth" means the fourth lunar day associated with the Gaurī-vrata;
"the worship of the cow" refers to the Bahulā-caturthī associated with that same rite.
The worship of Vatsa is known as Vatsadvādaśī.

However, some say that the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight should be taken when joined with the fifth, and the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight when joined with the third, based on such scriptural statements as: "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day [itself] is to be understood [as the observance]."
That is incorrect;
for regarding the statement concerning the fourth lunar day joined with the third, the previously mentioned arrangement alone is correct.

As for the *saṅkaṣṭacaturthī*, however, that which extends through moonrise should be taken, because in its own ritual manual (*kalpa*), it is prescribed as having the time of moonrise as its defining period.
Thus concludes the determination of the fourth lunar day (*caturthī*).
Now follows the determination of the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*).

For all rites dedicated to the gods, such as fasting and so forth, the fifth lunar day should be taken as joined with the preceding [day], according to the statement of Yama: "In the case of *yuga* and *bhūta* [tithis], [the tithi] is joined with the preceding."
In the Skanda Purāṇa as well: "O Lord, the fifth [tithi] should likewise be observed when conjoined with the fourth."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa as well: "The fifth [tithi] should be joined with the fourth, but not with the sixth."

The eleventh, the sixth, the new moon, and the fourth [lunar day] should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day; those joined with the preceding day [are to be observed on the earlier day].

Furthermore, in this statement by Vasiṣṭha, it is declared that when the fifth lunar day—distinct from those enumerated and included under the term "others"—is observed as a fast, it is connected with the preceding [day]. Therefore, although it is generally said: "Indeed, the lunar day should be observed on its final portion by those desiring the fruits of the gods," [the rule remains as stated].

Thus, because the *Śivarahasya* and *Saura Purāṇa* state that the end of a lunar day (*tithi*) is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) for fasting, it is understood that when there is a conflict between two lunar days, the one overlapping with the next (*paraviddhā*) should be taken for fasting.

Nevertheless, since this is a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*), it is indeed proper that the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) be joined with the preceding day for fasting, according to the specific statements previously cited.
It is with this very intention that the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is employed in the phrase "mostly at the end" (*prāyaḥ prānta*).
As for the contradictory statement, "But the fifth [lunar day] should be observed when joined with the sixth, O Nārada," that refers specifically to the fast of Skanda.

"In the Skandopavāsa, the fifth [lunar day] joined with the next [tithi] is to be accepted," because this is stated in the remainder of that passage; and it pertains to the vow dedicated to the deity Nāga:
"The fifth of the bright fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa is proclaimed as Nāgapañcamī."
Having abandoned that [fifth], the fifth [vow] together with the fourth is beneficial.
Because of this statement,
it should be understood that in the vow of the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the earlier [lunar day] is to be taken due to the mention of "audible" (śrāvaṇa).
However, some maintain that there is a systematic arrangement of contradictory statements regarding the fifth day based on the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights.
That is incorrect:
"The fourth [tithi] should be joined with [the fifth], but the fifth is not joined with the subsequent one;
likewise in rites for the gods and the ancestors, during the bright fortnight as well as the dark."
Thus, because the statement cited by Mādhava and others declares that the fifth day occurring in either of the two fortnights is to be joined with the preceding [tithi],
the mention of rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*) here is made by way of illustration;

just as in ancestral rites, in accordance with the afternoon and other requirements, one sets aside the fifth day joined with the sixth and adopts the fifth day conjoined with the fourth, so it is also in the case of rites for the gods (*daiva*).

Nor should it be suspected that, because the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is the time for the ritual in rites for the gods (*daiva*), and because the scriptural injunction regarding the time of the rite is more authoritative, the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) must be accepted as being joined with the following day;

for the various specific statements cited previously are even more authoritative. And it is precisely in such a case that the statement concerning completeness (*sākalya*), namely “having reached which lunar day...,” becomes applicable; otherwise, the statement on completeness would be rendered without scope (*anavakāśa*).

For this very reason, the statement that "the fifth [lunar day] itself is joined with the preceding [fourth] only in the case of fasting (upavāsa), whereas in rites for the gods (daiva), it is joined with the succeeding [sixth]" is also improper. This is because the phrase "in a rite for the gods" (daive karmaṇi) indicates that the fifth is joined with the preceding in all divine rites whatsoever; furthermore, the statements regarding the fifth being joined with the subsequent are restricted in scope by the specific injunction concerning the Skanda-fasting.
[Objection: But surely, from the rule of pairs found in the Vyāsa-nigama, it is understood that the fifth should be taken when it is joined with the fourth.
However, from the Yuga-śāstra cited by Āpastamba and others:
"The first day (Pratipad) should be joined with the second; the second day should be joined with the first; and that third day which is joined with the fourth bestows the fruit [of the vow]."
And the fifth [tithi], O Nārada, should be joined with the sixth.
Thus, it is understood that in such a case, a fifth-case ending joined with a sixth-case ending should be taken;

consequently, when there is a contradiction between two pairs of scriptural injunctions, because another statement serving as a regulator is required, it is appropriate to establish the rule according to the *Śukla* and *Kṛṣṇa* scriptures.
True.

The established rule based on the Śukla-kṛṣṇa-śāstra was stated precisely to refute that [other view]; thus, in the statement of Hārīta, "likewise in the bright fortnight and the dark," it is logical that the conflicting dual-scriptural tradition of Āpastamba and others pertains specifically to the Skanda-vrata fast. Therefore, the previously mentioned settled rule alone is superior.
This concludes the determination of the fifth lunar day.
Now the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) is determined.
And that [sixth] is to be accepted in conjunction with the seventh in all divine rites other than the Skanda-vrata, according to the Yuga-vākya:
"The Ekādaśī, Aṣṭamī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Dvitīyā, and Caturdaśī [are to be taken with their successors]."
The thirteenth and the new moon days should be observed as fasts when they are joined with the subsequent [lunar day].
This is also because of the statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The inclusion of the term 'fasting' (upavāsa), however, is stated in the *Dvitīyā-nirṇaya* to be an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa) for all rites dedicated to the gods.
A sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) that is pierced by the Nāga [the fifth tithi] occurs on both fortnights."
In rites for the gods, one should place that [line] at the end; in rites for the ancestors, it is joined with the preceding one.

Thus, because Sumantu has prohibited the *pañcamī-viddhā* (the sixth tithi overlapping with the fifth) while enjoining the *saptamī-viddhā* (the seventh tithi overlapping with the sixth)— referred to by the final word— in rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva-karman*):

"The sixth tithi overlapped by the Nāga [fifth], and the seventh overlapped by Śiva [sixth], as well as the tenth overlapped by the eleventh, should never be observed as a fast under any circumstances."
Thus it is stated in the Śivarahasya and the Saura Purāṇa:
"The sixth lunar day pierced by the serpent (the fifth), the Sun (Sunday) pierced by Rudra (Tuesday),
and Viṣṇu (Monday) pierced by Kāma (Friday)— these days are not to be accepted."
Thus, because of the prohibition against the *pūrvaviddhā* (the day overlapping with the previous tithi) in the *Nigama*,
the mention of "fasting" (*upavāsa*) here is also to be understood as before.
The *nāga* is the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*).
Śiva and Rudra are the eighth;
Divākara is the seventh;
Kāma is the thirteenth.
Viṣṇu is the twelfth [digit].
As for the piercing (vedha) of the fifth:
"A nāga [pierces] with twelve nāḍīs, and a dik likewise with fifteen."
A person born under the eighteen nāḍīs defiles the subsequent lunar day.
According to this statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, [the period] consists of six *muhūrtas* and not merely three *muhūrtas* in general.
As for the *Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī*: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight is *Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī*; the fourteenth day is *Śivarātri*."
These [fasts] should be observed as joined with the preceding day; the breaking of the fast should take place at the end of the lunar day (tithi).
Thus, according to the statement from the *Vrāhma-vaivarta*, the [eighth lunar day] must be taken as joined with the fifth (*pañcamī-yutā*).
"The eighth of the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) refers to the eighth day occurring within the dark half of the month;
or, according to some, it refers to the Janmāṣṭamī, which is connected to the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow well-known in the *Vrata-prakāśa* and dedicated to the deity Rudra.

This statement is for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding that very sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is generally forbidden for all divine rites when it is pierced by the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) for twelve *nāḍīs*.

Thus, since even in the rite of Skanda the sixth day pierced by twelve *nāḍīs* is forbidden, it should be understood that only that which is joined with a fifth day of less than that duration is to be accepted.
Otherwise, if that [sixth day] were to be accepted everywhere simply because it is pure, the statement would result in being rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, the statement "the *nāga* [tithi] is spoiled by twelve *nāḍīs*" does not intend to declare that the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) measuring twelve *nāḍīs* spoils the subsequent lunar day in all cases;

for such a declaration would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Rather, it is intended as an injunction that it is spoiled by twelve *nāḍīs* only where its status as a spoiler has already been established.

However, in the case of the *Skanda-vrata*, because it is stated that only the fifth day conjoined with the preceding one is to be accepted, there is no spoilage; thus, the rite must be performed even when the fifth day is pierced by twelve *nāḍīs*.
As for the statement:
"The eleventh, the third, the sixth,
and the thirteenth [lunar days] should be observed even when overlapped by the preceding day, provided they do not exist on the following day."
This statement by Vasiṣṭha does not apply to all deities.

For, since it is impossible for the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhī) to have a decrease exceeding three muhūrtas when the fifth day (pañcamī) of the preceding day is pierced by six muhūrtas, the sixth day must necessarily still possess at least three muhūrtas on the following day; thus, the phrase "if it should not exist" would be untenable.

However, if [the proper time] such as the period for a single-meal vow (*ekabhakta*) or midday (*madhyāhna*) does not exist on the following day, then even that "preceded by the previous day" (*pūrvaviddhā*), which is prohibited everywhere except for the *Skanda-vrata*, must be observed; this is appropriate as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
This is because the scripture concerning the [specific] time (*kāla-śāstra*) is more powerful.

The very same intention is determined for Hemādri as well, who asserts that the piercing [of the sun] at twelve *nāḍīs* and so forth applies to cases other than the *nakta*, *ekabhakta*, and similar observances.
The sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is *Candra-ṣaṣṭhī*; it should be taken as that which extends until moonrise.
Similarly, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the Candra-ṣaṣṭhī vow; the conjunction with the preceding day (pūrva-vedha) is recommended.
When the sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) occurs at moonrise on one day and continues into the forenoon of the following day,
that very day should be observed as a fast with great care during the dark fortnight when the moon rises.
Thus, according to this statement,
the determination of the genitive case is concluded.
Now, the locative case is determined.
And that [tithi], in all cases pertaining to rites for the gods, must be taken as being overlapped by the preceding day,
according to the rule of "the pair" (*yugma-vākya*) which states "the sixth and the seventh.
But the sixth, O dear one, [is joined] with the seventh.
But when they overlap one another,
O best of the twice-born, the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) should be observed as the one that pierces the preceding day.
According to the statement in the Brahma Purāṇa: "The fifth, the seventh, the tenth, the thirteenth, as well as the first and the ninth lunar days, should be observed as 'facing' (sammukhī) tithis."
Thus, from the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "The sixth, the eleventh, the new moon day, and likewise the eighth, when overlapped by the preceding [tithi]," etc. But surely— [this objection follows].
The seventh lunar day that is overlapped by the next is not to be observed as a fast; likewise, these five lunar days [of the dark fortnight] are not to be fasted upon.
Thus, since fasting on a [tithi] overlapped by another is prohibited, let it be that the one overlapped by the preceding [tithi] is to be accepted in that case as well.
Regarding that too:
"The seventh [tithi] should be observed when joined with the sixth, but not when joined with the eighth."
They say that for the worship of Pataṅga here, fasting on the sixth lunar day is required.
From the statement in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O dear one, the seventh lunar day must always be joined with the sixth, [when it falls on] Sunday (pataṅga)."
Wherever the sixth and seventh [notes] are present, there the sun is situated.
And because of this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa, let it be that [the rule] refers specifically to the fast of Saurī (the Sun-goddess).
This is not correct; for [it is said]:
"The seventh is not joined with the eighth, nor is the eighth joined with the seventh."
In all ritual observances, the eighth day is auspicious from that point onward.
This is because the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa* passage prohibits the "paraviddhā" (the tithi overlapping the following day) for all vows;

and since the phrase beginning with "for the worship of Pataṅga" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is logical that the prohibition of the "pūrvaviddhā" (the tithi overlapping the preceding day) applies to all [vows].

However, when the [tithi] begins after sunset on the previous day and, due to the waning of the lunar day (*tithi-kṣaya*), the eighth day is joined by [the seventh] for three *muhūrtas* on the following day such that neither a pure (*śuddhā*) nor a *pūrvaviddhā* eighth day can be obtained;

Then, according to the maxim "But when there is a subordinate element, an improper assumption [of its primary status] is not allowed," since it is improper to abandon the principal in favor of the subordinate, it is logical to adopt the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) that is overlapped by the seventh (saptamī), even if this transgresses the prohibition and even in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement, because it serves as the time for the subordinate rite. Furthermore, the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha should be taken as that which extends into the break of dawn (aruṇodaya).
The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to an eclipse of the sun;
bathing there at the time of dawn is prescribed.

According to this statement, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the worship of the Gaṅgā should be performed; there, the time that extends through midday is to be accepted, following the practice of the learned.
Thus concludes the determination of the seventh lunar day.

Now follows the determination of the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī). Regarding that, for all simple vows (vratas), the bright fortnight (śukla) [tithi] is taken as the later part of the day, while the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa) is taken as the earlier part. As it is said: "The eighth day of the bright fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight..."
One should not observe the [lunar day] overlapped by the previous one; it should be observed when conjoined with the following one.

The eighth day and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight should be observed when they are joined with the preceding lunar day; they should never be observed when joined with the following lunar day.
"This is the eternal law regarding duties such as fasting," according to the statement of the Nigama;
however, during the festival of Śiva-Śakti, all [the rules] are superseded by the supreme (parā).
On the conjunction of the eighth and ninth lunar days, during the period of great energy,
there is a great festival for Śiva and Śakti in the sacred field of Śiva on both fortnights.
Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
"In the case of a fast, however, on both fortnights, the eighth day (Aṣṭamī) should be taken only when conjoined with the following [tithi];
for in a fast, the seventh day (Saptamī), by virtue of its conjunction, destroys the merit of the subsequent day."
This rule for fasting is prescribed for both fortnights.
Thus, because the *Nāradīya* statement prohibits the *saptamī-viddhā* (overlapping with the seventh lunar day) in both fortnights,
as for the mention of fasting (*upavāsa*) in the previously cited *Nigama* statement— "the eighth [day] in the dark fortnight"— that refers specifically to the fast dedicated to Rudra.
In all rites dedicated to Rudra, the lunar day (tithi) should be observed as it faces the following one;
in other ritual procedures, one should fast according to what has been prescribed.
Because of this statement:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight, the sixth day of Skanda, and the fourteenth day of Śivarātri..."
These [fasts] should be observed as joined with the preceding day; the breaking of the fast should take place at the end of the lunar tithi.
In the *Madanaratna*, it is stated that this citation from the *Bṛhan-nārada-purāṇa* refers specifically to the Janmāṣṭamī.
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa is the Dūrvāṣṭamī;
and that [day] should be taken as the earlier one.
The Śrāvaṇī, the Durgā-navamī, the Dūrvā, the Hutāśanī,
the Śivarātri, and the day of Bali should be observed when they overlap with the preceding [tithi].
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhadyama*:
"The lunar day that is the eighth of the bright fortnight occurring in the month of Bhādrapada should be known as Dūrvāṣṭamī; the subsequent [eighth] is not so prescribed."
Thus it is from the *Purāṇasamuccaya*.
As for that which says:
"On the eighth day, during the *rauhiṇa* muhūrta, whether it be the former or the latter [half],"...
That Dūrvāṣṭamī should be observed, avoiding the Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla constellations.
Thus, that statement regarding others should be understood as referring to the conjunction with the *jyeṣṭhā* asterism and so forth on the preceding day;
for the *dūrvā-aṣṭamī* is always to be avoided when conjoined with the *jyeṣṭhā* or *mūla* asterisms.
Likewise:
Durvā grass worshipped under the constellation of Indra (Jyeṣṭhā) destroys one's offspring; it does not fail to do so.
At its root, it takes away the husband’s life; therefore, one should avoid it.
Because of this prohibition,
this [observance] should not be performed during the Sun’s passage through Virgo (kanyārka) nor when the star Agastya rises.
Likewise, the eighth lunar day known as Dūrvā occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
It should be performed only during the sun's transit through Leo, never during its transit through Virgo.
For it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O dear one, when Agastya has risen, one should worship her who was born from the nectar."
She shall endure widowhood and former grief for fifteen years.
And because the fault [of such a view] is stated in that very same place;
herein, the Jyeṣṭhā-vrata is described in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
