The eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kanyā, when it falls under the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, is remembered as Mahatī;
for the sake of warding off misfortune (Alakṣmī), one should worship Jyeṣṭhā on that occasion.
Thus it is said;
and this [day] joined with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā is to be accepted. If such a state occurs on two days, the latter one should be performed.
The eighth day should be observed together with the ninth; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, it should be joined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism.
"On whichever day one should perform the complete worship of Jyeṣṭhā during the night"— so says the Skanda Purāṇa;
and the conjunction with the asterism occurs after midday.
If it occurs before midday, it belongs to the preceding day alone.

On whichever day Jyeṣṭhā occurs, whether after or before midday, the sacrificial food (haviṣya) and worship belong to that day; however, if [the conjunction] is deficient, they belong to the previous day.
Because of this statement,
that which is occasioned by the lunar day (tithi) should be performed on the lunar day alone in the absence of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra),
whereas that which is occasioned by the lunar mansion should be performed on the lunar mansion alone.
The annual vow dedicated to the deity Jyeṣṭhā on the lunar day is prescribed,
as is the Nīlajyeṣṭhā vow performed when the constellation alone is present.
Mādhava states that this Nīlajyeṣṭhā-vrata, as described in the Matsya Purāṇa, is likewise dependent solely upon the lunar day (tithi).
Regarding this, when on the eighth day the day of the Sun (Sunday) and the lunar mansion (Punarvasu) coincide, it is called Nīlajyeṣṭhā; it is rare and its merit lasts for a long time.

Thus, in the statement of Skanda defining its characteristics, because the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) indicated by the locative case in the word "therein" (*tatra*) is understood to be the primary element— just as in the rule "one should offer the *jaya* oblation there" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.4.13)—
Madanaratna and others maintain that this is indeed a lunar-day observance (*nakṣatra-vrata*).
Because the term *nīlajyeṣṭhāpada* refers to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, at the conclusion of the Mahālakṣmī vow, the moonrise-pervading [tithi] is to be taken;
or, whether it is overlapped by the preceding or the following [tithi], that which exists at moonrise is always to be accepted.
Even if it lasts for only three muhūrtas, that [time] is worthy of worship, as it leads to higher rebirths thereafter.
This is because of the statement in the *Saṅgraha*:
"The *ūrdhvaṃgāminī* [tithi] is that which rises with the moon and extends upward for three *muhūrtas*; if it continues beyond that, it is the latter [tithi], otherwise it is the former.
As for that which—
When the sun has entered Virgo, one should not begin the worship of Lakṣmī;
nor should one complete that vow when the sun stands at the edge of the leaf of the Hasta constellation.
This lunar day, free from the four defects, bestows all prosperity.
It is proclaimed that [this yoga] destroys one's sons, good fortune, kingdom, and lifespan;
therefore, with every effort, it should be avoided when the sun is situated in Virgo.
If the ninth day is defiled, it should be especially avoided;
likewise, one should not observe a fast on the eighth day when there is a three-day conjunction or an omitted day (avama).

"The ninth [tithi] joined with the eighth destroys one's sons; when the sun is in Hasta, it destroys oneself"—this statement regarding the prohibition of the ninth tithi joined with the eighth refers to cases where it does not extend for three *muhūrtas* beyond midnight (*ardharātra*).
Furthermore, the prohibition concerning the "three-point contact" (*trispṛk*) and other such conjunctions applies to the initial commencement [of the tithi].
If one were to perform the observance in the midst of the sixteen-year vow already commenced, there would be public censure.
Thus ends the section on Mahālakṣmī-aṣṭamī.
As for Āśvina-śukla-aṣṭamī, it is Durgā-aṣṭamī; and according to the general rules of determination, it should be observed when overlapping with the ninth lunar day (navamī-viddhā).

And although this [Ekādaśī] is indeed considered overlapped by the following day simply by the determination of the general rule, nevertheless, it must not be performed even if it is overlapped by the seventh lunar day (saptamī) to the slightest degree.
And thus:
In the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*: "One who,
out of delusion or even ignorance, observes the Great Aṣṭamī while it is joined with even a trace of the seventh [lunar day], falls into hell."
Where the seventh [tithi] exists by even a fraction and the eighth follows thereafter,
this is declared to be a "thorn" (śalya), which brings about the destruction of sons and grandsons.
The eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh destroys sons, destroys cattle, destroys the kingdom along with its king, and destroys both those born and those yet unborn.
This is because of the prohibition against [a tithi] mixed with the seventh [lunar day].
And as it is said:
"If the eighth [tithi] occurs after the sun has risen on the seventh [day]," [it is not to be observed].
Regarding the statement, "One should perform the Durgā festival there, but not on another day," it refers to starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina—
having worshipped on the eighth day during the dark fortnight while the moon is in Virgo (Kanyā).
On the ninth day, one should awaken the Goddess with the sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Thus, in the Devīpurāṇa, the awakening of the Goddess on the eighth day of the dark fortnight is prescribed; that refers to this specific subject.
And as for the statement:
"On the Bhadrā [tithi], the rite of worship of Bhadrakālī should take place in the middle [of the night]."
Therefore, the wise should observe the eighth day of Durgā as pierced by the seventh lunar day.
Thus it is said;
and as stated in the Madanaratna:
"The bright eighth day (aṣṭamī) of the month of Āśvina brings about auspiciousness."
It should be performed on the seventh lunar day and so forth, but especially with the Mūla constellation.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Nirṇayāmṛta*:
"I am Bhadrā and Bhadrā is I; there is no difference between us at all.
When I am worshipped in the form of Bhadrā, I shall bestow all accomplishments."
Thus says the Devīpurāṇa; likewise, in that very same work:
"O Great King, having abandoned the *viṣṭi* [yoga]," and so forth.
Whoever performs my worship, the full fruit thereof shall not belong to him; by that act, I have been insulted.
By this, it is stated that even [a tithi] pierced by the seventh [lunar day] is to be accepted,
provided there is no eighth [lunar day] in the form of even a fraction (kalā) or a minute (kāṣṭhā) on the following day.
As for that which—
When the sun sets having reached the eighth lunar day,
one should perform the Durgā festival on that very day, and not on the following day.
"One should know that famine will occur in that place where one worships on the ninth day"—
this statement applies when the ninth day exists [only] on the tenth day; that is,
when the ninth day does not exist at sunrise on the following day.
Therefore, O King, one should observe the eighth day together with the seventh.
Thus it is stated in the *Madanaratna* based on a compendium of traditional law (*smṛti*).
In reality, however, based on the *Devīpurāṇa* cited previously, it appears that this refers specifically to the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣāṣṭamī*).
And regarding this, it is stated that one who has sons should not observe a fast;
as it says in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"One who has sons should not perform a fast on the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī)."
In whatever manner possible, one who has purified their self and observes the vow should worship the Goddess.
Thus it is said.
And this [observance], being rooted in the primary source, is declared to be most highly praised in the Skanda Purāṇa within the Hemādri:
"When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, that which is the eighth day of the bright fortnight..."
When conjoined with the Mūla constellation, that day is known as Mahānavamī.
"The Goddess, when worshipped on the ninth day, bestows the desired fruit.
Thus it is said that this [ninth day] should also not be performed when conjoined with the seventh day.
In the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, regarding the festival of Durgā:
"The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) should always be avoided by the wise even if it is conjoined with Mūla;
it is likewise defiled if it is touched by even a fraction of the seventh lunar day (Saptamī)."
Thus ends the determination of Durgāṣṭamī.
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, when joined with a Wednesday, is Mahābhadrā.
As it is said in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, when [it falls] in the month of Puṣya..."
If it should be a Wednesday on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
then that [day] is proclaimed as highly meritorious and "Mahābhadra."
Thus it is said.
This very [lunar day] conjoined with the asterism Bharaṇī is Jayantī.
And so it is stated:
In that very same [text]:
"O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, when it is the auspicious eighth day of the month of Puṣya."
A meritorious constellation is born, which is called "Fierce" (Raudra) in the world.
Then indeed that most meritorious and auspicious Jayantī Aṣṭamī occurred.
Thus:
*raudram* (the fierce) is Bharaṇī because its presiding deity is cruel;
*ārdra* is the Kalpataru (wish-fulfilling tree).
That is not so,
because its conjunction with that [time] is impossible there.
Now, the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī is determined.
Although this [is so],
for it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, when conjoined with the lunar mansion Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī)..."

From the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, which states, "On the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada at midnight," it is understood that [the rite] pertains to both Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.

Nevertheless, for the sake of parsimony in postulating a single source, one should understand that these [rites] are to be observed in Bhādrapada by taking the month as ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsyanta*), and in Śrāvaṇa by taking the month as ending with the new moon (*amāvāsyānta*).

And thus, the statement “In rites pertaining to lunar days (tithi), [the month] begins with the dark fortnight” does not here enjoin that the month of Śrāvaṇa ends with the full moon; rather, it is more parsimonious to assume this refers to matters other than the present one.

As for Bhādrapada, although by the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of Bhādra it would follow that it ends with the new moon—since the burden of assuming a root-scriptural text (mūla-śruti) is not a fault when it serves as a result-oriented purpose—it nevertheless applies to rites on other lunar days due to the statement: “In rites pertaining to lunar days, [the month] begins with the dark fortnight.”
Just as there is recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of the term *tattanmāsapada*, so too here recourse to figurative indication is not a fault.
And that [time] is of two kinds: the pure (*śuddhā*) and the one pierced by the seventh lunar day (*saptamīviddhā*).
Each of these two is further divided into two types, depending on whether it extends beyond sunrise or not.
Even such [an asterism] is of two kinds, distinguished by the presence or absence of conjunction with Rohiṇī;
among these,
there is no doubt that [the prohibition applies] as long as it does not exist at all after sunrise.

Because the eighth day does not exist on the following day; however, when the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas is conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism—whether it be pure or overlapping—it is that very day which is [the one to be observed], provided the conjunction exists on either of those two days.
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, conjoined with the Prājāpatya asterism..."
If it can be observed for even a single moment, that [fast] yields great fruit.

On that day of the eighth lunar tithi when the Rohiṇī asterism occurs, one should observe a fast, for even a single moment of it, when joined with the conjunction, is indeed obtained as a source of great merit.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.

Consequently, Hemādri, Mādhava, and others maintain that if the conjunction with Rohiṇī occurs on the subsequent day alone, the [Ekādaśī] of the previous day—though it may pervade the midnight (*niśītha*) and be "pure" (*śuddhā*)—must be abandoned.
However, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) observe the fast on the former day alone.
Their intention is as follows:

since midnight constitutes the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*) here according to the method to be explained, and because the scripture concerning the time of the ritual is stronger than all others, while that [time] is absent during the *parīdana*, the [observance] must be on the preceding day. Nor should it be argued that it should be on the subsequent day in accordance with the scripture regarding the conjunction with Rohiṇī.

Because it establishes the relationship between qualities and their results, it serves as a definitive authority, much like the treatises on planetary conjunctions such as those concerning Wednesday (Budhavāra) and so forth;
otherwise,
[the statement] "and the state of being a ghost has been destroyed for those who have entered the womb of ghosts by men" would be inconsistent.
By those by whom the eighth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, has been observed;
How much more so on Wednesday, and especially on Monday?

"How much more so, then, the eighth day conjoined with the ninth, which grants liberation even to those of low birth"— according to this statement from the *Padmapurāṇa*, one would have to abandon the eighth day occurring at midnight on the previous day when it is joined with Rohiṇī, and instead perform the subsequent [eighth] day even if it is joined with Wednesday or other such days;
yet this is not an acceptable conclusion.

Since it is understood from the passage beginning “It grants liberation to ten million lineages, how much more so on a Wednesday,” etc., that this serves to establish a relationship between a secondary quality (*guṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*), similar to the case in *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 4.3.8 (adhi. 6), “If one should desire, ‘May Parjanya be rainy,’” the claim made by Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi regarding the determining role of the conjunction with Wednesday and other factors is thereby refuted.
The authors of the *Tithitattva* and others also consider conjunctions with Wednesday and other days to be non-determinative.
And thus:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhas, when conjoined with the constellation Prajāpati..."
Even the statement from the *Viṣṇurahasya*, "It may be obtained even for a moment," should be explained as being intended to establish a connection between the qualities [of the rite] and its fruit.
As for that which—

Regarding the statement in the *Skānda Purāṇa*: "If at sunrise the eighth [lunar day] is present even slightly and the ninth is complete," the mention of "sunrise" (*udaya*) therein refers to the rising of the moon, because it forms a single syntactic unit with another scriptural passage: "likewise at the rising of the Lord of Stars (*tārāpati*).
Nor is it the case that—
Whether by day or by night, if even a fraction of Rohiṇī is not present,
one should perform the rite during the night, especially when it is joined with the Moon.
Based on this statement, one might argue that only when there is an absence of conjunction with Rohiṇī on the following day should the Aṣṭamī joined with the night be accepted.

However, that [statement] merely reiterates the duty to perform the Śuddhāṣṭamī vow as established by logic, even when there is no conjunction with Rohiṇī on that day, however slight; thus, the opinion of the learned is faultless.
Whether Rohiṇī is conjoined on both days or not conjoined at all, the Śuddhādhikā [Aṣṭamī] occurring on the earlier day is to be taken, because there is no reason to bypass it.
In the case of an overlapping [tithi], however, it is that very same day on which Rohiṇī is joined at midnight; this is because of the excellence of the conjunction with Rohiṇī.
Regarding the conjunction in the former case:
"If Rohiṇī is present at midnight on the eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh..."
That meritorious eighth day shall endure as long as the moon and the sun.
Thus, according to the Vahni Purāṇa, which serves as an exception to the prohibition of the eighth lunar day being joined with the seventh as will be stated hereafter:
"If Rohiṇī is conjoined with the night (niśītha) on both days, then the latter [day] alone [is valid];
however, the eighth lunar day joined with the seventh must be carefully avoided."
Even when accompanied by a lunar mansion, the eighth day joined with the seventh should not be observed.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*,

for this very reason, when there is an overlap (*viddhā*) on both days, if the conjunction with Rohiṇī occurs after midnight on both days, or if it occurs at midnight on the eighth day alone while being absent on the other, then the latter [day] is preferred. If the conjunction exists on only one of the two days, that very day is the one to be observed.
In every case, this same principle is to be observed regarding the eighth day when it is devoid of conjunction with Rohiṇī, whether at midnight or during the existence of either of the two days.
And it is not the case that:
"If the asterism of Rohiṇī is not obtained, the eighth day that is passing into its setting should be performed."
Having observed the fast there, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place at the end of the lunar day.

Thus, it should not be argued that based on the statement from the *Viṣṇurahasya* cited by Gauḍa, "if Rohiṇī is not obtained, the preceding [lunar day] alone must always be taken," because this statement is rootless, as it has not been recorded by Hemādri and others; or, even if it were rooted, it would refer to a case where there is no conjunction with Rohiṇī at midnight on the following day.
In this matter, two things are primary: worship at midnight and fasting.
When the eighth day of the dark fortnight coincides with the Rohiṇī asterism at midnight, worship of Śauri on that occasion destroys the sins accumulated over three lifetimes.
Thus, from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* and from the previously cited statement, "That [fast] should be observed, for it yields great fruit":
one should worship the God three times a day, especially during the day and night,
and likewise at midnight with various kinds of flowers.
Thus, the worship mentioned in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* is merely an ancillary (*aṅga*) [to the fast], because it lacks a connection to a separate fruit.

Nor should it be argued that, since there is a difference in the fruits of worship and fasting—even if they were to have the same fruit—the two would be enjoined independently, leading to the contingency of performing each one separately, as in the case of the *Citra* and *Udbhid* sacrifices. For it is said: "Having performed the worship of Hari while observing the fast, one does not suffer therein."

Thus, from the statement regarding the future (*bhaviṣyavacana*), a combination (*samuccaya*) is understood, as in the injunction: “One should offer the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) for twelve nights,” which is like the case of the *ādhāna* and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices.
Furthermore, according to the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, because of the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*), this rite is purely optional (*kāmya*).
[The time is: the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) in the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), conjoined with a lunar mansion belonging to Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) and falling on a dark fortnight.
It should be performed every year for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus.

Thus, because the repetition (*vīpsā*) is heard, the necessity [of the injunction] is established. Nor should it be argued that, since the fruit is heard here as "for the sake of contentment" (*tuṣṭyartha*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by two distinct purposes— the fruit and the motive—
or that there would be a syntactical split caused by two distinct objects of reference (*uddeśya*) belonging to different classes.
For that [cause], which consists in having multiple objects of different classes, is not a defect.
Nor should it be argued that, if this were obligatory, there would be scriptural injunctions for expiation (prāyaścitta) in the event of its non-performance;
for even though no specific [expiation] is mentioned, one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) must be performed for the removal of all sins.
Since this and other such [scriptural passages] are heard in general terms, they apply here as well; thus, [the conclusion] is faultless.
This concludes the determination of Janmāṣṭamī.
Now follows the determination of its ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
In that case, regarding the fast of the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) alone, if the eighth day continues on the day of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*), the rite should be performed at its conclusion.
As stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *Jayantī* and *Śivarātri* should be observed when they are conjoined with the *bhadrā* [lunar] period."
Having observed the fast until the end of the lunar day, one should likewise perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
Thus [it is said].
Here, the word *jayantī* refers specifically to the eighth lunar day of birth (*janmāṣṭamī*), because the rule for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) is prescribed at the end of the lunar day alone.

However, when the fast is observed on the eighth day conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, if both [the lunar day and the asterism] persist until the time of breaking the fast, then it should be performed at the end of both.
The eighth lunar day, when conjoined with Rohiṇī, should be observed as pierced by the seventh;
one should perform the ritual vigil on that day, and the breaking of the fast at the end of the lunar day.
Thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Furthermore, this breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) at the end of both [the lunar days] occurs before midnight, provided that the time sufficient for a meal is obtained at the end of both;
one should not perform the breaking of the fast at night, except in the case of the *Rohiṇī* vow.
In this case, one may perform it even at night, avoiding only the middle of the night (mahāniśā).
Thus, from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* cited in the Gauda compendiums:
"The *mahāniśā* (midnight) is the one-hour portion of the night occurring after the [first] three-and-a-half *yāmas*.
Indeed, the *mahāniśā* should be known as the middle [point] between the two middle *yāmas*."
According to this traditional teaching (smṛti), the Rohiṇī-vrata here is indeed the Aṣṭamī-vrata mentioned therein, due to the context.
And thus:
"In all fasts, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is prescribed during the day."
Otherwise, there would be a loss of merit, except for the maintenance and breaking of the fast.

The arrival of another guest at night is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), while during the day it is of the nature of light (taijasa). One should perform the breaking of the fast during the dark period; otherwise, one would attain a dark state.

Thus, the prohibition against breaking the fast at night found in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* and other texts refers to occasions other than the *Janmāṣṭamī*. However, when neither end [of the lunar day] is obtainable at such a time, then it should be performed even at the end of either one. As it is said: "O Bhārata, the breaking of the fast is recommended at the end of the asterism or at the end of the lunar day."
Thus, concerning the Janmāṣṭamī, from the Vahnipurāṇa:
"But when a time sufficient for the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) is not obtained prior to the great night (mahāniśā), then one should perform it even at that [time].
When there is an overlap of the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (nakṣatra), or even until the end of the asterism..."
Or one may perform the breaking of the fast even at midnight on the following day.
Thus, according to the statement cited by Hemādri:
"At midnight" means during the *mahāniśā* (the dead of night);
for it is appropriate that this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition of eating at that very time.
The phrase "until the end of the lunar mansion" (*nakṣatrāntam*) is also an elliptical expression for "until the end of the lunar day" (*tithyanta*).

However, the Gauḍas, having read the text as "one should perform it at midnight" (*ardharātreṇa tat kuryāt*), say that if the end of either [the lunar day or the lunar mansion] occurs at midnight, then the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should not take place at midnight, but rather during the day itself;
for they argue that this preserves the syntactic unity of the exclusion [rule], namely, "having avoided the dead of night" (*varjayitvā mahāniśām*).

As for the statement in the *Kālādarśa*: "The observer of the vow should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) either at the end of the lunar day (*tithi*) or at the end of the festival," that refers to one who is incapable [of observing the stricter rule], according to the *Madanaratna*.

Hemādri, however, states that breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) at the end of both [the lunar fortnight and the festival] pertains to those who are capable; for one who is incapable, it is at the end of either one; and for one even more incapable than that, it is at the end of the festival.

Thus [ends the section from] the illustrious *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrīmad Hemādri—who is the sun causing the blooming of the lotus-heart of the earth encircled by the four oceans, the son of Śrīman Mahārāja Madhukara Sāha, the grandson of Śrīman Mahārājādhirāja Pratāparudra, whose lotus-feet are honored by the clusters of rays from the crest-jewels of the entire circle of subordinate vassals.

In the *Samayaprakāśa* section of the *Vīramitrodaya* treatise composed by the illustrious Mitramiśra—who was commissioned by the glorious Mahārājādhirāja Vīrasiṃhadeva; who is the son of Śrī Haṃsapāṇḍita and the grandson of Śrī Paraśurāmamiśra; who is the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of all sciences; who is a lion to the great elephant of universal poverty; and who is the life-giver to learned men—concludes the determination of Janmāṣṭamī.
Now, the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) is determined.
That [eighth day] should be taken when conjoined with the seventh;
for there is the statement regarding pairs: "the Vasus and the Randhras.
Also, in the Padma Purāṇa:
The eighth lunar day pierced by the ninth, or the eighth joined with the ninth,
is like Umā-Maheśvara— resembling the Lord who is half-woman and half-man.
Thus it is said;
and also in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, in the Dvādaśī-kalpa: "The eighth [tithi] should be observed together with the ninth, and likewise the ninth [with the eighth]."
"Likewise" means together with the eighth day.
Even by way of prohibition, the fact that the ninth day is pierced by the eighth has been stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* and other texts:
"O dear one, the ninth day should not be observed [if it is thus pierced]."
"But on the tenth [lunar day] it may sometimes be so," according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*;
"when the ninth and the eleventh are pierced by the [preceding and following] directions."
Then it must be especially avoided, just as the water of the Gaṅgā is avoided by one who drinks liquor.
Thus says the Padma Purāṇa.
The tenth lunar day (daśamī) is the direction;
both the rule regarding the contamination (vedha) of the eighth by the ninth and the prohibition of the contamination of the tenth are shown in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa].
The eighth [lunar day] pierced by the ninth should be observed by those desiring the fruit;
one should never, O dear one, perform the ninth when it is pierced by the tenth.
Thus [it is said].

Now, even if the ninth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-navamī*) is pierced by the eighth day (*aṣṭamī-viddhā*), let the ninth day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa-navamī*) be pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī-viddhā*). For it is said: "In the bright fortnight, that lunar day (*tithi*) is to be accepted upon which the sun has risen."
If it is argued that this is on the strength of such scriptural statements, we say no;
for in the previously cited statements, the performance of dharma on the new moon day is explicitly prohibited.
Now, if it is argued that since the aforementioned prohibition is general in nature—applying equally to both the dark and light fortnights—it may be restricted to the dark fortnight, do not say so.

Even the restriction you mentioned—that "the lunar day (tithi) in the bright fortnight is to be accepted"—is itself merely a general rule; therefore, it is established that the ninth day (navamī) of both fortnights is indeed to be taken as joined with the preceding day (pūrvaviddhā).
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra is Rāmanavamī, and it should be accepted when it extends across midday.
When the sun has entered Aries (Meṣa) and the ascendant is called Cancer (Karkaṭaka):
The Supreme Person appeared through a portion of himself in Kausalyā.
This is because, according to the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*, midday (*madhyāhna*) is the time of birth;
and because, on the *jayantī* days, the very time of birth constitutes the ritual time for the act of worship,
as is observed in the case of the *janmāṣṭamī* and other such occasions.
That very midday conjunction is said to be exceedingly meritorious if it is joined with the asterism Punarvasu;
as stated in that same [text]:
"If the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra is joined with Punarvasu..."
That very [time], through the yoga of midday, becomes most supremely meritorious.
Thus,

if that Rāmanavamī touches the midday [meridian] on both days, or does not touch the midday on both days, or touches only a portion of the midday on both days, then it should be accepted as being joined with the Punarvasu nakṣatra.
If even a slight conjunction with the Punarvasu constellation is observed on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that day is meritorious and grants all desires.
According to this statement from the *Agastyasaṃhitā*,
when such a conjunction with Punarvasu occurs on both days, then that [conjunction] which takes place at midday should be accepted;
for the conjunction with a lunar mansion at the time of birth is as praiseworthy as the conjunction with Rohiṇī.
When the conjunction with Punarvasu occurs at midday on both days, or when it occurs at midday on both days after having passed midday, then too the later [tithi] alone is taken.
When it occurs at midday on both days, or having passed midday on both days, and the conjunction with Punarvasu likewise occurs only after passing midday, then too the later alone is taken.

When it is conjoined with midday on both days, not conjoined with midday on both days, or conjoined with only a portion of midday on both days—or when there is no conjunction with Punarvasu at all on either day—then in every such case, the later alone is taken.
But when the [nakṣatra] occurs at midday on the following day, even if it is joined with the [proper] asterism on the preceding day, then the following day alone is [the valid one]. However,
when it occurs at midday on the preceding day and there is again a conjunction with Punarvasu on the following day, then the following day alone is [the valid one],
because in every case an eighth-day overlapping [tithi] is prohibited.
The ninth [tithi] overlapping with the eighth should be avoided by those devoted to Viṣṇu;
the fast should be observed on the ninth, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the tenth.
This is because of the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*.
Furthermore, regarding these clearly stated positions, one should not suspect excessive redundancy.
On this point, some say as follows:
"The ninth [lunar day], when pierced by the eighth, should be avoided by those devoted to Viṣṇu.
Regarding this, for the Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to Viṣṇu, the ninth day pierced by the eighth is not to be observed as a fast; rather, that which is pierced by the tenth is to be observed.
However, they believe that for those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, even the ninth day pierced by the eighth may be observed as a fast.
That is incorrect.

Since that qualification can be justified as being intended to provide instruction that "all this must be performed by those who are devoted to Viṣṇu," it is inappropriate to accept it as a qualification of the agent that would result in the prohibition of the *aṣṭamī-viddhā* (the overlapping eighth lunar day) for non-Vaiṣṇavas.

In reality, however, because the word "Viṣṇu" refers to Viṣṇu in the form of Rāma under discussion, the term "devoted to" (*parāyaṇaiḥ*) refers to those initiated into His mantras; furthermore, this is heard even in the injunction regarding the possession of qualities (*saṅguṇa-vidhi*).

Regarding the statement, "On that day, the vow of fasting must always be observed," because the word "always" (sadā) implies a requirement for a temporal limit within its constant application, it connects with the present context. Consequently, due to the use of the word "always," the permanence implied therein applies to this vow specifically for those who have received initiation into the Rāma-mantra.
Indeed— it is said:
"When the day of Śrī Rāmanavamī has arrived, a mortal of deluded intellect who does not observe the fast is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells."
If one performs other vows without first observing the Rāmanavamī vow, which is the supreme among all vows,
one shall not partake in the fruit of those [other] vows.

If it is asked: "Why is this [obligation] not directed toward everyone, given that in such passages there is a presentation of the fault incurred by non-performance, and given that in the statements indicating its obligatory nature one hears general terms such as ‘mortal’?"—do not say so.

For that obligatory nature is indeed directed only toward those initiated into the Rāma-mantra, as indicated by the phrases "by those devoted to Viṣṇu" and "on that day it must be performed," and not toward everyone.
Even in the world, many cultured people (śiṣṭas) are observed who, being devoid of initiation into the Rāma-mantra, do not fast on the Rāmanavamī.
Whatever fruit is obtained by performing great gifts repeatedly at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, that one attains from the vow of Śrī Rāmanavamī.
The optional (kāmya) performance prescribed by such statements as these, however, applies to all [qualified persons].

If it is argued: "Just as the phrase 'by those devoted to Viṣṇu' has a connection with the injunction for the obligatory (nitya) entitlement, so too let there be a connection with the injunction for the optional entitlement," we say: no. This is because the optional performance is prohibited on a fragmented lunar day (khaṇḍatithi), and the statements defining the determination of fragmented lunar days serve solely as supplements to the injunction for the obligatory performance.
This is because the phrase "by those devoted to Viṣṇu," which is contained within that [text], is appropriately construed only with the word "constant" (*nitya*).

Here, as for the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*): when the fast is observed on a day joined with the previous tithi, then the breaking of the fast must be performed only after passing the ninth lunar day (*navamī*), both because of a general statement and because of a specific statement that "the breaking of the fast is on the tenth day itself.
Furthermore, there is no possibility whatsoever here of breaking the fast at night or the like.
Thus concludes the determination of Rāmanavamī.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is Durgānavamī; it is also known as Mahānavamī.
And so it is said:
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"The eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, when conjoined with the Mūla asterism, is known as Mahānavamī; it is exceedingly rare even throughout the three worlds."
Thus;
the mention of the "root" (mūla) is an elliptical indication. Regarding the worship of Durgā, it is stated in that very same [text]:
In the Durgā-pūjās, the ninth lunar day conjoined with the three asterisms beginning with Mūla is proclaimed as "Mahatī" (the Great); on that day, one should worship Durgā, the crusher of Mahiṣa.
And this [day] must be taken as the one pierced by the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) in the case of fasting and similar observances.
Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
The Śrāvaṇī, Durgā-navamī, Dūrvā, and Hutāśanī should be observed when joined with the preceding lunar day; the same applies to Śivarātri and the day of Bali.
Thus it is said:
"O dear one, one should never perform [the rite] on the ninth day, nor ever on the tenth."
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the offering of the bali-oblation, the ninth lunar day (navamī) associated with sunrise should be taken;
if the [following] tithi is empty (riktā) at sunrise, the [preceding] one shall be full (pūrṇā)."
In that place, the offering of the bali-oblation should be performed, which brings about auspiciousness.
"O King, if an animal sacrifice is performed on the eighth lunar day, there will be the ruin of one's sons"—
thus it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa. Furthermore, regarding that same [text]:
If even a single muhūrta or a mere kalā of the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja occurs, that entire day should be known as Dīkṣā by those seeking fortune, knowledge, and victory.
Thus ends the Saura Purāṇa;
that too is solely concerned with the offering of the bali sacrifice.
Furthermore, as for what was said...
On the ninth day, the offering of the bali is recommended during the afternoon;
one should avoid the tenth day in this regard—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the *Madanaratna*, it is stated that the words of Nārada refer to the prohibition of those [days] exceeding the pure [period]. Enough of this digression;
the detailed exposition is to be found in the *Navarātranirṇaya*.
Thus concludes the determination of the ninth lunar day (navamī). Now the tenth lunar day (daśamī) is determined;
regarding that day, there is no statement concerning the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, as there is for other lunar days.

For regarding other lunar days (*tithi*), in some cases the one overlapping with the previous day is to be accepted, while in others the one overlapping with the following day is to be accepted; however, in the case of the tenth day (*daśamī*), there is no such restrictive statement.
Therefore, when the tenth day extends across both days and covers the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*), it may be accepted as either the preceding or the succeeding one according to one's preference.
"A complete tenth day should be accepted, whether it is the later or the earlier."
Because that lunar day is joined [with the asterism] and not defiled, it is "facing in all directions" (sarvatomukhī).
Thus, according to the Skanda Purāṇa, [the tithi] is complete at the time of the ritual performance because no specific rule is heard; therefore, it applies to both days.
In other cases, however, the earlier [tithi] is taken.
"And the tenth [lunar day] itself must be observed as being accompanied by Durgā, O best of the twice-born," because it is stated thus in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
"Accompanied by Durgā" (*sadurgā*) means overlapped by the ninth [lunar day]. Now, one might object:
If it is argued: "Since the rule 'The full tenth day is to be taken,

whether by the following [eleventh] or the preceding [ninth]' results in a lack of settled determination, and since that [lack of determination] culminates in an option which is corrupted by eight defects, and because the mere proliferation of personal whim is improper,
one must certainly rely upon some authoritative scripture (*śāstra*) as a regulator"— this is true.
In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun has not yet risen is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun has set is to be taken.
Thus, the established rule has indeed been stated by Mārkaṇḍeya;
therefore, there is no independent expansion of human will at all.
For this very reason, it has been stated by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"But when the meaning of the scripture is indifferent, human desire is the regulator.
This being the case, those [texts] which prohibit [fasting] on a day overlapped by another tithi—
The Nandā-viddhā, the full-moon twelfth day (dvādaśī) in Capricorn during the bright fortnight,
and that which has lost its moonlight due to Venus— these are indeed remembered as fruitless.
Thus it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Pūrṇā" refers to the tenth lunar day (daśamī), and "Nandā" refers to the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī); it is understood that [the fast] on a day pierced by these is fruitless.
The fifth lunar day that begins on the new moon, the Bhūta-Sāvitrī, the full moon of Vaṭa,
and likewise the ninth and tenth days, are not to be observed as fasts when they are joined with the following day.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:

"The sixth lunar day pierced by the Nāga (the fifth), the seventh pierced by Śiva (the sixth), and the tenth pierced by the eleventh (the ninth) should never be observed as fast days under any circumstances."

Thus, the statements found in the *Śivarahasya*, the *Saura Purāṇa*, and other texts refer exclusively to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) and do not concern the bright fortnight (*vyāpti* and so forth).
In this context, it is appropriate to understand the mention of fasting as primarily indicative of all religious rites; this is the summary.
Thus concludes the general determination regarding the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*).
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha is called Daśaharā;
for on that tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, on a Tuesday and under the constellation Hasta,
this pure river descended from heaven.
It removes ten sins; therefore, it is known as Daśaharā.
And the ten sins have been declared by Manu as follows:
harshness, falsehood, and also calumny in every respect;
And incoherent chatter; thus, that which consists of speech is fourfold.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules,
and adultery— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— these are the three types of mental action.
Thus, from the Skanda Purāṇa. Regarding this, a specific yoga is described in that very same work:
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the tenth lunar day, when the moon is in conjunction with Mercury and the asterism Hasta,
under the Garānanda yoga and the Vyatīpāta karana, with the Moon in Virgo and the Sun in Taurus.
Having bathed during the ten-fold conjunction (*daśayoga*), a person is liberated from all sins.
And in this regard, that [conjunction] alone should be accepted in which there is an abundance of yogas. The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is Vijayā-daśamī.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Purāṇasamuccaya*:
"On the tenth day, Aparājitā should be properly worshipped by men,
having taken recourse to the northeastern direction (īśānī) with effort during the afternoon."

And if this very [Ekādaśī] is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism during the latter part [of the day], then that alone is to be accepted. "If on the day of rising there is a slight [presence of] the tenth [tithi] and the Ekādaśī is complete,
when at the time of [the conjunction] it is in the Śravaṇa asterism, that lunar day is named Vijayā."
Thus it is stated by Kaśyapa. In other cases, the [tithi] joined with the ninth day (navamī) should be accepted.
Aparājitā is to be worshipped on that full [lunar day] which is joined with the ninth day.
Thus, from the *Purāṇasamuccaya*.
This concludes the determination of the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*).
Now, the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) is determined.
And that [Ekādaśī] must be accepted as conjoined with the next day in all ritual activities, according to the *Yugma-vākya*: "The twelfth [day] joined with the eleventh.
O Lord, the Ekādaśī joined with the tenth day should not be observed.
Those who desire dharma, pleasure, and wealth should not observe the third, sixth, eighth, eleventh, or fourteenth lunar days when they are overlapped by the preceding day.

Thus, because of the prohibition of the *pūrvaviddhā* (the Ekādaśī overlapping with the previous day) in both the *Skanda Purāṇa* and the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, for the worship of Vāstu performed by Vaiśyas on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, that which extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) should be accepted. For it is said therein: "And at that afternoon, Vāstu is the sustainer of the lineage of the Vaiśyas."
He is to be honored with water-offerings, garlands, garments, and various colorful ornaments.

Thus, with reference to her, it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa* that the rites such as the "Sleeping of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuśayana*) and others should be performed starting from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
In that regard—
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Blessed Lord Hari always lies upon his serpent-bed in the Ocean of Milk."
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, one endowed with faith and devotion should awaken Keśava, who has been asleep, during the night.
Also in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight,
the gift of a waistband to Viṣṇu shall be the destroyer of great sins."
*Kaṭidāna* means the turning over of the limbs.
However, in the *Varāhapurāṇa* and other texts, the rites of lying down (*śayana*) and so forth are prescribed for the twelfth days (*dvādaśī*) of the bright fortnight during these very months:
"In the month of Āṣāḍha, on the twelfth day, [this rite] is auspicious and brings about all peace."
Whoever, having understood this according to the prescribed rule, should cause my ritual action to be performed;
That man shall not perish throughout the cycles of worldly existence, age after age;
and likewise, O King, this is the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī).
This was fashioned by me, who lie upon Śeṣa, for the sake of awakening all people and for their welfare.
Likewise, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa as cited by Hemādri:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, however, there are the festivals of the falling asleep and the turning over [of the deity]."
Furthermore, the claim made by some that the word "twelfth" (*dvādaśī*) here refers to the "eleventh" (*ekādaśī*) is not tenable;
for there is no evidence for such a meaning, and it would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
It has been stated that the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is the prescribed date for the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) to the Lord of Wealth (*Dhanada*).
The second lunar day (tithi) is remembered as the most excellent among all days, belonging to the goddess Śrī.
The third should be for Bhavānī, the fourth for her son,
the fifth for Dharmarāja, and likewise the sixth for Guha.
The seventh is declared for Bhāskara; the eighth is remembered for Durgā;
the ninth is for the Mothers (Mātṛs); and the tenth is remembered for Vāsuki.
The eleventh day is for the sages, the twelfth for the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu),
the thirteenth for Anaṅga (Kāma), and the fourteenth is said to be for Śiva.
O best of jewels, the full-moon day (pauṇamāsī) is prescribed for me;
and for whichever deity there is a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and a particular lunar day (tithi), [those are prescribed for them].
Furthermore, this would result in a contradiction with the statement in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The turning over on the bed and so forth of that deity [should take place] at that time.
Therefore, the prescription of a different time is indeed more appropriate.
In some places, however, the sleeping and waking [of the deity] are said to occur on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika respectively.
And so says Yama:
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Hari reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch in the Ocean of Milk;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, he abandons sleep. One should always worship Him during these two occasions.
It swiftly dispels sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
here, the full moon days of Āṣāḍhī and Kārttikī are intended,
because the practice is most abundant on those very occasions.
At the end of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana enters his own illusory power, yogic sleep, upon the body of the serpent Śeṣa.
He remains asleep for four months until the month of Kārttika arrives;
at that time, distinguished rites such as sacrifices and the like do not proceed.
This is because it is explicitly stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* that "at the end of the fortnight" (*pakṣānte*).
By this, the interpretation of the *Kalpataru*—that "this [day] of Āṣāḍha is the Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī" and "this [day] of Kārttika is the Kārttikī Ekādaśī"—is refuted.
Consequently, it is established that the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) is also a single [valid] time for the rite.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, however, the sleeping and waking [of Viṣṇu] are said to occur over a period of five days beginning from the eleventh day:
"On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Janārdana [is placed to sleep];
and likewise the gods, the sages, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases."
Having gone there, they constantly offer hymns of praise for five days and hold a festival filled with song and dance.
Then, for four months, they attend upon his yogic sleep;
and the sages equal to Brahmā attend upon him as he sleeps.
During those same five days of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the inhabitants of heaven, including Indra, go there and awaken the Lord of Gods.
Therefore, one should act accordingly and likewise hold a great festival at that time as well.
Furthermore, the statement of some that there is no sleeping or waking here, but rather worship for four days starting from Ekādaśī itself, is not tenable;

for from the passages “then for four months” and “they awaken the Lord of Gods,” it is understood that those two [sleeping and waking] are to be performed immediately after the festival accomplished over five days.
Therefore, it is logical that this too constitutes a distinct period of time.

These periods are established according to one's capacity and in accordance with tradition. Furthermore, these cycles of sleep, turning over, and awakening should be performed during the nights, the twilights, and the days.
"Sleeping at night, rising during the day, and changing position at the twilights"— so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
Viṣṇu does not sleep by day, nor does he awaken at night.
Thus it is from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

And so, the statement in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, "One should awaken [the deity] while it is asleep at night," must be explained as being in syntactic agreement with the statement of the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*: "One should awaken [it] during the day when it has been asleep at night."
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of [inappropriate] conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Moreover, in relation to that [negation], it is appropriate that the property of the word (*padadharma*), namely its very presence (*sannidhāna*), should be sublated;

for otherwise, if the property of the word were not sublated by virtue of that [negation], it would follow that the word itself is even less sublated, which would result in the total abolition of *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation).
Some, however, out of a lack of confidence in the statement "sleep at night," practice waking [the deity] even during the night;
but that is improper, as such a statement is not supported by Hemādri or any other authoritative compendium (*nibandha*).

In this context, when Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and Revatī arise respectively in the initial, middle, and final portions of the night on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), the sleeping, turning over, and waking [of the deity] are considered most auspicious.
And so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*:
"In the first quarter of the month of Maitra (Vaiśākha), Viṣṇu sleeps here; and in the middle of the Śruti (Jyeṣṭha), he turns over."
And at the conclusion of the month of Pauṣa, the slayer of the enemies of the gods awakens after four months.
O King, during the months beginning with Ābhākha, and in the month of Mādhava,
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, the festivals of the falling asleep and the awakening [of Viṣṇu] are celebrated.

When, during the portions of the night and so forth on the twelfth day, there is no conjunction with the specific portions of the respective constellations, but rather a conjunction with the constellation as a whole, then the sleeping and other rites should be performed precisely during those portions of the night and so forth when there is a conjunction with the constellation alone;
for it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa: "When there is no conjunction by quarter (pāda), it may occur even through the constellation itself."
Viṣṇu does not sleep during the day, nor does he awaken at night;
when there is a conjunction with the asterism on the twelfth lunar day, the conjunction of the lunar mansion's quarter is not a cause for concern.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.

When, during the portions of the night and so forth on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), there is not even the presence of a single lunar mansion (nakṣatra), then the sleeping and other rites should be performed on that very twelfth day at the time of twilight (saṃdhyā).
And so it is said:

In the Varāha Purāṇa: "At the time of the junction on the twelfth lunar day, when the [required] constellations are not present, the rites of lying down, turning over, and so forth are to be performed during the dark and bright fortnights."
"At the time of junction" (sandhisamaye) connects with "lying down" and so forth;
"time of junction" (sandhisamayaḥ) means the period of twilight (sandhyākālaḥ).
This meaning is also accepted by Hemādri and others.
Thus ends the period for Viṣṇu’s sleep.
On this very Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the commencement of the Cāturmāsya vow is prescribed in the Mahābhārata:
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, a man who has fasted and is self-restrained should perform the Cāturmāsya vow, whatever it may be.
Even if it is impossible [to perform it on that day], it should be performed with great effort even on the day of the Sun in Libra (tulārka).
Now, the vow of Ekādaśī is determined.
Regarding that—

In statements such as from the Nāradīya Purāṇa, "On every fortnight, one should perform fasting on the eleventh day," where the hearing of the term *upavāsa* (fasting) occurs, there the vow (*saṅkalpa*) of not eating for eight watches (*aṣṭayāmika*) is enjoined;
for it is accepted that the word *upavāsa*, which is a synonym for a specific type of religious observance (*vrata*), denotes the act of making a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
However, there are sentences joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) that are used in conjunction with terms such as "vow" (*vrata*), "restriction" (*niyama*), and "duty" (*dharma*), for example:
"One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights; this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics."
In such cases as well, just as in the injunction “one should not look at the rising sun,” it is the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) itself that is enjoined by means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for the censure of eating found there, according to the maxim “censure does not function to censure,” it is intended as praise for the vow (*vrata*), and does not imply an independent prohibition due to the resulting prolixity (*gaurava*).
One should not drink water from a conch shell, nor eat a tortoise or a pig.
One should not eat on the eleventh day of both fortnights.

In passages such as these, however, because they occur in a context primarily concerned with prohibitions and because there is no co-occurrence with words such as *vrata* (vow), the prohibition refers specifically to eating.

This is because there is no evidence for a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) therein. Nor can it be argued that such a resolve must be assumed for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*) by positing a single underlying basis [for both cases].
Because that [eating] occurs at a subsequent time;

otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati* section (*Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra* 6.1.51–52). In this context, what is prohibited is merely the practice of eating as established by tradition and worldly custom, and not the cessation of all eating whatsoever.

Therefore, when for a householder both the vow and the prohibition of eating apply on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇaikādaśī) and so forth, there is the injunction to consume something at least, as stated:
"But when fasting is prohibited, one should provide some small amount of food. This is the rule regarding the consumption of something.
Nor should it be argued that the eating [of meat] must be understood as being restricted solely to what is eaten for the sake of sustenance, based on the impossibility of this injunction otherwise;
for this statement has its purpose in excluding fasting performed out of passion, hatred, and so forth.
And this prohibition is indeed obligatory (nitya), according to the principle of the section concerning the prohibition of eating *kalañja*.
And this [prohibition] applies to all, both in the dark and the bright fortnights,
for any mortal over eight years of age who has not yet reached eighty,
who, being a doer of evil, eats on the day of Viṣṇu within my kingdom.
He shall be censured by me, punished by me, and banished from the country by me.
Thus, according to the statement of Nārada:
"A householder, a student, and likewise one who has established the sacred fires,
shall not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight."

This is also from the Agni Purāṇa. Here, some maintain that the mention of "eight years" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and the mention of "eighty" is an indicative mark for one's capacity (*śakti*).
That is not so,
because there is a lack of valid evidence;
nor is it the case that—
A householder who wanders about and practices austerity while fasting would become one who has violated his vow through the neglect of the Prāṇāgnihotra.
It should not be said that there is a contradiction in this statement; for it says:
"By eating once a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for..."
And by a single fast, the pādakṛcchra is proclaimed.

This [statement] is intended to preclude the repetition of the fastings obtained through the rule of "expansion in their own place" (*svasthānavivṛddhi*), for the purpose of achieving the threefold nature in the performance of the *prājāpatya* penance prescribed by rules such as "this is tripled is the *prājāpatya*.

For this very reason, in the expression "he should perform austerity while not eating," the present-tense suffix (*vartamānakālapratyaya*) has the sense of practicing non-eating for as long as the austerity is being performed.
The statement, "By the omission of the Prāṇāgnihotra," is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), like the passage, "For by that food is prepared.

That which is called the Prāṇāgnihotra is a specific rule based on eating, enjoined as obligatory, in accordance with the injunction: "Whatever food may first arrive, that is to be offered as an oblation."
Furthermore, its omission does not constitute a fault when there is an absence of food that serves as the physical basis [for life]; therefore, it is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).
Hemādri, however, says that this statement is intended to prevent the ascetic practice of fasting unto death for the celibate student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*).
As for what was also said—
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the religious student—these three attain perfection only while eating; for them, there is no perfection for those who do not eat.

This statement of the Sāṅkhyāyana is intended to prevent the suspension of Vedic study, the Agnihotra, and other such duties that would otherwise result from the absence of food due to lack of strength;
for there is a declaration made as a reason: "There is no accomplishment of these [rites] for those who do not eat.
Since the Agnihotra and similar rites are based on Śruti (Veda), it is appropriate that they take precedence over and override the Smārta (traditional) prohibition of eating.
Thus, the injunction for obligatory fasting proceeds without contradicting the *agnihotra* and other such rites.

However, an optional rite—even if Vedic (*śrauta*)—is indeed a sublater of even the obligatory *agnihotra* and so forth, because, in consideration of the relative strength of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the relative strength of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) takes precedence.
Furthermore, the cessation of an optional Smṛti rite by an optional Vedic rite is precisely what is intended, owing to the greater force of its Vedic character.
By this, the claim made by some—that obligatory (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*) Smārta fasts are superseded by Śrauta rites such as the Agnihotra—is refuted. Enough of this digression;
therefore, in both interpretations of the prohibition, all persons possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*).
Regarding the vow, however, for those other than householders, there is entitlement during both fortnights when it is performed as a regular practice;
but for a householder, it applies only during the bright fortnight. One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
This is the duty of the forest-dwelling ascetic; the householder, however, should always take [the vow] on the bright fortnight alone.
Thus it is stated by Devala:
"On the eleventh day of both fortnights, one should not eat;
the celibate student, the woman, and the householder should always [abstain] from the bright fortnight alone."
And as it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Just as the bright [twelfth day], so too the dark twelfth day is always dear to me. The bright one should be observed by householders, for it increases enjoyments and progeny."
"Likewise, Kṛṣṇā was pointed out in various ways by those seeking liberation," according to the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
As for those [verses] which—

Some maintain that general statements such as "as is the bright fortnight, so is the dark; there is no difference whatsoever" must be restricted in their application to those other than householders. Thus, since fasting is not established for the householder by virtue of these general statements, the injunction for the householder to fast specifically during the bright fortnight is derived from the rule: "The householder should always observe the bright [fortnight]."

Others, however, maintain that—due to the restriction by the particle *eva* (just as in the case of *A. 9, Pā. 4, Adh. 2*: "One should not say 'thirty-four,' but rather one should say 'twenty-six'"), because of the obstruction of the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) and the resulting fault of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*), and because an injunction for a householder to fast on a white *ekādaśī* is impossible, and because there is no other injunction [to serve as a basis], an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) is untenable; therefore, the general injunctions for fasting on both types of *ekādaśī* cannot be restricted (*upasaṃhāra*) to forest-dwellers and ascetics.

However, they say that because the rule "one who dwells in the forest" and "the ascetic" [also] mentions fasting on the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*), this refers specifically to the dark fortnight included therein;
thus, since the householder’s fasting on the bright fortnight (*śukla*) alone is already obtained from the general injunction, the phrase "only the bright fortnight" is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Others, however, say that since fasting is obtained for the householder even from the general statements, the statement "only the bright fortnight" is for the purpose of restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*), like the Vedic passage: "In this very place they sow, and from this very place they draw up."
First, it is established that for a householder, [the observance] is indeed purely white (śukla);
as for the statement:
"On the day of the sun's transit (saṅkrānti) and on the day of the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the dark fortnight, one should observe a fast..."
And during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, a householder who has sons should not perform [these rites].

Regarding such statements prohibiting the fast on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*), Mādhava and others maintain that although they generally prohibit the dark fortnight for householders, their purpose is to indicate the particular gravity of the fault for a householder who has sons.
However, that is not correct.

Since the general injunction has been restricted to those other than householders, and since the statement "one should always take only the white [Ekādaśī]" finds its purpose as either a restatement or an injunction for the white [Ekādaśī] specifically for the householder, and since the position of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) is untenable due to the resulting split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*),
and because fasting on the black Ekādaśī is impossible for a householder who has sons, the scriptural statement regarding the "black Ekādaśī day" applies to the householder who has sons.
Because it is impossible for [the statement] to have the purpose of proclaiming an excess of defects;
for the scriptural passage says:
"That which is the eleventh day of the dark fortnight occurring between the Śayanī and Bodhinī [Ekādaśīs]..."
That very [Kṛṣṇā] must be observed as a fast-day by a householder; never any other Kṛṣṇā.

By this statement, since the observance of Kṛṣṇa falling between Śayanī and Bodhinī is prescribed for the householder, Hemādri and others maintain that it serves as a *paryudāsa* (prohibition with a specific exception) for the householder who has sons.
Furthermore, this [rule] refers to those other than Vaiṣṇavas:
"By men constantly endowed with devotion and dedicated to Viṣṇu..."
And on every fortnight, one should observe a fast on the eleventh lunar day.
Thus it is said:
"As is the white, so is the black; as is the black, so is the other."
But he who approves when [the Lord] is treated as equal is indeed called a Vaiṣṇava.
Thus, from these two statements in the *Nāradīya-tattvasāgara*, it is understood that this [vow] includes fasting on both [Ekādaśīs] along with Kṛṣṇa.
In this manner, the Ekādaśī vow for specific desires (kāmya) should be performed by everyone during both fortnights.
"Likewise, a householder who has sons and is accompanied by kinsmen [should observe it]."
On both occasions, one should indeed observe the Vaiṣṇava vow as desired.
Thus, from the statement cited by Hemādri:
"On a Sunday, on the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), or on the dark fortnight..."
A householder who has sons should neither observe a fast nor perform the breaking of a fast.

By such statements, whether through prohibition (*niṣedha*) or exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is an abstention from fasting on Sundays and other such days; this refers to the fasting occasioned by those specific [prohibitions], but not to the Ekādaśī fast which has that very day as its locus.
This prohibition of fasting on account of that [occasion] has been declared;
however, for one engaged in another activity, there is neither a rule nor a prohibition.
Thus, from the statement of Jaimini; for this very reason:
"Endowed with the day of Bhṛgu and the moon, and joined with the sun's transit (saṅkrānti)..."
The Ekādaśī should be observed with a fast throughout; it increases one's sons and grandsons.
Thus, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* is also consistent [with this]. Furthermore, a fast occasioned by Sunday and other such days has been stated by Saṃvarta:
"The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), and especially the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*)..."
These lunar days are praised, as is likewise Sunday.
In this regard, bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, worship of the deities,
fasting, and likewise giving— each one is traditionally held to be purifying.
Thus,

in the phrase "the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) and the fasting (upavāsa)," because of the association with the word *pāraṇa*, which is a synonym for completion, the word *upavāsa* refers to the commencement of the fast. Therefore, the intended meaning is that one other than a householder who has sons— such as a widower or a celibate student— should perform the vow of fasting on Sundays and other such days.
But there is no separate prohibition against breaking the fast on account of that [specific day],
because there is no such thing as a breaking of the fast specifically occasioned by Sunday and so forth.
Nor is it the case that—
Having fasted for seven days while keeping the senses fully restrained in seven ways,
one is liberated at that very moment from the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes.
The breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) associated with the Saturday fast prescribed by such statements is occasioned by Sunday.
Likewise:
"Always during the two solstices, always during the two equinoxes..."
During lunar and solar eclipses, during the vyatīpāta yoga, and on the festival days (parvan).
Whoever, with a serene mind, fasts for a day and night and performs bathing, ancestral rites, giving, and likewise recitation, for him that [merit] shall be imperishable.

Thus, it must be stated that the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) performed on the day preceding the *saṅkrānti* is indeed caused by the *saṅkrānti*. However, because of scriptural injunctions such as "one should break the fast on the following day," the sun's transit on a Sunday or other day serves merely as the temporal locus for the following day; the breaking of the fast is not directly occasioned by that specific day itself, since there is no scriptural statement such as "one should break the fast on a Sunday."

Furthermore, since there is no scriptural injunction for fasting on the tenth day (daśamī) that would necessitate breaking the fast on the Kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī, such a fast-breaking is impossible by any means;

nor can it be argued that the prohibition applies only to a fast-breaking occurring on the basis of that [Kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī] fast, and that this is why the text mentions "fasting" (*upavāsa*) alone in the phrase "of the fast undertaken on that account," because if that were so,
it would follow that there could be no breaking of the Ekādaśī fast on a Sunday when the twelfth day (dvādaśī) occurs.
Therefore, the explanation exactly as stated is the correct one. Furthermore, regarding the statement:
"When a *śrāddha* has been performed on a *vyatīpāta* day, a householder who has sons should not fast."
By this statement, the prohibition of fasting on a day of *śrāddha* applies exclusively to cases other than the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*). As it is said:
"When fasting is obligatory and a *śrāddha* is occasional, one should then perform the fast after smelling [the food] that has been partaken by the ancestors."
Thus it is stated by Vṛddhayājñavalkya:
"O Guha, on whichever day the Śrāddha for the father or the mother occurs,
on that very day, my son..."
This shall be the Ekādaśī vow.
Or whatever other vow there may be, O Skanda, listen now to how it should be performed so that the *śrāddha* or the fast is not violated, O Guha.
Thus, O Śikhivāhana, when a matter is disputed, this is considered the supreme means, desired for the welfare of all men.
When the day of the śrāddha arrives and one must observe a fast,
then, having performed the śrāddha, one may consume whatever remains of the meal.
O Śikhidhvaja, having taken all that food with his right hand, he should then smell it;
by this means, O Śikhidhvaja,
the śrāddha becomes a source of satisfaction for the ancestors, and no violation of the vow occurs.
And because it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Furthermore,
whatever woman observes a fast or performs a vow while her husband is alive..."
She takes away the life-span of her husband and goes indeed to hell.
This statement also refers to cases where the husband has not given permission;
for a wife should always perform vows and other rites only with her husband's consent.
Thus it is stated by Kātyāyana:
"Indeed, a woman who is not authorized by her husband, father, or son,
whatever vow or other rite she performs shall be fruitless."
Thus it is from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
Here, the mention of the father and others refers to cases where the husband is not present and to the case of a widow, because of the statement: "A woman does not deserve independence.
And this [rite] must be performed by the widow during both fortnights.
O high-minded one, both a widow and an ascetic who neglect the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) are indeed cooked in the Andhatāmisra hell until the dissolution of all beings.

Because of this statement, due to the mention of the term *raṇḍā* (widow) in close proximity, it follows that for a married woman, as for a householder, there is entitlement only during the bright fortnight; thus, the position is faultless. Now, the dual nature of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) regarding the vow is determined.
And that [time] is of two kinds: complete (*sampūrṇā*) and pierced (*viddhā*).
Among these, it is "complete" when it begins from the two muhūrtas prior to sunrise and continues until the time of sunrise;
that is, it is associated with the two muhūrtas preceding the moment of the sun's rising.
The Ekādaśī that is complete is indeed [the one to be observed], while any other is proclaimed to be "viddhā" (pierced).
Thus, from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Therefore,
all [lunar days] beginning with the first (pratipad) [are reckoned] from sunrise to sunrise."
These are known as "complete" when they exclude the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).

Thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, an exception (*paryudāsa*) is made regarding the "completeness" (*sampūrṇatva*) mentioned in general terms, specifically in the case of the Ekādaśī that coincides with the day of Hari (Harivāsara). Here, of the two characteristics established in general that constitute completeness— namely, that it begins from sunrise and that it persists until sunrise— it is the former alone that is excluded on Ekādaśī, and not the latter as well.
Because it must be consistent with what will occur in the future,
it is established that the Ekādaśī is complete only when it exists from the time of dawn (aruṇodaya) until the subsequent sunrise.
As for that which—

It will be explained that the statement, "beginning from the time of sunrise, sixty nāḍikās [constitute] what is called a complete Ekādaśī," is an injunction for a secondary alternative (anukalpa) intended to establish completeness.

However, when pierced by the tenth [lunar day] at the touch of dawn (*aruṇodaya*), that which extends through the entire dawn but concludes before the second sunrise is neither pierced nor complete; rather, it is merely a fragment. Therefore, it is logical that what is conjoined with two *muhūrtas* prior to sunrise is "complete."

As for the statement— "If there should be a scent of the directions at the time of dawn (aruṇodaya)" and so forth— in such scriptural passages, the term "aruṇodaya" also refers specifically to a period of two muhūrtas.
As for that which is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Four *ghaṭikās* in the morning are desired as *aruṇodaya* (the dawn)," and likewise:
"The piercing [of the time] occurs at dawn for three and a half ghaṭikās.
Here too, this is an indication of two muhūrtas.
This is because of the parsimony of postulating a single root cause.
Furthermore, this piercing at dawn (aruṇodayavedha) applies specifically to Vaiṣṇavas:
"If the dawn should be joined with the piercing of the tenth day..."
A Vaiṣṇava should certainly not fast; for that is not the Ekādaśī vow.
Thus it is stated in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"This [tenth day] is always censured even if it touches upon the rising of the sun."
Mādhava and others maintain that this statement regarding the *sūryodayavedha* (the piercing by sunrise) refers to those other than Vaiṣṇavas, based on the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).
However, some hold that the *aruṇodayavedha* (the piercing by dawn) is common to all,
because there is a general statement concerning the types of piercing (*vedha*).

The mention of Vaiṣṇavas, however, is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama) that for Vaiṣṇavas, there is only the *aruṇodayavedha* (the overlap at dawn). And thus, the two types of overlap (*vedha*) generally applicable [to others] apply to those other than Vaiṣṇavas. Among these, the *aruṇodayavedha* pertains to the subject of optional vows (*kāmyavrata*).
If Ekādaśī extends for three ghaṭikās prior to sunrise,
it is called "Sandigdha-ekādaśī" (the doubtful Ekādaśī) and must indeed be avoided by those desiring dharma.
For the sake of the prosperity of one's son and kingdom, one should observe a fast on the twelfth day;
by breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
This is because of the statement in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*.
Nor should it be argued that this [rule] is restricted only to Vaiṣṇavas;
for in their case, fasting in general is prohibited by the statement, “One must certainly not fast.”
When there is an increase of both the Ekādaśī and the Dvādaśī, that [Ekādaśī] is the subject of the obligatory fast for everyone.
One should avoid the Ekādaśī joined with the tenth day when the moon is waxing;
when the moon is on the wane, one should observe the fast joined with the tenth day.
Because it is stated thus in the *Itibhaviṣya*:
"That Ekādaśī which is joined with the remainder of the Daśamī— on that day, one should observe the fast of Ekādaśī."
When, on the thirteenth lunar day, there is not even a single muhūrta of the twelfth lunar day.
This is because of the statement in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"In this regard, since it is said 'when [the Ekādaśī] should not be [thus],' it follows by implication that if it were [so], then the Ekādaśī pierced by the tenth day (*daśamī-viddhā*) must not be observed.

However, in the absence of a piercing by either the Ekādaśī or the Dvādaśī, the piercing at dawn (*aruṇodaya-vedha*) does not apply; rather, only the piercing at sunrise (*sūryodaya-vedha*) is operative.
Otherwise, it would follow that piercing by sunrise (sūryodayavedha) is purposeless.
Thus, in the absence of an increase [in lunar days], that which is pierced by dawn (aruṇodaya) alone is pure;
