however, when there is piercing by sunrise, even in the absence of an increase, the subsequent [day] alone is [pure].

"Even when [the previous day] is not available, one should perform [the rite] on the joined [day]; even when not available, one should enter [the fast] on the joined [day]," according to this statement.
"Joined" (saṃyuktā) means pierced by the dawn (aruṇodaya).
They say that *graveśinī* is [the day] pierced by sunrise;
in any case, it is beyond dispute that a day pierced by the dawn (*aruṇodaya*) must always be avoided by Vaiṣṇavas.
Even if pure, the Ekādaśī should be abandoned when there is an increase [of the lunar day], whether it be the Ekādaśī or the Dvādaśī.
Where the full Ekādaśī extends into the Dvādaśī due to an increase,
one should observe the fast on the Dvādaśī and perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on the Trayodaśī.
Thus it is stated by Nārada:
"O Brahmin, when [the moon] is full prior to its rising..."
It is defined as being joined with two muhūrtas;
however, when there is an increase of only twelve [muhūrtas], one should proceed by considering it complete— thus is the dwelling [described].
When the Ekādaśī is lost and the Dvādaśī follows,
one should fast on the Dvādaśī if one desires the supreme goal.
Thus it is said.

Nor should it be argued that this refers only to the domain of the Smṛtis; for it will be stated later that, regarding such a subject, those [Smṛti texts] prescribe fasting only when one is already pure.
A Vaiṣṇava, however, is one who has received initiation into a Viṣṇu-mantra;
for it is said: "One who has indeed obtained initiation as prescribed in the Vaikhānasa and other Āgamas is a Vaiṣṇava. And so forth.
And thus, it should be understood that if the sons and others of a Vaiṣṇava are not themselves Vaiṣṇavas, then there is no certainty regarding them.

In this context, the prohibition of the *viddhā* (intercalary) day serves both as a rule for the vow (*vrata*) and as a rule for the person (*puruṣārtha*), according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*).
Its status as a rule for the vow follows from the immediate context (*prakaraṇa*).
As for its utility for human goals:
"The tenth lunar day, when conjoined with the remainder of the [preceding] day, was fasted upon by Gāndhārī;
her hundred sons perished. Therefore, one should avoid it."
Where the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is followed by the tenth (daśamī),
there shall be the destruction of one's offspring, and after death, one shall go to hell.
Because of such recollections of undesirable consequences for a person as these:
"In ancient times, this [fast] was given to Jambha together with the remainder of the tenth [lunar day];
having fasted on that [day] through negligence, a twice-born man should perform an expiation."
Having performed a quarter of the *kṛcchra* penance, a man should give a cow together with her calf;
half a *suvarṇa* of gold should be given, accompanied by a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds.

Some maintain that this is because of the injunction for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, the reality is as follows: according to the maxim that “the mention of a fruit regarding a subsidiary act is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*),” the hearing of [consequences] such as hell upon the transgression of a prohibition intended for the ritual (*kratvartha*) is merely an explanatory praise of censure (*nindārthavāda*). Furthermore, even though the expiation is not studied within the context of a specific ritual initiation (*anārabhyādhīta*), it is rightly held—by the logic of the animal sacrifice dedicated to a specific deity (*adhikārapaśu*)—to be solely for the sake of the vow to be performed on the following day, just like the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice. Enough of this digression.
Thus concludes the determination of Ekādaśī according to the Vaiṣṇavas. Now, with respect to the Smārtas:
therein, both types of Ekādaśī—distinguished as *śuddhā* (pure) and *abhedā* (non-differentiated)—are each of nine kinds.
The pure, the pierced, and likewise the divided—these three types are each further divided into three by being less than, equal to, or greater than;
thus, each one is again divided into three by the twelve [factors] being less than, equal to, or greater than, making twelve.
Because of this statement, in the phrase "equal to the deficient" (*nyūnasamā*) and so forth, the designation is one in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant.
In the moment immediately preceding the rising of a second sun, the *samā* [yuga] is completed; those completed before that are "deficient," while those occurring after the rising are "excessive."
And here, according to the view of Sakalamati, the piercing [of the moon] occurs only by the piercing at sunrise;
for it is impossible for there to be eighteen divisions by adopting the piercing at dawn (aruṇodaya),
as neither decrease nor increase could occur to that extent.

And these are: (1) pure, deficient, deficient twelvefold; (2) pure, deficient, equal twelvefold; (3) pure, deficient, excessive twelvefold; (4) pure, equal, deficient twelvefold; (5) pure, equal, equal twelvefold;

(6) pure, equal, excessive twelvefold; (7) pure, excessive, deficient twelvefold; (8) pure, excessive, equal twelvefold; (9) pure, excessive, excessive twelvefold. Thus, there are eighteen varieties even in the pierced [twelvefold] as well.
Regarding this, there are two summary verses on the final determination found in ancient treatises:
"In the first six [days], the rule is as before; in the following two, it applies to householders and ascetics respectively; on the ninth day, it should take place on the following day."

In the case of the three pierced [tithis], the first [pierced] should be established as belonging to the preceding day; in the two subsequent ones, they belong to the following day; the remaining [tithis] belong to the next day, while the seventh is determined by specific rule.
Thus [it is said].

Mādhava, however, states eight varieties: (1) *śuddhānadhikādhikadvādaśikā*, (2) *śuddhānadhikādhikadvādaśikā*, (3) *śuddhādhikādhikadvādaśikā*, (4) *śuddhādhikānadhikadvādaśikā*; likewise, there are also [the four] *viddhā* [varieties].
In both cases, the conclusion is exactly the same;
for non-superiority can occur through either equality or diminution. Among these, in the first position, there is no doubt at all.

In the second case as well, it is the first [tithi] alone [that is taken]. When the pure [tithi] is equal, inferior, or equal and inferior to the subsequent one, one should observe the fast on the eleventh; one should certainly not observe the pure Vaiṣṇava [tithi].
This is according to the statement of Skanda; "pure Ekādaśī" means that it is pure [without overlap],
and "equal or less" means not exceeding [the preceding day].
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is indeed the "Northern" (uttarā) and belongs to Viṣṇu;
as for those [scriptural statements]:
"If the eleventh day (ekādaśī) should be full and the twelfth day follows after it..."
For then, having abandoned the eleventh day, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day.
Statements such as these should also be applied to the case where the Ekādaśī itself increases,
because they form a single syntactical unit with another statement: "Even a full Ekādaśī should be abandoned if both [the Ekādaśī and the Dvādaśī] increase."
Or [these rules] may pertain to Vaiṣṇavas;
for it has been established that for them, fasting must take place on the following day when there is an increase of even twelve ghaṭikās.
Regarding this point, Anantabhaṭṭa, Mādhava, and others are indeed in disagreement.

Hemādri, however, maintains that regarding this second position, those scriptural injunctions prescribing the fast on the pure *ekādaśī* pertain to householders (*gṛhastha*), whereas those prescribing the fast on the pure *dvādaśī* pertain to ascetics (*yati*). As it is said: "Where the *ekādaśī* is complete and the *dvādaśī* occurs on the following day, there the *dvādaśī* should be observed for fasting, and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place on the *dvādaśī* itself."
"Living beings do not enter the womb," so said the Blessed Lord Hari;
for this reason, he says that from the statement "living beings do not enter the womb," there arises the understanding of the ascetic (yati).
Regarding this matter, a clear original statement is recorded in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya* under the name of Nārada:
"When the Ekādaśī is complete and pure, and there is nothing at all on the Dvādaśī,
yet the Dvādaśī exists on the Trayodaśī— how should one act in that case?"
"The former [Aśvayuj] should be performed by householders, and likewise the latter by ascetics.
However, according to the third position, for all [classes], it is only the latter.
Where the Ekādaśī is complete [on one day] and it occurs again at dawn,
the latter must be observed by all when the Dvādaśī follows thereafter.
Thus it is stated by Nārada.
Regarding the fourth alternative, however, the arrangement is distinguished by the division between householders and ascetics:
"On the first day, the [impurity] is complete, persisting throughout the full day and night."
And likewise on the twelfth day, O dear one,
she is seen once again.
"The east [should be used] by householders, and the north by ascetics, O Lord"—
so says the statement of Nārada.
The mention of "ascetics" (yatīn) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for those other than householders.
Because it is more reasonable to apply figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the secondary sense; having begun with the full [period], it is further stated:
"When there is one *ghaṭikā* remaining at the time of dawn..."
In that regard, fasting is prescribed for the forest-dweller as well as for the ascetic.

And because of the statement, "And for a widow, [the rite is] likewise there, provided that the twelfth day does not follow," and because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "for the two widows" (*vidhavāyośca*), the term "widower" (*vidhura*) is also included.
This is because they share the commonality of being deficient by one limb.
Some, however, hold that the mention of the householder and the ascetic is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for those with desire and those free from desire respectively.
[In the case where] the Ekādaśī is complete and on the following morning it occurs again—
One who has desires should fast on the former [lunar day], but one free from desire should fast on the latter.
Thus it is stated by Mārkaṇḍeya.
Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with the previously cited statement, the terms "with desire" (*sakāma*) and "without desire" (*niṣkāma*) refer respectively to householders and ascetics;
for [it is said]: "A householder without desire should always perform the later Ekādaśī."
O best of the twice-born, let the twelfth day occur at dawn or not; [it is still effective].
Thus they say that even for a householder who is free from desire, fasting is prescribed in the subsequent section of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
However, when there is a desire to please Viṣṇu, in such a case, fasting should be observed on both days.
"Where the Ekādaśī is complete and it recurs again at dawn..."
The thirteenth lunar day should be observed as a fast during the time of dawn; what [result] would there be in that case?
"One should observe the fast on two lunar days (tithis) there, being intent on pleasing Viṣṇu"—so says the *Skanda Purāṇa*.

However, some say that by the phrase "two [days] should be observed," there is no injunction for the repetition of a single fast; rather, it is intended to establish that two lunar days are to be fasted upon, with some fasting on the earlier and others on the later, because this maintains consistency with the preceding statement.
But as for that [Ekādaśī] which is pierced by more than twelve [muhūrtas], it should be observed as pierced [by the preceding day].
If, by chance, the three lunar days (tithis) should coincide on the Ekādaśī, then there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices; one should break the fast on the Dvādaśī.
Thus it is said by Nārada:
"If Ekādaśī is not obtained and Dvādaśī lasts for the full duration, one should fast on the Ekādaśī that is pierced by Daśamī; so said the sage Uddālaka."
And because of this statement by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"In this case, the non-superfluity (*anādhikya*) of the pierced [tithi] occurs through equality or through decrease (*kṣaya*).
Among these, when there is a decrease, that [pierced day] should be observed as a fast by everyone except for householders who have sons."
He who observes a fast on the day when Ekādaśī is diminished will see his sons perish, just like one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) under the Maghā constellation.
Because of such statements as these, which exclude those who have sons from fasting;
and thus:
"The Ekādaśī, even if pierced by the Diśā [Dvādaśī], does not increase beyond that."
This very lunar day on the waning moon should be observed as a fast by both ascetics and householders.
Thus, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, the term "householder" (*gṛhin*) should be understood as referring to a householder distinct from one who has sons.
For them, however, when the end of the day arrives on the twelfth lunar day itself, the [eleventh] should not be observed if it is joined with the tenth.
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as a fast when it is pure, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī).
This is because of the statement in the *Itibhaviṣya*:

"In this case, since the prohibition of overlapping [tithis] on the day of the sun's decline (*dinakṣaya*) pertains specifically to those who desire sons, it should be understood that the fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) likewise pertains to that same class of people.

However, when there is equality or no increase [in duration], even for those desiring sons, the fast must be observed on the preceding day; for by the rule beginning with "on the day of the sun's decline," etc., the overlapping fast is excluded for them precisely when there is such a decline.
Therefore:
"Even if there is but a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī remaining and it does not increase on the following day,
that lunar day (tithi) must be observed as a fast by householders who have sons."
Thus, the statement from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa cited by Hemādri is inconsistent;
for here, due to the prohibition of an increase (*vṛddhi*), there is the implication of equality (*sāmya*).
However, for ascetics (*yatīnām*), when there is neither equality nor excess, [the rule] is indeed the other one.
O King, the eleventh day mixed with the tenth is the former [to be observed], and the full twelfth day is the latter;
however, when the twelfth day is pure, it alone should be fasted upon by those desiring liberation.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
However, when there is neither decrease nor increase [in the lunar days], the former [rule] alone applies, according to the *Padmapurāṇa*: "By ascetics and by householders...
As for that which—

Even when observed at daybreak, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) must be fasted upon by those desiring liberation only if it is pure; however, the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), even if pierced by the tenth (daśamī), is never to be fasted upon.
Thus, the statement of Sumantu must be explained as referring solely to equality, by means of the word "decrease" (kṣaya) which indicates the absence of increase;
otherwise, the *Pādma* [Purāṇa] would fall into the error of being rendered purposeless.
Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with this statement, it is the *Pādma* itself that should be taken as referring to equality through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Because it would result in an inconsistency for the later [time] to apply to the destruction [of the moon] and the earlier to apply to the equality [of the digits],

the *Madanaratna* states that for ascetics (*yatis*), in cases of both equality and destruction, only the later [time] applies, based on the previously cited statements of Sumantu and the *Viṣṇurahasya*.

As for the mention of "ascetics" in the *Padma Purāṇa*, he says it refers specifically to the perpetual celibate student (*naiṣṭhika*), the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who is joined with the asceticism of restrictive rules (*niyama*).

As for what has been stated in the *Tithitattva* and other works— that based on the statement from the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, "In the absence [of a pure day], one should observe the fast on the joined [tithi]; and even when there is no [pure] day, one should not observe the fast on the entering [tithi]," there is never a rule for fasting on a pierced (viddha) tithi— this is what was said.
That is incorrect;
for this statement is rootless, as it has not been cited by Ācārya Cūḍāmaṇi and others. Or, even if it were rooted, its application would be restricted to those seeking liberation (mumukṣu).
Otherwise—
If unpierced days are not obtained because they are forbidden by [other] prohibitions,
then the Ekādaśī lunar day, even if pierced by five muhūrtas, must certainly be accepted.

Otherwise, there would result the futility of the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga—which was cited even by Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi and others—as it serves to provide an exception for the case where the first day (pratipad) is pierced by the rising of the sun.
As for that [first day] which is pierced and has more than twelve ghaṭīs, that is indeed the latter [the second day].
"When the eleventh day is lost and the twelfth day follows... [so it is said].
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be observed as pure for worship, if one desires the supreme state.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
However, the Gauḍas say:
"If the rejection of the [previous] fortnight remains and the Moon has not yet set, one should observe the Ekādaśī joined with the tenth."

Having recited the latter half of the verse thus, they say that in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) the [tithi] pierced by the tenth is to be rejected, whereas in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) the one pierced by the tenth is to be accepted.
Regarding this, the following must be stated:
is it prescribed here that the prohibition of the "pierced" [tithi] applies only to the bright fortnight, or is it that the injunction for the "pierced" [tithi] applies only to the dark fortnight?

In the first case, even if there is an increase in the length of the eleventh and twelfth lunar days during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it would follow that the overlapping day (viddhā) must be observed. In the second case, however, during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), even if there is no such increase, it would follow that the day must be abandoned.
Nor is this a desirable consequence, as it is not accepted even by those [who hold the former view].
As for that which is stated in the *Madanaratna*:
"In all cases, the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) mixed with the tenth (Daśamī) should be observed by men;
whether it occurs in the morning or not, since fasting is obligatory."

Having thus explained the statement regarding the morning of the thirteenth day—namely, whether the twelfth exists or not—it was asserted that even if the twelfth exists on the thirteenth, the fast must be observed on that very [thirteenth] day when it is pierced (viddhā).
That is incorrect, because it would result in a contradiction with the cited scriptural authority beginning with, "When the eleventh is lost... and so forth.
Furthermore, because the word "prātaḥ" (morning) does not indicate the third morning [of the lunar day],
the meaning of the statement is this:

even if there is a piercing by the tenth day (*daśamī-vedha*) at the time of the morning vow (*saṅkalpa*), whether the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) occurs or not, the fast must certainly be observed in every case.
In reality, however, since the statement “mixed with the twelfth day (dvādaśī) by men” is cited in the *Hemādri* and other works, there is no fault whatsoever.

As for that [twelfth day] which has an excess of overlap (*viddhādhikādhikadvādaśikā*), it is for all [authorities] the subsequent one, because the prohibitory statements regarding overlap apply there without restriction.
But as for that [twelfth day] which has an excess of overlap but not an excess of duration (*viddhādhikānadhikadvādaśikā*), it is to be fasted upon as the subsequent one by everyone.
In all cases, the Ekādaśī lunar day should be made to merge with the Dvādaśī;
this applies whether the Dvādaśī exists on the Trayodaśī or not.
Thus it was said by Pojha:
"When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend into the remainder of the night and the thirteenth day follows,
one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices by breaking the fast on the thirteenth."
And because of this statement from the Kūrma Purāṇa:

"In this case, if due to the waning [of the moon] there is no excess of the twelfth lunar day, then according to the teaching of the Kūrma Purāṇa, householders who have sons should not observe a fast.
When the eleventh and twelfth days [overlap], and the thirteenth day remains at the end of the night..."
One who is endowed with sons and grandsons should not observe a fast.
Thus it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa;
however, [the fast] should be observed specifically at night.
When Ekādaśī increases and Dvādaśī undergoes waning, [the fast is observed at night].
That twelfth day should be known as exhausted; in that case, the nakta meal is prescribed.
Thus it is stated by Vṛddha-Parāśara.
However, some say that because of the statement, "But when fasting is prohibited," there is a prohibition of fasting caused by the loss of a day (dinakṣaya), and therefore one should eat something;
but that is not correct.
Because the injunction for fasting at night and so forth is specifically prescribed;
as it is said:
"If the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is increased [in duration] during the bright fortnight, and especially so during the dark fortnight..."
A renunciant should perform the latter [observance], but a householder should fast on the former.
Thus, that statement of Pracetas concerns the case of a pure [Ekādaśī], because it forms a single syntactical unit with many other statements such as, "Where Ekādaśī is complete," and so forth.
Mādhava, however, states on the basis of this very statement that this rule applies even when [the Ekādaśī] is pierced (viddhā).
And in this regard, in those cases where the possibility of fasting on a pierced day arises, the worship and the formal vow (saṅkalpa) of the rite should be performed at night.
If one has broken the fast, however, one should abandon that day and, with a concentrated mind,
worship Viṣṇu at night and perform the formal vow (saṅkalpa).
Thus, according to the Smṛti passage cited by Anantabhaṭṭa,
in those cases where there is the possibility of a pure fast (śuddhopavāsa), if on the previous day the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*) occurs before midnight, then,

based on general injunctions such as "the wise man should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in the morning" and "rites for the gods are to be performed in the forenoon," the observances must indeed be commenced in the morning.
But when the piercing by the tenth [tithi] occurs after midnight, then the worship and the formal vow (saṅkalpa) should be performed after midday.
For, due to the defect of contact with the tenth tithi,
one should avoid the four months following midnight for both the vow and the worship.
Thus, from the statement cited by Anantabhaṭṭa:
"And likewise, when [the Ekādaśī] is obtained on the eleventh day after midnight..."
In that case, one should not perform the preparatory fast (upavāsana) if even a fraction of the tenth day remains.

Regarding this statement in the Smṛti, Anantabhaṭṭa explains that the mention of "fasting" (upavāsa) is intended solely to prohibit the fast consisting of the morning formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and not to prohibit fasting altogether.
Hemādri, however, states that it refers to the first undertaking [of the vow].
Furthermore, the prohibition of desire expressed in the phrase "one should not break [the vow]" is most appropriately applied to the very first performance [of the rite].

Others, however, maintain that according to this statement, the *kapālavedha* (the overlap of the previous and following lunar days) is as inherently defiling as the *aruṇodayavedha* (the overlap beginning at dawn),
and for this very reason, it was not refuted even by the author of the *Kālanirṇayadīpikā-vivaraṇa*.
Therefore, they say that the *kapālavedha* is determined by local custom (*deśācāra*).
In reality,
however, for some, even at midnight, the piercing by the tenth [tithi] is accepted;
but at the time of dawn, there is no room for deliberation.
Those teachers who are dear to Hari say that this is "piercing the skull," but this is not my opinion, because the night is held to consist of three watches (yāmas).

Since this statement demonstrates the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) principle, it is logical that the injunctions regarding the piercing by the [moon] in the pot-sherd (*kapāla-vedha*) are merely for the purpose of praising the piercing at dawn (*aruṇodaya-vedha*).
Now follows the determination of the time for breaking the fast (*pāraṇā-nirṇaya*).
Even when the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) is very short, shorter, or shortest, the morning and midday rites should be performed by drawing them forward to the time of evening (*uṣaḥ-kāla*).
When the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is very short on the day of breaking the fast,
one should then perform both the morning and midday rites at the time of dawn.
Thus it is stated in the *Padma-purāṇa*.

Nor should it be argued: "How can such a ritual be performed when the time for the heat [of the summer] is so short? For by the force of the injunction, its performance is established through the sublation of the number and other such details.
For this very reason: "Indeed, this twelfth day (dvādaśī), when neglected by men, causes great loss; it effects the destruction of dharma."
Thus, the fault regarding the transgression of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
Furthermore, this reduction applies only to Smārta rites and not to Śrauta rites, because the latter are more authoritative;
moreover, the Smārta rule has its own scope as it pertains specifically to those who have not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni).
In this way, there is likewise no postponement of optional rites.

Furthermore, because of the mention of the morning and midday [offerings], there is no postponement of occasional rites—such as bathing and other acts prescribed for specific times when an equinox (*saṅkrānti*) or a *vyatīpāta* occurs—nor of annual rites and the like.
Similarly, even if the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is very long, the midday rite must indeed be performed in the morning.
For,

according to the statement cited by Mādhava: "The breaking of the fast for all fasts must indeed take place in the morning," when the morning time falls within the first quarter of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), then the breaking of the fast should be performed at its conclusion.
The first quarter of the twelfth day is designated as the day of Hari;
having passed that, one devoted to Viṣṇu should perform the breaking of the fast.
Thus, according to the statement in the Viṣṇudharma;
this concludes the determination of the breaking of the fast on Ekādaśī;
this concludes the determination of Ekādaśī.
Now follows the determination of the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
It should be accepted when joined with the eleventh day, according to the statement regarding the pairings: "The twelfth day joined with [the eleventh] is [dedicated to] Rudra.
And it should be observed, O Lord, as being conjoined with the eleventh day.
And this should always be performed by wise men who are devotees of Viṣṇu.
And thus from the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The Ekādaśī, the Ṣaṣṭhī, the Amāvāsyā, and the Caturthikā—these should be observed as fasts when joined with the following day; the others [are observed] when joined with the preceding day."
This is also because of the statement of Gārgya.
Furthermore, the mention of fasting (*upavāsa*) here is an elliptical indication for all ritual acts (*sakalakarma*).
And when the fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and the fasting on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) both apply on a single day, then both fasts should be performed by a single performance (*tantra*).

But when there is the contingency of two fasts due to the distinction between two full lunar days (*tithi*), Mādhava states that one should begin the *dvādaśī* vow after performing the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) with water while still observing the *ekādaśī* fast. This same principle should be applied everywhere whenever there is a contingency of two fasts.
The festival of *damanaka* is prescribed for the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
"The festival of *damanaka* occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra," and so forth, as stated in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*.
And in that context, what is intended is merely the day for breaking the fast (*pāraṇāha*).
If even a single ghaṭikā of the twelfth day (dvādaśī) cannot be obtained on the day of breaking the fast,
then the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) should be taken for the offering of the sacred damana grass.
For it is stated in that very [text]:
"And the offering of the *pavitra* is prescribed on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun is situated in Cancer.
(Śrāvaṇasya site pakṣe karkasthe ca divākare).
On the twelfth lunar day, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Vāsudeva is prescribed.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*.
Now follows the determination of the *Śravaṇadvādaśī*:
regarding this, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* says—
O Rāma, that twelfth day which is joined with the Śravaṇa constellation is indeed great;
having fasted on it, bathed, and worshipped Janārdana, [one obtains great merit].
The knower of Dharma effortlessly attains the fruit of twelve *dvādaśīs*;
and this yoga, though slight, is fruitful.
O King, it is the conjunction of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the asterism (*nakṣatra*), indeed a yoga itself.
If it is obtained for two watches, it should indeed be known as lasting for eight watches.
Thus, according to the statement in the Nāradīya Purāṇa concerning Śravaṇadvādaśī:
"Yoga" refers to the conjunction with Rohiṇī and so forth.

In that regard, if on a single day alone there is a conjunction with Śravaṇa—whether it be pure (śuddhā) or exceeding pure (śuddhādhikā), or pierced (viddhā) or exceeding pierced (viddhādhikā)—there is no doubt whatsoever regarding that [day].
When there is a conjunction with Śravaṇa on both days of the overlapping Ekādaśī, then that which is joined with Ekādaśī is to be accepted.
When the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) touched by Śravaṇa should touch the eleventh day (Ekādaśī),
that indeed is the Vaiṣṇava yoga known as Viṣṇu-Śṛṅkhala.
Thus it is stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*. However, in the *Hemādri*, the reading is "śravaṇāspṛṣṭā";
furthermore, it is explained that the word "vaṇā" is feminine in gender.
According to the Tantra, two fasts should be observed on that occasion.
However, when the conjunction with Śravaṇa occurs on both days of the pure fortnight, then only the latter [day] is valid;
for in the vow of Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī, that which pervades the time of sunrise is to be accepted.
Thus it is stated in the Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa.

However, when there is no conjunction with the Śravaṇa asterism on the twelfth day at all, then the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow should be performed on the eleventh day itself, provided it possesses that [conjunction].
When the Śravaṇa asterism is not obtained on the twelfth day anywhere:
That Ekādaśī, when conjoined with Śravaṇa, should be observed as a fast; it destroys all sins.
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya; and its specific designation is given in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is conjoined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, it is declared to be Vijayā; that lunar day bestows victory upon devotees.
Thus,

even when there is an excess of overlap with the tenth day (daśamī-viddhā), if there is no conjunction with the Śravaṇa asterism on the following day, such a day— even if it is overlapped by the tenth— should be accepted.
"Where the eleventh day is overlapped by the tenth, that lunar day (tithi) is not to be observed as a fast."
But when joined with hearing,
that auspicious [practice] bestows all desires.
Thus it is stated in the Vahnipurāṇa:
"When the fasts of Ekādaśī and Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī fall on different days, then one who is capable should perform both;
having fasted on Ekādaśī, one should likewise fast on Dvādaśī."
In that case, there would be no omission of the prescribed rule, for Hari is the deity of both.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*.

However, when one has undertaken the vow of Ekādaśī but is unable to perform both the Śravaṇa-vrata and the Dvādaśī-vrata, one should fast on Ekādaśī and perform only the worship on Dvādaśī. This applies even if the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Having observed the fast on the eleventh day, one should worship Hari there on the twelfth day.
Thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
However, one who has not undertaken the vow of Ekādaśī should fast on the twelfth day alone:
"Having fasted on the meritorious twelfth day conjoined with a [favorable] lunar mansion of Viṣṇu..."
A person undoubtedly attains the merit arising from Ekādaśī.
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya-purāṇa.
And regarding this, Hemādri maintains that even if the conjunction for hearing [the scripture] occurs at some time or other, the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) must be made specifically in the morning.
Furthermore, this [observance] is declared to be "great" when performed in the month of Bhādrapada.
The twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, when conjoined with the Śravaṇā nakṣatra, is to be known as "Mahatī"; it yields great fruit for those who observe a fast.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
And this [twelfth day] is highly auspicious when conjoined with Mercury;
for when the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa falls on a Wednesday, it is exceedingly meritorious.
That twelfth day is proclaimed by the name Atyantamahatī (the Greatly Exalted).

Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Regarding the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) following the fast observed on account of the *Śravaṇadvādaśī* vow: if both [the lunar day and the asterism] persist until the day of the breaking of the fast, then the breaking of the fast should be performed at the end of both; this is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*).
When the fast occurs due to the conjunction of a lunar day and an asterism...
But one should not break the fast until there is no longer even a single [particle] remaining.

Some say this is because of the statement in the *Nāradīya*: "Thus it is said. However, the *Madanaratna* states: "In this regard, although the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) appears to be at the end of either the lunar day (*tithi*) or the asterism (*nakṣatra*), nevertheless it must be performed at the very end of the lunar day, and not even at the end of the asterism alone in the middle of the lunar day.
For it is said: 'Whichever lunar days are declared meritorious due to their conjunction with an asterism [are so only when that conjunction occurs at the end of the lunar day].'"
One should break the fast at the end of the constellation Ṛkṣa (Mṛgaśiras), except when it coincides with Śravaṇa or Rohiṇī.

Thus, because [the breaking of the fast] at the end of Śravaṇā is excluded in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, one might object: "In that case, would it not also be improper to break the fast at the end of Rohiṇī? To this he replies: No, for in that case [of Rohiṇī], the [breaking of the fast] is indeed desired, as there is a statement from the *Vahnipurāṇa* situated within the section on the fast occasioned by the conjunction with Rohiṇī which says: "One may perform it at the end of the lunar day (tithi) or even at the end of the asterism. However, no such statement exists here [in the case of Śravaṇā].
Thus concludes the determination of Śravaṇadvādaśī.
Now follows the determination of other great Dvādaśīs.
Regarding this, the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa states:
Unmīlinī, Vañjulīnī, Trispṛśā, Pakṣavardhinī,
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī.
O twice-born one, eight of these twelfth days are of great merit and destroy all sins;
four others likewise arise through their conjunction with specific lunar days.
Through conjunction with the lunar mansions, these [Ekādaśīs] pacify even powerful sins;
indeed, the full Ekādaśī increases once again.
O best of the Bhṛgus, it is called Unmīlinī, which destroys all sins;
one should observe the fast on the twelfth day and break the fast on the twelfth day itself.
That [twelfth lunar day] is called Vañjulī, which destroys ten thousand killings;
it begins at sunrise, lasts for the entire day as the twelfth,
and ends with the auspicious thirteenth— she is celebrated as Trispṛśā.

When the *kuhūrāka* (the new moon) has reached its increase during the fortnight-increasing period (*pakṣavardhinī*), one should observe the fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) there, setting aside the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*).
These [twelfth days] are especially meritorious when conjoined with the Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Puṣyā, and Rohiṇī constellations.
"The twelve twelfth days (dvādaśīs), when observed as fasts, yield equal fruit individually.
Thus, there are eight: four by way of lunar day (tithi) conjunctions and four by way of lunar mansion (nakṣatra) conjunctions.
The first [Ekādaśī] refers to the eleventh day;
some say it begins at the break of dawn (aruṇodaya) and lasts until sunrise.
Furthermore, regarding one who is unable to observe two fasts during a Pakṣavardhinī, there is an injunction for the fast on the twelfth day alone, as heard in the case of the Śravaṇadvādaśī vow.
Puṣya is the first [nakṣatra], followed by Punarvasu;
regarding these, there is no further deliberation concerning the lunar days (tithis).
As for Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, it has already been determined.

But regarding the other [twelve] lunar mansions, when they are employed for the rite, there is no requirement for them to be present even for a brief conjunction as in the case of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī; rather, they must exist from sunrise until sunset, or until the same time on the following day.
This applies to the seven-day period of stars beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī.
These do not purify the entire lunar day merely by being in conjunction with it.
This is because of the general statement; however,
regarding the act of hearing [the scripture], it is stated that "it is so" due to a specific declaration,
since the hearing of results is mentioned in such passages as, "These eight Great Dvādaśīs are for those desiring specific fruits and are of great merit."
As for that which was said:
"Those in the world who, by my command, do not observe the eight twelfth days (dvādaśī),
their residence shall be in the city of Yama until the dissolution of all beings."
Thus, the statement indicating that there is a transgression for not performing [the rite] is its authority.
This concludes the determination of other major Dvādaśīs.
Regarding the worship of Vatsa on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through the *pradoṣa* period should be taken.
Because that [time] is prescribed for that very same occasion;
when it spans both days, the first day alone is [the valid time].
"Vatsapūjā and the Vaṭa [ceremony] must be performed on the first day," according to the traditional legal text (smṛti). Thus ends the determination of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Now follows the determination of the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*).
Among these, the bright (*śukla*) *trayodaśī* should be observed when joined with the preceding day; for it is said:
"O Sage, the *trayodaśī* should be performed together with the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*)."
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
Regarding the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the *Nigama* says:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight."
These [lunar days] joined with the subsequent [nakṣatras] should be performed as subsequent; likewise, the subsequent ones joined with the preceding [nakṣatras] should be performed as preceding.
And because of this specific statement;
as for that which was said by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"The second, the fifth, the tenth, and the thirteenth [lunar days] are [inauspicious] due to piercing (vedha)."
Regarding the statement, "On the fourteenth day, for the purpose of fasting, one should abandon the preceding and following lunar days," that refers specifically to the white (śukla) thirteenth day;
as stated in the Nigama: "In the dark fortnight, [one should avoid] the thirteenth day."
Thus, because the specific [rule] is stated with reference to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa),
when there is no thirteenth day on the following day, then the one overlapping with the previous [day] should be observed.
Regarding this, he says:
Vasiṣṭha:
The eleventh, the third, the sixth,
and the thirteenth [lunar days] should be observed even when overlapped by the preceding day, provided they do not exist on the following day.
Thus it is said.
This same decision applies to the fast as well.
As for that which—
The eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth, thirteenth, and new moon days— these should be observed as fasts when they are conjoined with the following day.
This statement from the *Viṣṇudharmottara* refers specifically to the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-trayodaśī*).
Otherwise, it is said:
"The second, the fifth, the tenth, and the thirteenth [are to be avoided] due to the taint of overlap (*vedha*)."
On the occasion of a fast, the fourteenth and fifteenth lunar days (tithis) should cause the preceding and succeeding days to be rejected.
This is because it contradicts the statement of Vṛddhavasiṣṭha.
Therefore, the natural consistency of both [texts] is established through the distinction between the dark and bright fortnights.
And here, the eligibility for the day joined with the previous tithi is not based on its merely pervading the evening (sāyāhna), but rather on its pervading the afternoon (aparāhṇa).
"The thirteenth day should be observed when it occurs during the afternoon," according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*. Therefore,
in the month of Caitra, the Madana Trayodaśī should be taken as that which extends through midday.
In that same context,
it is stated: "At midday, one should worship with devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth."
But that [Ekādaśī], because it falls within the bright fortnight, should be joined with the preceding day;
likewise, the Śanirathodaśī, when overlapping with the evening (pradoṣa), should be observed as joined with the preceding day. As for the definition of the evening:
"The period of *pradoṣa* lasts for three *muhūrtas* once the sun has set," so it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Then, when the sun has turned red, the observer of the vow, having bathed and restrained his senses,
should go to the place of worship and adore Śiva at the time of dusk.
Thus,
when the [fasting day] extends into both days during the evening (pradoṣa), or even if it touches only a portion of that time, the latter [day] is to be taken.
A wise person should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the vow of fasting and so forth in the morning.
Thus, because the practice begins from the time of the initial resolve,
the lunar day (tithi) that extends through the evening (pradoṣa) on both days is always the one to be observed.
In this regard, it should be observed on the later [lunar day] at night, because of the statement of Jāvāli: "Since that [observance] applies to both [days].
Furthermore, even when there is contact with only one part [of the time], it should be accepted where there is a greater duration.

Excellence consists in the worship of the deity, the consumption of food, and its duration throughout the entire period. However, when these qualities are equal, the latter [of two options] is preferred.
The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa is known as Anaṅga-trayodaśī.
Beginning with "In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
in the bright fortnight," it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "Since this was performed by Anaṅga, it is therefore called Anaṅgatrayodaśī."

Even though, according to the general determination in this case, the day overlapping the afternoon would result in the *pūrvaviddhā* (the one joined with the preceding day), nevertheless: "The eighth day of the dark fortnight, the *bṛhattapā*, the *sāvitrī*, the *vaṭapaitṛkī*,
the *anaṅgatrayodaśī*, and the *rambhā*— these should be observed as fasts when joined with the preceding [day]."
According to this statement by Saṃvarta, even that [thirteenth day] which extends into the evening (sāyāhna) is to be accepted if it is joined with the preceding [day].
Otherwise, since the [desired result] would already be obtained through the general rule alone, this specific statement would be rendered purposeless.
Thus, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika should be taken as that which extends into the evening.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, at the onset of night, one should offer a lamp for Yama outside; thus, untimely death is destroyed.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. This concludes the determination of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī).
Now follows the determination of the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"In a vow, the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight should always be taken when it is overlapped by the next [day]."
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight—these should be observed when joined with the following day; the subsequent [lunar days] when joined with the preceding."
Thus, in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"The [rite] should always be performed on the thirteenth day, but never when joined with the fourteenth."
That full moon day may be joined with the fourteenth day, and the fourteenth day may be joined with the full moon.
Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The third, the eleventh, the sixth, the full moon, and the fourteenth [lunar days]."
It should not be observed when overlapped by the previous day; it should be observed when joined with the following day.
Thus,
in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The Ekādaśī overlapping with the Daśamī, and likewise the Aṣṭamī overlapping with the Saptamī..."
When the sixth [lunar day] falls on the fifth, and the fourteenth on the thirteenth;
A person should not perform these rites on days that are pierced by the previous [tithi]:

the sixth [tithi] pierced by the Nāga (the fifth), Maheśvara (Śiva) pierced by the Sun (the seventh), and the fourteenth pierced by Kāma (the thirteenth). These mixed [tithis] are remembered as impure.
Thus:
Maheśvara is on the eighth;
the eighth and the fourteenth [are observed] during the bright fortnight.
The fourteenth days of the bright fortnights of Caitra and Śrāvaṇa are to be taken when they extend throughout the night;
and thus says Baudhāyana:

Thus, the "Yugma" (pair) statement—"on the fourteenth and the full moon"—should be understood as referring specifically to the Sāvitrī vow. However, the "Amā-yugma" (New Moon pair) statement—"the first day [of the lunar fortnight] is also [joined with] the new moon"—should be seen as referring to matters other than the Sāvitrī vow.

And here, the prohibition against the [day] being overlapped by the previous one does not apply when that [previous day] exists for only three muhūrtas; rather, it applies when the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) exists for eighteen nāḍīs, because of the specific statement: "The past [tithi], by means of eighteen nāḍīs, vitiates the subsequent lunar day."

Mādhava, however, states that this statement—regarding where the [fast] pierced by the [previous] lunar day (bhūta-viddhā) should be observed, as in the case of the Sāvitrī-vrata—is intended to mean that a period measuring eighteen nāḍīs is not to be accepted there;
but that has already been refuted.
The Vaṭa-Sāvitrī-vrata is performed on the fifteenth days of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
In that regard, the one overlapping with the previous day (pūrvaviddhā) should be observed:
the eighth day of the dark fortnight, Bṛhattapā, Sāvitrī, Vaṭapaitūkī,
Anaṅgatrayodaśī, and Rambhā— these are to be fasted upon when joined with the preceding [tithi].
Thus it is stated in the Nigama:
*sāvitrī* refers to the full moon day associated with that vow;
*vaṭapaitṛkī* refers to the new moon day associated with that very same [vow].
O King, in the past, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, she observed this vow with great devotion; I have now related it to you.
Thus, having introduced the Sāvitrī-vrata according to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"And likewise on the new-moon day in the month of Jyeṣṭha, O virtuous lady, a woman who has fasted for three nights should worship [Sāvitrī] at the root of a banyan tree according to this rite."
And because it is so stated in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*; furthermore, this is also mentioned in the *Hemādri* regarding the full moon day of Bhādrapada.
However, the Gauḍas [hold a different view]:
One should designate that Sāvitrī as being in either Aries or Taurus;
those women who worship Sāvitrī on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha [attain their goal].

Based on the statement of Parāśara, "Those who observe a fast at the foot of a banyan tree shall not suffer widowhood," they say [the rite] should be performed on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī). However,
regarding the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) prescribed in connection with the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, that which extends into the afternoon (aparāhṇa) is to be accepted.
Then, in the afternoon, one should have an auspicious protective amulet made from excellent, unbroken grains of white mustard seeds adorned with gold.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*.
And here, because of the hearing of the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), this [rite] is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the *upākarma* previously performed.
Therefore, some hold that just as there [in the *upākarma*] the avoidance of planetary transits (*graha*), solar ingress (*saṃkrānti*), and so forth is required, so it is here as well.

Others, however, say that because there is no authority for [the lunar days] being auxiliary parts, and because the phrase "from that" refers to the unbroken lunar fortnights which are established by the sense of the context and thus not themselves subject to injunction, there is no prohibition regarding the *graha* and *saṅkrānti* [days].
Furthermore, this [observance] should not be performed on the *bhadrā* day; for it is said:
"On the *bhadrā* day, two [rites] should not be performed: likewise the *śrāvaṇī* and the *phālgunī*."
Thus it is stated in the *Saṅgraha*.
In this very [kalpa], the manifestation of Hayagrīva occurs:
"In the month of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism Śravaṇā, Hari was formerly born with the head of a horse."
According to this statement,
the Śravaṇākarma is prescribed for this very [lunar day]; therein,
that which extends until sunset is to be accepted.
Regarding the statement, "The Śravaṇā-rite is performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa," the Āśvalāyana Sūtra prescribes, "Having cooked the *sthālīpāka* after sunset.
However, ritualists maintain that because this rite is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the primary sacrifice, its performance should take place on the subsequent festival day.
The *upākarma* ceremony is performed on this very [lunar day].
Regarding that, Yājñavalkya says:

The commencement of the study of the chapters (of the Vedas) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or by means of the Śravaṇa constellation, or when the medicinal herbs appear under the Hasta constellation, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
That which is studied is the *adhyāya*, namely the Veda;
*upākarma* is the name for the rite that consecrates the Veda;
*śrāvaṇyām* means on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

Although any lunar day (*tithi*) conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa could be obtained from the sūtra “*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*” (Pāṇini 4.2.3), nevertheless, it is specifically the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa that is intended here,
because it is mentioned explicitly in the statements of Pāraskara and others.
And so says Pāraskara:

"Now, therefore, follows the commencement of study (*adhyāyopākarma*): when the herbs have appeared, under the asterism Śravaṇa, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, on the fifth day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta.
This is because the asterism Śravaṇa is mentioned separately [from the full moon day].
In this same way, it should be understood for the full moon days of Āṣāḍhī, Prauṣṭhapadī, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by means of Hasta":
on whichever day is conjoined with the asterism Hasta.

However, some say that because the lunar day (*tithi*) is required even for the knowledge of the time through the form of the asterism (*nakṣatra*) such as *Hasta*, until some specific day is determined therein, the fifth [lunar day] alone is associated by virtue of its proximity; thus they say, "on the fifth lunar day conjoined with *Hasta*.
The phrases "when the herbs have appeared" and "of Śrāvaṇa" are to be connected everywhere.
Baudhāyana also states the alternative time:
"Having performed the upākaraṇa on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, one should study the Vedas."
Manu also says:
"Having performed the Upākarma ceremony according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months."
Thus;
by the word "api" (also), the months of Bhādrapada, the asterism Śravaṇa, the asterism Hasta, and the fifth lunar day are included.
Kātyāyana also says:

"Having performed the introductory rite during the northern course of the sun, one who knows the Dharma should then study," so says Gobhila; he also says, "on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, under the asterism Hasta."
Regarding the term *prauṣṭhapadīm*, the word "having reached" (*prāpya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, the meaning is: on some day in the month of Bhādrapada when it is conjoined with the asterism Hasta.
Āśvalāyana, however, states: "Now, therefore, follows the commencement of the term (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*): when the herbs have appeared, on the fifth day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Hasta."
Thus, regarding the *upākarma* as the primary subject, it is said: "That is called the annual (*vārṣika*).

By this, since Śrāvaṇa is prescribed first between the two months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada which are connected to the rainy season, the author praises the performance in Bhādrapada, which is established by the application of that designation.

In the month of Bhādrapada as well, [the rite] occurs only on the asterisms Śravaṇa and Hasta and on the fifth lunar day; for, in the Āśvalāyana-sūtra, after specifying the months, asterisms, and lunar days, when another month is mentioned, it is logical that only the previously mentioned month is superseded, because among those of intermediate similarity, that [month] has the quality of being more immediately present than the asterisms and so forth.
Furthermore, because they [the asterisms and days] are required, only they are taken.
And these times are established according to their respective *grahas*.
For those [texts] in whose branch (*śākhā*) many times are mentioned, their adoption follows the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) due to the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*),
since there is no other purpose for the order of recitation.

And likewise, according to the Bahvṛcas, on a certain day in the month of Śrāvaṇa when it is joined with the asterism Śravaṇā; and in that case, if there is an obstacle such as a solar transit (saṅkrānti), an eclipse, or birth-impurity (sūtaka), [the rite is performed] on the fifth lunar day joined with the asterism Hasta, or, if that is impossible, on the fifth alone.

Or, if it is not possible [to perform it] with only one's hands, and in the absence of the appearance of medicinal herbs, it may also be performed in the month of Bhādrapada when the asterisms and other factors are thus [favorable].
And "there" means on that very day.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Bahvṛcagṛhyakārikā*:
If, however, medicinal herbs do not appear during that month due to lack of rain,
then it is desired that [the rite] be performed in the month of Bhādrapada under the asterism Śravaṇa.
Thus,
when the conditions such as the possibility of hearing [the teaching] are present in Śrāvaṇa, the commencement should be made in Bhādrapada;
for since it is prescribed for that [latter month] in the absence of those conditions, it is considered secondary (gauṇa).
For the followers of the Yajurveda, however, the sequence begins with the full moon of Śrāvaṇa;
for the Sāmavedins, it begins with Hasta.
Even though in some places the Sūtra mentions them in a reversed order—

Those who know the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas perform the Upākarma rite in due order during the asterisms of Hasta, Śravaṇa, or on a parvan day, provided it is not joined with an eclipse or a solar transit.
According to this statement, this very sequence is to be adopted.
Regarding the faults [incurred] during a solar transit (saṅkrānti), an eclipse (grahaṇa), or impurity (āśauca), they are cited in the Smṛtis quoted in many treatises such as the *Madanaratna*:
"During a solar transit, an eclipse, as well as during birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka)..."
One should not perform a group Śrāddha, according to the words of Nārada.
If the Upākaraṇa ceremony should take place on a Parvan day associated with the first [of the two] defects,
the twice-born in that kingdom will be seized by suffering, grief, and disease.
Thus it is said.
Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated by Gārgya: "If a solar transit (saṅkrānti) or an eclipse occurs prior to midnight..."
One should perform the Upākarma rite; if it is performed later than that, it does not cause any fault.
Likewise:
"If the eclipse or the transit occurs before midnight, one should not perform the *upākarma* then; rather, one should do it on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or under the asterism Śravaṇa."
However,
one must certainly avoid these nine days beginning with the thirteenth for all auspicious rites, as well as during lunar and solar eclipses.
Likewise:
"The piercing (vedha) beginning with the twelfth lunar day and ending with the third is prescribed for a lunar eclipse;
that beginning with the eleventh and ending with the fourth is proclaimed for a solar eclipse."
"Regarding the partial eclipse of these two [the sun and moon], three days are prescribed for both cases"—
such prohibitory statements refer to other auspicious rites.
And so says the Smṛti:
In obligatory rites, occasional rites, the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, sacrificial acts,
the commencement of Vedic study (upākarma), and its conclusion (utsarga), no distinction regarding the positions of the planets exists.
Thus,
if an eclipse occurs on the day preceding or following [the full moon], the *Utsarga* (formal conclusion of Vedic study) should not be abandoned there.
And when a festival (*parvan*) is defiled by an eclipse or a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), the restriction regarding the time has been stated in the *Smṛtimahārṇava*:
If a solar transit (saṅkrānti) or an eclipse occurs on a festival day (parvan),
it is desired that [the rite] be performed in that same month on the fifth lunar day conjoined with the asterism Hasta.
Likewise:
"If either a solar transit (saṅkrānti) or an eclipse occurs on the full moon day,
the Upākarma ceremony should be performed by the Vājasaneyins on the fifth day."
Thus;
by the phrase "by the Vājasaneyins," those for whom the fifth lunar day is prescribed [for the *saṅkrānti*] are indicated.
"Whether it be a *saṅkrānti* or an eclipse..."
This is because [the rule] attains syntactic unity with general statements such as "if on the full moon day" (*yadi parvaṇi*).
Otherwise, if both were prescribed— as in the case of the Vājasaneyins' rule "only on the fifth"— there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Nor is it correct to argue that the concluding statement, “If a transference or an eclipse occurs on the day of the new moon,” is a case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because a conclusion is more logically appropriate than secondary indication;

otherwise, one would have to admit secondary indication even in the sentence concerning the Āgneya sacrifice for the sake of making it consistent with the statement, “He divides the sacrificial cake into four parts. In the present case, however, since even the pure fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) would be subject to injunction, this would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); therefore, secondary indication is indeed appropriate. Consequently, for those whose *Gṛhya-sūtra* does not mention the fifth case-ending, they should follow the previously cited *Anuvākya*.
O best of the twice-born, the commencement of Vedic study (upākaraṇa) is traditionally prescribed for the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha or Prauṣṭhapada.
Thus, according to the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, it should be performed on the full moon day of either Prauṣṭhapada or Āṣāḍha;
however, for the followers of Baudhāyana, it is to be done specifically on the full moon of Āṣāḍha alone, as that specific Āṣāḍha is prescribed by them.
For the Sāmavedins, it should be performed when the sun is in Leo (Siṃha) and the moon is in the constellation Hasta.
Regarding the term *prauṣṭhapadīm*, according to Gobhila as previously cited— "on the *prauṣṭhapadī* [day] under the asterism Hastā"—

the *prauṣṭhapada* here refers specifically to the solar month when the sun is in Leo (*siṃha*). When the sun is in Leo and the moon is in the Puṣya asterism, one should go outside during the forenoon.
The Chandogas, having assembled, should perform the ritual abandonment (utsarga) of all the Vedic meters.
For it is stated in the words of Gārgya: "In the bright fortnight, the afternoon *upākarma* rite is performed under the asterism Hasta.
And this [rule] applies specifically to the Chandogas.
As for the statement, "The *upākarma* may take place in the afternoon, but the *utsarga* must indeed be in the morning," that too refers specifically to the followers of the Sāmaveda (*chandoga*).
For others, however, it should take place in the forenoon alone because it is a rite pertaining to the gods;
for the forenoon is also prescribed by the statement of Pracetas: "The commencement (upākaraṇa) should indeed be on the full moon day, but specifically in the forenoon."
Moreover, by examining the statement of Gārgya, it is appropriate to understand that this refers to subjects other than the Chandogas;
however, in the *Prayogapārijāta*, it is stated that for all [schools], it must be performed only in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
In this regard, when the *parvan* (the junction of lunar phases) is divided, only that which occurs at sunrise (*audayika*) is to be taken.
And so it is said in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"On the fourteenth day, the two Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were born."
While the lotus-born Brahmā was accepting the Vedas, those two seized his two ears.
Having slain those two Asuras who dwelt in the depths of Pātāla, the Lord himself,
the Teacher of the World, recovered those Vedas and gave them back to him.

Furthermore, on the day of the rising [of Jupiter], Brahmā obtained the sacred revelation; therefore, the commencement of Vedic study (upākaraṇa) is not desired on that day when it is joined with a lunar mansion.
One should avoid an inauspicious time out of fear regarding the bringing of the Vedas;
as it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"When the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, on the full moon day at the break of dawn..."
A wise person should perform his bath according to the prescriptions of the Śruti and Smṛti.
Then one should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with excellent water;
for the Upākarma rite, the libation to the sages is prescribed to be performed during the day itself.
The phrase "at the end of Śrāvaṇa" refers to the nominal lunar month.
Furthermore, even when Hasta and Śravaṇa are incomplete, they must be taken as occurring at sunrise.
Thus it is said:

In the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "One who recites the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas should perform the Śrāvaṇa rite on the first day of the lunar fortnight conjoined with the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā and accompanied by the constellation of Tvaṣṭṛ."
The *Citrā* [sacrifice] belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ;
however, one should state that "the Śrāvaṇa" is not the name of this particular rite, but rather the name of the Śravaṇā rite,
because Vyāsa himself has assigned that designation to it as well.
And likewise, Vyāsa says:
"But that rite which is performed during the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra] conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā..."
The effort exerted over a year is destroyed in that very instant.
Whatever rite of Śrāvaṇa may be performed when conjoined with the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā,
one should know that rite, known as the Upākaraṇa, to be fruitful.
Thus [it is said].
And this is the scriptural rule regarding the time of sunrise, applicable when it is impossible for the ritual action to coincide with the entire duration of the time.
In this context, the injunction for the time of sunrise to coincide with the *parvan* applies to all followers of the Yajurveda branches.

This is because, by the previously cited statements such as "on the first day of the lunar fortnight conjoined with Dhaniṣṭhā," the *audayika* (sunset) parvan is prescribed specifically for those belonging to the Yajurvedic branches (*yajuḥśākhin*).
Nor is it the case that:
"The followers of the Taittirīya [branch] should perform the Śrāvaṇī on the *audayika* parvan."
The followers of the Ṛgveda should perform the Śravaṇa rite on a day free from eclipses and planetary transits.
One might argue that because this statement from the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa* mentions only the Taittirīyas, it must refer exclusively to them;
however, this is not so, for the mention of the Taittirīyas here is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Otherwise, how could the Bahvṛcas be included on an equal footing? For indeed, the co-mention (*samabhivyāhāra*) of things of equal status is what is logical.

For it is not possible [to say] that "this must be done by Brāhmaṇas, this by Kṣatriyas, and this by Kaṭhas," while it is appropriate to say "this must be done by Vaiśyas. Likewise, the co-occurrence of the terms "by the Bahvṛcas" and "at the Śravaṇa" is appropriate, as is "by the Yājuṣas" and "at the Parvan. Furthermore, the author of the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* set out to prescribe the duties related to the ritual acts specifically for the Bahvṛcas, and not for the Taittirīyas.

And thus, whatever regarding that time and so forth connected with the Taittirīyas is heard there, that portion is merely a restatement (anuvāda). And a restatement is only of what has already been established; and in this case, that establishment [of the time] comes from statements such as those in the Kālikā Purāṇa which enjoin the "sunset-to-sunrise" (audayika) nature of the festival day (parvan).
Even the Kālikā Purāṇa enjoins the "sunset-to-sunrise" nature specifically for the festival day as established by one's own respective Gṛhya-sūtra.
And the attainment of the *parvan* applies without distinction to all followers of the Yajurveda;
thus, it is appropriate that there be a restatement (anuvāda) specifically for them.
As for that which was said—
The Śrāvaṇī, Durgā-navamī, Dūrvā, Hutāśanī,
Śivarātri, and the day of Bali should be observed as commencing with the previous tithi (pūrvaviddhā).
Thus,
even that [text] does not enjoin the *pūrvaviddhā* (the day on which the previous lunar day overlaps) for those other than the Taittirīyas; rather, it concerns subjects other than the *upākarma*,
or else it concerns the *upākarma* performed by the Chandogas.

Moreover, in this case, it is logical that the injunction refers specifically to the *parvan* occurring at the time of sunrise (*audayika*), because such a meaning is required and because of the syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*).
Nor should it be argued that the verbal formulation should be: "If they were to perform the *upākaraṇa* on a *parvan* occurring at sunrise, [it would apply] only to the Taittirīyakas.
For if one were to thus refer back to a qualified subject, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Nor should it be argued that the grammatical formulation is "the Taittirīyakas [should perform it] on an *audayika* [day]," and that the fact of being an *audayika* day is obtained through proximity to the *parvan*;
for even though the *upākarma* rite is proximate, it is impossible for the *parvan* to be obtained through such proximity.

If that were the case, since the state of being "arisen" (*audayikatva*) would be obtained there as well through the proximity of the term *śravaṇa* itself, the latter half [of the verse] would be redundant.

Nor should it be argued that, for you as well, there is the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) in enjoining two qualifiers—namely, being on a lunar day (*parvan*) and being devoid of the transition (*saṅkrānti*)—regarding the state of being "arisen";

for here too, just as in the case of the injunction of a qualified substance where both "one-year-old" (*ekahāyanī*) and "tawny-eyed" (*piṅgākṣī*) are etymological (*yaugika*) and denote a substance, so it is here as well.

There is nothing inconsistent in the view that it is the very *parvan* (the full moon day) itself, as qualified by two words whose meanings are well-established from other sources through their etymological derivation (*yaugika*), that is being enjoined. Others, however, maintain that it is the *upākarma* rite itself, as qualified by its being performed on the *parvan* day by the Taittirīyaka priests, that is being enjoined.
Nor is there a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *taittirīyaka* due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) in a qualified injunction;
for if that were the case, it would follow that there would also be a figurative indication of the three castes (*traivarṇika*) in such passages as "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya.
Furthermore, there is a restatement (*punarvidhi*) of what is prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras because of the difference in the performers.
"Otherwise," they say, "there would be the consequence of the destruction of multiple memories regarding a single object.
That is not so;
for since memories proceed independently, it is logical that there should be a separate injunction for each memory.

Furthermore, since the *pariśiṣṭa* (supplement) proceeds by depending solely upon the *śeṣin* (the principal subject) in the form of completing what remains, it does not possess the status of an injunction there without restating that [principal subject].
In this context, even that which is *audayika* (arising from worldly conditions) should be understood as included up until the time of *saṅgava*.
And thus:

Gārgya says: If the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa occurs after the saṅgava period, then it alone is to be accepted as the one beginning at sunrise; otherwise, there shall be no [observance] beginning at sunrise.
Also in the Nigama:
"If the first day (pratipad) of the month of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada is pierced by six muhūrtas [of the preceding day],
that is the time for the commencement (upākarma) and the conclusion (utsarjana) of the Vedic studies."
Thus,
"parvan" is an elliptical expression for the hands,
the ears, sunrise, the time of contact (saṅgava), the moment of touching (sparśa), the hearing of the Veda, and the day of the moon's change (parvan) when the moon is in the sun's asterism.
The chanters of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda should perform the Upākarma ceremony in the month of Nabhas, in their respective order.
Thus, according to the statement cited in the *Pṛṣvīcandrodaya*. Furthermore, this *upākarma* should not be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*); and so says Kātyāyana:
"There shall be an increase [in the number of verses] upon the lapse of time during the rite of *upākaraṇa*.
And thus—
There is no excellence in the ten *hārās*, nor in the four *yugādis*;
for it has been stated that this [excellence] applies from the start of Taurus (*vṛṣa*) to the *upākarma* and the great sixth day (*mahāṣaṣṭhī*).

Thus, because this statement presents the reason that it is prescribed according to the solar calendar (*sauramāna*) and then enjoins non-advancement [of the term], and because it is prescribed for the *Chandogas* by means of the solar calendar, this statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga refers to that [specific] subject.
However, some maintain that, like the "dullness" (*mauḍhya*) of Venus and so forth, it does not concern the second performance of the *upākarma*.
And thus—
In the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*:

"O twice-born ones, [the following are times when study is forbidden]: during the stupor of Jupiter and Venus, or during childhood, or even in old age; likewise during intercalary months (*adhimāsa*), creeping months (*saṃsarpa*), impure months (*malamāsa*), and so forth."
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, [this applies] in cases such as the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), the transgressing month (*saṃsarpa*), and the deficient month (*malamāsa*).

"The first commencement [of a rite] should not take place [if it is done at such a time], for it causes the destruction of the ritual act. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of retrograde and accelerated motion is intended.
A detailed account, however, is to be found in the examination of the intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the Mādhavīya:
"When the commencement of Vedic study (upākaraṇa) is due, if the sun is situated in Cancer, the upākarma should not be performed; it should be performed when [the sun] is joined with Leo."
Thus [it is said]. But surely:
"One should perform the Śrāvaṇī rite on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa according to the prescribed rule."
The Upākarma ceremony should indeed be performed when the sun is situated in Cancer.
By this statement of the Nigama, since the performance [of the rite] is prescribed when [the moon] is situated in Cancer, how can there be a prohibition?
True;
this is not a prohibition.
However, this is merely a specific instance of the *siṃha-vidhi* rule, as in the case of the injunction: “One should not say ‘gire-gire’” (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 3.2.10; cf. *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 9.1.18).
In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard: “One should praise with the *yajñāyajñīya*.
Therein, by the term *yajñāyajñīya*, the *Sāman* produced upon the verse containing the word *yajñāyajña*—namely, “*yajñāyajñā vo girāgirā ca dakṣase*” (*Ṛgveda* 6.48.1)—is designated.

And in that [text], there is the reading of the word *girā*. There, by the Sāmavedic chanters studying the *yonigāna*, it is sung together with the syllable *ga* as "gāyīrā girā"; thus it is said: "The *aira* [verse] should be sung."

By this statement from the Brāhmaṇa, singing (*gāna*) is enjoined by means of the word *irā* after the elision of the letter *ga* from the word *girā*. Thus, since there is no distinction between the *Yoni-gāna* and the *Brāhmaṇa-gāna* due to their equal authority, and a performance by way of option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise result, the text—having declared the sublation (*bādha*) regarding singing that excludes the letter *ga* through the passage, “One should not say ‘girā girā’;
if one were to say ‘girā girā,’ he would thereby cause his own self to be struck down”—enjoins the word *irā*, devoid of the letter *ga*, as the object to be sung.

Thus, here too, since the two statements— "at the commencement of the Veda" and "on the Śrāvaṇī [full moon]"— possess equal force, the Upākarma would apply as an option in both Leo and Cancer; [therefore, the text specifies] "north of the Narmadā."
The intention is that by this statement, the rule is established according to the difference in location (*deśabheda*).
And thus, since both Leo (*siṃha*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*) are applicable, and there would otherwise be no fixed rule, he states the establishment based on the difference in location;
Bṛhaspati says in the *Prayogaparijāta*:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, the rite should be performed when the sun is in Leo;
and when the sun is situated in Cancer, one should perform the Upākarma on the southern bank.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows:

since the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) applies everywhere, it would follow that the dedication applies even in the southern region; this being the case, by means of this sentence, [it is established that] whatever one should dedicate in the south, that should be done in Karkaṭa, and whatever [one should dedicate] in the north, that should be done in Siṃha.
As for that which states:

"When the sun is in Leo and the moon is in Puṣya, one should go outside in the forenoon"—the reading found in the *Nirṇayasindhu* and other works is: "In the forenoon, when there is no rift [in the clouds], one should go outside."
And it has been explained that "in an *avivara* [place]" means one free from defects such as seizing [the breath].
Those who chant the *Chandoga* [Samaveda], having assembled together, should perform the *utsarga* (concluding rite) for all the *chandasa*s.

Regarding the statement, "In the bright fortnight, however, the Upākarma rite is performed in the afternoon under the asterism Hasta," since the phrase "when the sun is in Leo" applies to both cases, the injunction for the Sāmavedins that the rite occurs when the sun is in Leo serves the purpose of setting aside the regional distinctions between Karkaṭa and Siṃha; thus, its status as a mandatory rule (nitya) is not at all untenable.

Furthermore, this *upākarma* must be performed by students (*brahmacārin*), householders (*gṛhastha*), and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Its obligatoriness arises from its being a means of replenishing the mantras that constitute an ancillary part of the obligatory rite known as the *brahmayajña*.
And its nature as a means of replenishment has been stated:
Kātyāyana says: "By that upākarma rite, performed annually according to rule by the twice-born along with the utsarga, there occurs a restoration of the Vedic meters."
Whatever ritual action is performed by the twice-born with unexhausted meters,
even when they are merely playing, that is always the cause of their success.
Because of the injunction "having initiated [the student], one should study," all [initiations] must necessarily be performed even for the purpose of compulsory study;
and study is required for everyone.
In that regard, for celibates (*brahmacārin*), the necessity of their initiation is established precisely because it is for the sake of that [study].
