Regarding householders, however, Āśvalāyana has stated that they may undertake the study of the Vedas: "One who has returned home (samāvṛtta) should study according to the rule of the student (brahmacārin), following the proper method; others say he may approach his wife, but some say that [the latter] pertains to the Prajāpati vow. By the same specific rules by which a student would study, one who has returned home should likewise study, being joined with those very same observances.
The other students, however, should study according to the rule—that is, in the manner prescribed by their own specific injunctions.
Likewise, the householder who has taken a wife should also follow the regulations stated for the student's stage of life, and not the rules pertaining to mendicancy and so forth; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, because the purpose is the retention and study [of the Veda], the performance of these fixed duties is declared for everyone.
Gobhila states:

"The performance of the Utsarga rite for the Veda is prescribed even for forest-dwellers; because it is an ancillary to the retention and study [of the Veda], it is also required for householders and students."
Thus [it is said].

This refers to lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*); for as for those who are temporary students (*upakurvāṇa*), [the practice] is already established simply because it is for the purpose of study.

"Even from the statement, 'They should be taught while [the teacher] has taken hold [of the student],' the performance of the householder-teacher is declared. Thus ends the section on the time for the *upākarma* ceremony.
Now follows the *utsarjana*.
Regarding this, Manu states:
"On the day of Puṣya, a twice-born man should perform the external dismissal (utsarjana) of the Vedic meters;
or, when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, he should do so in the forenoon."
(a. 4, ślo. 96) *Puṣye* means in the month of Pauṣa;
"outside the village" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
*Utsarjana* is the cessation of Vedic study during the dark fortnight;
it does not mean a total suspension of study.
Having thus performed the *utsarga* of the Vedas outside [the village] according to the scriptures—
He should cease for a night of birds, or even for one day and night. (4.97) Thereafter, being self-restrained, he should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights;
he should recite the Vedāṅgas and the secret Upaniṣads during the dark fortnights. (4.98)
Thus, according to the statement of Manu;
the phrase "on the first day" is also connected here with "Puṣya.
When the *upākarma* is performed on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, then [the *utsarga*] takes place on the morning of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya.
When [the Upākarma] is on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, then [the Utsarga] is on Māgha; thus the option is fixed.
Having performed the Upākarma according to rule on either the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months. (4.95)
Thus, since Manu himself has prescribed that the study [of the Veda] lasts for four and a half months—
wherein "four and a half" means those in which a half of a fifth is included, that is to say, four and a half—
Yājñavalkya, however, speaks of other times as well:
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarga) outside, near water, according to the prescribed rule.
Thus,
the Rohiṇī [nakṣatra] in the month of Pauṣa occurs specifically during the bright fortnight,
because there is no authoritative evidence to override the bright fortnight prescribed by Manu.
In the phrase "on the Aṣṭakā," the term "of the month of Pauṣa" is also to be connected;
thus, it means "on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa.
Āpastamba says:
He concludes on the full moon day of Taiṣa, or under the asterism Rohiṇī;
the term "on the full moon day of Taiṣa" is also connected with "under the asterism Rohiṇī," according to the previously cited statement of Yājñavalkya.
Baudhāyana states: having performed the upākaraṇa on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, he should release [the Veda] on the full moon day of Taiṣa or Māgha.

It should be understood that after performing the *upākarma* on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, one may perform it again on the full moon of Taiṣa or Śrāvaṇa, and then [suspend it] on the full moon of Māgha.
This is stated with reference to the rule of Āśvalāyana: “One should study for six months.
Regarding the *utsarjana* (the ritual suspension of study), Āśvalāyana says:

Regarding the statement, "Having offered food to these deities on the eighth day of the middle [fortnight], they descend into the water," although this indicates the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha,

the author of the Vṛtti has explained that it is nevertheless referred to as being in Māgha itself by intending the locative case in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya-saptamī*), just as in the expression, "They perform the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice on the *uttaravedi*."
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Baudhāyana-gṛhyakārikā*:
"The suspension (*utsarjana*) of the study of the Veda is prescribed on the full moon day of Māgha."
And these positions are established according to their respective Gṛhyasūtras.
Regarding the time for the Utsarga (concluding rite) of the Sāmavedins, however, Gārgya says:
When the sun is in Leo and the moon is in the Puṣya asterism during the first watch of the night, one should go outside;
there, the assembled Chāndogas shall perform the utsarga of all the Vedic meters.
Thus it is said.

However, when the sun is situated in Leo (Siṃha) and the asterism Hasta is first, followed by Puṣya, then the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) should be performed while the moon is in Cancer (Karkaṭa); so it is stated in the *Chandogagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.
When Puṣya occurs before Hasta in the month of Prauṣṭhapada, then, in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
the twice-born should perform the formal abandonment (utsarga) of the Vedic texts.
Thus:
if Puṣya, which precedes Hasta in the month of Prauṣṭhapada, should fall within Śrāvaṇa, then one should perform the utsarga (formal abandonment of the Veda) in Śrāvaṇa itself; this is the meaning.
The months of Prauṣṭhapada and Śrāvaṇa refer, by intention, to the solar months beginning with Pisces, and thus denote specifically the signs of Cancer and Leo.
Since the rule for the *upākarma* ceremony is prescribed by them according to the solar measure [of time],
an alternative period is stated for those whose habit is constant study in the *Khādira-gṛhya*:
"One should perform the utsarjana either under the Puṣya asterism or on the day of the upākarma.
This alternative is scriptural (śrauta), based on the Vedic revelation cited by Mādhava: "He who studies his own Veda for a year [attains the fruit]."
And because this rite is divine and because of the previously cited scriptural statements, it must be performed by everyone during the forenoon alone.
It has been stated in the determination of the time for the *upākarma* that, when the *parvan* (the junction day) is divided, the [time] coinciding with the *saṅgava* period is to be taken.
Regarding this rite, he states its necessity for the purpose of Vedic study and its requirement to be performed every year:
Kātyāyana says:
"The annual *upākarma* rite, which is performed by the twice-born according to the rules along with the *utsarga*,
serves to restore the Vedic hymns (*chandas*) to their full strength."
Whatever rite is performed by the twice-born with Vedic meters that are not exhausted in their potency—
even if they are being recited— it always brings about success for them.
Thus ends the determination of the time for the Utsarjana ceremony.
Regarding the New Moon day of the month of Āśvina ending with the Darśa, that which extends into the morning time is to be taken for the Abhyaṅga rite.
On the first day of the month of Kārttika, during the new moon for the sake of nourishment and prosperity, when the moon is in the constellation Svātī, one should perform an oil-bath at sunrise.
Thus it is stated in the Brāhma [Purāṇa].
However, for the offering of a lamp, that which extends until dawn should be taken;
likewise, O Lord of Men, at the time of dawn, one should observe the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Having performed the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha with curd, milk, ghee, and other such offerings,
Having offered lamps at twilight and having worshipped Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite,
one should eat while well-adorned and graced by white garments.
This is because of the statement in the *Itibhaviṣya*:
"If [the new moon] exists for two days, the later [tithi] is [to be observed];
however, if it occurs for only one *daṇḍa* of the night, the *darśa* shall be on the following day."
Then, having abandoned [the previous day], on the following day there is the "Happy Night" (*sukharātrikā*),
according to the statement of the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"In this very latter part of the night, the expulsion of *Alakṣmī* (Misfortune) should be performed."
When midnight had thus arrived and the people’s eyes were half-closed in sleep, there arose the sounds of conchs and drums played by the women of the city.
"Alakṣmī is driven out from the courtyard of one's own home by joyful women," according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*. Therefore,
for the full moon day of Kārttika, which marks the burning of Tripura, the lunar day that extends into the twilight (saṃdhyā) should be taken.
"However, on the full moon day at twilight, the Tripurotsava should be performed," according to the statement of Brahmā; thus,
the Holākā takes place on the full moon day of Phālguna.
And in that case, the one that extends into the evening (pradoṣa) should be taken,
according to the statement: "At the arrival of night, the Holākā sacrifice, facing in all directions, should be performed."
And this [rite] should not be performed on Bhadrā, because of the previously cited statement: "On Bhadrā, two [rites] should not be performed.
And thus:
"The rite prescribed for Bhadrā and the worship of Holākā [should be avoided]."
The statement regarding the absence of a restrictive rule (*itiniyamābhāsa*) is to be rejected;
for in that case, if *pradoṣa* occurs on both days, the later [tithi] is preferred because the earlier one is associated with *bhadrā*.
However, when *pradoṣa* and the conjunction with *bhadrā* occur on the earlier day alone, [the earlier is preferred].

And if, prior to sunrise, even a small portion of time free from the Bhadrā period remains for the kindling of the Holākā fire, then it should be performed at that very time, even if the *pradoṣa* (dusk) has already passed; for:
"When [the fourteenth day] occurs on the fourteenth, more than one and two watches (yāmas) past..."
One should also kindle it at dawn, at the end of the day, and even at the end of the night.
Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
"When the tail of Viṣṭi occurs after midnight has passed..."
At dusk, one should kindle the fire, which bestows happiness and good fortune.
Such statements as these are without foundation.

However, when the time for Bhadrā is not obtained before [the previous day] nor does it pervade the evening (pradoṣa) after [the following day], then the rite should be performed precisely during the tail-end (bhadrāpuccha) of the Bhadrā on the previous day.
Whatever rites there are on earth, whether auspicious or inauspicious—
All of those are accomplished during the tail of Viṣṭi; of this there is no doubt.
This is according to the statement of Lalla.
Furthermore, this should be understood to apply when the full moon (paurṇamāsī) concludes even before one and a half watches (sārddhayāma) have passed later on.

However, when the full moon lasts for that duration or longer, and the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) increases in length on the second day, then that [rite] should be performed even during the evening (pradoṣa) of the pratipad.
When the full moon occurs at three and a half watches on the second day, and the first lunar day (pratipad) is increasing, then that is known as Holi.
This is because it is stated thus in the *Itibhaviṣya*:
"The Śrāvaṇī, the Durgā-navamī, the Dūrvā, and the Hutāśanī..."
Śivarātri must be observed on the day that pierces the previous [tithi], as must the day of Bali.
These and other such passages enjoining the "pierced" (viddhā) [tithi] as the previous one should be understood to apply when Bhadrā is absent on the preceding day.

However, when Bhadrā occurs on the previous day and there is a lunar eclipse on the second day, Divodāsa maintains that the Holākā rite should be performed on the former day at the tail-end of Bhadrā (bhadrāpuccha).
Others, however, hold that it should be performed only during the time of the eclipse itself.
For all castes alike, there is impurity upon the sighting of Rāhu;
having bathed, one should perform one's rites, but one should avoid cooked food.
They say that by this statement, it is understood that [the rite] is to be performed after the bath.
Thus ends the determination of the *holākā*.
Now follows the determination of the *parvan*.

Although it is understood from the two statements, "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day," that the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices along with their ancillaries are prescribed for the *parvan* (the junction day), nevertheless, through syntactic unity with other statements— namely, "The deities receive [the offerings] on the preceding day; one should sacrifice on the following day" and "The beginnings of the fortnights (*pakṣādi*) are to be sacrificed upon, while the ends of the fortnights (*pakṣānta*) are to be observed as fasts"— there is merely the commencement [of the rite] on the *parvan*.
By means of those two, the completion [of the rite] is prescribed on the very first day (pratipad).
Here, the "taking up of the deities" (*devatāgrahaṇa*), the "placing of fuel" (*anvādhāna*), and the "mental resolve regarding the deities" (*devatāsaṅkalpa*) are performed.
The "ends of the fortnights" (*pakṣāntāḥ*) are the full-moon days (*paurṇamāsyaḥ*); the "beginnings of the fortnights" (*pakṣādayaḥ*) are the first days (*pratipadaḥ*).
The plural number is used with reference to individual instances.
*Upavāsa* (fasting) is the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) regarding the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) that constitute an auxiliary part of the sacrifice.

Alternatively, since it will be stated later that the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the juncture (*sandhi*), and because that [juncture] is extremely subtle, [the term refers to] the commencement as well.

In that case, because it is impossible to perform [the rite] at that [exact point], the two lunar days (*tithi*) situated on either side of the juncture— consisting of the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) and the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*)— are prescribed here by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the purpose of the complete performance of the ritual.
And thus, even in the statement “one should sacrifice at the juncture” (*sandhau yajeta*), the word “juncture” (*sandhi*) likewise indicates those same two lunar days.
And in this way, the injunction "one should sacrifice near the junction" is also supported.
With this very intention in mind, Baudhāyana says:
Because the time of transition is subtle, it is called the "domain" (viṣaya) of the junction;
the ancients have declared that proximity constitutes the domain, whether by the preceding day or by the following one.
Thus,
the *anvādhāna* may be performed on either [the preceding or the following] parvan.
Even there, the time for the *anvādhāna* is not the entire parvan, but rather its first third.
The time for sacrifice, however, is the fourth part of the *parvan* day and the first three parts of the *pratipad* day.
And so says Laugākṣi:
They know that there are three parts of the fast and four of the sacrifice;
one should omit the last two parts both in the sacrifice and in the performance of the vow.
Thus, regarding the fasting day (aupavasta) and the preparatory rite (anvādhāna):

"the two final [parts]" refers to the final portions of both the festival day (parvan) and the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad). In the sacrifice, the final portion of the *pratipad* is to be avoided.

The meaning is that, in the ritual act of *anvādhāna* belonging to a vow, the final portion of the *parvan* is to be avoided; and this applies when the rite is to be accomplished over two days (*dvyahasādhyatve*).
However, in the case of a single-day performance (*sadyaskālatve*), [the rule is different].

It will be stated that the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite) must take place on the fourth *parvan*, even if it falls at night; and that *anvādhāna* occurs only in the morning, according to the statement of Gobhila: "On the day that the *upavasatha* occurs, on that very day, having offered the morning oblation (*prātar-āhuti*) in the forenoon itself..."

In this way, the sacrifice too takes place only in the morning. That which consists of the fourth part of the *parvan* and the first three parts of the *pratipad* should be known as the time for sacrifice, declared as "morning" by the wise.
This is because of such statements and because of Vedic texts such as "Sacrifice in the morning," and because the time of morning is divided into five parts.
From the time of writing [the documents] until three ghaṭikās after sunrise, it is declared to be the morning time; that constitutes the fifth part of the day.
According to this statement,
among the divisions beginning with the four [hours],
that very same [period] joined with one and a half [hours] is designated as "Prātar" (morning).
Thus [it is said].
As for the usage of that term among moderns, it is merely figurative, because it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings.
In this way, when the time for the *anvādhāna* of the sacrifice has been determined, if the fullness of both the *parvan* and the first day (*pratipad*) is present, then there is no doubt whatsoever.
But when those two [the moon and the sun] are eclipsed, there are four types of cases:
before the turning [of the eclipse], during the turning, after it, or at night.
Among these, in the first two cases, the sacrifice is performed on that very day, and the anvādhāna is performed on the preceding day.
If the ritual occasion (parvan) concludes either in the forenoon or at midday, one should fast on the preceding day; the sacrifice is prescribed for that very day.
This is according to the statement of Laugākṣi.
In this context, the terms *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon) and *madhyānha* (midday) refer respectively to the period before the sun’s turning point (*āvartana*) and the period after that turning point.
For it is said: "The forenoon is indeed that which precedes the turning point; the afternoon follows from that."
The junction between those two is midday, which is called the turning point.
Thus, because of this statement read within that specific context,
it should be understood from this very statement that the word "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) occurring in this context also refers to the portion of time following the midday transition (*āvartana*).
However, as for the latter two positions— although...
If the sacrificial session (parvan) concludes in the afternoon or at night, one should fast on that day;
it is prescribed that the sacrifice takes place on the following day.

From the statement of Laugākṣi, it is understood without qualification that one should perform the *anvādhāna* on the day of the conjunction (*sandhi*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*) the following morning; nevertheless, if the conjunction occurs in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), then provided there is no sight of the moon on the following day, the *anvādhāna* takes place on the day of the conjunction and the sacrifice in the morning. [As it is said:
"If the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) lasts for two *muhūrtas* and extends into the afternoon of the first day (*pratipad*)."
The ritual preparation (anvādhāna) takes place on the fourteenth day, after the appearance of the moon.
Because of this statement by Baudhāyana, since the sacrifice is prescribed for the day of the conjunction (sandhi) when the moon is visible;
here, the anvādhāna on the fourteenth day should be understood to occur only when some portion of the new moon (amāvāsyā) enters into that fourteenth day— namely,
when the fourteenth day extends into the fourth watch (yāma).
The new moon (amāvāsyā) is desired for the śrāddha ceremony precisely when it is waning.
Thus it is stated by Baudhāyana. The mention of the *śrāddha* is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anvādhāna*.
For this very reason, Mādhava [states]:

On the fourteenth day, when the new moon is not visible during the fourth watch of the night, and on the following day when the first lunar day (pratipad) occurs, the ritual for the ancestors (kavya) and other rites should be performed.

Regarding this statement of Baudhāyana, some explain that the new moon (amā) is not seen in its entirety, but rather appears as a very small sliver. Hemādri, however, states: "The fourteenth day is full, and the second day is subject to waning."
The *caru* offering should be for *iṣṭi* on the new moon day; the ritual for the ancestors (*kavya*) and so forth should be performed on the full moon day.

Because of this statement, even when the fourteenth day does not enter into the new moon (amāvāsyā), he says that if the moon is visible on the first day (pratipad), one should perform the anvādhāna on the fourteenth day and the sacrifice (iṣṭi) on the following day.
The phrase "the second day is approaching [the new moon]" is an indication of the visibility of the moon.
However, when the junction occurs at night, the anvādhāna must always take place.
This is because of the statement of Laugākṣi: "In the afternoon or at night.
Nor can this [statement] be taken as referring merely to the absence of moon-sight, as in the case of the afternoon junction (*aparāhṇa-sandhi*);

for if the *anvādhāna* rite is to be performed during the afternoon junction when there is no sight of the moon, what need is there to mention the junction occurring at night? This follows by the very logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*).
Because if [the rule] were applied when [the moonrise] occurs at the junction of night, it would result in the scriptural injunction regarding that junction becoming purposeless.
For this very reason, it does not concern the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) alone either,
since its establishment is already achieved by the mention of "the afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*).
And in this regard, when there is equality between the *saṃdhi* and the lunar day (*tithi*), it remains exactly as it stands.
However, concerning cases of increase (*vṛddhi*) and decrease (*kṣaya*), Laugākṣi states a specific rule beginning from the *parva-saṃdhi*:

Of those *ghaṭikās* that follow the tenth part [of the day], whether they be deficient or likewise excessive, half of them should be subtracted or added respectively; that [correction] applies on the first day, both in cases of decrease and increase.
Thus;
its meaning has been clarified by Mādhava:
"Whatever *vṛddhi* exists at the *pratipad*, one should add half of that to the *parvan*."
Having then subtracted half of that from the elapsed [period], let the conjunction always be determined.
Thus, "having cast" means having made it deficient.

Now, one might object: if, on the previous day, the junction occurs in the afternoon, and on the following day only the fourth part of the *pratipad* remains, how then can a determination be made according to the rules regarding the junction (*sandhi*), given that there would be no time for the sacrifice on the following day?
If this is so, it is true:
where the conjunction (sandhi) occurs in the afternoon, one who performs the sacrifice on the morning of the following day—
even if on the fourth part of the *pratipad*— does not incur fault.

Since Vṛddha-Śātātapa states that there is no fault even in the fourth part [of the day] by declaring the absence of defects, the performance of the rite is prescribed for that time as well. Furthermore, this applies to the full moon (paurṇamāsī).

Regarding the new moon (amāvāsyā), however, because the sacrifice is prohibited when the moon is visible, it has been stated that the sacrifice must take place precisely at the conjunction during the afternoon.
Hemādri, however, considering that the statement "where the junction [of the day] occurs in the afternoon" is not a Vedic (ārṣa) utterance but rather a verse by Maṇḍana,

has stated that even on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), if the time for sacrifice exists on the following day when the junction falls in the afternoon, the sacrifice should then be performed on that very day; but in the absence of such a time, it must be performed on the preceding day alone.
It is universally agreed that on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), there is a sacrifice performed upon seeing the moon;
for this very reason, an expiation (prāyaścitta) for that occasion has been stated by Kātyāyana:
If on the day of sacrifice the moon is seen in the western quarter,
one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and give a staff to a twice-born man.
Thus [it is said].

Nor should it be argued that since the moon might also be visible on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), and since Gobhila has excluded the *anvādhāna* rite for that day by stating, "One should fast only when one no longer sees the moon in the east," how then could that rite be performed there?

"According to the principle that 'when there is a conflict between a subsidiary and its quality, the quality must yield because it exists for the sake of the subsidiary' (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 12.2.9), in such a case, even there, it is appropriate to perform the subsidiary act of *anvādhāna* [the placing of fuel];
for this very reason, the Śruti says: 'Some, having seen that, fast.'"
Āpastamba also, following the injunction "one should fast," states:
"On the day when [the moon] is seen, that is the new moon; or on the day when one thinks, 'I shall not see it tomorrow. Nor is there [a contradiction] in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa:
"This is indeed the sacrifice called Sumanā; for one whom the moon rises after while he is performing the sacrifice, there comes prosperity for him in this very world.
Likewise, in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa: "When the moon departs from the east before the new moon day, then he sacrifices."

Thus, since it is understood from the statement regarding the excellence of the sacrificial procedure on the day of the moonrise that one should perform the sacrifice then, how can there be a prohibition of the sacrifice on that day?

On this point, some maintain that because only prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is mentioned here, and because such prosperity is possible even on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), this passage does not intend to prescribe the performance of the sacrifice on a day when the moon is visible.
That is not correct.
Because the verb *udayati* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* has as its primary sense the act of direct perception;

for this very reason, even in another Vedic text it is said, "He, born from the oblations, was seen afterwards," where there is a clear recognition of the sacrifice despite the mention of seeing the moon. Therefore, Hemādri maintains that these [passages] intend a scriptural vision.

In reality, however, since it has been previously established that the performance of the sacrifice occurs even on the day when the moon is visible during the junction of night, it is logical that [the aforementioned texts] refer to that case. Mādhava, the author of the Āpastamba-bhāṣyārthasaṅgraha, and others, however, maintain that according to the Taittirīya and Aitareya passages cited earlier, for those belonging to the branches of Āpastamba and Āśvalāyana, the sacrifice takes place only when the moon is visible at the junction of the afternoon.
However, others such as Baudhāyana and Kātyāyana state that the sacrifice does not take place at all upon the sighting of the moon.

In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated that the determination is always made by the rule concerning the junction (*saṃdhi*); therefore, even when the junction occurs in the afternoon, the fire-kindling (*anvādhāna*) must always be performed.

As for those scriptural statements prohibiting the sacrifice on the day the moon is seen, they are said to be merely supportive of that [junction-based] determination and not themselves the deciding factors.

Now, if the determination of the time for sacrifice is made in this manner, then due to the increase of lunar days (*tithi*), should there ever be an increase in the fortnight (*pakṣa*), it would follow that the sacrifice might even take place on the seventeenth day from the day previously intended for sacrifice. And that— "The desired sacrifice is performed on the sixteenth day; [if missed], it is middling on the fifteenth day."
On the fourteenth day, the sacrifice for the younger brothers is performed; on the seventeenth day, it is inauspicious.
If it is argued that this contradicts the statement of Āpastamba, we say no;
for the mention of the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) is intended to refer to the *anvādhāna* (preparatory rite).
If it were intended to refer to the sacrifice itself, the sacrifice would not be established on the fourteenth day, and thus the mention of it as occurring "there" [at that time] would be untenable.

Therefore, the meaning of the statement is that the anvādhāna (the preliminary rite) is performed respectively on the sixteenth, fifteenth, and fourteenth days during the cases of increase, normalcy, and decrease [of the moon].
As for the prohibition of anvādhāna on the seventeenth day, it is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda), because that [anvādhāna] is not applicable there in any way whatsoever.
For this very reason, Baudhāyana says:
In this context, the days for the *aupavasatha* (fasting) rite are the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth, but not the thirteenth or seventeenth.
Where the *aupavasatha* rite would be the thirteenth day before the day of sacrifice,
or even the seventeenth, one should avoid it with great effort.
Thus,
this *anvādhāna* on the sixteenth day and so forth should be understood as applying when the rite is performed over two days (*hyahakālatva*).
However, when it is performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatva*), the *anvādhāna* indeed takes place even on the seventeenth day.

And that quality of being performed on the same day is stated by Kātyāyana with respect to a specific full-moon day: "If the junction [of the day] occurs after the *saṅgava* period and before the sun has turned back [from its northern course]."
That full-moon day is to be understood as the lunar date for the rule regarding the immediate performance (sadyaskāla).
And this quality of being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatva*) is optional.
The placing of the fire (*anvāhiti*), the spreading of the grass (*āstaraṇa*), and the fasting (*upavāsa*)—these indeed take place on the previous day during the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
However, if the junction of the lunar phase (*parvasandhi*) occurs before midday (*āvartana*), then the entire rite may be performed on that very same day.
Thus it is stated in the *Saṅgraha*.

And so, having begun with the statement, "One should fast on either the earlier or the later full moon," the general rule regarding the full moon— "or immediately, or in the morning"— must be understood as applying specifically to the case where the conjunction occurs before the sun's turning point (*āvartana*), because this results in the parsimony of assuming only a single scriptural injunction.
And this [rule] pertains to those other than the Vājasaneyins;
for them, however:
"That day on which the junction of the parvan occurs before midday is this third [kind]."
That Kharvikā sacrifice belongs to Vājasaneya; having fasted on that day, the sacrifice takes place on the following day.
Thus, because the author of the *Bāṣyārthasaṅgraha* has stated there too that it occurs during two periods of time,

[the phrase] "this third" refers to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) alone and not the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), since it is this very [full moon] that was previously prescribed as being twofold by virtue of its connection with the afternoon and the night.
For this very reason,
Āpastamba has stated: "The Vājasaneyins prescribe the Kharvikā as the third [lunar day], beginning specifically with the full moon (paurṇamāsī)."

This also applies when there is a two-day duration [of the conjunction]: it concerns only the attainment of the third part of the *pratipad*, not the attainment of the fourth part, because that [attainment of the fourth part] is prescribed by the statement, "If the conjunction should occur in the afternoon" (*sandhir yady aparāhṇe syāt*).
And in this case, when the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) occurs at the junction of the lunar day (*parvan*), then the final ritual element must be performed on the *pratipad* itself;
provided, however, that the sacrifice is completed while the *pratipad* has not yet fully entered [the day].
Furthermore, having performed the re-consecration, the entire sacrifice must be carried out by those most skilled in ritual.
Thus, from the statement of Gārgya, "having led forward the fire" is the remainder.
This concludes the determination of time for the archetype (prakṛti).
Now, for the ectype (vikṛti).
In that regard, when the two-day duration is obtained by extension (*atideśa*) for the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices— such as the *iṣṭi* and *paśubandha* sacrifices—
the rule "When one should sacrifice with an animal or with Soma, he should sacrifice on the new moon day or the full moon day" prescribes the single-day duration (*sadyaskālatā*).

Likewise, it has been established in the fifth chapter, near its end, that there is no fixed rule regarding the injunctions, such that the *paurṇamāsī* [full moon] may serve as a model for a *darśa* [new moon] sacrifice, and the *amāvāsyā* [new moon] may serve as a model for a *paurṇamāsa* [full moon] sacrifice.
Baudhāyana, however, adds "or under a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatre vā*), thus mentioning the lunar mansion as well;
and that refers to the period beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Viśākhā.
"Kṛttikā is the first and Viśākhā is the last; these are the divine lunar mansions (devanakṣatra); whatever one intends to do, one should perform it during them.
Thus says the Taittirīya Śruti.
And [so too] Revatī.
For it is stated in that very same context: "Whatever is posterior to Soma, one should perform that in the Revatī [nakṣatra].

And this does not apply with respect to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because the nakṣatra prescribed outside of a specific context (anārabhyādhīta), which has its own scope, is set aside by the full-moon day and other times prescribed within the context (prākaraṇika) which have no other scope—just as the fifteen-fold chant (pāñcadaśya) sets aside the seventeen-fold chant (sāptadaśya), or the low tone (upāṃśutva) sets aside the tone of the Dīkṣaṇīyā.
Regarding that, there is a specific distinction concerning the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*:
the *paurṇamāsī* is that which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon; the *amāvāsyā* is that which is their closest conjunction.
According to this statement by Gobhila, since it is understood that [the words] denote moments of extreme proximity or remoteness,

and since the performance of the ritual with all its constituent parts (*sāṅgaprayoga*) is impossible therein, the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) is prescribed for the day-and-night junction (*sandhimat*) indicated by the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* through the sentence "If [one sacrifices] with an *iṣṭi*"; therefore, [the sacrifice should be performed] either at the time of the *āvartana* or prior to it.

Since the injunction for the *vikṛti* (the modified sacrifice) is also at that very same juncture of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*), there arises the possibility of performing both the *prakṛti* (the archetype) and the *vikṛti* simultaneously.

However, because the *prakṛti* was commenced on the previous day and because it is impossible to perform another ritual action in the interim, and because the morning time is expressly prescribed for the *prakṛti*, the ritualists (*yājñika*) declare: "Having performed the *prakṛti*, the *vikṛti* should be performed."
They cite a statement based precisely on logic:

"If the junction of the lunar day (parvasandhi) occurs before the turning point (āvartana), then having performed the primary rite (prakṛti) at that time, one should perform the modified rite (vikṛti)."
If the sacrifice were to take place on a later day than that,
then the modified rite (vikṛti) would follow the model rite (prakṛti) on the following day.
Thus it is said.

Nor should it be argued that because the *vikṛti* (the modified sacrifice) takes precedence over the *saṃdhi* (the junction-time) subsequent to the *āvartanī* (the turning of the sun), there would be a sublation of the scripturally enjoined time for the *anvādhāna* (the preparatory rite) belonging to the *prakṛti* (the model sacrifice).

For the *anvādhāna* is a subordinate (*aṅga*) element, and its time is overridden by the time of the *vikṛti*, which rests upon the primary (*pradhāna*) sacrifice, according to the principle: "In case of a conflict between a subordinate and a quality, the former prevails because it exists for the sake of the latter" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.2.9).
Since sublation is appropriate according to this principle,
even though the *sutyā* is thus unprecedented (*apūrva*), it must nevertheless be performed on that very same day because of the scriptural injunction "if [there is] an *iṣṭi*.
However, the *āgrayaṇa* occurs before the full moon sacrifice and after the new moon sacrifice.

"At whatever time the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs, having sacrificed with that [offering], he should then sacrifice with this [offering]; if it be the full moon (paurṇamāsī), having sacrificed with that [offering], he then sacrifices with the Full Moon sacrifice.
Thus says the Śruti.
"With this" refers to the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
Hemādri maintains that the Āgrayaṇa performed before the Paurṇamāsa belongs to the occasion of an immediate (sadyaskāla) full moon;
however, the Mīmāṃsakas state otherwise regarding the time for the modified sacrifices (vikṛti). For instance:

In the Śruti text, "The nights of King Soma, the half-month, were his wives; he did not approach them on the new-moon day (amāvāsyā) nor on the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī)," the use of the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* for those nights indicated by the pronoun *tat* establishes their status as designations for lunar days (*tithi*), a fact well-known even among cowherds and women. Furthermore, since the Gobhila-sūtra is appropriately explained as being intended to establish the grounds for the occurrence of specific parts [of the day], it does not have the purpose of denoting mere moments (*kṣaṇa*); therefore, [the parvan] refers to the *parvan* occurring at sunrise, which is to be accomplished prior to and including the *āvartana*.

Because it is inherently subordinated [to the primary rite], even if it is absent on the preceding lunar day (*pūrva-parvan*), it is appropriate that the sublation of the prescribed morning time by the principal *audayika* (at-sunrise) time should occur; therefore, the performance of the modified rite (*vikṛti*) takes place on the preceding lunar day alone. Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Virasiṃha—the son of the illustrious Madhukara Sāhu, who was the son of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāparudra, whose lotus-feet were honored by the clusters of rays from the crest-jewels of the entire circle of subordinate kings, and who was a sun causing the blooming of the white lotuses of the hearts of the earth encircled by the four oceans.

In the *Samayaprakāśa* section of the *Vīramitrodaya* treatise composed by the illustrious Mitramiśra—the son of Paraśurāma Niśra, who was the son of the scholar Haṃsa Paṇḍita; the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of all branches of knowledge; a lion to the great elephant of worldly poverty; and the life-breath of learned men—ends here the determination of the [auspicious] lunar days (*parvanirṇaya*).
Now follows the determination of the time for eclipses (*grahaṇakālanirṇaya*).
Regarding the nature of the eclipse therein, the *Sūryasiddhānta* states:
"The moon, situated below the sun, becomes like a solid mass that obscures it;
facing eastward, the moon enters the shadow of the earth, and thus the eclipse occurs."
Of this sun;
"that" refers to an eclipse.
When the moon situated below becomes the obscurer of the sun, then there is a solar eclipse.
The meaning is that when the moon, moving toward the east, enters the shadow of the earth cast by the sun situated in the west, then there is a lunar eclipse.
Also, in the *Barāhasaṃhitā*: "In its own eclipse, the moon enters the shadow of the earth; and in the eclipse of the sun, it enters the sun."
Thus:
"in the seizing of its own [disk]" means in the seizing of the moon;
"it enters the sun" means it obscures the sun.
Regarding the time of the eclipse, Vṛddhagārgya says:
"At the junction of the full moon and the first day of the lunar fortnight, Rāhu possesses a complete orb."
And it swallows both the moon and the sun between the new moon day and the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Thus, the division of time is stated in the Brahmasiddhānta:
"The duration of time at the end of the full moon (parvan) is equal to that at the beginning of the first lunar day (pratipad)."
The conjunction of the sun and moon on this day is exceedingly meritorious due to their meeting.
Thus,
the eclipse occurs in the latter half of the *parvan* (the junction) and in the former half of the *pratipad* (the first lunar day);
the meaning is that the center of the eclipse is at the conjunction (*sandhi*) of the *parvan* and the *pratipad*.
*Anehā* means time.
In this regard, bathing is mandatory:
"One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as during birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)."
One who does not bathe incurs death; one who bathes does not incur sin.
Thus, from the *Laiṅga*:
"If a person does not bathe during an eclipse or at the transition of the sun (saṅkrānti),
he shall suffer from leprosy for seven births and be born as a partaker of misery."
Thus, the elder Vasiṣṭha has stated the fault incurred by failing to perform [the rite];
and regarding the rule for bathing water, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
One should perform a bath in the Gaṅgā during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
and one should likewise perform a bath according to the prescribed rules in other great rivers.
Thus [it is said].

Here, because of the inclusion of the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*), that which was stated in the *Smṛtiratnāvalī*—namely, that "this bath is without mantras"—is refuted. [The verse continues: "The three Gaṅgās..."
The three most meritorious rivers— the Veṇī, the Godā, and the Jāhnavī—
having reached the earth from the body of Hari, the Lord of Monkeys, are indeed celebrated as the Gaṅgā.
In the *Kālamādhava*, however, the reading is "gāṃ harīśāṅghrikāt. Here, *hari* and *īśa* are the two [deities] (*harīśau*). *Aṅghri* means foot; *ka* means head.
*Aṅghri* means foot and *kaṃ* means head; thus, *aṅghrikaṃ* [refers to the foot and the head]. The Gaṅgā reached the earth (*gām*) from the foot of Hari and the head of Īśvara.
Even though the Jāhnavī alone is such [a river], [it is so called here for the sake of the meter].
But this is not the case with the braid of hair or the cow.

Nevertheless, it has been explained that, according to the maxim "those with umbrellas are walking," the status of being the Gaṅgā is not contradictory even for those two who are mentioned together with the Jāhnavī.
Thus, from the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The earth" (*gām*) means the world;
"from the shoulder of Gaṅgādhara" is found as the beginning of the second half-verse in some versions.
"Great rivers" refers to those flowing toward the ocean, such as the Sarasvatī, Narmadā, and others, according to the statement: "Great rivers flow to the ocean.
Śaṅkha says:
In ponds, wells, and tanks; on mountain springs;
in rivers, streams, natural reservoirs, and lakes filled with water.
"Or one may perform it with warm water during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
This refers to one who is ill.
Purified by the rays of the sun and further purified by fire,
therefore one afflicted by disease should bathe with warm water even during the day.
Thus it is stated by Vyāghra. The particle *api* is displaced [in the compound];
the meaning is "even with warm water."

Alternatively, in the context of the upcoming statement regarding Yama, [the word "atha"] has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with birth and other events previously mentioned as causes of planetary affliction (*uparāga*).
As for the verse:
"Upon death, at birth, during a transit (*saṅkrānti*), and during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
And upon touching that which is untouchable, one should not bathe with warm water.
Thus, the statement of Yama refers to those who are not afflicted by illness.
Vyāsa says:
"All water is equal to the Gaṅgā; all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā."
Every gift made during an eclipse of the moon or the sun is equal to the earth itself.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the statement that water alone is equal to the Gaṅgā, there is an expression of excellence (*prāśastya*); since praise for what is not already enjoined would be purposeless, a rule (*vidhi*) must be inferred from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) itself, namely: "one should bathe with any water whatsoever.
He now describes the progressive sequence of the excellence of merit (*puṇya*) regarding water:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Water drawn from the earth is more meritorious than that which remains in the ground; water from a spring is more meritorious than that; water from a lake is more meritorious than that; and river water is more meritorious than that.
The water of sacred fords is meritorious, and the water of great rivers is purifying; the water of the Gaṅgā is more meritorious than that, and the ocean is more meritorious than even that.
"Cool water [is more meritorious] than hot water; merit from another's water is boundless.

In this passage, the praise of the superior merit of one who stands on the ground and so forth is intended to imply the injunction regarding [water] that has been drawn up and so forth—since such [standing on the ground] would otherwise be impossible—but it does not constitute a connection between a quality and its fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha*).

For one who seeks only the fruit of bathing, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to bathe in a well when a well and the Gaṅgā meet; however, there is a superior merit resulting from specific sacred sites (tīrthas) during specific months—
as stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
An eclipse in the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent; however, O great sage, an eclipse in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā is highly praised.
In the month of Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious; in Māgha, the auspicious Sannihitā;
in Phālguna, the meritorious Varuṇā; and in Caitra, the meritorious Sarasvatī.
In Vaiśākha, the Candrabhāgā, the best of rivers, is exceedingly meritorious;
in Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; and in Āṣāḍha, the river Tāpikā.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is named Sindhu; likewise, in Bhādrapada, it is the Gaṇḍakī;
and in Āśvina, it is the excellent Sarayū.
Regarding the expression "Gaṅgā-Yamunā," there is a singular collective formation (ekavadbhāva).
This is because of the rule stating, "Every copulative compound may optionally be treated as a singular.
Devikā and Devahūtī are well-known in the region of Ayodhyā.
Sannihatya is Kurukṣetra.

Although in passages such as "In the month of Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious," the primacy of the location is perceived, nevertheless, in accordance with the introductory statement "An eclipse in Kārttika is most excellent," one must understand that the eclipse itself is the primary factor in all cases. Regarding specific holy sites for specific types of eclipses, it is said right there:
O great sage, when the moon is joined with Rāhu, and when the sun is seized by Rāhu so that it becomes shrouded in darkness, the Godāvarī is exceedingly meritorious.
"By contact with the waters of the Narmadā, they become fulfilled in their purpose.
Thus it is said in the Mātsya Purāṇa.
The Gaṅgā, Kanakhala, Prayāga, and likewise Puṣkara,
as well as the meritorious Kurukṣetra— these are all [purified] when the sun is seized by Rāhu.
In that very place: "The sin committed over ten lifetimes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, or whatever sin has been accumulated over a thousand births..."
"That [sin] shall perish when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu during the Sannihati [conjunction].
Thus,
he describes the Cūcamaṇi yoga occurring on specific days during an eclipse:
Vyāsa says:
When there is an eclipse of the Sun on a Sunday, or likewise an eclipse of the Moon on a Monday, it is known as *cacamaṇi*;
one obtains infinite fruit therein.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "The fruit that is obtained by men at Kurukṣetra through the gift of cows, elephants, sesame seeds, grain, jewels, gold, and land..."

In that regard, by bathing in the ocean during a lunar eclipse, one obtains sixfold the fruit that is obtained here at Kurukṣetra; since this statement is an improper description as if it were already established (*siddhavannirdeśa*), the injunction "one should give cows and so forth at Kurukṣetra" must be inferred.
Furthermore, the *śrāddha* rite is mandatory during an eclipse.
One should indeed perform the Śrāddha ceremony even at the cost of one's entire possessions during the appearance of Rāhu;
for he who, out of atheism, does not perform it, sinks like a cow in the mud.
Thus it is stated in the Mahābhārata:
"When a distinguished Brāhmaṇa has arrived, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon, or at the solstices..."
If they perform a Śrāddha at will during afflictions caused by planets at the time of birth or the lunar mansion, [they obtain great merit].

Regarding this statement, because it would otherwise contradict what was previously stated, it is understood through the connection with the phrase "and by one's own desire" that the expression "and a desire for the *śrāddha*" has the same meaning as the statement which establishes that the time [for the rite] depends on one's independent will; thus there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, concerning the *śrāddha*, the *Kūrma Purāṇa* also states:
However, a funeral rite for the sake of a specific occasion must be performed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or upon the death of one's kinsmen; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell.
Thus, giving is also essential:
"At the beginning of the solstices and other such times, one should always give whatever desirable wealth is present in the house."
And likewise at the commencement of the sixty-fourth year, and during the liberation of the moon and the sun.
Thus it is stated in the *Śātātapīya* based on constant scriptural authority.
Furthermore, this bathing and other rites should be performed even at night; as it is said:
"Bathing and giving gifts [are prescribed] during a solar eclipse by day."
"Likewise, bathing and giving gifts are prescribed for Soma as well during the night," according to the statement of Devala;
and "giving gifts" is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for performing Śrāddha.
"One should avoid performing a *śrāddha* at night, except during an eclipse (*sūtaka*) of Rāhu," according to the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
"Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and *śrāddha* performed during the sight of Rāhu yield infinite merit."
The night belongs to the Asuras elsewhere; therefore, one should avoid it.
Wise men should certainly not perform a śrāddha during either twilight or at night;
however, it may be performed during both if there is an eclipse of the moon.
This is also established by the two statements of Śātātapa and Viṣṇu:
"This [rite] should be performed even during an intercalary month (malamāsa),
as well as during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the time of death, and upon the birth of a son."
It should be given even during an intercalary month; what is thus given produces inexhaustible merit.
Thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
And here, even optional rites such as bathing should be performed. [As it is said:
"The bathing that is done at every dawn, during the twilight, and when the sun has risen..."
And during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, [a fast] equal to that is accomplished by the Prājāpatya penance.
Thus says Dakṣa:
"For a Śrāddha offered upon the sight of Rāhu remains until the moon and stars perish;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire."
Thus it is stated by Viṣṇu:
"Land, cows, gold, grain, or whatever else is desired—
all that should be given at the time of acceptance by one who desires his own welfare."
And because of this statement in the Mahābhārata:
"Regarding these, the specific times are stated in another Smṛti: 'When [the sun] is being eclipsed, there should be a bath; when it is eclipsed, a fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed.'"
When one is being released, there should be a gift; when one has been released, bathing is prescribed.
Thus [it is said].
The fire-oblation (homa) is also an indicator for the worship of the gods.
There should be bathing during eclipses and the like; in between, there should be the fire-oblation and the worship of the gods.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. And the Śrāddha should be performed after the Homa;
having performed the ritual bath in the Gaṅgā or another sacred place, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one should perform the oblation of sesame seeds.

Then, according to one's ability, the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) should be performed specifically for the six deities, using the *vyāhṛtis*, the *grahamantras*, and other mantras prescribed in one's own Vedic branch.
"One should give gifts according to one's ability— gold, food, cows, and land"—
so it is stated in the *Candraprakāśa* based on another Smṛti.
As for that which is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* concerning bathing and other rites:
The merit at the eclipse (upamarde) of the moon or sun is a hundred-thousandfold; at the moment of total immersion (grahaṇe), it is ten-millionfold; in the middle, it is infinite.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding this, Mādhava states that whatever is prescribed at the beginning, middle, and end is for the sake of the excellence of the respective fruits and so forth.
As for the statement of Vyāsa:
The gods are satisfied at the moment of contact, as are the ancestors;
humans, however, at the middle time, while the rākṣasas are satisfied at the time of release.
Thus,
this refers to the best, middling, and lowest times in relation to bathing and other such acts;
others say that "a hundred-thousandfold [merit] in the case of an eclipse" refers to a different time altogether.
Regarding the lack of qualification for other rites when bathing is not performed, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"Impurity arises for men during the eclipses of the moon and the sun;
having bathed at the contact of Rāhu with both, a man becomes fit for giving gifts and other such acts."
Thus it is said:
"kalpate" means "becomes eligible.
For all castes alike, there is no period of impurity (sūtaka) upon the sighting of Rāhu.
And from the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "Having bathed, one should perform the ritual acts," and the bath is to be performed with one's clothes on (*sacaila*).
"During the *rāhusūtaka* (eclipse), there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for all castes;
however, one must bathe with one's clothes on"— so says the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.
During the eclipse of Rāhu (a solar or lunar eclipse), one must remain with one's clothes on;
this applies equally to the bath taken upon release [from the eclipse].
It is recorded in the Smṛtis that during an eclipse there is impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca), and upon its release, there is impurity due to childbirth (sautika).
The sequence of ritual actions is performed by merely touching the point of contact between those two.

Thus, from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, because of the mention of impurity (*āśauca*) arising from contact and liberation, and because it is understood that this necessitates the performance of duties such as bathing with one's clothes on (*sacailasnāna*),
the opinion of the *Madanaratna*— that the bath upon liberation itself must be performed with one's clothes on—
is refuted.
Even a woman in her menses should bathe with water drawn from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).

There is no defect such as impurity (sūtaka) regarding the performance of oblations, recitations, and the like during an eclipse. During an eclipse, one should bathe even with water drawn from a non-sacred source, having lifted it up from a tīrtha.
Thus, from the statement in the *Sūryodayanibandha* within the *Bhārgavārcanadīpikā*:
"When the occasion for a ritual bath has arisen, if a woman is in her menses..."
Having performed the bath with water filtered through a vessel, one should observe the vow.
Thus it is stated in the *Mitākṣarā*.
Regarding the occurrence of the annual anniversary (*pratyābdika*) on that same day, Gobhila says in the *Madanapārijāta*:
If the annual anniversary śrāddha for one's parents falls on the day of a solar eclipse, the son should perform it with food; if that is unavailable, he should do so with gold or even with raw grain.
Thus; here, the words *darśa*, *ravi*, *pitṛ*, and *suta* are for the purpose of illustration,
because the underlying principle is the same.

Therefore, it has been explained in the *Madanapārijāta* itself that even during a lunar eclipse, the annual *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha and other rites must be performed on that very day with food and other offerings.
This is likewise stated in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*, the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, and the *Prayogapārijāta*.
As for those [verses] which are recited by some:
When the moon rises eclipsed at the commencement of the annual festival (pratyabda), there should be fasting on that day; however, for the subsequent year, it should be on the following day.
Likewise:
"If the sun and the moon both reach their setting while already eclipsed,
then that [rite] must always be performed on the very next day."
"But because of the [first] observation, it is on the second day; but because of the defect of menstrual flow, it is on the fifth.
Since these [rules] are not seen in the extant Smṛtis nor in their commentaries (nibandhas), they lack authority, characterized by non-observance as long as no source for them is found.

At the time of *śrāddha* for the new moon, the solar ingress (*saṅkrānti*), and so forth, as well as during an eclipse, success is achieved through the *śrāddha* performed specifically for the eclipse; by this incidental performance, the obligatory (*nitya*) rite is also accomplished.
Furthermore, even during the impurity caused by birth or death, one must perform the bath and other rites occasioned by an eclipse.
There is no fault in seeing Rāhu (an eclipse) during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mataka*).
Purity shall exist only so long as liberation is not perceived.
Thus it is stated in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*.
And it is not the case that:
"One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, even during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)."
One who does not bathe meets with death; one who bathes incurs no sin.
Thus, it should not be said that the previous statement in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* is redundant;

for it is meaningful either by way of the maxim of "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), or by its intent to establish that birth and death are distinct causes [for impurity], or by its intent to prescribe specific penances for the failure to perform the ritual bath.

By this, the opinion of Jīmūtavāhana—that during an eclipse occurring within a period of impurity (aśauca), one should perform only the ritual bath and not acts such as giving gifts or performing *śrāddha*—is refuted.
This is because purity is declared without distinction;

furthermore, the declaration of a purity that extends from the moment of contact until the release [of the eclipse], expressed by the words "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "until then" (*tāvat*), would be meaningless if it were intended for the bath alone, since the bath itself occurs at the time of contact.
All castes, even during birth-impurity or death-impurity, or upon the sight of Rāhu [during an eclipse],
should perform the Śrāddha after bathing, offering gifts free from deceit.
This is also because it contradicts the statements written by Kālādarśa, Madanapārijāta, and Candraprakāśa:
"During an eclipse, the impurity is that of a corpse (śāva); once it has ended, it is remembered as the impurity of birth (sautika).
Merely by contact with those two, one should perform the sequence of rites after sipping water."
Furthermore, because it is illogical for there to be a sequence of injunctions that depends on multiple factors;

as for the statement found in the *Saṃvatsarapradīpa* and other texts— "In both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), there is no fault during an eclipse of Rāhu"— [it refers to a different context].
Only the ritual bath should be performed, excluding the giving of gifts and the ancestral śrāddha ceremony.
Thus, if it were with root, then it would be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

In reality, it is rootless, because it is stated in the *Prayogapārijāta* as well, and because [the rule] "devoid of giving and funeral offerings" (*dānaśrāddhavivarjita*) would otherwise be redundant.
Voluntary acts such as great gifts (mahādāna) and the like do not occur out of desire, because they are non-contingent (anaimittika).

For great gifts and the like are not prescribed with an eclipse as their specific occasion; rather, the time of an eclipse is merely an auxiliary factor (aṅga), just as it is in the case of the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti) and so forth.
Because the mention of the eclipse occurs in a textual sequence similar to that of "the tongs of time" (kālasandaṃśa),
and because the statement of Aṅgiras, "all castes," excludes impurities caused by birth or death and establishes that purity is for the purpose of specific ritual acts;
here, he says that in the absence of a qualified recipient, the gift should be given even to a Brāhmaṇa who is a Brāhmaṇa by caste alone.
Baudhāyana says:
Whether he be unlearned or learned,
whether he be worthy or unworthy, even if he is a Brahmin who falsely claims to be one, such a Brahmin deserves a gift at the time of receiving it.
Thus:
one who is not a *śrotriya* is one who has not studied the Veda;
for it is said, "A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the *chandas*. (Pāṇini 5.2.84)
84) Thus, because of the grammatical derivation of *śrotriya* as one who studies that [Veda];
and the status of being a worthy recipient (*pātra*) is well known from such passages as, "Not by learning alone," etc. (*):
"Worthiness of being a recipient does not come through learning alone, nor even through austerity. (*).
Where both of these [qualities] and conduct are present, that indeed is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient.
Thus it was stated by Yājñavalkya. Regarding the characteristics of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*vipra*), the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* states:
"One who is endowed with the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), as well as the Vedic studies and the initiation (*upanayana*)."
He who neither teaches nor studies would be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva).
Thus,
because he has lost the refinement that follows the acquisition of the Veda and because there is no restriction regarding his teaching and other duties, he is inferior to the *śrotriya*.
Here, the term "vipra" refers to a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone.
Those who know only the essence of the Gāyatrī and those who are occupied solely with the twilight prayers—
such Brahmins, ignorant of the truth, are engaged in agricultural labor and are merely bearers of the name.
Thus, according to the Caturviṃśatimata; and here there is no optional alternative of equal force: "A gift to a non-Brāhmaṇa is equal [in merit], but double to one who is a Brāhmaṇa in name only."
To a Śrotriya, one gains a hundred-thousandfold merit; but to a worthy recipient (pātra), one attains infinity.
Thus, because Dakṣa has stated that there is a gradation in the fruits [of these times]:
"At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun..."
One should give land, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a brahmin who is a worthy recipient.
Thus, regarding the rule for the recipient during an eclipse, that [text] is primarily concerned with optional (kāmya) gifts;
for it speaks while introducing the topic of optional gifts, and the mention of "land" is intended as an illustration.
Alternatively, the statement may be intended as a restrictive rule (niyama), meaning that the gift of land must be given only to a worthy recipient (pātra).
Otherwise, it would result in the fault of figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*).
At the time of an eclipse, cooked food must be abandoned,
because the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha— beginning with the injunction "one should avoid food from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)"— refers specifically to the occasion of an eclipse.
Food is impure;
for all castes alike, there is impurity upon the sighting of Rāhu [an eclipse].
Having bathed, one should perform one's rites, but one should avoid cooked food [prepared during that time].
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"That which is eclipsed by an eclipse,
as well as what remains from new funeral rites (*navaśrāddha*), and that which has been kept overnight during a planetary affliction (*graha*)."
Thus, according to the *Mitākṣarā* commentary on the Smṛti;
in some cases, Medhātithi states an exception:
Fermented rice-gruel, milk, buttermilk, inspissated milk, ghee, roasted barley flour, and oil cooked with fats— these are never defiled.
Thus [it is said].
Herein, there is a counter-exception regarding roasted flour and oil-cakes;
as for other matters, it is a restatement of what is already eternally established.
A specific rule regarding this is stated in another text: "Fermented rice-gruel, buttermilk, ghee that has been cooked,
and water covered with *kuśa* grass— these are not defiled during the appearance of Rāhu."
Thus it is said;
however, in some recensions, the reading is:
"Water mixed with sour gruel, sugarcane juice, and so forth, is not defiled by sesame seeds or *darbha* grass."
Thus [ends the citation].
Here, the word "is appropriate" (*yuktam*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Sesame seeds and *darbha* grass are to be used together because they are both to be employed.

Therefore, it is prescribed that at the time of Rāhu’s appearance (an eclipse), one should offer water with rice, sesame, and *kuśa* grass; the phrase "it does not incur fault" is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) intended to demonstrate the absence of fault, meaning that a fault would indeed arise if sesame and *kuśa* were not employed.
Furthermore, avoidance [of such food] applies to eating:
that which is the leavings from a *śrāddha* for the deceased, and that which has been kept overnight during an eclipse.
And one should never eat the remnants of what has been eaten by a married couple.
Because of this statement,
and because an expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed for that very act,
it must therefore be avoided even in the case of a prescribed ritual action.

"Because of the statement of Āpastamba: 'That which is unfit to be eaten by the noble ones (āryas) should not be used for sacrifice'—the term 'yajati' (to sacrifice) is an indicator for prescribed ritual acts; thus, in the context of receiving [gifts], there is a prohibition against eating what is forbidden to oneself."
In the *Śivarahasya*:
"One should perform japa and other rites for as long as the solar or lunar eclipse lasts;
one should not sleep nor eat, but should eat after bathing once both [the sun and moon] have been released."
Thus it is said.
In this regard, there is a specific rule from the Śātātapa-smṛti:
"One may eat when the moon has been released [from eclipse], provided that it is not the dead of night."
Thus it is said.
Mārkaṇḍeya has described the "great night" (mahāniśā): "The great night consists of two ghaṭikās during the middle watches of the night."
Thus:
the meaning is that two [units] on each side combined make two, or one on each side makes one.
The *Kalpataru* states that four *muhūrtas* following the half-watch (*sārddhaprahara*) constitute the "great night" (*mahāniśā*).
One's meal should be taken only in one's own home;
one should not eat at that time when the moon or the sun is eclipsed. Once they have been released, one should bathe and afterwards eat in one's own dwelling.
Thus, from the *Brahma Purāṇa*: by this, there is an abstention from the food of others. It also prohibits eating even prior to the eclipse:
Bṛhadgautama says:
During a solar eclipse, one should not eat for four watches prior [to the eclipse];
during a lunar eclipse, however, for three watches, except in the case of children, the elderly, and the sick.
Thus,
the state of being "prior" is relative to the limit of the new moon during an eclipse;
however, the lunar eclipse occurs after the first watch of the night.
One should eat before the turning back [of the shadow] in the first [period], and below the first [mark] in the first [period].
Thus, because Mārkaṇḍeya spoke in this manner regarding the lunar eclipse:
"from the first" means after the first watch (*prathamayāma*), that is, in the second watch;
"in the first" means during the first watch of the night.
"From the first [part] of the day" means during the first watch of the day.
However, in the *Kālādarśa*, following the verse "But the eclipse of the moon should occur," it states: "It should be after sunrise but before midnight."
It should occur in the fourth watch, or below the fourth watch.
And this statement is recited by the name of Vasiṣṭha.
The mention of "above" means that one should eat below the fourth watch of the night.
And here, eating is not being enjoined; rather, since eating is already prompted by natural desire, the time is being restricted.
Nor indeed is that [the case],
for it would entail the displacement of the midday ritual;
rather, on the grounds of parsimony in postulating a fundamental rule (*mūlakalpanālāghava*), eating after the stated time is prohibited.
Alternatively, this [statement] provides a limit for the prohibition of eating without restriction, namely: "One should not eat before the eclipse of the sun.

This is like the provision of a limit by the term *svardṛś* ("the sun") for the closing of the eyes prescribed by the rule: "While the *Rathantara* is being chanted, one should close one's eyes; one should look toward the *svardṛś*.
In this case, the act of eating (*bhujis*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), just like the act of looking. (A. 1, Pā. 6, Adhi. 2)
Regarding the specific rule in the *Matsya* and *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇas* concerning those such as children who are unable to remain without food:
if the eclipse occurs in the evening (*sāyāhna*), there is no meal in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*);
if it occurs in the afternoon, there is none at midday (*madhyāhna*); and if it occurs at midday, there is none during the forenoon (*saṅgava*).
"If there should be [an eclipse] at the time of the junction (saṅgava), one should eat, provided no meal has been taken previously.
Regarding the phrase "if there is a [lunar] eclipse," [it refers to an eclipse occurring] in the afternoon and so forth.

The term "meal" (*bhojana*) is to be supplied [to the prohibitions] such as "not at midday" and so forth. The meaning is that for those unable to observe the [strict] rule regarding the evening meal and so on, there is a prohibition against eating specifically from the afternoon onwards in sequence; therefore, there is no fault in eating prior to that time.
Furthermore, this applies during a solar eclipse and not during a lunar eclipse, because [the timing] is impossible during the afternoon and so forth in the case of the latter.

By this same principle, even during a lunar eclipse, so that there may be no contradiction with the primary injunction for children and others, one should divide the night into five parts; it should be understood that when the eclipse occurs in the fifth part, one must not eat in the fourth, and when the eclipse occurs in the fourth, one must not eat in the third—
just as is seen in the case of a solar eclipse.
This is according to the principle: “Or [it is so] because of the sense, since it is a part of the conceptualization” (Nyāya Sūtra 1.4.2.3).
One cuts with a sacrificial ladle;
one cuts with a knife.

Regarding the injunctions such as "he cuts with the hand," and so forth, concerning the substances to be cut—the clarified butter, the animal, and the sacrificial cake—it is initially argued that the implements for cutting, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, are not fixed, because there is no specific scriptural statement to the contrary. To this, it is replied: since an injunction for an impossible matter cannot exist, the injunctive power must necessarily [specify] the capacity [of the means].

Therefore, it must be accepted that [the Vedic injunction] has auxiliary factors; thus, the injunction itself, aided by its own potency (*śakti*), determines the specific implement to be employed according to its capacity.

Consequently, the ladle (*sruva*) is determined as suitable for the liquid substance of clarified butter (*ājya*), the sharp-edged axe (*svadhiti*)—a specific type of knife—for the meat to be cut, and the hand for the prepared sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). This is the established determination.
The same applies here as well.

By the force of the sense, there would be an assumption of an injunction—that is, an assumption of a fixed meaning—because it is a part of the whole, since the word assumed through the force of the sense is a part of the injunctive sentence; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
This is stated in the Skanda-purāṇa (Mādhava-khaṇḍa):
When a lunar eclipse occurs after midnight,
one should eat during the forenoon, and by no means at midday.
O Śikhivāhana, when the moon's conjunction occurs during the latter part of the night or during the day, one should not take food during that daytime.
Thus [it is said].
And Hemādri, citing the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, states:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should not eat during the first four watches."
Some sages say there are three, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
Thus,
this should be determined according to whether one is capable or incapable [of fasting].
When the rising of the moon has been swallowed [by Rāhu], there is no eating during the day.
"One should not eat during the day before the moon has risen from its eclipse," according to the statement of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha.
As for that which [is stated]:
When Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun at the time of twilight,
then one should not eat during the day, except for the sick, women, and children.
Thus, the prohibition against eating during the day on the occasion of a lunar eclipse refers specifically to the case where the moon rises already eclipsed (*grastodaya*),
because this assumes a single underlying source and is thus simpler.
In this matter as well, the arrangement regarding those who are ill and so forth should be understood to be exactly as before.
Regarding the two [planets] being eclipsed,
Śātātapa says:
"Having bathed and seen [the eclipse], one should give [gifts] on the following day for those two when they have set during an eclipse."
Thus;
"of those two" refers to the moon and the sun.
As for that which—
One should not eat for a day and a night when there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun;
however, having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having seen the release [of the celestial body], one may eat.
Thus it is said;
however, that too refers specifically to the period when [the moon] is eclipsed.
But in the case of a lunar eclipse, it should be understood that the "day and night" (ahorātra) consists of that night and the day following it.
In this context, the root *dṛś* (to see) signifies the characteristic of rising.
If the sun and the moon reach their setting while already eclipsed,
then a person, having bathed at the rising on the following day, may take food.
Thus, because eating is prescribed at sunrise by Bhṛgu;
and also in the Kālādarśa, Gārgya says:
When Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun at the time of twilight,
one should not eat on that day, nor ever during the night.
Thus [it is said].

Here, the phrase "at any time" (kadācana) is for the purpose of prohibiting the observance of restrictive vows (dhāraṇaparāṇavratasya) and the breaking of a fast (pāraṇa) on lunar days such as the full moon or under specific constellations.
Regarding eating during an eclipse or when it is pierced [by another planet], an expiation has been stated in the Mādhavīya:
Kātyāyana states:
Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten on that very same day [after the eclipse], one is purified by a three-night fast.
Thus [it is said].
Here, the mention of "day" (dina) is an indicator for the period during which eating is prohibited, other than the time of an eclipse.
At the time of a total solar eclipse (grastāsta), all daily religious duties (āhnika) must be performed except for eating.

When the moon has been eclipsed and has set, having ascertained the time of liberation, one should perform the ritual bathing, fire-oblations, and other rites; then, at the rising of the moon, one should eat again.

Thus, according to the statement of Śātātapa cited in the *Madanaratna*, the mention of the moon here is not intended to be restrictive, because the purpose is fulfilled by the mere occurrence of an eclipse ending in sunset. And in this way, even for the sun, when there is an eclipse ending in sunset, the morning bath and other such rites must be performed.
Regarding this, the optional fast is prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa: "It is obligatory during both solstices, as well as during the two equinoxes,
during eclipses of the moon and sun, during the vyatīpāta yoga, and on the festival days (parvan)."
For one who, with a serene mind, fasts for a day and night and performs bathing, ancestral rites, giving, and recitation, that merit shall become inexhaustible.
Thus it is said;
and also in the Laiṅga Purāṇa:
"Having fasted for one night, having bathed, and having given according to one's ability..."
