It is like the withdrawal of a serpent from its slough; it is the emergence from the sheath of evil.
Thus it is said.

Regarding this, some maintain that because of the suffix *niṣṭhā* in *upoṣita* and the suffix *ktvā* in *upoṣya*, which both denote a prior action, the fasting must take place on the preceding day (*pūrvedyus*).
Others, however, argue that based on its inclusion in the list beginning with "the solstices" (*ayanādi*), the suffix *lyap* is applied in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*).
And, as in the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open," they say that the fast is to be observed on that very day, intending merely the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*);
the meaning is that this refers to the suffix *kta*.
This alone is logical,
because in the *puraścaraṇa* [rite], fasting is prescribed beforehand, as stated: "When there is an eclipse of the sun or the moon, one should first fast."

And this [rule] applies to a householder who is separated from his son; however, a householder who has a son should not observe a fast on the day of the Saṅkrānti, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
or during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
Thus it is because of Nārada’s statement regarding exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
To this, it must be said:
this is not an exclusion.
This is because, as in the case of the statement "one does not choose the Hotṛ," there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*);
on the contrary, as in the case of "one does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice," it is because [the prohibition] is not proximate (*asannihitatva*).
Or, even if it were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), nevertheless, an independent fast (*svatantra-upavāsa*) occasioned by the *saṅkrānti* and other such events would be more appropriate.

Otherwise, there would be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) even in cases such as the fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) when it coincides with the solstice (*ayana*), during an eclipse, during the fast that is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to a great gift (*mahādāna*), or during the fast of the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances.

For this [eleventh-day fast] possesses the status of an ancillary because it is understood as a fast that serves to purify the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), as expressed in the injunction: "having fasted for a day and night.

This is because, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the passage, "When one who is initiated (*dīkṣita*) sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," the initiation is understood to have the purpose of bathing by way of purifying the agent, just as in the present case.

For this very reason, it is stated in the section on Ekādaśī that the prohibition of fasting during solar transits (*saṅkrānti*) and similar occasions applies only to fasting performed for those specific purposes. Consequently, we observe that even householders who have sons perform the fast as an ancillary part of *puraścaraṇa*, as practiced by the learned without hesitation. Therefore, the fast consisting of abstaining from food for a day and night and bathing, which constitutes an ancillary element, is indeed permissible even for a householder who has sons.

But that man who, having fasted for a single night on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) or similar occasions, beholds Rāhu and performs the ritual bathing and Śrāddha according to the rules, attains inexhaustible merit.
Thus, according to what was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya, the fasting— whether independent or prompted by that [eclipse]— belongs to him in that very context as a *paryudāsa* (an exception). However,
the prohibition of eating prompted by an eclipse certainly applies to him on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) as well, since there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
And all this, beginning with the ritual bath, applies only during a solar eclipse visible to the eye; it does not apply when [the sun] is obscured by clouds and the like, nor for those who are blind.
However, in the case of a lunar or solar eclipse, [the rites should be performed] as long as [the eclipsed body] remains within the range of vision.
Thus it is said:
"For a *śrāddha* offered during the appearance of Rāhu lasts as long as the moon and stars;
bathing, giving, austerity, and the *śrāddha* performed at the sight of Rāhu yield infinite merit."
This is because, in occasional injunctions (naimittika-vidhi) such as "having seen [a solar eclipse], one should bathe," the verb *dṛś* is employed to denote visual cognition (*cākṣuṣa-jñāna*);
otherwise, it would be redundant,
since the mere cognition is already obtained by the mention of the occasion itself, and one is entitled to perform the occasional rite only upon the ascertainment of that occasion.
And the act of seeing belongs to the agent of the bathing and so forth, because of the hearing of the suffix *ktvā*.

Even in cases such as "at the sight of Rāhu" (*rāhudarśane*), where there is no hearing of the suffix *ktvā*, the term *dṛśi* denotes merely the act of seeing common to both oneself and others; nevertheless, by the maxim "what is seen in one instance [is understood elsewhere]," the seeing belonging to the agent is obtained.
For this very reason, when there is an eclipse of the moon at night on a Sunday, there is no occasion for ritual bathing and other such acts.
For this same reason it is said:
"If there should be an eclipse of the sun at night, or likewise an eclipse of the moon during the day..."
Both of these were shown to the king, as well as whatever was most subtle.
Thus is the statement that the predictions of astrologers are unreliable;

otherwise, if the root *dṛś* (to see) were taken as signifying mere cognition, the undesirable consequence would be unavoidable that one would have to perform ritual bathing and other rites upon an eclipse occurring in another location.
In the passage, "Neither of the two should be reported to the king," the statement regarding non-reporting would be for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) [in your view].
In my view, however, it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣ�ṭārtha*); since reporting an unfit person to the king is fruitless, the non-reportability is restated as a matter of established fact.
And it is not the case that—
When there is a solar eclipse at night or a lunar eclipse during the day,
one should not perform ritual bathing, nor should one ever give gifts on such occasions.

It cannot be said that there is a cessation [of the rule] based on this statement, because that would result in the fallacy of treating the prohibition (*niṣedha*) and the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

Now, if by the word "seeing" (*darśana*) one intends to mean the fitness to be the object of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñāna*), then there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to eclipses occurring at night or during the day; yet, even so, there arises the problem that people in other locations would possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the rite simply by virtue of the eclipse being visible to those in their own location.
This is because, according to the opponent's view, the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is not intended to be expressed.

Nor should it be argued that in whatever place a lunar or solar eclipse is perceptible through visual cognition, that place constitutes the occasion for the *udita-homa* (the offering at sunrise), just as sunrise is;
for it is more appropriate to accept the identity of the agent as the verbal condition, rather than postulating a non-verbal spatial location as the limiting factor.

Now, if it is intended that there be a fitness for being the object of a visual cognition by the same agent, then let there simply be the status of being its object as the qualifier, since that is presented first; what is the use of "fitness," which is presented later?
For by that much alone, the over-extension [of the rule] to a solar eclipse occurring in another location is avoided.

Therefore, the ancients hold that acts such as ritual bathing should be performed only when the eclipse is actually visible to the eye, and not when an eclipse occurs behind clouds or for those who are blind.
They should be addressed as follows:
"One should bathe after having seen [the sun]"—

here, by means of the suffix *ktvā*, which is prescribed under the governing rule concerning the connection between verbal roots (*dhātusambandha*), there is a relationship between seeing and bathing, just as in the case of "one performs the *Agnihotra* for as long as one lives."

In this case, by means of the suffix *ṇamul*, a direct connection is perceived between the two, just as there is between living and the *homa* offering. That [connection] cannot, however, be understood as being by way of a condition (*nimitta*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as seeing a jar; nor can it be understood through the eclipse (*uparāga*), according to the principle "we do not tolerate the qualification of the oblation (*havis*) [by a mere incidental attribute]," just as the affliction (*ārtti*) is qualified by the oblation. (Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra 6.4.6) Nor can it be understood through the eclipse, according to the maxim: "We do not tolerate the qualification of the oblation. Just as the affliction is qualified by the oblation, so too [the affliction] is not here qualified by the eclipse.

It must be stated that the act of seeing (*darśana*) is what is qualified [by the number], because otherwise there would follow the consequence of repetition of bathing and other rites for every single instance of seeing— just as there is repetition of the *japa* mantra upon seeing impurity when the rule says, "Having seen impurity, one mutters the *avaddham manaḥ*," and as there is repetition of the *Soma* sacrifice at every occurrence of its performance.

Furthermore, it would follow that those who observe the vow of not looking at the eclipsed sun (*noparaktam ādityam īkṣeta*)— who intentionally avoid looking for fear of the great effort required by bathing and other rites— would be rendered ineligible [for the rite] if they were unable to see an evil planet.
Furthermore, because it is prohibited to look at impure things— according to the rule, "The Rāhu and the stars are not impure"— impurity cannot serve as its cause;
for all [planets] are indeed impure at the time of an eclipse.
Impurity due to death is prescribed upon taking up [the corpse], and that due to birth upon releasing it;
by merely coming into contact with these two, one should perform the ritual sequence after sipping water.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.

Nor should it be argued that, since a prohibition is logically applicable only to matters prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*), there can be no engagement in a scripturally enjoined (*vaidha*) vision; for the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) itself is not something to be enjoined.

Now, it cannot be said on the basis of the *Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa* that the nature of an eclipse is what causes impurity, for that would result in the occurrence of impurity for people in one region due to an eclipse occurring in another region;
rather, it is the very sight [of the eclipse] that is the cause.
For all castes alike, there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) upon the sighting of Rāhu.
Because of this statement;

as for the statement regarding the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), its purpose is to show that impurity arises from mere contact, let alone from seeing it—this is why the suffix *-mātra* is employed. If it is argued that since impurity also has seeing as its cause, just like bathing and so forth, there is no impurity prior to the seeing; thus, because the prohibition does not apply before the seeing, there is the possibility of seeing, and therefore it [impurity] would indeed be the occasioning cause.

Nevertheless, because one who is subject to impurity (*āśauca*) caused by birth or death is prohibited from being seen, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that such a person lacks the qualification for bathing and other rites. Nor can this consequence be accepted as desirable, for it is said: "One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and likewise during birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)."
One who does not bathe incurs death; one who bathes does not incur sin.
This is because it contradicts the statement in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*.

Now, one might object: although looking at [the sun or moon] is generally forbidden during periods of impurity—as in the rule "one who is impure shall not look at Rāhu or the stars"—there is no fault in seeing Rāhu during both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*).

If it is argued that, because this [text] shows a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the sight [of the corpse] during the impurity caused by birth or death, there is no obstruction to eligibility even during such impurity—[we reply:
no. For by this, the act of seeing is not counter-exceptionally permitted; rather, it is the bathing and other rites occasioned by that [sight] which are addressed.
Purity shall exist only so long as the release [from the body] is not seen.

Thus, because the remainder of the statement establishes purification in the form of eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), there is no fault in the fact that the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*) would not otherwise be applicable due to the operation of prohibitions regarding impurity from birth and so forth; consequently, the explanatory reference (*anuvāda*) "there is no fault at the sight of Rāhu" is untenable, and the lack of eligibility remains as previously stated.
Nor does this apply even when both [the sacrificer and his wife] are subject to impurity regarding the prohibition of the sight [of Rāhu].

It should not be argued that eligibility [for bathing] will exist because of the scriptural statement, "One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and also during birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka)," for otherwise,
even a blind person or one who is impure would incur that obligation even when the sky is covered by clouds.

Because there is no such statement regarding impurity caused by the touch of a Śūdra and the like, and because such [impurity] would not be applicable [in that case], and because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of someone in another country; and because in those cases, by qualifying [the eclipse] with "being visible to those in the same location" and so forth, it is understood that the nature of the eclipse itself is the cause, let it be the same everywhere—what is the use of this "half-old woman" logic (*ardhajaratīnyāya*)? Furthermore, since it is heard in some places that the eclipse is the cause and in others that visibility is the cause, one of these two must necessarily be the case.

Since the coloring (*uparāga*) is common to both seeing and non-seeing, it is logical for that which is eternal to serve as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) according to the principle of "he who by this" (Brahma Sūtra 5.3.13, sūtra 37), but not for the non-eternal act of seeing.

For this very reason, it was stated in the section on the *ātithyā* sacrifice (*A. 1, Pāda 7, Adhikaraṇa 13*) that its conclusion by means of the *iḍā* is achieved through the obligatory preceding *iḍā* alone, and not through the non-obligatory subsequent *iḍā*.
Furthermore, since "seizing" (*grahaṇa*) is independent, it is appropriate for it to function as a causal condition (*nimitta*), whereas "seeing" (*darśana*), being dependent upon a relation, is not.
And this has been explained in the subsequent section regarding the word "subsequent" (*uttara*).
(9.2.5) Furthermore, if the very nature of an eclipse were the *nimitta* (the occasioning cause), the explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) “there is no fault in seeing Rāhu” would be untenable.
Nor can it be argued that when a vision [of Rāhu] occurs—whether through negligence or intentionally by transgressing a prohibition—the occasional rites such as bathing are enjoined;

for the removal of the sin (*pratyavāya*) produced by the transgression of a prohibition requires a specific means, and rites such as bathing require a specific purpose. This is illustrated by the case of the horse-sacrifice offering (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*) and the recitation of mantras, regarding which it is said: “one does not give a maned beast.”

For, just as [the injunction] "one should not touch the sacrificial post" (A. 9, Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 3) serves to avoid the demerit (*pratyavāya*) arising from the transgression of that prohibition, it would follow that bathing and other such acts likewise serve that same purpose.

And thus, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the Niṣadha section, the injunction for bathing and so forth would be difficult to obtain for eclipses in general, as it would apply only upon the transgression of that [Niṣadha rule] through the acquisition of knowledge regarding bathing and the like.

Now, one might object: in the second prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), since it is understood from the explanatory passage (arthavāda) that the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi is intended for the expiation of a fault, and since a fault pertains to what is prohibited, and since the mantra statement—beginning with "Therefore, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is not to be touched"—is prescribed [in that context], it is appropriate [to conclude that the prohibition applies].
[The purpose of the rule] would be the avoidance of sin (*pratyavāya*).

However, in this case, since the injunction regarding the cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*naimittika*) is stated without reference to a prohibition, and because there is no syntactic unity with a prohibition, it does not have the purpose of avoiding the sin produced by transgressing that [prohibition].

Rather, since a prohibition is absent from any injunction whatsoever, or because the act of seeing has occurred through the transgression of a [general] prohibition, the general injunction—"one who has seen [the forbidden object] should bathe"—is easily established by restating (*anūdya*) that seeing which has already occurred.
If it is argued that this may be so, we say no;
for even then, since one who has not transcended the prohibition and remains in a state of impurity lacks the qualification [for ritual acts], that deficiency is difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, such a view would contradict the statement in the Laiṅga Purāṇa.

Therefore, if it is the mere sight [of the sun] that generates impurity, then there would be a lack of eligibility for those who are impure; if, however, the conjunction existing in its own nature generates impurity, then the consequence would be a lack of eligibility for everyone.

What need is there for further elaboration? If one who acts with prior deliberation were to forcibly bring about the causal conditions [for merit], then no one would engage in bathing and other such acts that are sources of suffering; thus, the entire injunction would be rendered invalid.

Furthermore, regarding a *saṅkrama*, the merit belongs to the preceding and succeeding times, whereas in the case of an eclipse (*uparāga*), it lasts only as long as it remains within the range of vision.
The meaning that results is that bathing and other rites are to be performed at the very same time as the object becomes the focus of visual cognition.
Nor is this possible, because there is a contradiction between looking [at the moon] and bathing, as they are accomplished by facing upwards and downwards respectively.

Nor should it be argued that since the act of seeing (*dṛśi*) is common to both error and valid cognition, there is no contradiction with bathing for one who has the error of a reflection in water, or for one who possesses the valid cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the original object (*bimba*) thinking "this is that very same moon";
for in that case, the contradiction with performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and the like would be difficult to avoid.

And because of the prohibition, "neither eclipsed nor situated in water," for this very reason, an eclipse characterized by visibility— like the fire of a portent— is not the cause, since it does not transcend the previously mentioned defects; furthermore, because there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) if a specific [visibility] were intended as the condition.

Furthermore, the "seeing" (darśana) which qualifies the subject of the injunction is not intended to be significant, just as the "twofold nature" (ubhayatva) of the oblation [in the *ubhayādyā* sacrifice] is not intended; for it is not intended here.

Now, if you argue that in this way the "seeing" need not be the occasion (*nimitta*) because it causes confusion, then let it be so; however, just as in the injunction for the muttering (*japa*) qualified by seeing during the bringing of the twilight (*sandhyā-haraṇa*) performed by the mist-maker (*nīhārakartṛka*), it is precisely the eclipse (*uparāga*) that is the occasion, and the bathing (*snāna*) and other acts qualified by seeing are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the bathing and other acts enjoined by their respective specific scriptural passages.

Alternatively, only the perception [of the mark] is enjoined; let the ascertainment of the mark be exactly as you desire. And by the mere observation of the nature of the effect, the cessation of blindness and so forth will occur, just as the establishment of the sacred fires results in the destruction of each individual fire and the like.

Alternatively, if the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is understood, then because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), just as the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) functions to specify the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), the very act of seeing will serve to fulfill the qualification (*adhikāra*) by way of determining the occasion (*nimitta*). Since the prohibition "one who is eclipsed" and so forth does not apply to what is enjoined (*vaidha*), and since in this view the prohibition "one who is impure during the eclipse of the moon or stars" applies only after the seeing has occurred, all persons will possess the qualification.
If it is argued that "this path is correct," it is not correct.

In this context, the word *darśana* does not denote visual perception (*cākṣuṣajñāna*), because it is used by experts even for mere ascertainment—as in "the six systems of philosophy" (*ṣaḍdarśanāni*) and "the system of the ritualists" (*yājñikadarśana*)—and because of the Vedic scripture:

"The Self, indeed, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavya*). Furthermore, the term *īkṣati* (to see/contemplate) is employed to denote the knowledge of the Lord, as in "He performed *īkṣā*" (*sa īkṣāñcakre*) and "Because of *īkṣā*, [the cause] is not that which is non-scriptural" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*). Thus, *īkṣati* signifies seeing in the sense of knowing.
Also in the *Aitareya*:
"He recites the verse beginning with *ṛtā vā yasya rodasī*; this is the unimpaired eye. Therefore, when two people are disputing, whoever says, 'I have seen this with my own eyes,' they believe him.
Here, too, the mention of the "eye" would be purposeless [if the mantra were not for the purpose of seeing].

Since the visual cognition is obtained by the mere expression "I saw," and because the instrumental case is prescribed in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakṣaṇa)— as seen in the example "he saw the teacher with his pupil"—
therefore, even mere cognition is the object of seeing.
For this very reason—
"A woman becomes impure for three nights upon seeing menstrual blood"—
such is the Dharmaśāstra.

However, the frequent application of the term "eye" (cākṣuṣa) [to denote the sense of sight] arises from repeated usage, just as the word "go" came to mean "beast" in general due to its prior application to the specific animal "cow."

Or, even if it were to denote visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñāna*), nevertheless an injunction regarding "seeing" (*darśana*) is not possible; for since that [seeing] is already established as a possibility (*pakṣaprāpta*), an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is impossible, and because enjoining [it] with multiple objectives would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Now, suppose the view is held that bathing and so forth, qualified by the restriction of seeing, are what is enjoined.
Nevertheless, it is not easy to maintain that this excludes the blind and others;
for even with respect to them, the performance of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) proceeds.

Indeed, unlike in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), there is no requirement to include all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) in occasional rites, as that would contradict their very nature as being contingent upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
For that alone is a valid occasion (*nimitta*) which necessarily compels the performance of an action within its own existence;
for it is impossible for that which does not compel performance to be an occasion.
Indeed, not everyone is always capable of performing [the rite] with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).

Therefore, even with the omission of some auxiliary factor (*aṅga*), the entitlement for those such as the blind to perform the occasional rite (*naimittika*) remains difficult to deny, even when the factor of seeing—such as in the case of a sky covered by clouds—is lost.

For this very reason, there can be no restriction of the occasion (*nimitta*) based on the requirements of the occasional rite, as that would contradict the scriptural statement regarding the occasion.
As it is said: "He whose two fires... (Jaimini Sūtra 6.4.8).

In this case, however, since the mere following of the fire (*agnyanugamana*) is the occasion (*nimitta*), and because the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration)—which is established as producing both fires—lacks the capacity to generate each individual fire, the injunction of the primary act itself would be untenable.

Furthermore, since the noun not in grammatical apposition with the verb refers to something remote, there is no distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara*) and thus no differentiation of acts (*karmabheda*). Consequently, out of necessity, the occasion must be restricted.

Moreover, there is no contradiction here with the blind and others by virtue of the primary acts such as bathing, which would necessitate postulating that [the injunction] refers to subjects other than them.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the blind and others would also be entitled to the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires);
for that [act] lacks inherent necessity (*nityatva*) in its own nature, and if it were so, it would result in an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
And this has been explained by Bhaṭṭa Someśvara.

Furthermore, according to the principle of "each principal act" (*pratipradhānanyāya*), there would be the consequence of repeating the observation [of the eclipse] for the sake of the ritual bath (*snāna*), the *śrāddha*, and so forth.

Even though the time of the eclipse is a single great duration, the constituent parts of the Sākamedha sacrifice—such as the Anīkavatī and others—which are prescribed over a period of two days, must be performed at their respective times, such as morning and so on.

Because it is encompassed by the rules for the performance of the ritual with its constituent parts (*sāṅgaprayoga*), such as the rule beginning, "When [the moon] is being swallowed, there shall be a bath," which governs the application of the bath and other rites according to their distinct timings;

nor is there a case of "once-and-for-all" application (*tantratā*) here on the analogy of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as in the cases: "A Brāhmaṇa should consecrate the fires in spring" and "He cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations" (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 11.3.3).
Because there is no mention of an independent time;
nor is there an extension of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) as in the case of the *yūpāhuti* offering (Aṣṭādhyāyī 11.2.7),

as there is in the passage, "Having churned the fire near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he offers the *yūpāhuti*," where such an extension occurs due to the identity of the location "near" in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*).
In this case, however, there is a discrepancy due to the difference in the location of the primary elements (*pradhāna*).
Nor does the principle of the *svaru* apply here (A.

11, Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 5). In that [other] instance, because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a single unit (*tantra*), its first chip (*śakala*), which is produced as a byproduct (*anuniṣpādī*), is also singular; therefore, it is logical that the *svaru* shares that same unitary character.
But here it is not so, because there is no such reason.
Therefore, repetition is difficult to avoid.

Nor should it be argued that there is no need for repetition because seeing [the deity] is merely an ancillary part of the ritual bath, and because its occurrence after the *śrāddha* and other rites is established by the very fact that it follows the bath.
"Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and the *śrāddha* ceremony yield infinite merit during an eclipse of Rāhu," because this establishes that [the *śrāddha*] is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the [eclipse].

Now, if it is argued that since the "sight" (*darśana*) serves as the basis for establishing the entitlement (*adhikāra*) by virtue of being the determining condition (*nimitta*), and since it is an ancillary, there should be no repetition once that determination has occurred even upon a single sighting—[we reply: No.

Because the ascertainment of the occasion (*nimitta*) existing at the time of performance is required—just like the recollection of the matter to be performed—otherwise, one who possesses life even at midday would incur the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the *agnihotra* sacrifice.

If, in that case, the entitlement belongs to one who has the ascertainment of life delimited by the evening time, then here too it is the same: the entitlement to the ritual bath and so forth belongs to one who perceives the eclipse as delimited by the time of being swallowed (*grasyamāna*) and so on. Thus, the two cases are equal.

Furthermore, since there is no certainty regarding the presence of the specific qualification— namely, the absence of obstacles that cannot be removed by effort as determined by astrology and so forth— in the sacrifice performed on the occasion of the contact of the moon with the *sphya* (sacrificial wooden sword), which must be performed prior to the invocation (*āvāhana*), no one would engage without hesitation in such acts as the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and the three-night fast, which are auxiliary to the great gifts (*mahādāna*) to be performed before an eclipse.

Furthermore, if the "sight" (*darśana*) were the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), then in such injunctions as "one should bathe during an eclipse" (*uparāge snāyāt*), there would result the necessity of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "eclipse" (*uparāga*) to mean "sight.
If it is argued that since the eclipse itself is the occasioning cause, the same [necessity for indication] applies to the "sight" as well, that is true;

however, in sentences containing the locative case, such as "one should bathe upon seeing Rāhu" (*rāhudarśane snāyāt*), according to the rule "and [the locative is used] when one state indicates another state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*, Pāṇini 2.3.37), [the locative is justified].

37) Thus, by virtue of the locative case prescribed for the purpose of characterizing an action (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*), just as in the example "he went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*), where the act of milking characterizes the time of departure, it is necessary that the verb *dṛś* (to see) here also serves to characterize time.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to perform acts such as bathing at that specific moment, it is more appropriate in this context to understand the locative as indicating "fitness" (*yogyatā*) according to the maxim: "that which has already once commenced [is understood to continue]."

The meaning of the sūtra is this: the locative case should be used where there is an indication (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, a secondary mark (*upalakṣaṇa*)—of an action such as "going," by means of another action such as "milking" expressed by a verbal root (e.g., *go-bhāvena*), for the purpose of indicating the time and so forth that delimit that going.

For this very reason, in cases involving words ending in the locative and joined with the word *dṛśi* ("seeing"), there is no injunction regarding the act of seeing; because that which is already established cannot serve as a mark, while that which is not yet established cannot logically be so. This is because the locative case prescribed for indicating an action—as in the case of words like *abhi*—obstructs the injunctive force [of the verb].

And thus, even in the case of words ending in the suffix *ktvā*, it is easy to assume an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "eclipse" qualified by fitness, according to the logic established for sentences containing the word "seeing," because of the parsimony of assuming a single basis. Furthermore, there is no injunction to see [the eclipse] in words ending in *ktvā*, because the suffix *ktvā* is not injunctive; whereas the subsequent portion beginning with "bathes" (*snāti*) is injunctive, as it enjoins the bathing and so forth. Moreover, in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there would be the fault of indicating (*lakṣaṇā-patti*), and there would also be the consequence of assuming further injunctions regarding the posteriority in time and the commonality of agent, which are already implied by the sense.
But in the case where [the word] is defined by secondary indication (upacāra), it is merely the definition itself that [constitutes the meaning],
since the qualities such as occurring at a later time are obtained solely through the force of the cause (nimitta).
And thus, this is the meaning:
In order to avoid the total meaninglessness of this restatement:
"When there is a solar eclipse at night, or likewise a lunar eclipse during the day,
one should not perform an ablution, nor should one ever give a gift."

Thus, by the exclusion of an eclipse occurring in another location, one should learn from the scriptures that an eclipse capable of being perceived by the eye occurs in the same location, and perform bathing and other rites at those respective times.
Regarding an eclipse occurring during the birth-constellation (*janmarāśi*) and so forth, there is a defect; the propitiatory rites (*śāntika*) for that case are to be found in the *Śāntiprakāśa*.
In this context, regarding the reception of mantra-initiation (*mantradīkṣā*):
The month, lunar mansion, and so forth need not be purified. At a sacred pilgrimage site, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, at the festivals of Tantudāma and Parvan,
one who is performing a mantra-initiation need not purify the month, lunar mansion, and other such factors.

The mere recitation of the mantra at the time of an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva— that is called "instruction" (upadeśa).
Thus, according to statements in the *Sārasaṅgraha* and other works. Regarding the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) here, it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacāndrikā*:
"During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, being pure and having first fasted..."
Likewise, one should stand in water reaching up to the navel that flows toward the ocean.
Alternatively, having bathed in sacred water and being pure, having first observed a fast,
one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra from the moment of [the moon's] eclipse until its release.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the materials];
at the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and the satiation of Brahmins.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, one should worship and satisfy the guru;
in this way, the mantra will be perfected and the deity will become gracious.
Thus it is said in that very same [text]:
"In the event of being unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform recitation (japa) four times the number of the oblations."
And for the twice-born, [the merit] is sixfold and eightfold respectively.
Japa takes the place of the fire-oblation (homa) precisely at the time of the oblation, because it acquires the attributes [of the oblation] through substitution; furthermore,

since the fourfold merit is prescribed for japa delimited by the time beginning from its commencement and ending with its conclusion, and since that [delimitation] is impossible in that [context of the oblation],
preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) does not take place when the moon rises or sets while eclipsed.

Because it is not established that [the process] begins with contact and ends with liberation; and because only those [factors] such as contact and liberation that are capable of being seen are the causal conditions, according to the statement: "as far as the range of vision extends."

For this very reason, some maintain that even the *śrāddha* and other such rites do not apply to those performing the *puraścaraṇa*, because the obligatory (*nitya*) is sublated by the optional (*kāmya*). However, in reality, since the injunction for the optional rite fulfills its purpose even with respect to one who is ineligible for the *śrāddha* and so forth, it does not possess the power to sublate the obligatory. There is a difference [between these cases], however: in the case of the *godohana* vessel or the *ukthya* sacrifice, because they are dependent respectively on the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*) and the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, they cannot find a place without sublating the *camasa* cup and the *agniṣṭoma* conclusion; thus, they do indeed sublate. This constitutes the disparity.
Regarding the prohibition of specific times for auspicious rites, Hemādri states:
"In all auspicious ceremonies, one must certainly avoid nine days beginning with the thirteenth lunar day, as well as during eclipses of the moon and the sun."
Likewise:
"The piercing (vedha) beginning on the twelfth and ending on the third lunar day is prescribed for a lunar eclipse;
that beginning on the eleventh and ending on the fourth is proclaimed for a solar eclipse."
Thus,
this [rule] is to be established according to whether the task is mandatory or non-mandatory.
This concludes the determination of the time for receiving [the precepts].

Now follows the determination of *ekabhakta* (eating once a day). Its nature is described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "That which is eaten according to rule after the midpoint of the day has passed [is *ekabhakta*]."
Therefore, that which is called "eating once a day" (ekabhakta) should indeed take place during the daytime alone.
In this context, by the etymological name "ekabhakta" (one-meal), the cessation of a second meal is indicated.
By the word "niyamena" (by rule), there is the attainment of the general dharma of the prescribed vow.
Therefore, the meaning of the term "ekabhakta" is eating during the day accompanied by the absence of a second meal.
Regarding this, Devala states the specific detail:
"That which is eaten according to rule when half the day has passed..."
That is declared to be a single meal (ekabhakta), provided it is reduced by three mouthfuls.
Thus it is said;
and for this [fast], midday is the primary time:
"In the case of Ekabhakta, the lunar day (tithi) that extends throughout midday is always to be accepted."
Thus it is stated in the *Padma-purāṇa*.
That [time] also is not the full [day];
rather, it is specifically the time after midday, according to the statement: “when half the day has passed.”
Regarding this, Hemādri states that midday is defined by a threefold division [of the day], whereas Mādhava maintains it is by a fivefold division.

Others, however, say that because there is no decisive evidence favoring one over the other, the period following the sun's turning point (āvartana) is the primary time (mukhyakāla), regardless of whether the division is fivefold or threefold.
As for the secondary time (gauṇakāla), it extends from that point until sunset, since it is permitted that [the rite] may be performed during the day alone.
In that case, if it pervades both days or does not touch either, the [observance] belongs to the first day alone,
because there is a pervasion of the secondary time (gauṇakāla). And even when the primary time is not touched, the performance of the *ekabhakta* occurs precisely at the primary time.
Whatever decrease or increase occurs in the lunar day (tithi) and so forth on the subsequent day,
that same amount should be taken on the previous day for one's own rites, even if it was not perceived there.
Thus, according to the statement cited by Hemādri:
"On the preceding day, [the calculation refers] to the previous lunar day (tithi) and so forth.
Regarding decrease, increase, and equality, some maintain that these are always in relation to sixty ghaṭikās, and not in relation to the previous lunar day and so forth.
Hemādri, however, maintains that when the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*) spans two days, the determination is made according to the *yugma* (pairing) rule;
for while there is a fixed rule regarding the worship of the pairings beginning with the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) and so forth,
there is an injunction for the increase by two days (*dvy-ṛddhi*) in cases such as the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha and the *vṛddhi* ceremonies.

By the phrase "in the case of the *niyama* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *ekabhakta* (single-meal fast); since it can be said that the application of the rule regarding pairs (*yugma-vākya*) extends even to the *ekabhakta*, [the opponent's position is untenable].
As for the non-contact (*asparśa*) and the equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*), he claims their determination is based on the pervasion of the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*).
That is not correct.
This would result in the fallacy of "half-old-woman-ness" (applying a rule only partially), nor is this the scope of a pair of statements,
because the rule concerning time is more authoritative.
For just as a determination is possible by following the pervasion of the primary time (*mukhyakāla*) rather than showing regard for the statement regarding paired days (*yugmavākya*),
so too is it possible by the pervasion of the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*).
Otherwise, indeed—
"A time subsequent to the primary time is the secondary (gauṇa) time for the preceding rite.
Since the secondary time is already obtained from this very general statement, it would follow that prescribing it again specifically for the "one-meal" (ekabhakta) period would be redundant.
Therefore, it is established that where there is a specific injunction regarding the secondary time, the determination is made by its full extent as well.

The *ekabhakta* (single-meal fast), which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) element, should be performed at midday on the lunar day determined as the primary time for the rite. However, the *ekabhakta*, which is the primary element itself, may be performed even during the secondary period (*gauṇakāla*), according to the maxim: "In case of conflict between a subsidiary and its primary, the rule follows the purpose of that primary."
(1.2.9.25) For this very reason, where the primary [time for the one-meal practice] is the afternoon and so forth, the performance of the one-meal (*ekabhakta*) even at night is not contradictory.
However, that one-meal which serves as a substitute for fasting must be performed at midday on the lunar day appropriate for it.

Thus concludes the determination regarding eating once a day (*ekabhakta*). Now follows the determination regarding fasting by night (*nakta*); that consists in eating at night characterized by the absence of eating during the day.
However, some say that there is no rule that *nakta* must necessarily be of the nature of eating;
rather, its being of the nature of eating is merely common.
For this very reason, they maintain that the description of the *navarātra-vrata* as a *nakta-vrata*, as stated by Mādhava and others, is consistent.

And in that case, the lunar day (tithi) that extends through the evening (pradoṣa) should be observed; for there is the statement of Vatsa: "In the vow of Naktavrata, the lunar day that always extends through the evening should be taken."
Pradoṣa consists of three muhūrtas following sunset;
when the sun has set, there shall be a period of three muhūrtas known as pradoṣa.
One should perform the nakta rite during that time—such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
Thus it is stated by Vyāsa:
"But when the sun shines, casting a double shadow..."
In that context, one should understand "nakta" as [the practice of eating at night]; it does not mean eating during the night.
Thus, in the *Sauradharma* and other texts, a period of time consisting of the final muhūrta of the day, characterized by double the shadow, is prescribed; that is secondary (*gauṇa*).
"The wise declare that a night is a day minus one muhūrta;
O Gaṇādhipa, I consider 'night' (*nakta*) to be [the time] from the appearance of the stars."
Thus, from the statement regarding the future, it is understood that the time characterized by the sight of the [lunar] asterism is primary because it is his own accepted view;
the two muhūrtas preceding the final muhūrta are a more secondary time.
"Where [the asterism] extends through the three muhūrtas of the evening (pradoṣa) during the day..."
"Then one should observe the vow of eating only at night," according to the statement in the *Kaurma Purāṇa*.
The secondary nature (*gauṇatva*) of this [time] as well follows from the reasoning already stated above.
The state of being secondary, however, arises from the remoteness from the primary time.
Even within the primary time, the first two muhūrtas are most primary.
But the night-vow (niśānakta) should always be understood as occurring during the first half-yāma.
Because of this statement:
"One should avoid these four actions during the twilight (saṃdhyā)."
Food, sexual intercourse, sleep, and study as the fourth.
Thus, regarding the prohibition of eating during *saṃdhyā*, the word *saṃdhyā* there refers to the period of time extending up until the appearance of the stars;
for this is consistent with another scriptural statement: "From the appearance of the stars, it is the evening *saṃdhyā*; that which stands beyond that [is the night]."
"The evening twilight (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*) consists of three *ghaṭikās* from the time the sun has set.
Thus, the term "twilight" (*sandhyā*) applies even during those three *ghaṭikās*; this is to be understood in cases such as "thunder during twilight" (*sandhyā-garjita*).

Others, however, maintain that since the prohibition concerns eating prompted by desire (*rāga-prāpta-bhojana*), and since eating at night (*nakta-bhojana*) is prescribed [as a religious duty], it does not fall within the scope of the prohibition.

For this very reason, even though there is a prohibition against eating at night on days such as Sunday, Hemādri and others have stated that the performance of *nakta* (eating at night) is permitted therein.
Consequently, they say that *nakta* must indeed be performed even during the *saṃdhyā* period consisting of three *ghaṭikās*.

However, in reality, since there is no contradiction between the injunction and the prohibition, the *nakta* should be performed only after the three *ghaṭikās*, because one thereby obtains the primary time (*mukhyakāla*).

Otherwise, even the prohibition "he does not give a maned beast" would fail to apply to the gift of a horse that has been prescribed; for in the rule "of him [there are] one hundred and twelve," the word "his" (tasya) refers back to the horse as well, which would result in the obligation of giving one hundred and twelve horses on the new moon, full moon, and other such occasions. Since there is thus a contradiction between the injunction and the prohibition, it is proper to interpret it in that way. As for what was said—
O Brahmin, those men who observe a fast on a Sunday should eat at the end of the day,
because of the prohibition against eating at night.
This statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* refers specifically to the solar *nakta* (nocturnal fast) prescribed for the seventh lunar day of the sun (*bhānu-saptamī*) and similar occasions:
"When a lunar day (*tithi*) touches three *muhūrtas* during the day and likewise [three] at night, one should perform that solar *nakta*; however, the eating must take place on the very day."
Thus, Sumantu, by means of the word *eva* (only), prohibits eating at night—which would otherwise be generally applicable during *saura-nakta*—thereby restricting it to the daytime.

Mādhava, however, states on the basis of the statement "those [who eat] on the day of the Sun" that on Sundays and similar days, *nakta* is to be observed during the daytime as a secondary period (*gauṇakāla*).
Likewise, even when *nakta* is performed under the authority of ascetics (*yati*) or widows (*vidhavā*), it must be done during the day alone.
A householder, endowed with the prescribed ritual, should perform it at night;
likewise, an ascetic and a widow should perform it during the day.
According to this statement, for householders, the evening (pradoṣa) alone is the primary time for the night-meal (nakta).
In that regard, if the primary time overlaps with both days, or if it does not touch either day at all, the latter [day] is to be chosen.

Because of the availability of a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*), and because there is no contact [with food], one does not eat during the primary time as in the case of *ekabhakta*; rather, it is specifically at evening.
If it should not occur at *pradoṣa*, then *divānakta* is prescribed.
The shadow of one's own body becomes twice as long when the sun grows dim.
They say "nakta" means "at night," but eating at night is not what is meant by "nakta"; knowing this, the wise man should therefore perform the act of eating in the evening.
"One who observes the *nakta-vrata* should perform the rite at night; the fruit [of the vow] certainly arises [then]," according to this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa.
Likewise, in the case of the solar *yati-nakta* as well, since the late afternoon (*sāyāhna*) is the primary time, that [lunar day] which extends over it should be accepted.
If that [time] extends over two days, or if it does not touch either day at all, then the previous [day] alone is the valid time,
because both the primary time in the form of evening (*sāyāhna*) and the secondary time in the form of *pradoṣa* exist on that day.
Furthermore, this determination should be understood to apply not only to *nakta* in the form of eating, but also to [acts such as] worship and so forth.
Because the underlying principle is no different;
whether it be another auxiliary rite or a substitute for the fast, the determination regarding *nakta* is exactly like that of *ekabhakta*.
Thus concludes the determination of *nakta*.
Now follows the determination regarding the coincidence of the *nakta* (night-meal) and *ekabhakta* (single-meal) observances.

In that case, when two conflicting [observances] prescribed for two different lunar days (*tithi*) fall on a single day, one should follow the primary rule (*mukhyakalpa*) for that which is connected to the earlier lunar day— since it was commenced first and its conflict has not yet arisen— and one should treat the other as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
And this [rite] should be performed on the following day if the secondary period (*gauṇakāla*) is not obtained; however, if it is obtained on that very day,
it should be done then, because when there is no absolute obstruction of the time, it is proper to follow the convenience of the performer.

Thus concludes the determination regarding the combination of eating only at night, eating only once a day, and so forth. Now follows the determination regarding food obtained without asking (ayācita): that consists of eating once [a day] what has been obtained in the absence of any solicitation.
Others, however, say that "unasked" (ayācita) refers specifically to the resolve to avoid begging;

since this, like the fast (upavāsa), must be accomplished over a full day and night, the lunar day (tithi) that encompasses both [the beginning and end of the period] should be taken. If it exists only on one of the two days, then the one that covers the daytime should be taken.
Because of the statement of Jābāli, “The lunar days (*tithi*) during the day are meritorious,” and so forth,
the eating of food obtained without asking (*ayācita-anna*) should be performed only once— whether by day or by night— at whatever time it is obtained, provided it is not at a forbidden time.
But if it is not obtained, there is no loss whatsoever; thus concludes the determination regarding what is unasked for. Now follows the determination regarding fasting on lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
And that [day] connected with the setting [of the sun] is to be understood; for it is said:
"O Rāma, one should fast on that day on which the sun sets, or on that [day] during which [the moon] is in conjunction."
The night together with the moon.
Thus, from the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"Or, when there is a connection with sunset on two days, [the fast is observed] on the former day alone, because of the existence of the overlap with midnight.
This is the determination regarding the observance of a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).

Now follows the determination of the *saṅkrānti* (the sun's passage into a zodiacal sign). Regarding that, the nature of the *saṅkrānti* is the conjunction between the first atom of the sign, such as Aries, and the central atom of the solar disc; this is well-known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
And for this reason, because there are twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*), those [months] also become twelve.
And so it is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
Twelve indeed are declared to be the equal conceptualizations of the transits (*saṅkrānti*).
"Conceptualizations" (*kalpanā*) means "divisions" (*bhedāḥ*).
And these are "equal," meaning they are common (*sādhāraṇa*) to the injunctions and prohibitions based on the general cause that is the transit.
In the *Māghavīya*, however, the reading is "the calculation of transits is equal" (*samā saṅkrāntikalpanā*). In that case, "equal" (*samā*) means pertaining to each single year.
The particle *eva* (only) is used for the purpose of indicating that there are exactly twelve transits even when there is an excess of intercalary months (*malamāsa*).
And in order to establish the specific excellence of the meritorious time for these [transits], intermediate designations were stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"Two solstices (ayana), two equinoxes (viṣuva), four 'sixty-eight' (ṣaḍaśīti) transits, and four 'Viṣṇu-steps' (viṣṇupadī); thus twelve transits (saṅkrānti) are recorded."
The two transits of Pisces and Cancer are the northern and southern solstices;
Libra and Aries are the equinoxes, and the others follow between them.
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is even greater than that of the equinoxes.
The movement of the sun in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius is declared to be the Ṣaḍaśītimukha;
it possesses sixty-eightfold merit in its results.
The *jhaṣa* is the crocodile;
between those two solstices and equinoxes lie the six subsequent *ṣaḍaśīti* and *viṣṇupadī* [days].
In the *Kālādarśa* and other texts, however, the reading is "tato 'pare" (the others from that).
The meaning is that the "gola" refers to the circle of zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*) joined with the equinoxes and solstices, and "apare" means those [points] situated within its center.
This is the distilled meaning.
In Cancer and Capricorn, respectively, the designations are the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana) and the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa);
in Libra and Aries, it is the equinox (viṣuva); and in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo, it is the station of Viṣṇu (viṣṇupada).
The *Ṣaḍaśītimukha* occurs in Virgo, Gemini, Sagittarius, and Pisces.
Furthermore, those born in these [signs] according to the distinction of days (or the distinction of lunar mansions) each receive seven designations.
And so it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Ghorā is [the goddess presiding] over the Sun, Dvāṅkṣī over the Moon, and Mahodarī over Mars."
In Mercury it is named Mandākinī, and in Jupiter it is Mandā.
On Friday it is Miśritā, and on Saturday it is Rākṣasī; Mandā is to be known in the fixed (dhruva) signs, and likewise Mandākinī in the mutable (mṛdu) signs.
One should know that *Dhyāṅkṣī* is swift; *Ugrā* is proclaimed to be terrible; *Mahodarī* is to be known by her movements; and *Rākṣasī* is characterized by cruel constellations.
And it is indeed taught as mixed, if there is a transition by means of mixed [factors].
Thus:
the fixed [nakṣatras] are the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī;
the soft [nakṣatras] are Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa.
The swift [nakṣatras] are Abhijit, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya;
the fierce [nakṣatras] are the three Pūrvas, Bharaṇī, and Maghā;
the movable [nakṣatras] are Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Svātī, and Śatabhiṣaj.

The cruel [nakṣatras] are Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, and Āśleṣā; the mixed are Kṛttikā and Viśākhā. The specific distinctions regarding auspicious times associated with these designations will be explained later.

And in this case, because the conjunction of the atom at the center of the solar disc with the first atom of the zodiacal sign of Aries and so forth occurs over such an extremely subtle duration of time that it is difficult to discern, it is impossible to perform even a single prescribed act such as ritual bathing there; consequently, it is all the more impossible to perform many such acts.

Therefore, performance at a proximate time is established by implication, just as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa) prescribed for the *sandhi* (junction) period, which must be performed at a proximate time since they cannot be performed precisely at the junction itself.
And regarding the inquiry as to whether that imminent time pertains to both [the ingress and egress] or to only one, and for how long it lasts— Devala states:
"The moment of the *saṅkrānti* is subtle and difficult to discern even by those with the eyes of a physician."
And through union with that, thirty channels—both below and above—are purified.

The meaning is that, by joining together thirty *nāḍīs*— fifteen above and fifteen below the subtle time (*sūkṣmakāla*) conjoined with the *saṅkrānti*— the authors of the treatises have sanctified them, making them fit for the performance of rites such as ritual bathing. Furthermore, this statement regarding the fifteen *ghaṭikās* of merit on both sides should be understood according to the perspective of that school in which the solar disc is considered to be half the size of the true motion (*spaṣṭabhukti*), since the dimensions of the solar disc differ according to various opinions in the *Jyotiḥ-śāstra*.

In this view, it is well-established in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that fifteen *ghaṭikās* prior to the subtle moment, the eastern part of the solar disc enters the zodiacal circle beginning with Aries, and after that time, the western part likewise enters the zodiacal circle beginning with Aries for exactly as many *ghaṭikās*. This very process is called "enjoyment" (*bhoga*).
And likewise, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"The past and future experiences are said to consist of fifteen channels (nāḍīs)."
Thus:
"The channels to be known as sixteen are below, and sixteen are behind."
The time of the sun's transition [into a zodiacal sign] is proclaimed by the learned to be meritorious.
Likewise:
Sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after the transit [of the sun] are proclaimed as the meritorious time (puṇyakāla) by the mere sight of Rāhu.
Likewise,

statements such as those of Śātātapa, Marīci, and Jābāli— "At the transition [of the sun], the auspicious time consists of sixteen *kalās* on both sides"— are to be explained according to the intention of that school which holds that the solar disc has a motion equal to its own fifteenth part.

Therefore, it is established that sixteen or fifteen *ghaṭikās* on either side, according to the difference in the size of the [solar] disc, constitute the time of merit (*puṇyakāla*) for each [occasion]. This meaning is also accepted by Hemādri, Ratnākara, and others.
However, Mādhava, Madanaratna, and others—

"Due to that conjunction, thirty nāḍīs are proclaimed both before and after [the transit]," according to this statement of Devala; thus, thirty nāḍīs prior to the time of the *saṅkrānti* are meritorious, and thirty nāḍīs after it are also meritorious. As for those statements previously cited which establish the merit of sixteen or fifteen *ghaṭikās*, they say that these are intended to demonstrate a greater degree of merit.
Furthermore, this statement regarding the merit [accruing] before and after [the transit] applies universally to all transits (*saṅkrānti*),

as there is no distinction [between them]. However, those statements to be mentioned later— which prescribe specific times for particular transits by placing [the merit] sometimes after, sometimes before, and sometimes at both— serve the purpose of demonstrating a greater degree of merit.
The consensus of all the digest-writers (*nibandhakāra*), such as Hemādri and Mādhava, is likewise [as stated above].

As for what has been asserted here by the Maithilas, such as Śrīdatta and Ratnākara, and by the Gauḍas, such as Smārta and others— that the statements of Śātātapa and others cited previously, which establish the merit of sixteen *ghaṭikās* on both sides, refers exclusively to the Viṣṇupadī [tithi].

Since specific details have been stated for all other transits (*saṅkrānti*) according to the method that will be explained, it is logical— by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*)— that general statements indicating the merit of sixteen *ghaṭikās* apply exclusively to that [specific case] alone.
And therefore:

"The time for merit [is] sixteen [nāḍīs] before and after the sun's transit (saṅkrānti)," according to this statement from the Skanda Purāṇa, there is also a summary of these [rules] due to brevity— this is not so; for by Śātātapa:
At the beginning of the solstices, whatever desirable substance is always to be given in the houses,
as well as at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti* periods and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.

Since the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the opening phrase "at the solstice, etc. includes the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) and the Viṣṇupada, it is understood that the injunctions for giving gifts and so forth apply to all transits (*saṅkrānti*). Furthermore, because giving and other such acts are not possible within a subtle moment (*sūkṣmakāla*), there is a requirement for a gross time (*sthūlakāla*). In this regard, the subsequent statement, "The sixteen [ghaṭikās] preceding are to be known," clearly establishes that the injunction of a gross time consisting of sixteen ghaṭikās on both sides applies to the subject of all transits.
Furthermore, the restriction of a clear general rule is not logical;
as the venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has stated:
"A general rule that is unclear may be restricted by a specific one."
Thus,
because a restrictive conclusion (upasaṃhāra) is untenable, it is logical that [the merit] pertains to all [transits].

And so, since the status of being meritorious for sixteen ghaṭikās on both sides is established by statements common to all transits, the specific statements [regarding particular days] are intended to indicate a superior degree of merit.
In that regard,
Vasiṣṭha says: "But at the equinox in the middle, the merit is in Viṣṇu in the east, and in the southern solstice."
When the six-eighty-faced [conjunction] has passed, and when the northern course has passed.
"In the middle, on both sides" means up to that point.
However, the Easterners [state]:
"When the mouth of the month of Āṣāḍha has passed and the two equinoxes have occurred..."
Based on this statement from the *Devīpurāṇa*, some say that [the term] refers to what has already occurred (*vṛtta*).

However, in reality, Anantabhaṭṭa’s interpretation alone is correct: that *vṛtta* means "occurring" (*vartana*), with the suffix *kta* used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), thus referring to the present time;
for this achieves consistency with the statement of Vasiṣṭha.
"In Viṣṇu" means "in the Viṣṇupadī [river].
And this statement regarding the prior sanctity of the Viṣṇupadīs is for the purpose of indicating their superior excellence.
The auspicious time for the Viṣṇupadī lasts sixteen [muhūrtas] both before and after [the sun's entry].
Thus, because the *Skanda Purāṇa* states that the period of merit consists of sixteen *ghaṭikās* both before and after [the transit], the following rule is established:

during the *viṣṇupadī* transit, the sixteen *ghaṭikās* following [the transit] are more meritorious than other transits, while the sixteen *ghaṭikās* preceding it are most meritorious. This meaning is also accepted by Hemādri, Madanaratna, and others.

Others, however, state that because the statement regarding the merit of the time preceding the Viṣṇupadī (the transit of the sun) lacks any root authority, whereas the Skanda Purāṇa states that sixteen ghaṭikās on both sides [of the transit] constitute the meritorious time,
the highest degree of merit occurs once the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed;
even there—
When eighty-six [nāḍīs] have passed, eighty nāḍīs are said to be called "meritorious" (puṇya) within the Viṣṇupadī; sixteen are likewise [meritorious] both before and after it.
Because in this statement, by the word "ca" (and), the fact that [this gift] is more meritorious than both is indicated in comparison with other transferences;
likewise,
Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha also says:
Regarding past and future merit, there are two solstices: the northern and the southern.
There are thirty nāḍīs in Cancer, and twenty more in Capricorn.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*, however, the fourth quarter states: "But in Capricorn, there are ten more. Bṛhaspati also says:
"In the [southern] solstice, twenty [days] are prior; in Capricorn, twenty are posterior."
"In the solstice" means in the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Here, in all these cases, the arrangement of contradictory statements should be understood as being intended to show a greater abundance of merit.
Consequently, it is established that even the period consisting of sixteen *ghaṭikās*, which is established by the general statement, possesses even greater merit than the twenty [mentioned].
Because of its proximity.
Furthermore, regarding the region of the equinox—
that very same [point]—
In the present [solar transits] of Libra and Aries, there are ten nāḍīs on both sides.
Regarding the *ṣaḍaśīti* [period], Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha states:
"When the *ṣaḍaśīti* has passed, eighty nāḍikās are said [to remain]."
The *aṣṭi* consists of sixteen [syllables];
it is called *aṣṭicchandas* because it possesses sixteen syllables.
This reading is also accepted by the *Madanaratna* and other authorities.
In the Hemādri, Mādhava, and other works, however, the reading is "sixty.
Regarding this, Hemādri has explained it as fifteen for each [of the four quarters], totaling sixty.
But in the case of Viṣṇupadī, since no specific number is heard, only the sixteen ghaṭikās mentioned in the general statement are auspicious at the beginning.
And here is the summarized meaning:
ten *ghaṭikās* before and ten after the [solar transits] of Libra and Aries are meritorious; twenty *ghaṭikās* before the [transit] of Cancer and twenty after that of Capricorn are meritorious.

In the *Ṣaḍaśīti* there are sixteen *parā* [transits], and in the *Viṣṇupadī* there are the former [sixteen]; thus, regarding those transits (*saṅkrānti*) designated as *manda* and so forth, which are connected with the days of the week and the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)— [The text continues: ...in these transits, whatever [is prescribed]... [the remainder of the sentence is omitted in the source].
Three, four, five, seven, eight, nine, and twelve *ghaṭikās* respectively— this indeed is their ultimate merit.
This statement from the *Devīpurāṇa* should also be understood as intended to demonstrate the superiority of merit.

In this context, if these [women]—whether they are "enjoyers of the prior" (*pūrvabhoginī*), "enjoyers of the subsequent" (*uttarabhoginī*), or "enjoyers of both" (*ubhayatobhoginī*)—are born during the day, specifically at the midday and other such times, then they are born during the day itself because of obtaining the auspicious times prescribed for those respective instances.
When, in the case of a woman who is a "prior enjoyer," she gives birth to a "subsequent enjoyer" immediately after sunrise, [the same principle applies].

If a child is born before dawn while the mother is still in her period, and the two auspicious times—daytime and the period immediately following—are not obtained, then one must adopt the time prescribed by the general rule: namely, the subsequent time for a woman who has already menstruated, or the preceding time for one who is currently menstruating;
one must not, however, mistakenly take the night-time due to a confusion regarding the auspicious periods.
And likewise, Vasiṣṭha says:
"When the sun enters a new sign during the day, the entire day is proclaimed to be meritorious."
When the sun enters a new sign at night, the first half of the day is prescribed for bathing and giving gifts.

For here, since the merit of the day during a transit occurring at midday or other such times is already established by the statements regarding the merit of the preceding and following *nāḍīs*, this [verse] does not intend its literal meaning; rather, it is for the purpose of prohibiting the merit of the night that might otherwise be presumed due to the occurrence of a praiseworthy time within the aforementioned scope.

Therefore, immediately after the sun rises, when a daughter is born either to the mother who previously enjoyed [the husband] or to the one who will enjoy him later, the ritual bathing and other rites must be performed during the day itself.

However, in the case of those women who enjoy [the husband] on both sides, since there is equality between both times, there is no contingency of performing the rite at night because a praiseworthy time is available even by day;
Mādhava, Madanaratna, and others also hold this view.
Regarding the transition at night, although there is the statement: "Whichever nāḍīs are present, those are remembered as most meritorious," [the following applies].

Bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts should be performed at night during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the passage of the sun into a new zodiacal sign (saṅkrānti), at marriages, during times of calamity, on occasions of prosperity, and during optional vows (kāmyavrata).
And because of this statement, it follows that even the night is a time of merit; nevertheless—when there is a transit of the sun at night, one should perform that rite during the day.
According to this statement by Gobhila, the auspicious time (*puṇyakāla*) occurs only during the day;

however, that does not mean the entire day, for according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "If the sun's transit (*saṅkramaṇa*) occurs at night, [the merit] for bathing and giving gifts lasts for half the day," it is only half [of the day].

And even then, it is established that if the transition occurs before midnight, it belongs to the preceding day; if after [midnight], it belongs to the following day; but when it is exactly at midnight, it belongs to both. Thus he says:
"In that case, if it is below midnight, the ritual action belongs to what is above midday."
And in the case of ascending, it is for two watches above the rising.
When the sun enters [a new sign] at the exact moment of midnight,
they say that both days are meritorious, with the exception of Capricorn and Cancer.
Midday is the turning point;
and that belongs to the preceding day,
while sunrise belongs to the following day, due to their proximity.
"Complete" (*sampūrṇe*) means at the junction of the two halves of midnight.
Mādhava, however, states that midnight consists of two *ghaṭikās*: the first *ghaṭikā* of the third watch and the last *ghaṭikā* of the second.
Furthermore, the two days are not complete, but rather delimited by [that] half.
"During a transit [of the sun] at night, the merit of bathing and giving belongs to the half-day [preceding it].
Since this is stated as a general rule at the outset regarding the merit of the half-day during a nocturnal transit,
Anantabhaṭṭa, Hemādri, Madanaratna, and others also hold this view.
But Kālādarśa, Mādhava, and others state:
"If the transit (saṅkrama) occurs at midnight, the six watches (yāmas) preceding and following it should be known as the time of the transit; one should perform bathing and other rites therein."
Thus, based on the statement from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, some say that when the transit occurs at midnight (*arddharātra*), the entire two days are meritorious.
However, in reality, since Anantabhaṭṭa has declared this [view] to be baseless (*nirmūla*), the interpretation of Hemādri and others alone is superior and widely accepted.
Therefore, when the transit occurs exactly at midnight, the latter half of the preceding day and the first half of the following day are meritorious due to their proximity.

That too is not by way of conjunction (samuccaya), but rather by way of option (vikalpa); otherwise, there would be the contingency of repeating the primary injunction. Furthermore, that [time] is determined as follows: if the lunar day (tithi) coinciding with the time of the sun's passage (saṅkrama) is non-different from the latter half of the preceding day, then the latter half of the preceding day is to be taken;
but when it is non-different from the first half of the second day, then the first half of the following day is to be taken. Thus is the rule established.
And so it is stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should know the merit to be at the beginning [of the lunar day] if the lunar day (tithi) remains undivided."
When midnight has passed, it should be understood as being on the following day.
This is the meaning of the first half [of the verse]:

if, at the time of the transit occurring at midnight, there is only a single lunar day (*tithi*) spanning both the latter half of the preceding day and the moment of the transit itself, then one should know that the merit (*puṇya*) belongs first to the latter half of the preceding day.

If, however, [the tithi] is non-different from the first half of the following day, then it is established by implication that it belongs to the first half of the following day. If, after midnight, [the tithi] is different [from the tithi of the previous day], yet remains non-different [throughout the following day], then it is established by implication that it belongs to the first half of the following day. But if, after midnight, [the tithi] is either different or non-different [from the tithi of the previous day], then it belongs to the following day alone; such is the meaning of the latter half [of the verse].

However, when a lunar day (tithi) belonging to the time of the midnight transition occurs during both the latter half of one day and the former half of the next, the established rule is as follows: for those [lunar days] enjoyed by the first [day], it is the latter half of the preceding day; for those enjoyed by the second [day], it is the former half of the following day; and for those enjoyed by both, there is an optional choice.
Ananta Bhaṭṭa, Madanaratna, and others also hold this view.

As for what was stated here by Śrīdatta— that when the lunar day (*tithi*) is not divided, the merit lies in the first half of the preceding day, but when it is divided, it belongs to both according to the *Devīpurāṇa* statement, "When complete, [the rite] should be performed on both"— it refers to both cases.
That is not so;

for when the *Devīpurāṇa* prescribes that the gift should be given in both cases by stating, "But when [the time] is complete, it should be given to both," the simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) is untenable due to the resulting necessity of repeating the primary act (*pradhānāvṛtti*). Since an unrestricted option (*avyavasthita-vikalpa*) would thus arise, the subsequent statement, "One should know the merit to be in the first [case]," [establishes the rule].
Because it is more concise to establish a mere formal rule, the distilled meaning here is as follows:
if the transit occurs before midnight, it belongs to the latter half of the preceding day; if the transit occurs after that, it belongs to the former half of the following day.

Regarding the transition at midnight: if the transit occurs on a lunar day (*tithi*) that is not distinct from the latter half of the preceding day, then [the merit accrues] in the latter half of the preceding day;
however, if the transit occurs on a lunar day that is not distinct from the first half of the following day, then [the merit accrues] in the first half of the following day;
but when it occurs on a lunar day that is not distinct from the halves of both days...

At that time, the transition (*saṅkrama*) occurs in the *pūrvabhoginī* [nāḍīs] during the latter half of the first day, in the *uttarabhoginī* [nāḍīs] during the first half of the second day, and in the *ubhayabhoginī* [nāḍīs] there is an optional choice (*aicchika-vikalpa*).
As for that which—
When the sun's transit occurs at night while it is in the signs of Sagittarius, Pisces, Aries, or Virgo— specifically when moving from the east toward the north— it is known as Viṣṇupadī.
The wise have declared that five nāḍīs in the forenoon and likewise five in the afternoon are auspicious for rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.

Thus, the Vedic statement establishing the priority of the forenoon and afternoon *nāḍīs* occurring at sunset and sunrise on the preceding and following days should be understood as intended to demonstrate an excellence [of those times]. The same is stated in the *Madanaratna*.

Furthermore, this rule regarding the transition (*saṅkrānti*) during the night pertains to cases other than the solstices (*ayana*), because the previously cited statement of Vasiṣṭha provides an exclusion for the entire determination of the night by stating: "excepting Capricorn and Cancer during the solstices."
Therefore, when there arises the expectation of how these two [rites] are to be performed, Mādhava and Madanaratna state:
"If the sun's transition into Cancer should occur at dawn or at midnight, one should perform it on the preceding day."
When the sun enters the sign of Cancer after leaving Aquarius—
at either dusk or midnight— bathing and giving gifts should be performed on the following day.
