In accordance with such statements from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, even when the transit [of the sun] occurs at midnight or after midnight during the period of Karkaṭaka, the merit belongs on the day itself; whereas during Makara, even if the transit occurs before midnight, the merit belongs on the following day alone. And thus, since the rule regarding daytime merit is established even for a transit occurring at night, the prohibition of bathing and other rites at night is inferred by implication.
In some statements, however, there is also a duty to be performed at night;

for instance, in this very same statement of Vasiṣṭha, regarding the daytime duty common to all transits (saṅkrānti) which is occasioned by the transit occurring at night— due to the exclusion “except for Capricorn and Cancer”—
there is a duty to be performed even during that night.

For this very reason: "During an eclipse, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), at marriages, after calamities, during auspicious increments (vṛddhi), and in optional vows (kāmyavrata), acts such as bathing and giving gifts should be performed even at night."
Thus, even the general statement of Yājñavalkya refers to the *ayana*s (solstices);
otherwise, since other *saṅkrānti*s are prescribed as meritorious only during the day, this [statement] would result in being rendered devoid of scope.
Although, according to the cited statements from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa and others, that [merit] also exists there...
Although there is indeed a rule regarding the merit of daytime [donations], nevertheless, because of the exclusion "except for Capricorn and Cancer," there is also the merit of nighttime [donations].
Therefore, it is appropriate that the general statement refers to the solstices (ayana).
Thus, when there is an option between the merit of nighttime and the merit of daytime during the solstices, the determination is made according to local custom.
Hemādri, however, states:
"They say two days are meritorious, excluding [the transits in] Capricorn and Cancer.
This exclusion does not apply to the entire determination regarding the night, but rather only to the two days occasioned by a transit occurring at midnight, which are immediately proximate.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
as there is merit for two days when other transits (saṅkrāntis) occur at midnight, it is not so during the solstices (ayana).

However, when that [solstice] occurs at midnight, according to the previously cited statement from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, the following day is meritorious in Capricorn (makara), while the preceding day is meritorious in Cancer (karka).
For in the *Bhaviṣyottara* passage, it is established that for the Makara-saṅkrānti occurring at dusk (*pradoṣa*) or at midnight (*ardharātra*), the merit belongs to the following day;
whereas for the Karka-saṅkrānti occurring at dawn (*prabhāta*) or at midnight, the merit belongs to the preceding day.
This being the case—
Having passed through Sagittarius, Pisces, Virgo,
and Gemini, the five nāḍīs at the end of the day are remembered as most meritorious.
Furthermore, this would result in a contradiction with the statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "And likewise, five [muhūrtas] at sunrise, both in rites for the gods and in rites for the ancestors.

Therefore, the statement from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* must be explained as follows: regarding the phrase "at dusk or at midnight," the two words "or" (*vā*) have the sense of "either... or" (*yathātatha*), according to the lexicographical tradition (*nighaṇṭu*) which states: "The word 'or' is used in the senses of comparison and alternative."
Therefore, this is the meaning:
just as there is merit in the first half of the day preceding a Makara-saṅkrānti occurring at dusk, so too there is merit on the following day for one occurring at midnight.
The same applies to the statement regarding dawn.
Therefore, when the transit occurs at midnight, the auspicious time is the subsequent day for Capricorn (Makara) and the preceding day for Cancer (Karka);
however, if the transit occurs before or after midnight, the determination in both cases is exactly the same as for other transits.

Nor should it be argued that this would render vacuous the statements of Yājñavalkya and others which establish the religious merit of the night, because those texts specify that the auspicious time is only during the day whenever the transit occurs at night across all zodiac signs.
Because both types of statements are observed, the auspicious time for a transit occurring at night exists both during the night and during the day.
However, Hemādri and others maintain that because of the statement, "Sins are present [at night]," the night is more meritorious.
Anantabhaṭṭa, however, says that if it is impossible to perform the rite during the day due to negligence or other causes, it should be performed at night.

The Easterners (Prācya), however, maintain that when the *saṅkrānti* occurs during the portion of the day adjacent to night, since the night is also excluded by the prescribed time consisting of sixteen *ghaṭikās* and so forth, the scriptural statements regarding the merit of the night (*rātripuṇyatva*) are justified as referring to that [adjacent] period.
In this context, one should seek elsewhere for what is prescribed—such as bathing, *śrāddha*, and giving—and what is prohibited—such as travel and sexual intercourse.

Just as with the sun’s transition into a zodiacal sign (*rāśisaṅkrama*), so too upon its transition into a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-saṅkrama*), and upon the transition of other planets into a zodiacal sign or a lunar mansion, the performance of bathing and other rites is enjoined.
And at that time, Jaimini said:
"At the transit of the sun, the constellations and zodiac signs [should be calculated] both before and after, increased by sixty nāḍīs."
Likewise, the sages have declared that in a yuga, exactly one nāḍī of the moon's meritorious [period] consists of three dhārāpala measures.
The four nāḍīs of Mars are accompanied by six palas; those of Mercury are three nāḍīs and fourteen palas;
those of Jupiter are four and a half nāḍīs joined with seven palas; and those of Venus are four nāḍīs and one pala.
The auspicious [nāḍīs] of Saturn are said to be seven palas enriched by two nāgas;
performing recitation, fire-offerings, and giving at the beginning, middle, and end of these, one attains the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
The phrase "both here and beyond" is connected to everything [that follows].
"Rasendunāḍyaḥ" means sixteen ghaṭikās.
"Tridharāpalaiḥ" means by thirteen palas.
*Sapalā* means exceeding by one *pala*. *Manavas* are fourteen *palas*;
*nāgas*, being doubled, are sixteen.

When the transition of a planet occurs during the night, the ritual bathing and other rites must be performed at night itself, just as in the case of the transit of the sun, because there is no statement regarding its being meritorious during the day;
furthermore, this is an optional (kāmya) act, since the fruit of bathing and so forth is heard to accrue therein.
If a person does not bathe when the sun's transit occurs,
he will be born sickly throughout seven lifetimes and will remain destitute.
And because it is stated that "thus [the soul] does not hear," there is no transmigration.
This concludes the determination regarding transmigration. Now, the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is determined.
The state of being an *adhimāsa* (intercalary month) consists in being a month beginning with the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*) while lacking even a single solar transit (*saṅkrānti*).

This lack of a single transit occurs in two ways: by having no transit at all or by having two transits; thus, there are two types of *adhimāsa*: the *adhika-māsa* (intercalary month) and the *kṣaya-māsa* (expunged month).
And so it is stated in the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya-sūtra:
"In whichever month there is no solar transit (saṅkrānti), or indeed two transits..."
That month should be known as the intercalary month (malamāsa), and it shall be the thirteenth month.
Thus,
by the phrase "not a transit," the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is indicated;
by the phrase "two transits," the deficient month (*kṣaya*) is indicated.
In that regard, Bhṛgu states the nature of the intercalary month: "When two new moons occur while the sun remains in a single zodiac sign..."
At that time, the intercalary month (adhimāsaka) should be known as the destroyer of the rites for the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
Thus:
"two *darśas* (darśadvayam)" means "two conjunctions" (*darśānadvayam*).
This is because the word *darśa* primarily denotes a "conjunction," according to the definition: "*darśa* [occurs] at the meeting of the sun and moon."
For in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), it is well known that the conjunction (*saṅgama*) occurs precisely at the final moment of the new moon.
Furthermore, the month referred to here is specifically the lunar (*cāndra*) one, which is the cause of an intercalary month (*malamāsa*);
for a lunar month in which no solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) occurs is proclaimed to be an intercalary month.
Thus, according to the *Brahmasiddhānta*,
that [month] is indeed characterized by the bright fortnight and so forth;
it is proclaimed as the beginning of the month when Indra and Agni are offered oblations.
Agni and Soma are traditionally held to be in the middle, while Pitṛ and Soma are at the conclusion.
If the sun should ever pass beyond that [lunar month],
it is to be known as the first *malimluca* (intercalary month), while the second is remembered as the ordinary (*prākṛta*) month.
Thus, according to the statement of Laghu-Hārīta;
by the words "first" and "second," he indicates its twofold nature in comparison to the other months and its designation as the "subsequent month.
For this very reason—
Jyotiḥpitāmaha states: "Sixty days constitute a month according to the followers of Bādarāyaṇa;
having abandoned the first half, the ritual action should be performed in the latter half."
Thus [it is said]:
the Vedic statement, "A year consists of thirteen months," refers to months of thirty days each;
and its designation as a specific month is due to its being characterized by the [lunar] signs beginning with Caitra.
For it is thus:
for those whose first moment of the year begins when the sun is situated in Pisces and so forth,
twelve lunar months beginning with Caitra are traditionally taught for that year.

Thus, Vyāsa has stated the definition of Caitra and the other months through their connection with the characteristics beginning on the first lunar day (pratipad) when the sun is situated in Pisces and the other signs;
and this can also be applied to the intercalary month (adhimāsa).
As for that which was said:
"The month in which the sun's transit into Aries occurs during the lunar month is Caitra;
likewise, Vaiśākha and the others [follow] by connection with the transits into Taurus and so forth."

Thus, the definition of Caitra and the other months stated by Brahmagupta is based on the intention of *śuddha* (pure) months; it is conventional (*prāyika*) rather than primary (*mukhya*), because it does not encompass intercalary months (*malamāsa*).
Otherwise, the use of terms such as "Caitra" and so forth in the traditional usage (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) regarding an intercalary month would be untenable.
As for that which—
The year within which evil resides destroys the fruits of sacrifices;
it is possessed by Nairṛtas, Yātudhānas, and the like, and is devoid of its proper name.
Thus, the statement in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* regarding its being "nameless" is due either to its having names such as *malimluca* and others which are contradictory [to its nature],
or because even though a name exists, it is as good as non-existent due to its unfitness for the rites prescribed by that name.
Alternatively, the definition stated by Brahmagupta alone is primary, and not that stated by Vyāsa, because the latter is impossible during a period of decrease (*kṣaya*).
Furthermore, since an intercalary month consists of sixty days, and because the solar transits (saṅkrānti) of Aries and so forth can occur within it,
the names Caitra and others may be applied to an intercalary month.
Moreover, the status of an intercalary month as "impure" (mala) is due to its excessiveness.
For this very reason, the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa states:
"Those who know time declare that an additional month is the impurity of time."
And regarding its designation as "neuter," it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"Indeed, that month which, due to the increase of lunar days (*tithi*), does not enter [the next solar transit] for some time is called neuter."
In this context, only that intercalary month which occurs according to the *sphuṭa* (apparent) calculation should be accepted as an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*),
and not that which occurs according to the *madhyama* (mean) calculation,
because the latter is not applicable to the practices prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.

For instance, by such statements as "Where Indra and Agni are invoked," it is understood that the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*)—which occurs within the month beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) and ending with the new moon (*darśa*)—is fit for both injunctions and prohibitions. However, the transits (*saṅkrānti*) occurring according to the mean measure (*madhyama-māna*) do not necessarily coincide with the period from the first day of the bright fortnight to the new moon.
The fixed time of its occurrence is shown in the *Vasiṣṭha-siddhānta*:
When thirty-two months, sixteen days,
and four ghaṭikās have passed, one intercalary month (adhimāsaka) falls.

Thus, the meaning is that when this much time has elapsed following a previous intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), a second intercalary month occurs according to the mean measure (*madhyamamāna*). Furthermore, if in this statement there is an intention to refer to months ending with the new moon (*darśānta*), it would follow that the commencement of the intercalary month occurs after four *ghaṭikās* have passed on the second day of the dark fortnight.

Moreover, if there is an intention to refer to thirty-two months whose commencement and conclusion are not fixed by lunar days (*aniyatati-thi*), it would result in the contingency that the commencement of the intercalary month is also not fixed by lunar days.

Consequently, in either case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of violating the fixed rule regarding the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*) and so forth of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*).

Therefore, it is clear that only that [lunar month] which does not coincide with the solar ingress (*saṅkrānti*)—extending from the first day of the bright fortnight as calculated by the true [mean] measure until the new moon (*darśānta*)—is of use in the Vedic and Smārta practices concerning the domain of the intercalary month.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*:
The intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is clearly that month in which no solar transit (*asaṅkrānta*) occurs;
"clearly" (*sphuṭa*) means as determined by the true measure (*sphuṭamāna*).
However, the non-transit according to the mean measure (*madhyamamāna*) is useful only for the practical conventions of the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
Furthermore, this intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is not as certain as the intercalary month occurring according to the intermediate calculation (*madhyamamāna*).
As for those statements such as "it may occur in the thirtieth month," these are intended to indicate possibility rather than being fixed rules, because deviation is clearly evident.
A "destruction month" (*kṣayamāsa*), however, consists of two solar transits (*saṅkrānti*) and begins with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*) of the lunar month.
"An intercalary month (*dvisaṅkrāntimāsa*) called a *kṣayamāsa* (destruction-month) occurs occasionally," according to the statement in the *Siddhāntasiromaṇi*.
And that [month] occurs only during the three months beginning with Kārttika, not in others.
When this happens, there are two intercalary months on either side of the *kṣayamāsa* within the year.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi: "The intercalary month occurs in the triad beginning with Kārttika and not otherwise; at that time, there will be two intercalary months within the year."
And here, the year consists of twelve lunar months beginning with the first solar ingress (*pūrva-saṅkrānti*) and so forth, but not those beginning with Caitra;
for in the six-month period beginning with the Caitra following an intercalary month (*kṣayamāsa*), a second intercalary month is never possible.
And the time of its occurrence is stated in that very same [work]:
When the Śaka era has passed by [the number] measured by oceans, mountains, and joys (1474),

then it will be [the year] measured by lunar days, lords, limbs, eyes, and suns (12515); likewise, it will generally be [the year] measured by elephants, mountains, chariots, fires, and earth (13818).
By the years [since the epoch] measured by the Earth, the Vedas, the Moon, and the poets, cows, and the Earth.
Thus,
the number to be established here indicates the duration of the intervening period; in some cases,
it is [given] as 141 minus 19, i.e., by the "cows" (9).
The meaning is that there is an interval of 141 years in some cases and 122 years in others.
Accordingly, it should be noted that when the previously mentioned number 974 is added to 141, the result is 1115; adding 125 to that yields 1256; and adding 122 to that results in 1378.
"Abdhayaḥ" means four.
*Adrayaḥ* means seven; *nandā* means nine. Their occurrence in reverse order [is the sequence].
The meaning is that by these measured years, destruction first occurred.
The lunar days (*tithi*) are fifteen;
the lords (*īśa*) are eleven (1115). Measured by these, it will perhaps occur at some time.
The limbs (*aṅga*) are six; the dice (*akṣa*) are five.
Sūryas = twelve; all together in one place = 1,256;
Gajas = eight.
The mountains are seven; the fires are three; the earth is one.
In one place: 1378 / *kuḥ* = one;
*vedāḥ* = four.
Indu is one;
in one place [it is] 141; cows are nine.
*kuḥ* = *ekaḥ* / *ekatra* (19). The meaning is: "In the year measured by these [digits], someone will come into being."

And this *kṣayamāsa* consists of two months because it is joined by two transits (*saṅkrānti*) that serve as the defining characteristics of a month, such as the transit of the sun into Aries (*meṣa*).
For this very reason, the *Ratnamālā* states: "In whichever month there are two transits of the sun, there is a pair of months called *kṣaya*."

Thus, for this very reason, because there is no separate existence of the month of Kārttika and so forth— characterized by the preceding solar transit— with respect to the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and so forth— characterized by the subsequent solar transit— it is said that "the loss consists of two transits. However, others say:
"In accordance with the definition stated in the scriptural passage, 'Whichever lunar month is completed when the sun is situated in Aries and so forth,

that is to be known as Caitra and the others,' they say that in the case of a *kṣaya-māsa* (intercalary month), since there is no completion of the final *darśa* while the sun is in the preceding zodiacal sign, the month must indeed take the form of the subsequent month because its completion occurs only when the sun is in the following sign."
The designation *Aṃhaspati* for the intercalary month (*kṣayamāsa*), and the designations *Saṃsarpa* and *Adhimāsa* for the intercalary months occurring before and after it,
are stated in the *Bārhaspatyasaṃhitā*: "In whichever month there is no solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), or where there are two transits..."
Saṃsarpa, Aṃhaspati, and likewise Adhimāsa are condemned.

Thus, in this context, it is understood from the sequential mention that the names *saṃsarpa* and *hāspati* apply respectively to the two transits (*saṅkrānti*) that have not preceded [the intercalary month], while the subsequent transit constitutes the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). This is the view of the *Madanaratna*.
Furthermore, the *saṃsarpa* is not a defiled month (*malamāsa*), but rather a pure (*śuddha*) month, whereas the subsequent one is impure (*aśuddha*).
If there are two intercalary months (*adhimāsaka*) in a single year,
the preceding month is to be regarded as auspicious, while the latter is the defiling (*malimluca*) one.
Thus, from the statement of Jābāli:

when there is one intercalary month (*malamāsa*) in the six months beginning with Āśvina and another in the six months beginning with Caitra, then there is also another statement establishing the purity (*śuddhatva*) of the former [month],
found in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
There is no intercalary month prior to Caitra, but one may occur after it.
As stated in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*:
"When the sun has entered Libra, Virgo, Scorpio, or Sagittarius..."
An intercalary month is not prescribed when [the sun] is in Capricorn or Aquarius.

*Dhaṭa* means a balance (*tulā*). Nor do these two sentences ever intend to convey the absence of the occurrence of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) therein. [As it is said: "If a month should occur without a solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*) while the sun has entered Virgo (*kanyāgata*)."
At that time, rites for the gods and the ancestors performed when the sun is in Libra yield inexhaustible merit for the performer.
This is because it contradicts the statements of Pitāmaha and others.
Furthermore, this demonstration of the purity of the *saṃsarpa* [intercalary month] refers to occasions such as *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death) and *śrāddha* rites, excluding matters like marriage.
When there is a pair of intercalary months within a year, the one known as *kṣaya* occurs during the triad of months beginning with Kārttika.

"This [impure month] must be diligently avoided for three months during marriages, sacrifices, festivals, and auspicious rites," according to the statement of the Jyotiḥśāstra. Thus ends the determination of the intercalary month (malamāsa).
Now follows the determination of what should and should not be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
Regarding this, Pauṭhīnasi says: "All rites pertaining to the Śruti and the Smṛti are declared to be performed in the twelfth month."
Therefore, those [rites] performed in the thirteenth month are proclaimed to be fruitless.
And here, the status of the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) as the thirteenth is relative to twelve pure months (*śuddhamāsa*) conjoined with solar transits (*saṅkrānti*), but not absolute.
Although the cessation of all rites is understood from the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarvāḥ*) here, nevertheless:
"One should avoid all optional rites (*kāmya*), such as sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), during the intercalary month."
In accordance with such statements as will be mentioned hereafter:
"One should, being self-restrained, perform the obligatory and occasional rites during an intercalary month."

And from such statements of counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), there is the cessation of only those rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), but not of the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) ones.
Furthermore, even among those [latter], only those that have no other recourse (*ananyagatika*) are to be performed therein, not those that have an alternative recourse (*sagatika*).
And so it is said:
In the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra*:
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites for a man who has no other recourse.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month.
Thus,
it is stated that the obligatory and occasional rites have no other recourse [for performance].
In the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa and other texts: "Sacrifices not accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call, as well as the *parvan* and the *āgrayaṇa*,
should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), but one should avoid optional (*kāmya*) offerings."
Sacrifices without the *vaṣaṭ*-call refer to the *agnihotra*, *aupāsana*, *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth;
and this [rule] pertains to those rites that have already been commenced.
Regarding the commencement, it refers to the first performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *agnihotra*.
Thus, because the *Madanaratna* prohibits the very commencement [of the rite],
the "parvan" refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as well as the *sthālīpāka*.
The *āgrayaṇa* is performed when old grain is not available.
The permanence of these [rites] is to be understood from such factors as the scriptural injunction that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance.
Furthermore, they have no other recourse because their completion occurs during the period of the intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

For rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which are enjoined with respect to the occasion of one's being alive during specific times, their completion occurs precisely within the intercalary month itself.

However, those rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma for which the prescribed time, such as spring, is not completed during the intercalary month (malamāsa) because it continues into the following pure month, should not be performed in that [intercalary] month. For this very reason, since the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice— though prescribed for the rainy season consisting of two months— is still obtainable at its proper time even in the pure month, the justification for the forthcoming prohibition against performing it during the intercalary month is established.
And we shall examine this further below.
Yama states:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, bathing, ancestral rites (śrāddha), giving gifts, recitation of mantras (japa), and so forth [are meritorious]."
"Rites should be performed even during an intercalary month.
In this context, the mention of lunar and solar eclipses is an illustration for unattainable conjunctions (alabhyayoga) such as the Kapila-ṣaṣṭhī and others.
[The same applies] during illness, during an unattainable conjunction, or during the Sīmantonnayana or Pumsavana ceremonies.
Because, by the statement of Itimarīci, it is understood that [the rite] must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

Furthermore, this injunction regarding what is to be performed here refers only to those acts such as ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth that are occasioned by that [intercalary month], and not to optional rites (*kāmya*), because of the prohibition: "An optional rite is never [to be performed].
Likewise—

One should not avoid the intercalary month (adhimāsa) in the following cases: during pregnancy, in moneylending, for a servant, at the monthly *śrāddha* rite, at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony, or in obligatory (*nitya*) rites.
Bathing at sacred fords, the recitation of mantras, burnt offerings with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth, the birth-rite, the funeral rites, and likewise the first anniversary śrāddha;
"The *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of Maghā, as well as the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Regarding "in the womb" (*garbhe*), it refers to the sacraments of the embryo (*garbhasaṃskāra*), such as the *puṃsavana* and others.

In *vārdhuṣike* means in the business of usury, namely in the taking of interest; in *bhṛtye* means in that business, namely in the taking of wages; in *māsike* refers to the monthly *śrāddha* rite, such as the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).

Because the sixteen *śrāddhas* are specifically mentioned here as distinct [from the monthly ones], the *śrāddha* performed at birth (*jātakarman*) and likewise the *darśa-śrāddha* must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), according to the statement of Vyāsa: "The *śrāddha* performed at birth and likewise the *darśa-śrāddha*—that should be performed even in an intercalary month; such is the word of Vyāsa."
Furthermore, from the statement of Vyāsa, it is understood that even the *darśa-śrāddha* (new-moon śrāddha) must be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
As for the verse: "That month which occurs as a thirteenth, exceeding the [regular] year..."
On that thirteenth day, one should not perform the śrāddha when the moon has waned.

This statement by Kauthumi refers to the *śrāddha* performed on the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*) associated with specific months beginning with Kārttika for the sake of particular fruits; or it refers to the optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* enjoined for the attainment of all desires, which is likewise restricted to the new-moon day alone. It does not, however, refer to the obligatory (*nitya*) *darśa-śrāddha*.
Regarding this, from the previously cited statement of Vyāsa:
"In the intercalary month (malimluca), one should, being self-restrained, perform the obligatory and occasional rites,
as well as bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), the 'elephant's shadow' rite (gajacchāyā), and likewise the Śrāddha for the deceased."
Furthermore, because of such general statements, it is understood that [these rites] must be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
This is also the consensus of all the digests (*nibandha*) of the Southerners (*Dākṣiṇātya*).

However, the Gauḍas argue that the term "obligatory" (*nitya*) does not include the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and other rites that are merely necessary; for if that were the case, since the necessity of performing even the *preta-śrāddha* and similar rites would be established by that very term, their separate mention would be rendered redundant.
However, this refers specifically to those [rites] such as the daily bath and *saṃdhyā* that are performed day after day.

Consequently, since there is no general counter-exception for the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, its prohibition during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) follows from the cited statement of Kauthumi. As for the statement of Vyāsa, that refers to the *śrāddha* known as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
That month in which Indra and Agni are invoked is proclaimed as the beginning;
Agni and Soma are remembered for the middle, and Pitṛs and Soma for the conclusion.
If the sun should ever pass beyond that [lunar month], it is to be known as the first *malimluca* (intercalary) month; the second is recorded as the ordinary (*prākṛta*) month.

In the statement of Laghuhārīta, after stating "At the conclusion [of the sacrifice], Pitṛ and Soma," the phrase "having passed beyond that" indicates the nature of the intercalary month (malamāsa); thus, since the performance of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña— whose deities are Soma qualified by the Pitṛs— is understood to be required during the intercalary month, they say that for the sake of achieving syntactic unity with that [text], it is appropriate that the statement of Vyāsa also has this same purpose.
Regarding "perpetual" (*nitya*), it refers to perpetual giving:
the *śrāddha* and the gift should be performed day after day during the year;
even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*), they should be performed every month with cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold.
This is according to the *Mātsya-purāṇa*.
"In the year" means in the first year. "Daily śrāddha" refers to the water-pot śrāddha prescribed for every day.
And likewise, Kauthumi says: "One should give a water-pot for a year, as well as food that has been well-accumulated."
Even when the year has increased [in length], the monthly rite is performed every month.
And thus, thirty offerings of water-pots and food constitute one additional monthly rite.
For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "If an intercalary month should occur within the year, one should increase the duration by one day for the purpose of the monthly rite."

As for what was stated here by Jīmūtavāhana—that the monthly śrāddha performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) for one who has died does not increase with the addition of months because of the previously cited Kauthuma statement, "beyond a year"—that is not correct.

For there is no evidence that this statement refers to that [monthly śrāddha] due to the non-mention of the word "māsika" in this text; rather, by the reasoning already stated, it is more appropriate that its scope is restricted solely to the pārvaṇa śrāddha.
Bathing at a sacred ford (tīrthasnāna) is subject to repetition,
because a prohibition against non-repetition will be stated later.
Furthermore, that bathing has the sacred ford as its locus, since it occurs solely by virtue of the occasion provided by the sacred ford.
The *aupāsana-homa* is performed by a human being with substances such as barley, rice, sesame, and so forth, because of the mention of these materials.
The mention of the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*).
Thus it is stated in the *Smṛti* cited by Mādhava:
The Śrāddha rites, the Jātakarman, and those sacraments accompanied by vows should be performed even during the intercalary month (malimluca),
but one should avoid optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi).
*Śrāddha* refers to that occasioned by birth, because it is mentioned in conjunction with birth;
its separate mention is justified because, since it is not an integral part (*anaṅga*) of the *jātakarman*, it is not included in the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) that applies to the latter.
*Jātaka* means the *jātakarman*.
*Samskāras* are rites such as the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) and *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food), which are fixed for specific months beginning with the fourth; namely:
naming, *annaprāśana*, tonsure (*caula*), marriage, the tying of the sacred girdle (*mauñjibandhana*), the *niṣkrama*, the birth rite (*jātakarma*), optional rites, and the release of a bull.
When Jupiter or Venus has set, when the moon is in its infancy or old age, or during an intercalary month,
one should by no means perform the commencement or undertaking of vows.
Thus, the statement of Garga prohibiting the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other ceremonies should be understood as referring to those performed at their primary time;
for instance, that same author says:
One should perform the naming ceremony and other rites according to the proper time;
however, if they have been delayed, they should be performed during an auspicious month when the moon is in the Puṣya constellation.
The *antyakarma* (funeral rites) includes the cremation, the collection of bones, and so forth.
The *navaśrāddha* (new funeral rite) refers to the rituals performed on the fourth day and subsequent days following the day of death. Bṛhaspati states:
One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month (malimluca),
as well as the śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha), the śrāddha under the "elephant's shadow" (gajacchāyā), and likewise the śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha).
In this regard, concerning the "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā):
whoever should offer supreme food (paramānna) together with honey to the ancestors while facing south, under the shadow of the lordly elephant in the east; [that person attains the highest reward].
Thus, according to Viśvāmitra, the shadow of the elephant itself is to be accepted;
however, it is not as follows:
"When the moon is in the constellation sacred to the ancestors (Maghā) and the sun is situated in the hand (Hasta)."
That lunar day which falls on a Tuesday is indeed proclaimed as Gajacchāyā.
Thus it was stated by that very [author],
because when the sun is situated in Hasta, there is necessarily a transition into Virgo (Kanyā-saṅkrānti), and therefore an intercalary month (malamāsa) is impossible;
the Southerners (Dākṣiṇātyas) also hold this view.
The followers of the Smṛtis, however, state:
"When Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, eclipses the sun during the junctions of the lunar phases (parva-sandhi), that is called Gaja-chāyā; one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony at that time."
Thus, they say that [the Gajacchāyā] mentioned in the Vārāha[-purāṇa] is to be accepted.

In this regard, according to the Southern tradition (Dākṣiṇātyamata), even though the Gajacchāyā and so forth possess a specific time for their occurrence, their performance must be understood as mandatory due to the scriptural injunction.
In this way, it has been stated that obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites are to be performed during the intercalary month (malamāsa) because there is no other alternative.
However, those rites that possess a specific destination (*sagatika*) are eternal (*nitya*), yet they are not to be performed there [in the intercalary month].
Some of these have been shown in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*:
"Rites such as the Soma sacrifice, though eternal, [are not to be performed] in the intercalary month (*malimluca*)."
And [the rites] such as the Putreṣṭi, Āgrayaṇa, Agnyādheya, and Cāturmāsya.

One should avoid performing even those rites such as the Mahālaya, the Aṣṭakā-śrāddha, and the Upākarma, which are prescribed by the explicit mention of a specific month, during the period of impurity (mala).

For here, since sacrifices such as the Soma sacrifice are prescribed for specific seasons like spring consisting of two months, they possess a "resort" (sagatikattva) even when the [specific] time is pure;
this should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
The *putreṣṭi* is the *jāteṣṭi*.

Even though that [offering] is occasional (*naimittika*), since its sublation occurs immediately after the occasion due to conflict with the primary element (*śeṣin*), it is logical that it should include the pure time (*śuddhakāla*), just as the *parvan* is included; thus, it possesses a basis for performance (*sagatika*).
As for the *Āgrayaṇa*, however, because it belongs to the rainy season consisting of two months, its possession of a basis for performance is quite evident.
As for the statement regarding its necessity to be performed, it was stated previously that this will apply when old grain is not available.
The *mahālaya* and other rites will be explained later.

Even those optional (*kāmya*) rites that cannot tolerate delay because they conflict with their primary purpose—such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice and others—must indeed be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
As for occasional (*naimittika*) optional rites, they should be performed exactly as they arise.
In that very same way, the tasks should be performed; however, time is not prescribed as a restrictive factor.
This is according to the statement of Dakṣa.

Here, there is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "occasional" (*naimittika*) and "optional" (*kāmya*); thus, the meaning is that those optional rites which present themselves as duties to be performed due to causes such as bad dreams are what are intended.
Even for purely optional rites, their avoidance applies only at the commencement and the conclusion.
Those months which are called "sunless" are not approved by me for the commencement or completion of vows and sacrifices.
This is according to the established conclusion of the *Brahmasiddhānta*.
Furthermore, the [observance of] continuity must indeed be maintained even in that case;
whatever *prārabdha* karma there may be, its effect should take place during the intercalary month (*malimluca*).
For it is stated right there [in that text]:
"Therefore, if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs between the commencement and the conclusion of the optional *Cāturmāsya* vow, its performance is prescribed therein without interruption."
"For this very same procedure is prescribed even in the case of the Adhimāsa [intercalary month]," so it is said.
As for that which—
Any optional rite that was commenced prior to the intercalary month but remains unfinished;
"Even when an intercalary month (malamāsa) has arrived, that [rite] must undoubtedly be completed.

Thus, the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra*, which establishes the completion of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) even during an intercalary month, refers to subjects such as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *ahīna*, and *satra* penances, which depend upon the solar measurement of time (*sāvanamāna*).
*Kālamādhava* also holds this same view.
Hemādri, however, holds that while the mere commencement of a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmyakarman) is forbidden during an intercalary month (malamāsa),
its completion must indeed be performed even in such a month, based on the previously cited Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtra.

As for the prohibition of completion found in the statement from the *Brahmasiddhānta* regarding "that which has been commenced," he says that this is intended to demonstrate the excessive fault in completing within that very month what was commenced out of delusion during the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) itself.
Thus, once the status of [the intercalary month] as something to be avoided has been established in brief, these scriptural passages are cited for the sake of detailed exposition.
Jyotiḥparāśara states: The establishment of the sacred fires, consecrations, sacrifices, gifts, and vows;
as well as Vedic observances, the ritual release of a bull, and the tonsure ceremony.
One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month (malamāsa),
as well as when Jupiter or Venus is in its infancy, or when either is aged or has set.
One should avoid these [acts], such as visiting a deity and the first installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), just as one avoids them during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
However, the re-installation of the fires (*punarādhāna*) necessitated by the extinction of the fire must certainly be performed, because it is a contingent rite (*naimittika*).
The original consecration remains as before;
however, when contact with outcastes (caṇḍāla) and the like occurs, a re-consecration must indeed be performed there.
Sacrifices and gifts are accompanied by their respective destinations.
Because there is a statement regarding the reversal [of prohibitions] for those who have no other recourse:
"The consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth, as well as sacrificial rites..."
One should not perform great gifts or religious vows during an intercalary month.
Thus, by these words of Nārada, there is a prohibition specifically of the "great gifts" (mahādāna), intended to indicate a particularly grave transgression.

As for the claim made by Ananta Bhaṭṭa, Hemādri, Jīmūtavāhana, Śūlapāṇi, and others—that the term *dāna* here refers exclusively to the great gifts and that therefore only those are prohibited—it is incorrect;
for it is appropriate to prohibit all other gifts as well, since they too have their own specific destinies.
When Venus has entered the twilight period (saṃdhyāgata) or is situated in a month that is an intercalary month (malimluca),
one should avoid visiting deities, giving gifts, or making great donations.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to conclude [the rule] by means of the employment of the terms "gift" (*dāna*) and "great gift" (*mahādāna*) in such passages from the *Laghu-Hārīta*, these texts cannot be considered rootless; for they are found in the *Kālaviveka* of Jīmūtavāhana, in Smṛti manuscripts, and elsewhere.
Therefore, it is logical that the separate prohibition of the great gifts is intended solely to indicate an excess of sin (*pratyavāya*).

Others, however, say that since it would result in the sublation of the primary injunctions (*śeṣin*), when giving and other such acts must necessarily be performed, this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) applies only to other [ordinary] gifts and not to the "great gifts" (*mahādāna*), because those are specifically prohibited again.

Nārāyaṇopādhyāya, on the other hand, says that for one seeking liberation who performs other gifts without attachment to their fruits, these are permissible even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*); however, the great gifts are not so, because they are prohibited again.
In the *Kṛtyacintāmaṇi*, however, the reading for the word "giving" (*dāna*) is "journeying" (*yāna*).
The Vedic vows are the Mahānāmni-vratas. The release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) is optional.
Since the rite on the eleventh day cannot be prohibited—just like the sixteen śrāddhas—it would otherwise be rendered impossible.
Other auspicious rites as well, such as marriage and so forth, are likewise [prohibited].
For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhīmaparākrama:
"During an intercalary month (adhimāsaka), one should avoid marriage, a journey, tonsure, initiation (upanayana), and the like."
One should perform auspicious rites without leaving any room for doubt, but one should not perform special sacrifices.
Thus [it is said].

Here, since the matter is already established by the phrase "having scope" (*sāvakāśam*), the Smṛti-author states that the explicit mention of "remarriage" and so forth is for the purpose of prohibition even in cases where there is no scope.
Furthermore, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) belongs to the king, and that is the first [of the sacraments].
The first consecration of a king awaits a pure time;
however, because it is obligatory, the annual [consecration] may take place at any time whatsoever.
Thus, according to the statement cited in the *Madanaratna*;

in reality, however, even the second [lunar month] and subsequent ones are indeed prohibited during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), because there is an alternative course available. This is the statement.
However, even during times such as the setting of Venus (*śukrāsta*), the primary duty remains the visiting of deities;
specifically, first the visiting of those beginningless deities well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources.
For it is said: "Upon seeing the beginningless deity, there would be no grief even when Bhārgava [Venus] has set."
One should avoid bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) that have not been visited previously, even during an intercalary month (malamāsa).
Thus, from the Skanda Purāṇa:

for here, the prohibition—which depends on the censure found in the first half [of the verse]—is not to be conceived as independent; otherwise, because the word *anāvṛtta* (not returning) would connect only with what follows, even the seeing of the deity (*devadarśana*) when repeated would be prohibited. Rather, it is this very [prohibition], "one should abandon," which applies due to its immediate presence.

For this very reason, even because bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and visiting deities (*devadarśana*) are mentioned together in the injunction regarding what is to be avoided, the use of the word "also" (*api*) is justified. Furthermore, since both are equally the objects of the act of avoidance, it is logical that the non-repeated category of items serves as the delimiter for both; thus, the prohibition of visiting deities applies to the first instance [of such a visit] during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

Moreover, if the prohibition applied to repeated visits to deities, it would follow that those deities who have been worshipped from time immemorial would become unworthy of worship for that duration of time.

This is not an undesirable consequence; for the purpose of worshipping the beginningless deity, no fault of time exists. Likewise, the Ekādaśī vow is [efficacious] through the practice of constant repetition.
Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with the statement of Jyotiḥparāśara.
Furthermore, in this context, the mention of bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) in the Skanda Purāṇa is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for pilgrimage and other such acts;
for this very reason, the reading in the statement of Gārgya is "one should avoid pilgrimage" (tīrthayātrāṃ vivarjayet).
And there is an exception to this rule regarding Gayā;
for it is said thus in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
A wise person should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at Gayā at all times, even during an intercalary month,
on one's birthday, or when Jupiter and Venus are eclipsed.
The Śrāddha at Gayā must not be abandoned even when Jupiter is situated in Leo.
Satyavrata says:
"The annual Śrāddha that is performed for one's mother and father on the anniversary of their death..."
"In an intercalary month (malamāsa), [the annual rite] should not be performed," according to the statement of Vyāghra.
The mention of "mother and father" is illustrative;
therefore, what is intended is that the annual *śrāddha* must not be performed during an intercalary month.
And this is logical,
because of the scriptural statement, "touched by the month, the fortnight, and the lunar day," which prescribes [the rite] on that specific lunar day of each respective month.
One should avoid performing what is prescribed for a clearly named specific month during an intercalary month (*mala*).
Because of this prohibition; for as it is said:
"The wise know that the intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not [to be considered] in the annual śrāddha."
The śrāddha performed at the birth-rite (jātakarman), as well as the new-moon śrāddha (navaśrāddha);

"The annual *śrāddha* is prescribed even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*)," and so forth— such statements by Śātātapa and others are intended to mean that for those who died during an intercalary month, the annual *pratyābdika* rite must be performed again in that very same intercalary month, and not in the pure (*śuddha*) month.
"But the *śrāddha* which is performed year after year on the anniversary of death— if that [anniversary] falls in an intercalary month..."
One should perform it there for those who have died; however, for others, it should be performed later.
Thus, because Śātātapa himself has assigned it as the object [of the name],
if a Brāhmaṇa dies when the *malimluca* month has arrived,
since that month is designated as "deficient" (*ūna*), how then should one perform the annual rite (*ābdika*)?
When the Sun has entered that zodiacal sign in which the death of a twice-born person occurred,
one should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and the water-libations (udaka-kriyā) in that very same sign.
For those who have perished during an intercalary month (adhimāsa), one should rely upon the solar measurement (saura-māna).
That very day is [the proper time] for his śrāddha, the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), water libations (udaka), and so forth.
This is also because it forms a single syntactical unit with the statement of Vyāsa.

Furthermore, the interpretation offered by the author of the *Samayaprakāśa*—that this statement intends that for one who dies during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the annual anniversary rite (*pratyābdika*) must always be performed according to the solar month alone—is not tenable.
For if the day of death were never to arrive again within the subsequent year for one who died in an intercalary month, it would result in the omission of the *śrāddha*.

Therefore, the interpretation that for one who died in a *mala-māsa*, the annual *śrāddha* (pratyābdika) must be performed in that same *mala-māsa* and not in the pure (*śuddha*) month, is the superior and widely accepted view.
However, for those who died in a pure month, the second and subsequent annual rites should be performed in the pure month alone, while the first annual rite should be performed in the *mala-māsa*.
And so it is said:
Hārīta says:
"The first annual *śrāddha* (ābdika) must be performed by the twice-born even if the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) has not occurred;
likewise the monthly *śrāddha* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
The meaning is that this refers to the intercalary month (malamāsa) when the sun has not yet shifted [to the next zodiac sign].
Yama also says:
"That which is the first annual śrāddha, one should perform even during the intercalary month."
But when the thirteenth year has arrived, one should perform the annual śrāddha once again.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the first annual rite (prathamābdika) should indeed take place during the intercalary month (mala).
As for the second and subsequent annual rites (punarābdika), if an intercalary month falls on that same day, then one should perform them in the thirteenth pure month; such is the meaning.
The *Laghuhārīta* also states:
"Every year, in the twelfth month, the rite of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should be performed by sons;
in some cases, it may also take place in the thirteenth month, except for the very first year."
The rule that "the [śrāddha] is performed every year in the twelfth month" is a general principle when there is no intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
In certain cases, such as the second anniversary and so forth, if an intercalary month occurs, it should be performed in the thirteenth *śuddha* (pure) month.
The meaning is that the first anniversary (*ādyābdika*) must be performed in the twelfth month itself, even if an intercalary month has fallen within that period.

And this requirement to perform [the *sapiṇḍana*] in the twelfth month applies when an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) occurs, not when an intercalary month falls within the middle of the year. For if it were otherwise, since the lunar date (*mṛtatithi*) of death would not be found in the twelfth month, the *sapiṇḍana* would be impossible; furthermore, for one who died in Kārttika, there would be the undesirable consequence of performing the annual anniversary (*pratyābdika*) in Āśvina.
However, only when the final month itself is an intercalary month (malamāsa) is the first-annual rite (ādyābdika) to be performed therein.
This is the meaning:
for those who died during an intercalary month, whenever by the course of time that very month of death happens to be an intercalary month, then their annual rite must be performed at that very time.

However, for those who have died during a pure month, the second annual anniversary and subsequent ones are performed in a pure month, whereas the first annual anniversary is performed in the intercalary (mala) month itself.
And thus:
"If an intercalary month should occur when the day for the Śrāddha has arrived..."
One should perform two śrāddhas; by doing so, one does not go astray.
Thus, the statement of Vasiṣṭha should be explained as referring to the monthly rites (*māsika*).

As for those statements of Gālava and others, such as "That [rite] should be performed even during two months, according to the word of Vyāghra" and "The ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) belong to both," these too must be settled in the same manner.
Kauthumi states: "The rite for the increase of years (*varṣavṛddhi*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and so forth, should be performed when [the month] is additional, but not otherwise.
*Varṣavṛddhi* refers to the celebration of prosperity (*vardhāpana*) performed every year.
Hārīta states: "In an intercalary month (adhimāsa), one should not perform the Śrāddha, nor likewise the Abhyudaya-śrāddha;
the same applies to any optional rite (kāmya-karma), except for that which is performed during the first year [of mourning]."
Whatever Śrāddha rite there may be after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa—
whether it be an *iṣṭi* or otherwise— one should not perform it during the *malimluca* month.

In this context, it should be understood that by means of the prohibition of *abhyudaya* (prosperity rites), the prohibition of the *caula*, *upanayana*, and other such rites—which are constituent parts of those [rites]—is intended.
This is because it forms a single syntactical unit with the previously cited statements such as, "The *cūḍā* and the *mauñjī-bandhana*," and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the *nāmakarma* and other rites to be performed during the impure month (*malamāsa*) in the first year, the *ābhyudayika* rite must be performed specifically in that impure month; thus it is said: "Except for the first year."
This is the meaning [of the verse].

However, some say that the *ābhyudayika* rite performed on the day following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* during the first year must be performed even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). Hemādri, however, maintains that the phrase "from the first year onwards" connects with the expression "after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."

And likewise, he states that those monthly rites (māsika) related to the first year which are performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony must be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). However, Śūlapāṇi says:
"The first annual rite (*ābdika*) must be performed by the twice-born even when no solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) has occurred [in that month]."
In the same way, the monthly rites are performed first, as is the sapindikarana ceremony.
Thus, in the statement of Laghuhārīta, the preceding phrase is intended to prohibit the monthly *śrāddhas* that occur subsequent to the *sapiṇḍana*.
Therefore, he states that those [other rites] should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
Furthermore, this prohibition of *śrāddhas* occurring after the *sapiṇḍana* applies to cases other than the *yugādi-śrāddhas*.
These, however, should be performed even during an intercalary month;
there is no postponement on the Daśaharās, nor on the four Yugādis,
nor on the Upākarma and Utsarga, for this is desired starting from the month of Vṛṣabha.
Because of this statement;

for here, since it is designated as beginning with "vṛṣāt" (from Taurus), it is understood that the *daśaharā* occurs only in Taurus and Scorpio, while the *yugādayaḥ* occur only in Libra, Capricorn, Aries, and Leo.

Furthermore, the hearing of words such as "Jyeṣṭha" in statements like "In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha," and so forth, as well as in the context of the Daśaharā festival and others, refers by necessity to the solar month through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), since it is impossible for a pure month to exist when the sun is situated in Libra (Tulā) and other signs. Consequently, because the commencement of the Yuga-ādi falls precisely during the intercalary month (malamāsa), its non-deferral is established. In this regard, the statement concerning the non-deferral of the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites pertains specifically to the followers of the Sāmaveda (Chandogas).
For them alone:
when the sun is in Leo and the moon is in the Puṣya asterism, one should go outside in the forenoon;
the assembled Chandogas (Sāmavedins) should perform the utsarga of all the Vedic meters.

And because the *Gārgya* statement— "The afternoon *upākarma* rite is performed with the *Hasta* nakṣatra during the bright fortnight"— prescribes the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites when the sun is situated in Leo (*siṃha*),
for this very reason, the word "Śrāvaṇa" in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* passage beginning with "with the *Śravaṇa* [nakṣatra] of Śrāvaṇa" does not refer to a solar month.

Since the rule *vṛṣāditaḥ* can be explained as referring to the *Chandogas* who depend upon the well-known solar month, there is no evidence for taking the word "Śrāvaṇa" in a figurative sense. Therefore, the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites should not be performed during an intercalary month (*mala*) by the general followers of the Sāmaveda.
For this very reason—

The postponement of rites such as the commencement of study (*upākarma*) and others occurs when the time for their performance has increased; however, there is no postponement of the increases [of the lunar days] associated with the beginnings of the *yugas*.
Thus, the validity of such scriptural statements as those concerning the Ātīya month and others is established;
otherwise, if everyone were to rely solely on the solar month, these scriptural declarations would become meaningless.
Therefore, one must adhere to the system exactly as it has been stated.
As for that which is stated in the *Smṛtisaṅgraha*:

"O twice-born ones, [the rites] are suspended during the mental confusion of Bhṛgu and Bhārgava, whether in childhood, youth, or old age; likewise during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), the *sarpa* month, the impure month (*malamāsa*), and so forth."
If the first *upākṛti* is not performed, it causes the destruction of the ritual act.
This statement prohibits the first *upākaraṇa* (commencement) for the Sāmavedins alone.
Mādhava and others, however, disregarding the causal phrase "because [it begins] with the bull" found in the statement "not on the *daśaharā* days," [state]:
"The *śrāddha* performed every month on the anniversary of death, and that which is performed every year..."
And at the beginning of the Manvantaras, at the beginning of the Yugas, and during both months as well.

One should perform the *yaugādika*, the monthly (*māsika*), the fortnightly (*aparapākṣika*), the *manvādika*, and the *tairthika* śrāddhas either on both [the new and full moon] days of the month, or alternatively, on both months.
Thus, based on the words of Marīci and others, they state that the *yugādi* śrāddha must be performed on both occasions.

However, regarding the performance of a śrāddha at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the settled rule is that one should perform it only when the arrival at the ford occurs—whether during the bright or the dark fortnight.

In reality, however, because the inconsistency [of the former view] would arise with the statements of Manu and others, it is more logical that the śrāddha at a sacred ford be performed on both occasions by the force of this very text.
The rite pertaining to the other fortnight, which is based on the common characteristics of the dark fortnight, should be performed during two months.
However, regarding the occasion of the *mahālaya*, if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) falls within either Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, then:
"Whether it be Nabhas or Nabhasya that becomes the intercalary month..."
The seventh [day] belongs to the side of the ancestors, but elsewhere it is indeed the fifth.

Thus, because it is prescribed in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* for the seventh fortnight from Āṣāḍhī, its prohibition during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is quite clear. Even when the month of Āśvina is an intercalary month, the *Mahālaya* should not be performed in that "defiled" Āśvina under the mistaken impression that it is connected with the month of Kanyā; rather, it must be performed in the latter fortnight of Bhādrapada, according to the statement: "But elsewhere, [it is] the fifth.
Nor should it be asked: "How can there be a Śrāddha there if there is no conjunction with Kanyā?"
It should be asked: if the entire fortnight lacks conjunction with the maiden (Kanyā) [nakṣatra], how can the Śrāddha be performed there?

[The answer is: even though the entire fortnight lacks connection with the maiden, the performance of the Śrāddha therein is possible because the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada possesses contact with the solar transit (saṅkrānti) into the maiden.
For this very reason—
Whether at the beginning or in the middle, whichever fortnight the sun enters [the sign], that entire fortnight is to be honored; therein the Śrāddha rite is prescribed.

Thus, even according to the statement of Kārṣṇājini, it is declared that the Śrāddha should be performed there [in the fifth fortnight] even if the entire fortnight lacks conjunction with the month of Kanyā. However, in the view of Śūlapāṇi and others, since the fifth fortnight itself—regardless of its connection with Kanyā—is the time for Śrāddha, the performance of the Śrāddha there is indeed appropriate.

As for the other Śrāddha performed once during the latter half of the month when the moon has entered Kanyā in their view, that pertains to the latter half of the month when the moon has entered Kanyā.

Since the fifth fortnight is impossible during the impure Āśvina month, even if [the Śrāddha] occurs then, it must be performed specifically during the latter fortnight of [Āśvina] when the sun has entered Libra (*tulā*), in accordance with the statement to be cited hereafter.

In reality, however, the Śrāddha of the latter fortnight when the moon is in Virgo (*kanyā*) is not distinct from the Śrāddha of the fifth fortnight; for if there were a difference between the Śrāddhas, it would entail the fault of over-complication (*gaurava*) in postulating separate injunctions.
Furthermore, by the statement, “At the end or in the middle,” it is understood that the time for the Śrāddha of the fifth fortnight is indeed characterized by the presence of Virgo.
Nor does it follow that the performance of a Śrāddha would be required in the fifth generation in the absence of a connection through a maiden;
for in that case, a connection through a maiden is mandatory.
For if the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) occurs during Śrāvaṇa or Bhādra, the fifth fortnight would not be connected with Virgo (*kanyā*).
In that case, since the seventh fortnight is prescribed, the performance of the *śrāddha* would occur only when marked by Virgo; thus, there is no deficiency whatsoever.

However, when Āśvina is the intercalary month, the fifth fortnight is indeed connected with Virgo, because the sun enters Virgo on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) itself. Therefore, it is logical—and widely accepted—that there is only one *śrāddha*.

And even that [rite] should be performed only during that very fifth fortnight characterized by the month of Kanyā, since it is obtained as the primary [period], despite the fact that the month of Āśvina may be impure.
As for that which—
If the month should be one in which the sun has not yet entered Virgo,
then rites for the gods and the ancestors performed when the sun is in Libra yield inexhaustible merit for the performer.

Thus, the statement of Pitāmaha regarding the light (jyotiḥ), which indicates that [the śrāddha] should be performed when the sun is in Libra (tulā), refers to śrāddhas such as those performed at the ripening of rice (*vrīhipāka*) and others, excluding the Mahālaya.

Alternatively, since the Mahālaya is prescribed even during the secondary period (*gauṇakāla*) by the rule "as long as the scorpion is seen," this prohibition—intended for a rite performed in the impure month of Āśvina due to a misconception regarding the secondary period—is directed toward [rites other than the Mahālaya] when the sun is in Libra, as stated by the Kālādarśa: [The text continues: ...that which is performed by the Kālādarśa...

In the statement, "On the anniversary of the year [of death], on the day of the water-jar [ceremony], on the Anvādi days, on the Mahālaya days, and on the Yugādi days," the inclusion of the term *mahālaya* among the rites to be performed refers to the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) named Mahālaya;
this is also the view accepted by Mādhava.

And here, since in the *Jyotiḥpitāmaha* statement it is understood that even the rites for the goddess (*daiva*) which are to be performed by a girl must be performed in Libra (*tulā*), the installation of Durgā and other such rites should also be performed at that very time.
As it is said in the *Jyotiḥ*:
If an additional month occurs when Gemini is complete, then that Lord Hari sleeps in Cancer and wakes in Scorpio; however, when four months have passed,
the Lord of Śacī, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, rises in Virgo.
Durgā herself is at the arrival of the balance (tulā), and when it is exceeded, the remaining gods are the others.
In the *Pariśiṣṭa* as well:
"When the second Āṣāḍha has arisen, Hari lies down in Cancer;
Ākhaṇḍala [Indra] is in Virgo, and likewise Pārvatī is in Libra."
And here is the description of the intercalary Āṣāḍha: "When the sun, situated in Gemini, touches two new moons, that is to be known as the intercalary Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer."
According to this statement, the primary [meaning] alone should be accepted:
"In the six months beginning with Mādhava, if there should be two new moons (darśa) in a single month, that is to be known as a double Āṣāḍha."

Many authorities maintain that figurative (gauṇa) interpretations of such passages should not be accepted here. Regarding the specific rule for the annual anniversary śrāddha (pratyābdika) for one who died during the month of Kṣaya, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa in Hemādri states:
The first half-tithi is considered the first month, and the second half-tithi the subsequent month;
these two middle portions of the intercalary month (kṣayamāsa) are thus reckoned by the wise.
Thus it is said;
this should be understood to apply to the *vardhāpana* (birthday celebration) as well, just as it does to the annual anniversary (*ābdika*).
This concludes the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).

Now follows the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done regarding the thread ceremony (*maujhī*) and other rites when Jupiter, Venus, and so forth are in their respective states.
Bṛhaspati says:
"Whether Jupiter is in its childhood or old age, or when Venus has set, or when the sun has set..."
One should avoid visiting these deities, just as one avoids them during an intercalary month.
Upon seeing the beginningless deity when Venus has set, one should not grieve;
even during an intercalary month, one should avoid pilgrimage to sacred sites from which there is no return.
The Miśras maintain that there is merely the absence of the defect of returning to the sacred ford, but no actual fruit [accrues].
That is not so,
because there is no subverting evidence [to the contrary].
Lalla also says:

"When [a planet] is in its sign of debilitation, or in retrograde motion, or in excessive velocity, or when it is young, old, or set; then renunciation, pilgrimage to the gods, the performance of vows and observances, ear-piercing, and initiation [are forbidden]."

The tying of the muñja-grass girdle for women, the ritual rules for specific observances, and the consecration of Vāstu deities should be diligently avoided by the virtuous when Jupiter is situated in the sign of Leo.
Thus it is said.
An exception to this is stated in the *Brāhma*:
"Shaving the head and fasting [are required] at the Gautamī when the Sun is in Leo."
But when the moon has entered Virgo during the dark fortnight, there is no [restriction] for those dwelling on its banks.

The characteristics of childhood and so forth are stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "The conjunction of the other planets with the Sun is called their setting (*asta*). Prior to that is old age; after [the setting] due to their dullness (*mauḍhya*) is declared to be childhood."
The measure of this is also stated in that very same place:
"In the eastern direction, the childhood of Venus lasts for five days, while its old age is said to last ten days;
in the western direction, its old age lasts for five days, while its childhood is remembered as lasting ten days."
Childhood and old age are the two phases, occurring respectively before and after Jupiter.
Also in the Bārhaspatya [Tantra]:
"Venus, having risen in the east or the west, is a child for five or seven days;
its old age is the reverse. It is the same for Jupiter as well."
In this case, when there is a contradiction regarding measurement, the determination is made either by difference of location or by the influence of adversity.
For this very reason, Mihira says:

Many periods of time have been shown, both in childhood and even in old age; among those, the greater [periods] should be adopted, or the remaining ones according to the difference of place or in times of distress.
And Gārgya has stated the distinction of regions as follows:
"Venus and Jupiter are [respectively] young in the east and old in the west."
They say that in the Vindhya mountains and in Daśārṇa it lasts seven nights;
in Vaṅga and among the Hūṇas, six and five nights respectively; and in all other regions, three days.
Regarding the specific rule for the Gaṅgā, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"A wise person should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) in the Gaṅgā at all times,
even during an intercalary month (adhimāsa), on one's birthday, and when the Sun or Venus is eclipsed."
The Gayā-śrāddha must not be abandoned even when Jupiter is situated in Leo;
likewise,
[it should be performed] at the Godāvarī, at Gayā, and at Śrīśaila during both eclipses.
And among the teachers of the gods and asuras, no fault of delusion exists regarding the "grahaṇa"—
that is, with respect to the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra and other rites caused by an eclipse.
Therefore, Lalla says:

The rite of pilgrimage to a sacred ford is recommended during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the half-rising of the moon or sun, on the sixth lunar day known as Kapilā, upon the setting of Jupiter (the preceptor of gods and demons), and during the sun's transit into a new zodiac sign.
Thus ends the determination regarding the debilitation (mauḍhya) and other states of Jupiter, Venus, and the rest. Now follows the time for the Śrāddha ceremony.
In that regard, first, the time is the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
On this point, Śātātapa says: "That which is declared as the *darśa-śrāddha* is proclaimed to be the *pārvaṇa*."
And in the afternoon, giving gifts to the ancestors there is praised.
Yama says:
"At the end of the fortnight, one should offer to them [the gods] in the afternoon, but the ancestral rite (paitṛka) [is performed] later.
Kātyāyana says:
The Śrāddha consisting of the Anvāhārya rice-ball is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, but not too close to the time of twilight.
It is designated as *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* because it is performed after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*;
for this very reason, Manu says:
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, on the new moon day,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
(Verse 3, Śloka 122) Furthermore, "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) here refers to the third part of a day divided into three;
this is because of the expression "the third part of the day."
"At the waning of the moon" means on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
And it is not by the term "ancestral sacrifice" (*pitṛyajña*) [that this is meant]; for it is said:
"A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the ancestral sacrifice known as the libation (*tarpaṇa*)," etc.
One should always perform the Śrāddha rite consisting of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka on the day of the new moon.

Thus, according to the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, it must be stated that only the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is being described, and not the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For if the term "ancestral sacrifice" (*pitṛyajña*) in Manu’s statement were taken to refer to the libation, the term "offering of rice-balls" (*piṇḍānvāhārya*) could not function as its name;
for that [term] is a name by virtue of the principle of "being known through that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*).
And that [sequence] is not possible unless the status of occurring after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed;
therefore, the term *pitṛyajña* refers to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
However, in the statement of the *Mānava-śākhā*, the term *pitṛyajña* denotes only the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

And that [tarpaṇa] is not the libation in the form of the *pitṛyajña* included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) as stated by Medhātithi; for since that is already accomplished by occasion (*prasaṅga*) on the day of the *śrāddha*, it is illogical to enjoin its performance subsequent to it.
Rather, it refers specifically to the water-libation (*jalatarpaṇa*).

Furthermore, although the sequence following that [libation] is already established—since the *śrāddha* is prescribed for one who has bathed, and the libation is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the bath—it is nevertheless [stated as follows]:

"The *pitṛyajña* is the libation (*tarpaṇa*), or it may be the *śrāddha*, or even the offering (*bali*) to the ancestors. Regarding the attainment of these three types of *pitṛyajña* mentioned in this scriptural statement, the Gauḍas hold that the repetition of the term "libation" (in the rule for one with sacred fires) is intended to exclude other forms of *pitṛyajña* on the day of the *śrāddha* for one who maintains the sacred fire.

Others, however, argue that since the *tarpaṇa* (libation) included within the procedure for bathing is prescribed only for the followers of Kātyāyana, there is no evidence for its inclusion within the bathing procedure for others; consequently, it might occasionally follow after a *śrāddha*. Therefore, since a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is possible when such a contingency exists, rather than an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*), the statement in the Matsya Purāṇa is intended to restrict [the timing] precisely to the period following the water-libation.
Thus they say.
In every respect, the term "pitṛyajña" in the statement of Manu refers exclusively to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Therefore, it is established that the designation *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* for the Darśa-śrāddha is based precisely upon that [Piṇḍapitṛyajña].

Since such [a time] is possible only for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and is entitled to perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, these statements from the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* and Manu refer specifically to that subject;
they do not apply to everyone, because the designation [of "afternoon"] would otherwise be impossible for others.
For this very reason, the "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) consisting of the third part of the day mentioned in the *Pariśiṣṭa* belongs only to the *āhitāgni* who is entitled to the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

Furthermore, by the phrase "not too near the twilight" (*nātisandhyāsamīpata*), it is only the final muhūrta of the day that is prohibited for him, and not the three-muhūrta period constituting the evening (*sāyāhna*).

If that were the case, it would be impossible to perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the Śrāddha during the remaining eleventh and twelfth muhūrtas, as these fall within the afternoon— which consists of the third part of the day comprising five muhūrtas—
and because the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is prescribed specifically for the afternoon divided into three parts.
By this, Mādhava’s statement that the phrase "not too near the twilight" (nātisandhyāsamīpataḥ) is intended as a prohibition against the late afternoon is refuted.

The author of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* maintains that this rule for the determination of time, as stated in the *Pariśiṣṭas*, applies only to those for whom the New Moon sacrifice (*darśeṣṭi*) is prohibited on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) when the moon is visible.
Therefore, for those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and perform such rites, the Amāvāsyā (New Moon) is determined according to the *Pariśiṣṭa* in accordance with the time of the sacrifice;
and in that case, the time is specifically the afternoon divided into three parts.
However, regarding the waning of the moon, there is merely a recommendation based on the statement: "It is praised when the moon has waned.
And the waning of the moon is described in that very same place:
"In the eighth part of the fourteenth day, the moon becomes waned."
And again, at the eighth part of the new moon, it indeed becomes subtle once more.
Thus,
"exhausted" (kṣīṇa) means having only one-quarter of a digit (kalā) remaining;
for it will be described later as being of extreme subtlety in that very same manner.
And because there is a complete waning [of the moon] during the seventh part of the new moon, both [the seventh and eighth parts] are denoted by the term "waning.
However, it is stated that on the new moon days of the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, the waning occurs at only the eighth part of the new moon—
in that very same [text]:
