The new moon day of Āgrahāyaṇa and likewise that which occurs in Jyeṣṭha—
those who know the lunar days declare these two to be particularly distinguished.
In this context, the experts of the celestial sphere declare that the moon remains in the first watch with only a quarter-kalā remaining,
and at the very end of that [watch], it undergoes complete waning.
"Of these two" means *ābhyām* = *anayoḥ*. "Only those ending in that" means only those ending in *am*.

It has been stated that in a year joined with an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), even for these two [the *saṃkrānti* and the *amānta*], the intercalation (*kṣaya*) is exactly the same as for the other.
In that same work:
"In whichever year there are thirteen months, in that year the third [lunar day] should not be observed.
Here, *pavya* means a month.

Because it is deficient by a fourth part due to the third [digit], and remains as a mere third part of a digit (*kalā*), it would not be visible during the first watch of these two new moons; however, the meaning is that there is a waning (*kṣaya*) here in these two new moons just as in other months.
Regarding this, the author of the *Pariśiṣṭaprakāśa* states: "The full moon ends in the months of Jyeṣṭha and Mārgaśīrṣa."
Thus, it is established that the afternoon divided into three parts is the primary time,
while the waning of the moon is merely a matter of excellence.

In this case, regarding the pervasion of the afternoon, the entire duration of the day is pervaded by the absence of any decrease in the occurrence [of the moon] exceeding three muhūrtas; whereas on the other day, it occurs through non-contact with that [afternoon] or through partial pervasion. Therein, the non-contact [with the afternoon] arises due to the new moon being equal to, increasing beyond, or decreasing relative to the fourteenth day.

In that regard, first, that [lunar day] which occupies the entire duration on the previous day and does not touch even a portion of it on the following day belongs to the previous day alone. Likewise, that which occupies only a portion of it on the subsequent day also belongs to the previous day alone;
however, if the moon is visible on the day of sacrifice, the sacrifice must take place on the very day when only a portion is occupied.

If, however, due to the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the non-appearance of the moon, the sacrifice is performed on the *pratipad* itself, then it must be done on the very day when there is partial overlap (*ekadeśavyāpti*). Otherwise, the simultaneity of the three acts—the kindling of the fires (*ādhāna*), and so forth—would be untenable; this is also the consensus of the *Gobhilabhāṣya*.
As for that which...
If it covers only a portion of the previous day, that [fourteenth day] is all the more "prior";
and when the fourteenth day extends into the fourth watch and the new moon is waning, then the Śrāddha is prescribed at that very time.
This is also because of the statement in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:

"But that [tithi] which on the following day alone covers the entire duration of the time, while on the preceding day it either touches only a portion of it or does not touch it at all, that [following one] alone is to be taken.
However, when it covers only a portion of the time on both days but unequally, whichever is greater is to be accepted."

However, if [the fast] extends partially equally over two days, then if it is such by way of decrease (*kṣaya*), it is the former day according to the previously cited statement regarding the decreasing [fourteenth day], namely: “When the fourteenth day [extends into] the watch (*yāma*)...”; but if it is such by way of increase (*vṛddhi*), then it is the latter day.
As it is said: “If one should obtain the increasing new moon (*amāvāsyā*) on the following day...”
The ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) should take place three yāmas later, or even more than that.
This is because of the statement in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
"The exception regarding those two [the new moon and full moon] caused by the visibility or invisibility of the moon has already been explained.
Thus, when they are equal, the determination is likewise based solely on visibility or invisibility.

And when, in certain views, the performance [of the rites] falls on an Amāvāsyā mixed with the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), then—if it is possible to perform all the rites by waiting for the Amāvāsyā—then that [Amāvāsyā] should be awaited; if not, then everything must be performed even on the fourteenth day. Now follows the determination of the Amāvāsyā for those without sacred fires (niragnika) and for those with sacred fires (sāgnika) who, like the followers of Āpastamba, Asvalāyana, and others, are not bound by the rule of performing the triad [of rites] on a single day.
And here, that [lunar day] which extends through the afternoon divided into five parts is to be accepted.
When it extends through the afternoon on both days, if there is a decrease [of the lunar day], the former is taken; if there is an increase or equality, the latter is taken.
However, as for the new moon (amāvāsyā), whichever occurs during the two afternoons is [the one to be observed].
In the case of destruction, the former [direction] is prescribed; in growth and in equilibrium, the latter is traditionally taught.
This is according to the statement cited by Mādhava;
furthermore, here the "wane" (kṣaya) and so forth refer to the subsequent lunar day (tithi),
though some maintain they refer to that very [preceding] lunar day.
Even when there is an equal partial overlap on two days, this same decision applies.

However, when the new moon touches the afternoon on both days, the determination is made according to the distinction between those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgni*) and those who do not (*niragni*).
If, due to the waning of the lunar day (*tithi-kṣaya*), the new moon does not cover both afternoons:
Sinīvālī is traditionally assigned to one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), while Kuhū is assigned to one who is without such fires.
This is according to the statement of Jābāli; and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), women and Śūdras are included.
Women, Śūdras, and likewise twice-born men who maintain no sacred fires (anagnika) should perform the *kuhū* sacrifice.
This is according to the statement of Laugākṣi.
Furthermore, the Madanapārijāta maintains that the term *āhitāgni* (one who has consecrated the sacred fires) here is also indicative of one who maintains the Smārta fires.
The definitions of Sinīvālī and the others have been stated [as follows]:
Vyāsa states: "Sinīvālī is that [first lunar day] on which the moon is seen; Kuhū is remembered as that on which the moon has disappeared.
However, Hemādri maintains that for those who do not maintain the sacred fires (niragnika), the day that extends through the Kutupa period should be taken.
If that [lunar day] extends over two days, it is the former when there is a decrease [of its duration], and the latter when there is equality or an increase; thus he says.
This concludes the determination of the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Now follows the determination of the time for the Aṣṭakā rites.
Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states: "The Aṣṭakās are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons.

Here, Hemanta and Śiśira refer to the two seasons, which in this context consist of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, ending with the new moon (darśānta). "Aparapakṣāḥ" means the dark fortnights (kṛṣṇapakṣāḥ).
The phrase "in four" is intended to prohibit the performance [of the rites] during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
This is what is meant: the four *kṛṣṇāṣṭamī* days occurring in the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa—on those days, the *aṣṭakā* sacrifices are to be performed.
The term *aṣṭakā* is, according to the view of Āśvalāyana, the name for both the *śrāddha* and the *homa*, whereas according to the view of Kātyāyana, it is the name for the *homa* alone.

This is because in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*)—"on the eighth days [of the dark fortnights] are the *aṣṭakās*"—the ritual act in the form of the *aṣṭakā* is enjoined with respect to that time.
Furthermore, its reference to the ritual act is established by the grammatical derivation from the rule: "The word *aṣṭakā* [is used] when the ancestors are the deity."

And thus, although in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, following the opening “the new moon day and the *aṣṭakās*,” it is stated that “the times for the *śrāddha* have been proclaimed,” the word *aṣṭakā* appears at first glance to denote time;
nevertheless, like the statement “the substance and the excellence of the Brahmins,” it indicates by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) the time mentioned by Āśvalāyana.
However, in the *Padma-purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, the *prauṣṭhapadī-aṣṭakā* shall take place in the world of the ancestors.
By this, another *aṣṭakā* on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is mentioned.
And thus, it is established that there are five *aṣṭakās* in a year.
Āśvalāyana, however, has assigned another name to the Bhādra-aṣṭakā, namely *mādhyāvarṣam*.

Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya and others have explained that because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual details from the [ordinary] *aṣṭakā*, it is a distinct rite from the *aṣṭakā*.

Thus, according to those learned in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*), the Paurāṇic *aṣṭakā* and the *mādhyāvarṣam* should be performed together by the followers of Āśvalāyana on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada.

Gobhila, however, having stated, "One should desire to perform all those [Aṣṭakās] with meat during the winter which consists of four Aṣṭakās," subsequently mentions the alternative view of eight Aṣṭakās.
This statement, "The winter consists of four Aṣṭakās," is to be understood as referring to the position that the year has three seasons;
or else, following the rule "by combining Hemanta and Śiśira," it should be understood as referring to the position that the year has five seasons.
In the Smṛtis of Viṣṇu and others, where there is the mention of "the three Aṣṭakās and the three Anvaṣṭakās," that refers only to those occurring in the winter season,
because their presence here [in that context] is possible without any interruption.
Even though—
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "On the first [tithi] of the lunar fortnight presided over by Indra, one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables;
on the second, presided over by Prajāpati, one should satisfy them with pure meats."
On the third lunar day dedicated to Viśvedevas, one should offer cakes according to the prescribed order during the rainy season; likewise, on the fourth day, one should always offer pure vegetables.

Although no specific month is mentioned here, nevertheless, because another statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa* says, "On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables," and thus specifies that the offering of vegetables occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa, these three [offerings] are understood to pertain specifically to the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, however, it is clearly stated that these three [Aṣṭakās] occur specifically in the months beginning with Pauṣa:
"The new moon and the three Aṣṭakās are in the three months beginning with the month of Pauṣa."
And here, Pauṣa is intended as beginning with the bright fortnight (śuklādi),
according to the Viṣṇudharmottara: "When Āgrahāyaṇī has passed, there are likewise three Aṣṭakās in the dark fortnights."
Thus, in the *Brahmapurāṇa* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, three [days] during the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are mentioned, excluding the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna.
However, in the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyupurāṇa*, it is stated:
"The three Aṣṭakās alone are the root for the granting of sons."
For during the dark fortnight, the former [Pūrva-phalgunī], belonging to Indra, is considered the most excellent.
The second [offering] should be dedicated to Prajāpati, and the third to the Viśvedevas;
the first should always be performed with cakes, and likewise, the other should be with meat.
The third [day] should be observed with vegetables; this is the rule regarding the substances.
Furthermore, one should especially observe whatever other fourth [day] there may be.
Thus [it is said].

Although the month is not explicitly mentioned here either, nevertheless, regarding the third [day] which is described as the "vegetable aṣṭakā": "On the eighth day of Phālguna, one should cook vegetables oneself, or even one's wife."
By this [statement], because the eighth day of Phālguna is recognized as being among the *śākāṣṭakās*, three [such days] are mentioned, excluding the eighth day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
By the phrase, "And that which may be another fourth," the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada alone is intended.
"And always on the fourth day during the rains with pure vegetables."
In this context, because that very [tithi] is referred to as being the fourth, others, however,
maintain that there are three [days] beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

And thus, since there is the possibility of consistency with the previously cited *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, and given the parsimony of postulating a single scriptural authority (*eka-śruti-kalpanā-lāghave*), it is indeed improper to postulate separate scriptural authorities.

The fourth [Aṣṭakā], however, is indeed the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, and not the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna; otherwise, how could one say, “these three” and “this is the fourth”? For if it were as Gobhila suggests, one would have said “four” from the very beginning. Thus, even according to the Paurāṇika view, four Aṣṭakās are to be performed in a year.
In case of inability, however, there are two options: either the one mentioned in the Āśvalāyana Sūtra as "or on one [day]," or the Bhādrapada-kṛṣṇāṣṭamī mentioned in the Purāṇas.
Even among those, it is specifically the Phālguna-aṣṭamī mentioned in the Sūtras;
for Āpastamba states: "The eighth day that follows the full moon of Māgha and is connected with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra—that alone they call Ekāṣṭakā. Thus, it refers only to the Phālguna-aṣṭamī.
Because it has been so stated;
because it relates to two days, such as the two *aṣṭakās*;
that [lunar day] was explained by the author of that commentary in two ways: either by way of being an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) or by way of being a fragmented lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*).

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the rite] is connected with the Jyeṣṭhā [nakṣatra], but not for the purpose of implying that it must be performed only when the moon is joined with Jyeṣṭhā and not at any other time.
Thus ends the section on the Aṣṭakā.
Now follows the Anvaṣṭakā.

Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states: "The Anvaṣṭakya [rite] is on the following day," meaning on the day after the Aṣṭakā and other rites. Viṣṇu also says: "There are three Anvaṣṭakās; the three are on the preceding days."
"Pūrvedyuḥ" means "on the day before the Aṣṭakā";
that too is a name for the ritual.
The obligatory nature of the Aṣṭakā has already been stated.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"But for him whose [ancestors] return [unhonored], not being worshipped with the Aṣṭakā rites, his world shall be in vain and what he has acquired perishes."
Thus [it is stated].
And Āśvalāyana has prescribed another *śrāddha* on the day preceding the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, stating: "One should offer to the ancestors on the previous day.

Kātyāyana states:
"Whichever lunar day (tithi) occurs on the anniversary of death in a given month,
that same lunar day during the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa) should be diligently honored."
One should not interrupt the lunar day (tithi) due to incidental impurity;
the piṇḍa-śrāddha must be performed, and one should never allow its continuity to be broken.
But when one is unable to perform it on the paternal side,
one should offer the rice-balls according to the prescribed rule even on a day that is otherwise prohibited.
Thus it is said:
in this regard, when performing the *śrāddha* daily, one need not avoid the *nandā* and other [inauspicious] days;
"one should perform the *śrāddha* day after day during the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya."
Neither the Nandā and other such days should be avoided, nor indeed should the fourteenth day be avoided.
Thus, according to the statement of Kārṣṇājini,
in the other cases, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) must be avoided for those who have killed a snake with poison, a beast of prey, a serpent, an animal, or a Brāhmaṇa.
The ritual should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, it is censured.

It has been stated that, according to the statement cited in the *Kālādarśa* and other works by Itimarīci— “In the Mahālaya, the *śrāddha* for one killed by a weapon alone [is performed] on the fourteenth day”— there is a prohibition of *śrāddhas* for those other than those killed by weapons.
But in that case, it certainly occurs for a father or others who have been killed by a weapon;
for it is given there specifically to those who were slain by a weapon (A.
This is because of the statement by Yājñavalkya.

However, the avoidance of the Nandā and other [inauspicious tithis] does not apply to the systems beginning with the fifth lunar day (pañcamy-ādi-pakṣa), for that would entail the undesirable consequence of fragmenting the divisions and diminishing the prescribed duration.
For this very reason, in the system beginning with the sixth lunar day (ṣaṣṭhy-ādi-pakṣa), there is no avoidance of the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
As for that which is stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*: "In the twenty-sixth degree of Sagittarius, in the twenty-second of Capricorn,
in the eighteenth degree of Gemini, and in the fourteenth of Virgo..."
Having said this:
"From this point forward, those sixteen days of a maiden are equal to sacrificial rites; what is given to the ancestors during them becomes inexhaustible."
Thus, the sixteen days have been declared as the proper times for *śrāddha*; however, Śūlapāṇi and others maintain that these refer specifically to other types of optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddhas*.
As for the statement:
"The householder who does not perform *śrāddha* while the sun is situated in Virgo..."
Whence could he have wealth or sons, when he is oppressed by his father’s sighs?

By such statements, another *śrāddha* occasioned by the maiden [sign] is prescribed independently of the fifth alternative; and regarding that, Śūlapāṇi has stated that when the maiden transits [the sun] during the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), the [performance] is cumulative (*tantra*), whereas if there is a difference [of time], it is performed separately, and when the maiden [transits] once, the performance is done only once.

That [interpretation] is improper because it involves the burden of assuming multiple injunctions (*vidhi-bheda*), and because in the fifth lunar fortnight (*pañcama-pakṣa*) the entry of the sun into Virgo (*kanyā-saṃkramaṇa*) is inevitable;

thus, it is logical that only the fifth fortnight characterized by the presence of Virgo constitutes the time for the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, this is untenable due to the parsimony of postulating a single scriptural source (*eka-śruti-mūla-kalpanā-lāghava*) through syntactic unity with the cited statement: "Whether at the beginning or in the middle.
In this regard—

That period consisting of the sixteen lunar days in the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, when it is joined with the sun's passage through Virgo, is the time for the performance of the Śrāddha rite.

Thus, because the originative injunction for the *śrāddha* rite specifies the word "rites" (*karmāṇi*) in the plural, the *śrāddha* is performed throughout all the lunar days (*tithi*) involved, according to the conjunction of the specified number and dates, just like the *Āgneya* sacrifice.
As for the statement:
"That entire fortnight is to be honored with respect to the sixteen *śrāddhas*."

Thus, the hearing of a number (*saṅkhyā*) with respect to the object (*karman*) does not differentiate it, because [the number] pertains to the quality of the entire set of offerings being worthy of worship, even through its connection with only a single part; for it lacks the status of being intended to produce the ritual act (*karma-utpatti*).
This is because only a number residing in the originative injunction (*utpatti-gatā*) serves as a differentiator.

Furthermore, in the phrase "the sixteen *śrāddhas*," the *śrāddhas* are the objects of reference (*uddeśya*), as indicated by the use of a *karmapravacanīya* particle in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) which serves as the basis for the second case ending (*dvitīyā-nimitta*). Therefore, [the meaning is] "day after day."

Thus, due to the force of repetition (*vīpsā*) in such cases as “a fortnight less by one-third,” and due to the accusative case denoting absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) in such cases as “that entire fortnight is to be honored,” and because the sense of repetition is understood from words like “entire” (*sakala*), there follows a repetition of the performance of the *śrāddha* with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) on all lunar days (*tithi*). This is because, just as the performance of the *homā* with its parts is repeated at both evening and morning due to the difference in time, so too must there be a repetition of the performance when times are combined, since the time [of the rite] functions as the delimiter of the performance.
And thus, that which Hemādri stated regarding the practice— that at the end there is the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the unification of the Brāhmaṇas— is to be reconsidered;
for it would follow all the more that there is a single performance (tantratā) even for other remote auxiliary rites (ārādupakāraka) occurring before or after the primary rite.

And thus, even if a single consultation has been conducted with the Brahmins for the sake of ensuring freedom from obstacles during a fortnightly *śrāddha*, if the Brahmins subsequently incur ritual impurity (*āśauca*), they must simply be dismissed;
for there is no scriptural injunction for their formal invitation (*nimantraṇā*) once this has occurred.

Likewise, if the performer who has proceeded according to any particular method of practice should encounter an onset of impurity in the interim, then regarding the phrase "the preparation of the food at the *śrāddha*": [the rule applies].

Thus, because there is an absence of the primary commencement (*mukhya-prārambha*) as previously stated, and because of the absence of the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), the rule "there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) regarding what has been commenced" does not apply; therefore, the very abandonment of the practice once commenced is [the appropriate course].

However, after the cessation of the impurity, the Mahālaya Śrāddha must be performed properly according to the *sakṛt* (once) or other prescribed methods, since it has not been performed by any method whatsoever.
As for the ritual applications (*prayoga*) previously undertaken, they are indeed fruitless due to the absence of the necessary auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*).
However, in the event of an obstruction other than impurity (āśauca), the rite should be performed by means of a substitute; enough of this digression.
Regarding the Mahālaya, the secondary time for performing the Śrāddha is stated in the Hemādri:
Yama says:

When the sun is in the sign of Leo during the rainy season, while the moon is in Virgo, even one living at home on mere vegetables may perform [the rite] during both fortnights in the interval between the two fifth lunar days.
Thus,
it means between the two fifth days associated with the dark and light fortnights.

Here, the intent is to prescribe the secondary time (gauṇakāla) as being either before or after the new moon day, by means of distinguishing between what has been reached and what has not yet been reached relative to the fifth day.
Even in the absence of that [lunar day], from any day up until the transit of Scorpio (Vṛścika-saṅkrānti),
and as long as the sun remains in Virgo and Libra respectively,
that shall be the time for the Śrāddha; at that time, the city of the departed spirits (Pretapura) is empty.
Thus, from the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
Here, the syntactical connection is that the time for the *śrāddha* follows the sequence [of the months].
The meaning of "in *tulā*" is [to be understood] in the event of the impossibility [of performing it] in *kanyā*.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Even when the fortnight of the ancestors (*pretapakṣa*) has passed, as long as the sun remains in Virgo (*kanyā*)."
The ancestors indeed desire that the śrāddha offered by their sons be performed for so long.
Furthermore, O King, some desire that even when the sun has entered Libra,
the ancestors— tormented by hunger and thirst— receive the śrāddha offered by their own descendants.
For two months, the ancestors of men wait at the door of their house, having become like the wind, afflicted by thirst and emaciated by hunger.
O Lord of the Earth, as long as the sun has entered Virgo and remains in Libra.
Thus it is said;
even therein, there is a special distinction on the new moon day of Kārttika,
O King, which is known as Dīpānvitā.
The fifteenth day is renowned on earth; if one does not give [offerings] on that day during the Mahālaya, it is as if nothing has been given to the ancestors.
Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.

Although the offering of lamps is prescribed here even on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) of Kārttika, nevertheless, only the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is to be understood by the word "the fifteenth" (*pañcadaśī*).
This is because the dark fortnight is praised for rites concerning the ancestors (*pitrya*), and because that [new moon day] alone is renowned as the *Dīpāvalī*.

The *mahālaya* is the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, so called because the ancestors (*pitṛs*) dissolve (*laya*) therein to an extraordinary degree; or else, because it is the abode (*ālaya*) of the great festival (*maha*) of the ancestors.
Furthermore, a *śrāddha* performed right there on the day of Bharaṇī yields great fruit.
The Bharaṇī [nakṣatra] during the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa) is proclaimed to be great;
by whomsoever a śrāddha is performed on this day, he becomes one who has performed a śrāddha at Gayā.
Thus, from the Matsya Purāṇa. Now, the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī).
Regarding this—
When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
one should indeed perform a śrāddha with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Likewise:
"Or he who might nourish his body every day by selling himself—
by him also a śrāddha must be performed with various well-accumulated substances."
On the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā constellation—one should strive diligently;
there exists no time superior to these for performing śrāddha rites.
Likewise, (Atri 3.273):
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.

Although in such statements from the Śaṅkha, Brahma, and Manu Purāṇas, as well as other scriptural sources, the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) joined with the Maghā nakṣatra is heard of as the time for the śrāddha, nevertheless, that day alone is also a time for the śrāddha. For it is said: "The thirteenth day of the dark fortnight after the full moon of Prauṣṭhapadī," and "the dark thirteenth day following Prauṣṭhapadī."
"May there be born in our family some such supreme among men."
During the rainy season, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight,
one who is composed should perform a śrāddha with honeyed milk-rice.
Likewise—(A. 3, Ślo. 274):
"May he be born in our lineage who shall give us milk-rice with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, and when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east."

Thus, because it is heard even as a solitary injunction in the *Viṣṇu*, *Manu*, and other Smṛtis, the mention of "yoga" (conjunction) is for the purpose of indicating excellence. Likewise: "Especially on the thirteenth day of the rainy season and under the Maghā asterisms..."
Thus, because Yogī Yājñavalkya has stated by the word "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) that this [day] is for the purpose of excellence (*prāśastya*),
the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is the primary [occasion] dear to the ancestors.
In that [offering], his ancestors themselves remain satisfied for five hundred years.
When that [lunar day] is conjoined with the Maghā asterism, the ancestors, being gratified even by water and other offerings,
remain satisfied for ten million times ten million years.
Thus, having stated that [the time] is pure by means of the statement found in the *Candrikā*, and because of the mention of its excellence when in conjunction with the *Maghā* asterism,

the word "and" (*ca*) in such passages as "during the rains and under *Maghā*" does not signify mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) with the lunar day (*tithi*), but rather signifies a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*) characterized by the connection of multiple items to a single action independently of one another:
"with honey and meat, and with vegetables, and with milk and milk-rice."
"He will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā constellation."
Thus, because Vasiṣṭha’s statement declares that even the Maghā constellation alone is a time for Śrāddha,
it is not the case that [one should perform it] only with great effort on the thirteenth day during the rainy season under the Maghā constellation.
It should not be argued that, in such passages, even the rainy season (*varṣā*) would constitute a separate time for the *śrāddha* ceremony;

for in texts such as "in the rainy season, during the bright fortnight, on the thirteenth day" and likewise "on the thirteenth day of the rains," it is understood that [the rainy season] functions as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Regarding this, Śūlapāṇi states:
"When the month of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
one should indeed perform the Śrāddha rite with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa)."
Thus, because a direct injunction is heard in the words of Śaṅkha:
"May there be born in our lineage one who would give [to us] on the thirteenth day."
Likewise:
"May there be born in our lineage some supreme among men,
who, being composed, [performs this] on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight during the rainy season."
"He who shall perform the *śrāddha* with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) soaked in honey"—in these words of Manu and Viṣṇu, which establish the [observance] on the thirteenth lunar day alone; and likewise:
"He will give us this *śrāddha* during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."

Thus, since the statement of Vasiṣṭha— which conveys only the prohibition of *maghā*— is merely an *arthavāda*, and since it is possible for it to form a single syntactical unit with a directly perceived injunction,

it is improper to postulate a separate independent injunction; rather, it is more appropriate to assume that these isolated statements refer to *yoga* (the conjunction of asterisms) through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), thereby achieving parsimony in the assumption of a revealed text (*śruti*).

He says that the conjunctions of *gajacchāyā* and *kuñjaracchāyā* serve only to produce an excellence of fruit for the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), because they were prescribed by other sages;
however, this is incorrect.

For if, for the sake of the parsimony of postulating a single rule, one resorts to the indication of another [time] even when it is not required—thereby overriding the natural independence [of the primary time]—then [the argument fails].

In that case, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the *śrāddha* should be performed on the thirteenth lunar day specifically when it is joined with the yoga called *gajacchāyā*, and in a place where the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east, and not elsewhere;
for it is more parsimonious to postulate a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that, while being a general summary, refers specifically to this qualified subject.
Now—
For, having been determined as distinct and independent of one another by their very form, they seek their respective purposes while disregarding each other entirely.
By this reasoning, the postulation of various *śruti* passages corresponding to the words of those respective sages is also authoritative.

Consequently, even the statements prescribing the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight as the sole [time for the rite] possess the capacity to postulate their respective *śruti* passages without opposition; so much for that. Furthermore, this *śrāddha* is distinct from the *śrāddhas* such as the *mahālaya*.
When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, [one should perform it] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight;
for in such scriptural statements as "on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following Prauṣṭhapada," the Śrāddha of Mahālaya and others are not mentioned.
And this [Śrāddha] is obligatory.
"Having begun with the words: 'When the month of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, likewise on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight'—
Prajāpati has declared these indeed to be the obligatory times for the Śrāddha."
One who does not perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for these [deceased ancestors] falls into hell.
Thus, from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. And [this applies] to optional rites (*kāmya*), beginning with this very passage:
When pleased by the śrāddha, the ancestors always bestow upon men desired offspring, fame, heaven, health, and likewise wealth.
Thus it is stated by Śaṅkha. Furthermore, regarding the prohibition of the śrāddha ceremony here, Jyotir-Bṛhaspati says:
"The man who performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
One should know for certain that death has come to his eldest son.
Thus has that which pertains to a single class been shown.
And likewise, Kārṣṇājini says:
One should never commence a *śrāddha* for a single class of ancestors on the thirteenth lunar day;
for those who remain unsatisfied therein will surely harm the progeny of that person.
Thus;
this statement has been explained in two ways by Hemādri:
the word "eka" refers to that which is exclusive (kevala).
One should not perform [the śrāddha] for the paternal group alone, but should also perform it for the maternal grandfather’s group.

Since, according to the Āpastamba-sūtra and other texts, the purpose of the obligatory scriptural injunction is fulfilled even by the performance of the śrāddha for the paternal group alone when one is incapable [of performing more], there arises the possibility of sacrificing to only a single group.

Alternatively, the meaning is that one should not perform only the *pārvaṇa* rite for a single group, but rather the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites must be performed for all, including the father, paternal uncles, and others.
This is because of the supplementary statement, "they are not satiated.
Alternatively, this prohibition concerns the *sapiṇḍaka* śrāddha. [As it is said:
"The śrāddha on the two solstices (*ayana*), as well as on the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)," and so forth.
And on all the beginnings of the Yugas, except for the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Thus it is stated by Pulastya.

Some maintain that the Mahālaya Trayodaśī Śrāddha is not distinct from the Yugādi Śrāddha, because the former presents itself through its invariable concomitance with the status of being a Yugādi (the beginning of a Yuga).
Or, even if there is a distinction, nevertheless—
On the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā constellation, a twice-born man who desires progeny should never perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
so the wise have always known.

Thus, since Bṛhat-Parāśara specifically prohibits the offering of *piṇḍas* at a Śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, there is no fault in interpreting the prohibition of the Śrāddha as pertaining to that specific case, or else as referring to optional (*kāmya*) Śrāddhas.
Āpastamba states:
"On the thirteenth day, one obtains many sons and many friends, and his offspring are handsome; however, they die young."
Since a fault is mentioned in connection with the optional *śrāddha* (kāmya-śrāddha), it refers either to a householder who has sons;
for there is a prohibition against him by the Smṛti: "A householder who has sons should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day."
"However, for one who is childless, the thirteenth day is prescribed for the *śrāddha*;
if one who possesses offspring should perform it, there will be the destruction of his lineage.
This is because the defect regarding one with offspring is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* of the *Hemādri*.

In this context, the word *santāna* refers to a son, according to the Smṛti text: "A householder who has a son need not perform [these rites]. Here, there is a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the Trayodaśī, Mahālaya, and Madhūka Śrāddhas; however, in the case of a variation such as the Yugādi Śrāddha, that too applies.
Other specific details should be consulted in the *Śrāddhaprakāśa*.
Thus ends the thirteenth [chapter].
Now, the fourteenth: Marīci says:
For those who have killed a venomous snake, a beast of prey, a fire, an animal, or a Brahmin, the funeral rites should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, they are censured.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose slaughter is by means of poisons and so forth, ending with [slaughter by] Brahmins.
As stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"For those who meet an untimely death, or even death by weapons..."
And for those who have died by calamity, those who have met with death by poison,
those consumed by fire, and those who have met with death by water;
O lord of men, their *śrāddha* should be performed on the fourteenth day;
as stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "He whose young ancestors have died or were killed by a weapon [should perform it on that day]."
"Therefore, the rite should be performed on the fourteenth day.
Regarding "youth," the *Śrāddhaviveka* and other texts state it is from sixteen years of age up to thirty.
In all these instances, the gender is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), as it serves merely as a qualifying attribute of the person addressed (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇatvāt*).

In this context, because of scriptural statements such as "here an untimely death (āpamṛtyu) may occur," dying without disease is the motivating factor for the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*).
Thus, the Gauḍas maintain that the *caturdaśī-śrāddha* must indeed be performed even for one who has followed her husband in death.

Others, however, hold that an unrighteous death (*avaidhamaraṇa*) is the motivator for the *caturdaśī-śrāddha*; and while this generally applies to those who die by fasting, it certainly applies even to those who have perished according to the prescribed rule.
"Likewise for those who have met their end through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, or hanging"—
so it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
Similarly, this also applies to those killed in battle.

They say that this is because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: “For the *śrāddha* rite of those killed in battle, the fourteenth day is recommended. And this [rite] takes the form of an *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Furthermore: “The *śrāddha* performed on the fourteenth day after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one slain by weapons must be carried out according to the procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*.”
Thus it is stated by Gārgya.
Further details on this matter should be understood from the *Śrāddhaprakāśa*.
This concludes the fourteenth [day].
Now, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, there is the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for the maternal grandfather) performed by a daughter's son (*dauhitra*).
As stated in the *Saṅgraha*:
"Even if he is just born, a daughter's son [performs the rite] even while his maternal uncle is still living."
One should perform the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather on the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
Thus,
it is stated in the *Nirṇayadīpa*:
"On the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) should perform a single *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] during the time that encompasses the *saṅgava*."
One who has a father should always perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfather during the Saṅgava period.
Even though his two grandsons and his maternal uncle have already been born,
the first lunar day (pratipad) of the Noble One shall fall between the morning and the saṅgava periods.
Because of this statement.
Now, the times for the miscellaneous daily *śrāddha* (nitya-śrāddha):
regarding that, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*—
O Lord of the Earth, the transit of the sun (saṅkramaṇa) during a śrāddha ceremony is highly commended;
likewise, both equinoxes and especially the two solstices are so.
This is obligatory:
during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, on the three Aṣṭakās, and on both solstices,
a self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors.
"By him a *śrāddha* has been performed for a thousand years"—this is a secret that the ancestors declare; thus from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Its character as being for a specific desire (*kāmya*) is established by the words of Viṣṇu beginning with "the transit of the sun" (*ādityasaṅkramaṇa*).
The time for the *śrāddha* is characterized by the presence of the proper materials and qualified Brahmins.

Thus says the *Nigama*: "On whichever day the afternoon occurs, especially on the new moon day, on the *aṣṭakā*, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or on the lunar day (*tithi*)—when there is the availability of materials and qualified Brahmins—one should desire to perform it."

Rites prescribed on account of specific occasions—such as prosperity, a transition [of inheritance], the arrival of materials, or the presence of Brahmins—are mandatory by virtue of being occasional (*naimittika*).
This is also established from the statement of Hārīta:
"And when materials for a sacred occasion (*tīrtha*) are available, one should not wait for a [specific] time."
And having obtained a worthy Brahmin as a recipient, the Śrāddha rite is ordained to be performed immediately.
The word "sadyas" (immediately) is mandatory.
Yama says:
"A śrāddha offered at the sight of Rāhu is said to yield infinite results."
Viṣṇu says:
Indeed, a Śrāddha offered on the occasion of Rāhu’s appearance (an eclipse) is said to be infinite;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire.
"Sarvakāmīyam" means that which is prescribed for the fulfillment of all desires.
In the *Liṅga Purāṇa* it is said:
"Indeed, a *śrāddha* should be performed even at the cost of one's entire property during the appearance of Rāhu."
By the phrase "even with one's entire property," the necessity [of the rite] is indicated;
and the time characterized by the desire for a *śrāddha* is the *śrāddha*-time.
As stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:

O sons, when one encounters a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices, when the equinox occurs, at the transition of the sun into a new zodiac sign, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga;
When there is an abundance of materials suitable for a *śrāddha*, upon seeing an evil dream,
or when one is afflicted by planets at the time of birth, one may perform a *śrāddha* according to one's desire.
The word "ca" (and) is displaced [in its position];
the meaning is "and by desire.
This is because the necessity [of the suffix] is established when desire is the cause.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The śrāddha that is to be performed on full-moon days should be done when [the moon] is in its proper asterism,
in conjunction with the asterism of the month."
Regarding the specific rite for the full moon of Bhādrapada, the Brahmapurāṇa states: "Every year, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo,
the rite for the Nāndīmukha ancestors must be performed on the full moon day, according to the words of Varāha."
Those who are beyond the grandfather (the great-grandfather) are the three Nāndīmukhas;
they are known as the "Serene-faced" ones and are the abodes of auspiciousness.
"From the grandfather" means from the father's grandfather.
Yama says:
"On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, [one should feed] three or five twice-born men."
One should satisfy the ancestors first; that [offering] of his is said to be inexhaustible.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "O child, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, during an eclipse, and likewise during the Mahālaya—
in these statements, the mention of specific full moon days is for the purpose of establishing necessity or for the sake of emphasizing excellence."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who always performs the *śrāddha* during the dark fortnight of Āśvina and the first [fortnight] of Kārttika shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
At that time, Janārdana, the soul of all beings, abandons sleep;
therefore, a Śrāddha performed then is infinite—of this there is no doubt.
Devala says:
All odd lunar days (tithis) are more honored than even ones;
and as for time, both the months of Māgha and Prauṣṭhapada are most highly esteemed.
Of the two fortnights, the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight are honored by the *śrāddha* rite.
This examination of lunar days (*tithi*) has been declared; it is not explained with reference to the constellations (*nakṣatra*).
Uttarā, Śravaṇa, Tiṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), Hasta, Śatabhiṣaj, Svāti, Citrā, Pitrya (Maghā), and Aśvinam (Aśvinī).
These asterisms are always praised for rites pertaining to the ancestors;
however, other asterisms are occasionally mentioned for specific reasons.
Or again, that time at which one obtains a brahmin endowed with virtues and worthy of being a recipient becomes the honored time for the *śrāddha*.
"By reasons" means by such factors as the conjunction with the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha and so forth.
Now, the times for optional (kāmya) śrāddhas:
regarding this, Kātyāyana says—"Now there are optional rites: on the first lunar day (pratipad), women of incomparable beauty [are obtained]."
In the second [period] there is birth as a woman; in the third, as a horse;
in the fourth, as small livestock.
Sons on the fifth, prosperity from gambling on the sixth, and agriculture on the seventh.
On the eighth day, trade; on the ninth, one-hoofed animals; on the tenth, cattle.
On the eleventh day, attendants;

on the twelfth, wealth, grain, and base metals; on the thirteenth, preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth, young men die in it, as do those killed by weapons; and on the new moon day, everything.
Performing [the rites] on even days and under even lunar mansions, one attains all desires;
but by worshipping the ancestors on odd days, one obtains abundant progeny.
Yājñavalkya (Ācārādhyāya, Prāyaścittaprakaraṇa, verses 265–268): "Indeed, heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, land, strength,
as well as sons, preeminence, good fortune, prosperity, and excellence of children [are obtained through the performance of ancestral rites]."
As well as the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], commerce and the like,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers the Śrāddha shall obtain knowledge, wealth, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
One who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy shall obtain these desires by [worshipping] from Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī.
*Pravṛttacakratā* means possessing a command that is unimpeded everywhere.
Viṣṇu states: one who constantly performs a *śrāddha* on a Sunday attains health;
on a Monday, good fortune.
Victory in battle when Mars is [the lord]; all desires when Mercury; and the desired knowledge when Jupiter.
Wealth [is gained] under Venus, and life under Saturn. These are the times for the optional Śrāddha.
Now, regarding the beginnings of the Yugas: in the Viṣṇupurāṇa it is said—
the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, and the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha.
These four lunar days, which mark the beginning of the Yugas, have been declared by the Purāṇas to be of infinite merit;
on these days, a self-restrained man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors.
"By him, a śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years; this is a secret, so the sages declare.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Now listen, O Indra among kings!"
The beginnings of the Yugas are dear to the ancestors;
by the mere recitation of their names, the accumulation of sins is destroyed.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava,
the new moon day of Tapasya, and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya.
The beginnings of the Tretā, Kṛta, Kali, and Dvāpara ages are traditionally taught as being especially significant for bathing,
giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and particularly for the libations to the ancestors.
"Those which cause what has been done not to perish and yield great fruit for good deeds. *Tapasye* means in the month of Māgha.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: the third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika,
the fifteenth of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa).
"For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, making whatever is given [on them] inexhaustible.
Regarding this, he states the specific excellence resulting from particular lunar mansions:
Devala says:
The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha joined with Rohiṇī is auspicious;
likewise, the thirteenth lunar day of Nabhasya joined with Maghā is auspicious.
"For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to become inexhaustible.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
Beginning with "The Kṛta Yuga was established on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha," and so forth, [it continues]:
"These four lunar days are the beginnings of the Yugas; whatever is given or one's lineage on these days becomes inexhaustible."
That which occurs over a hundred years in each age would occur in a single day at the beginning of a yuga.
Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "The third day of Vaiśākha is indeed equal to the Kṛta Yuga."
That ninth [lunar day] in the month of Kārttika is equal to the Tretā Yuga.
O King, the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha is indeed equal to the Kali age;
these four, O Indra among kings, [are such].
The auspicious origins of the ages.
Therefore, these days have been called "Yugādis" (the beginnings of the ages) by the ancient sages;
consequently, fasting, giving gifts, performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), burnt offerings (homa), and recitation of mantras (japa) [are especially meritorious on them].
"But then, whatever is performed [on that day] shall become ten million-fold.
Hemādri states that by saying "it is equal to the Kṛta Yuga," the attainment of the complete dharma of the Kṛta Yuga occurs on this single lunar day (tithi).
Others say it is merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda).
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"When the moon and the sun [are together], and when Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati..."
When they shall come together in the single heap, then the Kṛta age will enter.
Thus it is said;
and here, because of the prophetic statement, "The full moon of Māgha [marks its end]," it follows that the terrible Kali Yuga likewise ends on the full moon day of Māgha.

Thus, from the *Brahmavaivarta*, the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* stating "the new moon of Tapas," and the *Brahma-purāṇa* and other texts stating "on the day of the waning moon in Māgha" and "on the new moon of the month of Māgha," it should be understood that the application of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) of Māgha is determined according to the specific Yuga.

And in this regard, because of the primacy of rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarma*), as stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "He has performed the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) for a thousand years; the sages declare this to be a secret."

"Regarding the annual rite for the ancestors, the month is traditionally considered to belong to the moon. Since this traditional teaching allows for both [reckonings] through the distinction between the bright and dark fortnights, [the time is determined as follows]:
"If the fifteenth day of the dark half of Māgha should ever coincide with the day of Varuṇa..."
O King, that supreme time of the ancestors is reached by the constellation Ṛkṣa; indeed, it cannot be attained by those of meager merit.

Having presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—since this is impossible when the Sun is in Aries (*meṣa*) and possible when the Sun is in Aquarius (*kumbha*), and since the status of being the beginning of a Yuga (*yugādi*) is possible for both the full moon and the new moon in this position—the beginnings of the Yugas should be understood according to the lunar month—the author states:
"There is no postponement on the *daśaharā* days, nor on any of the four beginnings of the Yugas;
for it has been stated that the *upākarma* ceremony on the Great Sixth (*mahāṣaṣṭhī*) begins from [the month of] Taurus (*vṛṣa*)."

Based on these words of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Hemādri maintains that only those [tithis] occurring within the solar month are to be accepted. Furthermore, for rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛkarma), these tithis should be taken as those extending into the afternoon (aparāhṇa), whereas for rites dedicated to the gods (daivika), they should extend into the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa).
Regarding the dark fortnight, the tithi is to be accepted in which the sun sets.
In the bright fortnight, that lunar day (tithi) is to be taken which the sun has risen upon.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti).
Others maintain that the arrangement is based on the distinction between the white and the black [paths].
For this very reason—

In the Nāradīya and Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇas: "The wise know that there are two beginnings of the Yugas in the bright fortnight and likewise two in the dark fortnight; those in the bright fortnight are to be observed in the forenoon, and those in the dark fortnight in the afternoon."
Thus [ends the section on] the beginnings of the yugas. Now, the ends of the yugas.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Wherever the sun is in the constellation Revatī while traveling through the zodiac signs, that is a day like the end of a Yuga; there, every gift yields infinite merit."
The meaning of *saṅkrānti* is the movement into the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*).
If the Sun occurs at an equinox (*viṣuva*) or at the northern solstice (*saumya*),
or on the seventh day of either the bright or dark fortnight, they know that to be a *yugānta* (end-of-age) day.
Thus:

O gentle one, if on the northern solstice (udagayana) the seventh lunar day—whether bright or dark—is conjoined with an eclipse, the equinox, the northern solstice, or Sunday, then that is the meaning of "the day of the end of the Yuga.
A specific detail is given in the Brahmapurāṇa:
At the sun's entry into Leo, the Kṛta Yuga ends;
then, at its entry into Scorpio, the Tretā Yuga ends.
The end of the Dvāpara age is to be known by its numerical duration as occurring at the transit of the sun into Taurus,
and likewise, the end of the Kali age occurs at the transit into Aquarius.

In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Whatever bathing, giving of gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth is performed on the first days of the Yugas or at the ends of the Yugas, the fruit of the end of the Yuga is said to accrue from that."
In the Brahma Purāṇa as well: "The Śrāddha performed on the Yugādis and at the conclusion of sacrifices is said to be inexhaustible."
Thus end the sections on the ends of the Yugas. Now, the beginnings of the Manvantaras, according to the Mātsya Purāṇa:
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, likewise the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Māgha, and also that of Bhādrapada.
The new moon of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh of Pauṣa,
the tenth of Āṣāḍha, and likewise the seventh of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha, and the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight [of Mārgaśīrṣa].
These are the beginnings of the Manvantaras, which cause what is given to be inexhaustible;
even by bathing in water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass on these occasions, [one gains great merit].
He who gives [an offering] dedicated to the ancestors shall attain the supreme goal;
bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors [yield great merit].
One should know that everything performed during the beginning of a Manvantara and so forth is indeed inexhaustible.
All bright fortnights, with the exception of the new moon day (amāvāsyā), are to be accepted [for ritual purposes].
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even their water," their obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is indicated.
Śūlapāṇi, however, states that because this [practice] lacks a scriptural foundation, it is merely optional (*kāmya*).
In another Purāṇa cited in the Hemādri:
"The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, as well as those of Śrāvaṇa and Kārttika..."
For these, such as the beginnings of the Manvantaras, cause that which is given to become inexhaustible.
Thus [ends the section on] the beginnings of the Manvantaras. Now, the beginnings of the Kalpas.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "Now, O King, the auspicious lunar days (tithis) beginning with the Kalpa are being described."
In these [waters], when a śrāddha is performed, the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
In ancient times, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Śvetakalpa came into being;
on its thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, Udāna was born;
and the Kalpa named Nārasiṃha occurred on the first day of the dark fortnight.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the ritual manual for Gaurī was also prepared;
and on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Nīlalohita [was established].
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, he who is named Garuḍa began his course;
on the second day of the dark fortnight, Samāna arose.
The Māheśvara [incarnation] appeared on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
the manifestation of Vāmadeva occurred on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O King, on the full moon day of that very month, the Kaurma incarnation took place;
and on the third day of the dark fortnight, the Āgneya incarnation was born.
On the new moon day, the Pitṛ-kalpa was proclaimed, resting upon that very [Sāman];
but on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Śuci, the Rāthantara-kalpa came into being.
In that same month of Kṛṣṇa, Somakalpa arrived;
on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, Raurava appeared.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of that same month, he became Mānava;
and having reached the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, he became known as Prāṇa.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight, however, he was named Puṣkara;
on the seventh day of the sky, the Bṛhatkalpa was attained.

O lord of the people, on the sixth day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, and on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, as well as on the [eighth] day of its dark fortnight, Vaikuṇṭha entered [the body].
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kalpa is named Kandarpa;
on the dark fortnight, however, during the sacrifice, there is the conception of the Lakṣmī-kalpa.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Kalpa was immediately attained;
and on the dark fortnight, the Sāvitrī-kalpa commenced its beginning.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya, Īśāna indeed appeared;
it was the commencement of the Asita Aghora Kalpa.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, Vyāna departed;
on that very same dark night, O King, Varāha arrived.
O high-minded one, Sārasvata appeared on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, while Vairāja shone forth even on the dark fortnight.
Thus, these thirty kalpas are the lunar days (tithis) of Parameṣṭhin;
I have declared those to be the most meritorious initial lunar days of them all.
When a *śrāddha* is performed on those [lunar days], the merit is established as lasting for an entire *kalpa*.
However, in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, other lunar days are mentioned as being the beginnings of a *kalpa*,
as follows:
For that which is proclaimed as the beginning of the Kalpa is indeed the beginning of Brahmā’s day;
it occurs on the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha and of Phālguna.
The fifth day of the month of Caitra, its final day, and likewise another;
the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, and the seventh days of Kārttika.
I remember these as the first days of the nine kalpas; indeed, they cause what is given to become inexhaustible.

"Of that very [month], the last" means the last new moon (amāvāsya) of that Caitra month. The third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the third of Phālguna, the fifth of Caitra, and its new moon— these are the four dark [days].
The three [days] of the bright fortnight— the thirteenth of Māgha, the tenth of Kārttika, and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa—
make seven;
for it is stated that "I remember only seven," thus there is no enumeration of other remembered kalpas and so forth.
Or, the word "eva" is for the purpose of indicating excellence.
Thus [end] the Kalpas and so forth. Now, the Vyatīpāta.

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: A gift given on the new moon day yields a hundredfold merit; that same gift at the end of a day (the solar transits) yields a hundred times that; at the time of the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign it yields a hundred times that; and at the equinoxes it yields a hundred times that again.
At the beginning of a Yuga, it is multiplied by one hundred; at the transition of an age, by one hundred times that;
during a lunar eclipse, by one hundred times that; and during a solar eclipse, by one hundred times that.
Those who know the Vedas understand that a gift given during the *vyatīpāta* yoga is incalculable (*asaṅkhyeya*).
"Ghnam" means multiplied.
Among the yogas beginning with *viṣkumbha*, the seventeenth yoga is called *vyatīpāta*.
Regarding the specific durations of its phases in *ghaṭikās*, the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) states:
"Twenty-two [ghaṭikās] for its arising, twenty-one for its wandering,
ten *nāḍīs* for its heating, and seven *nāḍikās* for its falling."
The divisions are those beginning with *utpatti* (origination).
"Increased by two" means twenty-two.
Regarding that, the result is stated in the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*:
The fruit is said to be a hundred thousandfold at its origin, ten millionfold during its flight,
one hundred millionfold when it blazes, and what is given becomes inexhaustible upon its descent.
Yājñavalkya, as cited in the Hemādri:
"At the moment of its rising, [merit is] a hundred-thousandfold; at the hour of its circumambulation, it is ten-millionfold;
at its setting, it is multiplied by a hundred-billion; and when it has set, acts such as recitation and giving become inexhaustible."
Vṛddha-Manu has stated otherwise:
"If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) falls on a Sunday under the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Niṣṭhā (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Ārdrā, or the head of the Serpent-deity (Āśleṣā), that is called Vyatīpāta."
Nāgadaivata is Aśleṣā;
mastaka is the first quarter of Ārdrā.
An amāvāsyā occurring on a Sunday and conjoined with the first quarter of any one of these nakṣatras is called Vyatīpāta.
Some, however, say that the head [of the constellation] is Mṛgaśiras.
The *Kalpataru* states that the conjunction of the transits of the sun and the moon, as understood through the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), is called *vyatīpāta*.
Bhṛgu says:
The time of the equality of the solstices has been proclaimed by the lords of sages to be similar to a solar eclipse;
at that time, Bhārgava says that offerings, oblations, recitations, and worship yield a merit of ten million times ten million.
Thus, in the *Smṛtyantara* cited in the *Hemādri*:
"If Jupiter and Mars are situated in Leo and the Sun is in Aries during the bright fortnight,"
The lunar day joined with the Karabha [nakṣatra] and designated as a "noose" (pāśa) is here called the Vyatīpāta yoga.
For by the gift of cows, land, gold, and garments in this world, a person, having abandoned all evil,
attains the state of a celestial being, the status of Indra, freedom from disease, and sovereignty over mortals.
"Pañcānanasthau" means seated upon a lion;
"pāśābhidhānā" refers to the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), according to Hemādri;
and "karabheṇa" means by the hand.
Now, regarding Vaidhṛti,
Viṣṇu says:
"What is given during Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta becomes inexhaustible."
Bhāradvāja also says:
"There is no end to what is given during Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti.
Some maintain that Vaidhṛti, like Vyatīpāta, is an equality of the [solar] transit.
Others say it is a specific type of yoga. Thus ends the section on Vaidhūti.
Now follows the Avamadinī day.
In that regard, concerning the time for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), Vasiṣṭha states:
"When three lunar days (*tithi*) coincide at the end of a single day, that is called a 'destruction of the day' (*dinakṣaya*); the fruit [of an offering] therein is said to be a thousandfold."
Now, regarding the time for the śrāddha of new grain,
the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
"It should be performed at the ripening of rice, and likewise at the ripening of barley."
O Great King, those two cannot be external in any way whatsoever without faith.
The meaning is that they are external and merely palliative.
*Vrīhi* refers to autumn-ripening grain, such as *ṣaṣṭika* rice and the like.
For this very reason—
Rice, paddy, mung beans, wheat, mustard, sesame, and barley—
these seven medicinal grains, when washed, destroy calamities.
Thus, in the *Pariśiṣṭa*, it is treated separately from the winter grains and so forth.
And this should be performed during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
Accordingly:
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Having recognized that the new grain has ripened beautifully during the bright fortnight,
one should go to the field according to the prescribed ritual, preceded by song and instrumental music."
Having quoted this—
“By that [water], one should likewise satisfy and worship both the gods and the ancestors”—
there follows a prohibition regarding the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) in the *Kāmadhenu*:
Since a human being should not prepare new grain during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa),
the ancestors do not accept it, and the giver shall go to hell.
In astrology:

One should not perform the *nava-śrāddha* on a Nandā tithi, on a Saturday, on the thirteenth lunar day, or during the three birth asterisms (*trijanman*), due to the destruction of sons, wife, and wealth.

Regarding "trijanmani" (at the three births), the *Kāmarūpīya* states it means on the birth-tithi, the birth-asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), or the birth-moon (*janmacandra*). Others, however, interpret "trijanmani" as referring to the first, tenth, and nineteenth asterisms.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Dīpikā*:

Having avoided the thirteenth lunar day, one's birthday, the Nandā tithis, the birth-star, and Saturday, the performance of Śrāddha is desired on the days of the Sun, Jupiter, Moon, Mercury, and Venus, as well as during the Maitra and Dhruva constellations.
Hari is Śravaṇa;
Ijya is Puṣya;
Indu is Mṛgaśiras.
Kara is Hasta; Antya is Revatī;
Maitra is Anurādhā.
The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī,
and the lunar days and asterisms to be accepted are also specified in the Jyotiṣa:
namely, Hasta, Svātī, Punarvasu, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, and Anurādhā.

A śrāddha performed with new grain is auspicious when conducted under the asterisms of Mūla, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Citrā, Kṛttikā, Śatabhiṣaj, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, and Aśvinī; and when the Moon is in conjunction with Mercury, the Moon, Jupiter, or other benefics, and when the lunar mansion is favorable.
And its secondary time is stated in the Smṛti:
"With śyāmāka, vrīhi, and barley, one must certainly sacrifice before the respective times [of their ripening]; for here there is no lapse of the *āgrayaṇa*."

The statement "with *śyāmāka* grains" refers specifically to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), according to the *Kāmarūpīya*, based on the scriptural injunction: "For the householder should sacrifice with barley in autumn and spring; the forest-dweller [should sacrifice] with *śyāmāka* grains in the rainy season.
Thus ends the time for the first-fruits offering (*navānna*).
Now follows the time for the *śrāddha* offerings for new water and so forth.
The ancestors long for food at the time of new water, at the first harvest, upon the roofing of a house, on the Aṣṭakā days, and under the Maghā constellation.
Therefore, one should always be diligent in giving to learned Brāhmaṇas during *navodaka*, which refers to the commencement of the rains— that is, when the sun is situated in the constellation Ārdrā.
"Covering the house" means the construction of a new house.
Thus ends the section on the times for *śrāddha* regarding new water and the construction of a new house.
Now follows the determination of the time for the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*).
In that regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Every year, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother and father,
as well as for a childless paternal uncle and indeed for an elder brother, [the śrāddha] must be performed."

In this context, regarding the injunction for performing a *śrāddha* ceremony where the recipients are the mother and others, it should be understood that the son and other relatives acquire the status of performer by implication.
In the phrase "of the brother" (*bhrātuḥ*) as well, the word "of one who has no son" (*aputrasya*), having been read previously, is to be connected here.
By the term "of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya*), it is understood that a *śrāddha* is not mandatory for a younger brother even if he has no son; however, this does not constitute an absolute prohibition.
A father should not perform [the Śrāddha] for his son, nor should an elder brother for his younger brother;
even out of affection, they may perform it, provided it is without the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
This is because it is consistent with the statements cited by Hemādri.
Here, by the term *mṛtāha* (the day of death), what is intended is the lunar day (*tithi*) of the same type as the lunar day that served as the locus of the death;
for there is no connection to the actual occurrence of death on the lunar day at the end of the year.

And the "sameness of kind" (*sājātya*) regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) does not consist merely in being the first day (*pratipad*) and so forth; rather, it consists in its falling within the same month and fortnight as that [specific] month and fortnight.

As it is said: "On whatever day one dies, touched by a specific month, fortnight, and lunar day—those who know declare that such a day, when it is actually present, is his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death)."
Thus, from the words of Vyāsa;
and here the word *ahaḥ* (day) refers to a full day and night (*ahorātra*).
And in this context—
O tiger among birds, he who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of his father’s death,
nor on the anniversary of his mother’s death at the end of the year—

Thus, because the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* mentions the "end of the year" (*vatsarānta*), the specific lunar day that serves as the locus of death does not itself serve as the locus for the *śrāddha*; rather, it merely establishes the identity of the *śrāddha*-day with the lunar day at the end of the year.

Therefore, as for what some say—that because the term "every year" (*pratisaṃvatsaram*) is heard without qualification, and by the force of the etymological designation "annual" (*vārṣika*) meaning "occurring in the year," the lunar day that is the locus of death also becomes the locus for the *śrāddha*, and consequently the annual *śrāddha* (*sāṃvatsarika*) applies even to the lunar day of death—[that is refuted].
The statement that "it should be performed on the eleventh day" because of the scriptural injunction "on the first [day], on the eleventh day," is to be understood as refuted;
for by the mention of "the end of the year" in the cited passage, there is no occasion for the Śrāddha to be performed on the anniversary of the date of death.
The statement, "On the first day, on the eleventh day," refers to the monthly śrāddha; for it is said:
"It should be performed on the anniversary of death every month for a year."

Because of this statement, [the rite] must be performed on the very lunar day (tithi) that constitutes the beginning of each respective month—the day of death itself. Therefore, regarding the performance that would otherwise apply even on the lunar day marking the initial occasion of death, the prescription for its postponement by the rule "on the first [day], on the eleventh day" is appropriate.
For this very reason, the etymological derivation of the term *māsika* (monthly) as "that which occurs in that same month" is established.

Regarding the *sāṃvatsarika* [śrāddha], since the word "end of the year" (*vatsarānta*) is mentioned in the scriptural statement, its etymological derivation as *vārṣika*—meaning "that which occurs at the end of the year"—is established.

Furthermore, in the phrase "on the day of death at the end of the year" (*vatsarānte mṛtāhani*), the meaning should be understood as "on the day of death occurring at the end of the year. For instance:

For here, there is no mention of the solar year (*saṃvatsara*), because it is impossible for the time of death to be determined by the increase or decrease of lunar days (*tithi*). Rather, it refers to the lunar month (*cāndra*).
For this very reason, there is the statement of Vyāsa: "In the annual rite for the ancestors and in the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya), the month is traditionally held to be lunar."

And for this reason, since the lunar year ends with the conclusion of the preceding lunar day (tithi), the day of death—which constitutes the beginning of the second year—does not constitute the end of the previous year; therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "the end of the year" and "the day of death.
Rather, the meaning of the statement is simply: "when the end of the year has occurred, [on] the day of death."
Therefore, the meaning accepted by those of the South is that the *śrāddha* should be performed on the first anniversary of the day of death;

Śūlapāṇi, however, maintains that the etymological derivation of these terms is simply "that which occurs in a month" (*māse bhavam*) and "that which occurs in a year" (*varṣe bhavam*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of performing monthly or annual rites on every single anniversary of the day of death, because what is intended is the lunar month and year spanning from one day of death to the next.
The ablative case in the phrase "mṛtatither" (from the date of death) indicates a limit, as in the expression "darśād darśaḥ" (from new moon to new moon) which denotes a lunar month.

Consequently, it is only the final date of death that constitutes the meaning of the terms "previous month" and "previous year," and not the subsequent month or year; whereas the previous date of death constitutes the meaning of the terms "subsequent month" and "subsequent year. Therefore, among those [dates] occurring within the first year...

On the second and subsequent lunar days of death, the first and subsequent monthly rites (*māsika*) are performed; and at the end of the first year, the first annual rite (*vārṣika*) is performed. However, regarding the rule "the first [rite] on the eleventh day," this prescribes a *śrāddha* that is distinct from the monthly rites, serving as the archetype for all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, and does not prescribe a postponement (*utkarṣa*) of the first monthly rite. Thus says [the author]. But Dhanañjaya, Śupatī, Halāyudha, Bhānu, Upādhyāya Jīmūtavāhana, Dhavaleśvara, and others [hold a different view]:
In whichever zodiac sign the Sun has entered when men meet with calamity,
it is in that very sign that the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and the water-libation rite should be performed for them.

From this statement, it follows that the annual rite (sāṃvatsarika) must be performed according to the solar month. Nor is this [rule] restricted solely to the anniversary of death occurring in an intercalary month (malamāsa), as there is no evidence for such a limitation. Furthermore, even when a lunar day (tithi) is omitted due to the reduction [of the moon's phases], there is no resulting omission of the Śrāddha rite.
If an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises, or if the lunar day (*tithi*) is omitted,
one should perform it on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), especially during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
Because that [rite] is possible on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) according to such a statement,
they say that when the term "annual" (ābdika) is used in a statement defining the lunar month, it refers specifically to rites performed every year, such as the Durgotsava and others.
And in this regard—
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its rising,
that entire lunar day is to be known as valid for acts such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches when setting,
that entire lunar day is to be known as valid for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study.

Thus, according to the statements of Devala and others, just as a lunar day (*tithi*) that is not present at the time of a ritual action is accepted by imagining its fullness, it is not so with the day-and-night (*ahorātra*) that serves as the locus for human death; in that case, the *tithi* existing at sunrise or sunset in the form of three *muhūrtas* or more is not accepted merely because of its connection to the death.
Rather: "For humans, at the time of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) or at the time of death, the *tithi* is recorded as being that which exists at that very moment."
Thus, by the statement of Vasiṣṭha, [the śrāddha] refers specifically to that performed at the time of death.
Now, regarding the determination of the annual time when the day of death and so forth are unknown:
in that case, if neither the lunar day of death nor the fortnight of death is known, but the month is known;
That annual [śrāddha] should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) occurring within that month;
and thus says Bṛhaspati:
