If the day of death is not known when someone has passed away while living abroad, and the month is known, then the rite should be performed on the new moon day of that month; if the day is known, it should be on the anniversary of the day of death.
The phrase "that which is prescribed for the day of death" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

And although here only the ignorance of the day of death is mentioned, nevertheless, since—as will be explained by the method to be stated—the omission of that [day] is inferred when the fortnight is known, the annual *śrāddha* would thus fall on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight;
therefore, this [rule] applies even when the fortnight is unknown.
Because it serves as the definitive factor here, the mention of the "day of death" is intended to indicate the fortnight as well.
The term "one who has gone abroad" (proṣita) is an indication of the causes for not knowing the day of death;
for this very reason—
In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"Even in the absence of physical separation, those two [the husband and wife] may become estranged when they have forgotten one another," and so forth.
And here, because of the general statement, this same decision is appropriate even for paternal uncles and others when the day of death and so forth is unknown.
And thus:
"O King, he who does not know the day, or even the month..."
But when his parents have died, O man of great wisdom, how can that man [be considered a son]?
Thus, in the interrogative passage from the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, the word "father" (*pitṛ*) should be understood as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Marīci states the subsequent time limit:
When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen and the day of death is unknown,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

Since the word "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) is heard here, the Śrāddha is performed even on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight; thus, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight alone is the primary [time].

However, if that [bright fortnight] is not known, then because the dark fortnight is praised for ancestral rites (*pitrya*) and because of the mention of "specifically," the eleventh day of the dark fortnight is the primary time.
But in its absence, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight serves as the time—this is the distinction.
This is also the consensus of all southern and Maithila authorities, such as Hemādri and others.

However, the Bhaṭṭa Smārta, intending to emphasize that the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇaikādaśī) is primary in comparison to the new moon (amāvāsyā) mentioned in the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati, stated "specifically" (viśeṣataḥ).
Nor is there any inconsistency in using the term "specifically" in the context of "an obstacle to the Śrāddha," for in that case, the new moon is indeed the specific time intended.
It should be stated that this is because there is no prohibition.
However, when an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen, such as a death or birth-impurity occurring in the interim,
some wise men say that one should perform it on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) once one is purified.
He states this because, according to the words of Vyāsa, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is prescribed for that occasion.
However, when the month of death is unknown but the day is known,
then [the rule] from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa is as follows:
But that man who knows only the day and not the month—
whether he performs [the rite] in Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha— [does so in vain].
In the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti* as well:
"Then, in the month of Āṣāḍha or Māgha, that day shall occur;
here too, when the bright fortnight is known, the specific lunar day (*tithi*) occurring therein is to be taken."
If not, it should be taken as belonging to the dark fortnight, because that is most highly recommended for ancestral rites (*pitrya*).

However, when there is ignorance regarding the month, fortnight, and lunar day connected with the death of all three [ancestors], then— if news of their being alive was not received even after their departure— the month, lunar day, and fortnight corresponding to those of the date of departure should be adopted.
As Bṛhaspati said:
"When neither the day nor the month of death is known..."
However, the day and month of departure should be determined according to the method previously described.
The mention of "day and month" is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for the fortnight, as before.
The meaning of the phrase "by the previously mentioned [method]" is as follows:
when only the month is known, [one determines] the lunar day (tithi) of that fortnight occurring within Bhādrapada or other months.
If only the fortnight is unknown, [the rite is performed] on that specific lunar day (tithi) occurring in the dark fortnight of that month;
if only the lunar day is unknown, it is performed on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of that month;
and if both the month and the fortnight are unknown, it is performed on a lunar day occurring in the dark fortnight of the month beginning with Bhādrapada.
If the lunar fortnight and the lunar day are unknown,

[the rite should be performed] on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of that month; however, if the month and the lunar day are unknown, it should be performed on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada and so forth.
However, when there is ignorance regarding the month, fortnight, and lunar day that are common to all three [the departure,

the news of life, and the news of death], and for one whose news of living was heard for a long time after the departure but whose certain death was subsequently heard, the month, fortnight, and lunar day corresponding to the date of hearing [the news of death] are to be taken for one who has not yet performed the funeral rites.
And likewise,
in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"Upon hearing news of death, those two [the *sapiṇḍana* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*] are to be performed according to the sequence previously stated."
The meaning of the phrase "in the manner previously stated" is as follows:
the determination made based on one or two cognitions, which was mentioned earlier, should be understood here as well.

Furthermore, on the very day that the news of the certainty of death is heard, the annual anniversary rite (*ābdika*) should be performed by one who has already completed the funeral rites for the deceased.

It should be understood as follows: however, for one whose funeral rites (*pretakārya*) have not been performed, once the certainty of death has been heard, the post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadaihika*)—beginning with the cremation of an effigy (*pratikṛti*) and so forth—must be completed, and then the annual rite (*ābdika*) should be performed in the second year on the lunar day (*tithi*) when [the news] was first heard; this is the distinction.

But when there is ignorance regarding the month, lunar day, or fortnight that correspond to the lunar day of the hearing for all three [ancestors], or when there is no certainty regarding the performance of the funeral rites, then in the matter of the annual rite—
The *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:

"One does not know the day or even the month of the deceased by any means; therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*amāvāsyā*), or in the months of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa."
The word "vā" (or) is intended to include that alternative view as well;
for this very reason, the mention of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is appropriate.
Otherwise, however—
On whichever day of a month, fortnight, or lunar date a person dies, they know that corresponding day of each year to be his *kṣayāha* (the anniversary of death).

Thus, according to the statement of Vyāsa, since even the fortnight (pakṣa) serves as a determinant for the day of death, it is impossible to abandon its knowledge once that fortnight is known; consequently, because [the rite] is obtained only on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month beginning with Bhādrapada, the insistence on the new moon (amā) is untenable.
Furthermore, this would be a prescription of a previously unknown alternative time in the case of ignorance of all three [factors], which is cumbersome.

Rather, even when only one of the others is unknown, the time such as the new moon is already prescribed; therefore, even in the case of ignorance of both, it is merely a restatement (anuvāda) of what is already obtained by implication.

And precisely because it is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), there is no fault in the word *amā* (new moon) indicating another time in the form of the secondary Śukla-ekādaśī— which is primary [only] as Kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī— nor in the words *māgha* and so forth indicating the month of Bhādra and so forth.
For this very reason, when commenting on this statement according to his own view, the Smārta author stated that the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is to be accepted only in the absence of Kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī.
"And yet not" means by no sign whatsoever, such as hearing of the death or departure of the deceased.
By this, it is also indicated that when the month associated with the death is known, the date of departure belonging to that month of death should be taken, and so forth.

Furthermore, in this context, if the date and other details associated with the death are unknown, but the date and other details associated with the departure are known—whether through the departure itself or through hearing of the death—then the date and other details associated with the departure alone are to be taken.

In the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati, it is understood that when the lunar day (*tithi*) and other details related to the time of death are unknown, only the lunar day and other details related to the departure (*prasthāna*) are to be taken;
for many [authorities] maintain that the departure is prior to the hearing (*śravaṇa*).
In reality, however, since the connection with the day of death is understood through the lineage on the day of the hearing, [the latter] is understood as the primary [criterion].

Even though there is a sublation of that specific relation characterized by being the delimiting factor for the *tiṣya* constellation belonging to the same class as the anniversary date, it is improper to abandon the general relation understood by implication— provided it is possible— just as one does not abandon the mere sequence observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) between the *ānubandhya* and *agnīṣoma* sacrifices in the *sādyaska* rite; therefore, when the date and so forth related to death are unknown, the date and so forth related to the *śravaṇa* asterism itself must be taken.
Nor is there any contradiction with the statement of Bṛhaspati;

for since the genitive case in the word *maraṇasya* denotes a mere relationship, there is no harm even if it refers to being mediated by the *Śravaṇā* [nakṣatra], just as in the case of the expression "the seventeen-aratni [pole] of the Vājapeya" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.9).

Therefore, when the lunar day and other details related to death are unknown, one should take the lunar day and other details related to the *Śravaṇā*; and when those are also unknown, one should take the lunar day and other details related to the departure (*prasthāna*).
The distinction is that even when that [month] is unknown, one should observe the time as prescribed in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*.
As for what Vācaspati stated here—that no action should be performed due to the ignorance of the month because of a lack of basis—that must be disregarded;

for, according to the previously cited statements of Bṛhaspati and others upheld by Kāladarśa, Mādhava, Smārta-bhaṭṭācārya, and others, specific months such as Bhādrapada are prescribed in cases where the month is unknown.

However, in the case of one who has gone to an unknown land and for whom neither life nor death can be determined, after waiting for fifteen years, the funeral rites such as cremation with a substitute image are performed; for such a person, the month, fortnight, and lunar day corresponding to those of the date of cremation and so forth are to be taken.
And likewise, Jātukarṇya says:
"If a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor his return,"
But after fifteen years have passed, having made a substitute image, [one may proceed].
And he should perform his consecration according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, he should carry out all the remaining rites just as if [the person] had died at that very moment. "Just as if at that very moment" means as if the person had died right then.
The remaining rites refer to those such as the monthly and annual ceremonies (*māsika-ābdika*).
As for the statement:
"For one whose news is not heard for up to twelve years..."
Through the burning of a blade of *kuśa* grass, there would be his certain determination.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"When the period of twelve years has passed for one who has gone abroad,
and the thirteenth year has arrived, one should perform the funeral rites."
If he should return alive, one should place him in a jar of ghee;
having lifted him out and bathed him, one should perform the birth rites and so forth.
He should observe the vow for twelve days, or for three nights; then, having bathed, he may marry her as his wife, or another woman in her absence.

Having established the sacred fires according to the rules, he should either perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice; or else, having gone to a mountain, he should perform the Aindrāgna animal sacrifice there.
"One should perform the *āyuṣmatī* sacrifice and then the desired rites"—
this statement of Vṛddha-Manu, which prescribes a waiting period of twelve years, refers to cases other than the father's death,
because in the previously cited statement of Jātūkarṇya, the term "father" (*pitari*) is specifically mentioned as a qualification.
Some, however, state the rule that for one less than fifty years of age, there is a waiting period of fifteen years, while for one older than that, it is twelve; but that is not correct,
because this [rule] lacks a foundation, as it is not established by any scriptural statement.
The phrase "while living," and so forth, applies even in the case of the father.
The practice of vows consists of the form of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the annual anniversary rite when the day of death is unknown.
Now follows the determination regarding obstacles to the *śrāddha*.
First, concerning the obstruction of the *kṣayāha-śrāddha* by impurity (*āśauca*), it should be performed on the day following the last day of that impurity.
And so it is said:
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: If,
however, impurity should arise when the Śrāddha for the ancestors is about to be offered,
then the Śrāddha for them is prescribed to be performed once that period of impurity has passed.
Having become pure, one should give on whichever lunar day (tithi) arrives;
that very tithi must be observed by him, and never any other.
Thus,
the qualification "to be given" (*deya*) is for the purpose of excluding *śrāddha* rites other than those on the anniversary of death;
for, according to the statement of Śaṅkha, it is understood that these [other rites] are not to be performed during the period of impurity (*āśauca*).
For example:
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors— these are suspended during periods of impurity, with the exception of the offering of funeral cakes for the deceased.
Thus [it is said].

Now, since there is no distinction in their being rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkarman*), the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) is likewise excluded; therefore, how can it be that only the *śrāddha* other than the one on the anniversary of death is to be accepted?
On this point, some say:

Since the phrase "the performance of the *piṇḍa* for the *preta*" refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a *preta*, it is established that this *ekoddiṣṭa* must be offered during the period of impurity (*aśauca*). Consequently, by extension (*atideśa*), it would follow that the annual *ekoddiṣ�ṭa*—which is a modification of that rite—must also be offered during the period of impurity.
[The opponent claims] that the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga serves as a restrictive injunction (*vidhi*) that the time for it is the end of the period of impurity.
That is not correct.

Since the *pratyābdika-śrāddha* performed according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure by an *aurasa* son who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) does not entail the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, there would be no possibility of its being offered [during a period of impurity], and thus it could not be performed at the end of the period of impurity;
yet this is not an acceptable conclusion, as it would contradict the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

Furthermore, since the obligation to offer all paternal rites—other than the *preta-ekoddiṣṭa*—is established by the statement of Śaṅkha, and since the *sāṃvatsarika-ekoddiṣṭa* is specifically enjoined as something not to be offered [during impurity], there is no possibility of its obligation being derived through extension (*atideśa*).

In reality, however, the phrase "the rite of offering rice-balls for the deceased" (preta-piṇḍa-kriyā) does not refer to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for the deceased, because that would entail the fault of metaphorical interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*). Rather, it refers to the mere offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-dāna*) in general.

Consequently, since even the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the deceased is not to be offered during the period of impurity (*āśauca*), there is no possibility of its being extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the annual *ekoddiṣṭa* as something that must be offered.
Therefore, such an interpretation is not tenable.

Others, however, argue that by the qualification "it should not be given," the prohibition applies to the *pārvaṇa* and other rites at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), rather than to the [specific rite] mentioned in the *Kāmadhenu*.

This is because this statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga is recorded in the *Kāmadhenu* specifically within the section on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha-prakaraṇa*), and in the original source (*ākara*) as well, it occurs in the section on the anniversary of death.
Thus, this is inferred to mean "it is exactly so.

And therefore, they say that by virtue of the context, it is only the *śrāddha* to be performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) that is prescribed here as being to be performed at the end of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), and not the *pārvaṇa* and other types of *śrāddha*.
That is not correct.
Otherwise, the term *deya* (to be given) would become redundant;
furthermore, it would be improper to assume that [the passage] belongs to the section concerning the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) merely because of its mention in the *Kāmadhenu*.
Therefore, how can the exclusion of the *pārvaṇa* and other rites be established solely by virtue of the qualification *deya*?
The fact that these [objects] are not to be given is clearly evident from the words of Śaṅkha.
However, regarding the obligation to give at the *mṛtāha* (anniversary) śrāddha, it is stated:
"When an obstacle to the śrāddha has arisen, or when the *mṛtāha* is unknown..."
One should perform it on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.
According to this statement by Laghuhārīta,

the term "day of death" (*mṛtāha*) here qualifies "obstruction to the *śrāddha*" as well, because it is situated in the middle [of the phrase] and thus lacks a specific distinction, and because it remains expectant of further specification. Alternatively, although the term "day of death" is connected only with the word "unknown," nevertheless, due to its immediate proximity, the obstruction occurring specifically on that day is what should be understood.

And therefore, since it is understood that the *śrāddha* for the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha-śrāddha*) must be offered whenever there is an obstacle [to its performance], it follows by implication that it must also be offered when there is an obstacle in the form of ritual impurity (*āśauca*).

Nor should it be argued that because the obligation to offer it is understood here with reference to specific times such as the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), the injunction regarding the time at the end of impurity cannot apply here according to the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;

for even though this [statement] is primarily concerned with a specific obligation to offer, an injunction regarding other times is indeed possible here by relying on the general obligation to offer which is implied.

Just as, although there is a specific connection with the *āgneyī* [verse] for the *stotra* and other rites, the injunction “one worships the *āgnīdhra* fire-altar with an *āgneyī* verse” relies upon the connection with the sacrifice in general— which is established by the sense of the matter— for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), and thus prescribes it as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the worship of the *āgnīdhra*; so too, since the time of the eleventh day and so forth mentioned here is prohibited by the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, “but never another [day],” it possesses a secondary status (*gauṇatva*) in comparison to the day immediately following the primary period of impurity (*āśauca*) which is proximate to the anniversary of death.
Since that which serves as the basis for the prohibition cannot be prohibited in every respect, the prohibition must have a possible scope [of application].

For this very reason, the *Smṛticandrikā*, *Kālādarśa*, *Hemādri*, and other authorities, having explained the statement of Laghu-Hārīta regarding the interruption of impurity (*āśauca*), have declared that the time of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth is secondary (*gauṇa*) in comparison to the time at the end of the impurity. By this, it is refuted by some who claim that when there is an interruption of impurity, the offering should be made on the lunar day marking the end of the impurity, and that the black *ekādaśī* need not be awaited because of the prohibition: "But never any other," which they argue refers to cases of other interruptions.
And as for what was stated by a certain partial follower of the Gauḍa school:
"When an obstacle to the Śrāddha has arisen— such as death or birth occurring in the interim—
the wise should not perform it on the eleventh day or even on the new moon day."
As for the claim that, based on the words maintained by many treatises, the rite must be performed only at the end of the period of impurity—
that too should be understood as refuted; rather,
the cited statement is to be explained as referring to a specific possible case.
Otherwise: "If,
when the annual *śrāddha* has arrived, a birth or death impurity occurs in the interim,
one should perform it after the period of impurity has ended, or even on the new moon day of that month."
Otherwise, the statement of Gobhila cited in the *Kālādarśa* would be rendered devoid of scope.
Therefore, when a Śrāddha is obstructed by impurity (*āśauca*), it should be performed at the end of that period of impurity.
If, due to negligence or other causes, the Śrāddha cannot be performed then, it should be performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Because that [observance] is prescribed with the condition of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) by the statement of Gobhila cited earlier from the *Kālādarśa*;
because, if even that is impossible, it is prescribed for the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) in the *Laghuhārīta-smṛti* as a remedy for any general obstacle;
and because, if even that is impossible, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śuklaikādaśī*) is indicated as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) by the specific mention of it as well.

As for what Vācaspati has stated—that the statement of Laghu-Hārīta refers to cases where the anniversary of death is obstructed by a period of impurity (āśauca) other than the one specifically prescribed—it is incorrect, because the prohibition "but never another [day]" would otherwise be untenable as it would prohibit a time that was not even applicable.
Śūlapāṇi also holds this view.

Furthermore, this rule regarding the performance of the rite at the end of the period applies when there is an obstruction of impurity that cannot be removed by human effort; it does not apply when the obstruction can be removed by human effort, since in that case the impurity ceases simply through the purification prescribed for the day of the śrāddha.

And thus, since even the impurity caused by injury cannot be removed by human effort, some hold that if an obstacle arises due to such impurity, the rite must be performed at the very end of that period.

Others, however, argue that there is no authority for treating injury-caused impurity as "impurity" (āśauca) in the technical sense; or even if it were considered such, when an obstacle to a Śrāddha has arisen—such as a death or birth occurring in the interval—[the rite should be completed].

They say that because the previously cited statement prescribes that the performance [of the rite] must take place at the conclusion of the impurity caused by birth or death (*jananamaraṇāśauca*) alone, it should not be performed at the end of the impurity caused by a wound (*kṣatāśauca*), but rather on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth.

And thus, according to the view that the performance must occur at the conclusion [of the impurity], even the rule regarding the performance on the preceding day is to be carried out on the following day; for on the preceding day, since there is doubt as to whether the wound has healed, there is no certainty regarding the necessity of performing the principal rite.
Nor should it be argued that it cannot be performed on the following day either, due to the absence of the time-period consisting of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*).
Because it is improper to abandon the principal act for the sake of conforming to a subsidiary detail;
nor should it be said that what is performed at an improper time is as if unperformed,
since a secondary (gauṇa) time is still available.

Otherwise, since it would be impossible [to perform the rite] on the *amāvāsyā* day when it must be completed immediately (*sadyaskālā*), there would result the omission of the *anvādhāna* and other rites that are to be accomplished on the preceding day.

And thus, as for what Bācaspati stated regarding the case of impurity due to a wound—that the duties of the preceding day are not even a constituent part [of the rite] because, due to the doubt concerning the absence of the wound, there is no certainty on the preceding day that the primary rite should be performed; and because on the following day, although there is such certainty, the time consisting of the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is absent at the moment of contact with the wooden sword (*sphya*)—[this is the position].
The claim that there is a sublation (bādha) of the invocation (āvāhana), as in the case of the *jyāyas*,
has been refuted;
for it is improper to omit an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) when a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) is available.

Furthermore, even the citation of an illustrative example is based on a misunderstanding of the source-text, because the *Ācārakāṇḍa* states that the invitation (*āvāhana*) must be performed immediately after the occasion [of the impurity] in the tenth chapter.

Thus, when a *śrāddha* is performed on the day following the final day of birth or death impurity, the rites belonging to the preceding day must be performed on that very same day; for since the impurity still exists on the preceding day, one lacks the qualification to perform them then.
As for those rites that are rendered redundant by the purpose (such as eating only once a day), they are simply omitted.
Vācaspati, however, states that the rite should be performed on the very day it falls, because purity (*śauca*) is not a mandatory requirement there, just as in the case of the *ekādaśāha* śrāddha.
And here, in the phrase "to be given for the ancestors," it is understood that the śrāddha determined by the day of death must be performed at the end of that period of impurity (*āśauca*).
Consequently, this also includes the monthly, the six-monthly, the three-fortnightly, and other such rites.

Therefore, if there is an obstacle to the monthly or annual rites due to impurity (āśauca), they must be performed at the end of that period; however, if that is impossible, they should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) or similar occasions.
But if the obstacle is other than impurity, the monthly *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed on the day following the monthly anniversary.
Thus says Atri:
If that day should be defiled by some cause such as birth-impurity (sūtaka) and so forth,
one should perform it after the impurity has ended, or on that very same day again.
Thus [it is said].
And here, the first period of time refers to the occasion of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and obstacles, because it is consistent with the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;
whereas the second refers to obstacles other than birth-impurity, as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

Although the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga is general in nature, it is indeed appropriate that the two options have distinct scopes, because a choice between these two alternatives is marred by the eight logical fallacies (*aṣṭadoṣa*).
Nor is there a lack of evidence for this [rule] having as its scope the monthly *ekoddiṣṭa* rites; for it is said:
"The monthly rite and the water-pot offering—whichever of these may be interrupted..."
They declare that [the rite] is to be performed according to the dependence on each subsequent [authority].
Because such a certainty is obtained through the attainment of syntactic unity with that statement,
for this very reason, there is a citation from Devala in the Hemādri:
"But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived, if an obstacle should arise..."
In another month, on that same lunar day (tithi), one should diligently perform the śrāddha rite.
Thus it is said.

Although at this point, during the occasion of stating the specific cause [for the rite], the term *ekoddiṣṭa* appears to apply generally to both the monthly (*māsika*) and annual (*ābdika*) rites, nevertheless, because of the statement "on another month," it refers specifically to the monthly *ekoddiṣṭa*.
Otherwise, he would have said "on another year."

Furthermore, this prescription of the time consisting of the intervening day of the monthly rite (*māsika*) is not for when the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) and so forth are unavailable; for that [eleventh day] has been specifically prescribed with priority over the monthly rite.
For this very reason, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* stated that the statement, "One should perform it on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)," refers to the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) śrāddha.
However, in the Gauḍa compendiums (*nibandha*), it is stated that if the rite is not performed on the eleventh day and so forth, it should be performed on the intervening day of the monthly rite.

Regarding this, the author of the *Candrikā* maintains that because the term "ekoddiṣṭa" is mentioned in the cited statement, the prescription for a different day and time applies only to those monthly rites (*māsika*) performed in the form of *ekoddiṣṭa*, and not to those performed in the form of *pārvaṇa*.

On this point, the Gauḍas hold that after performing the missed monthly rite (*patitamāsika*), one should subsequently perform the monthly rite for that specific day, because there is no authority for abandoning the established sequence [of rites].
They argue that in this case, since the rites share the same time and performer, it is more appropriate to treat them as a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Since the sequence is merely implied by the sense (*ārthika*), there is no defect even if it is set aside;

or, even if the sequence were a constituent part (*aṅga*), its sublation would still be entirely appropriate in accordance with the time, which is not something to be directly prescribed (*anupādeya*).

Nor should it be argued that because the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and so forth serve merely as a means of excellence (*atiśaya*), the time for the *śrāddha* is not sublated even when those [details] are set aside.
For even in accordance with such other [texts] as the *Aparārka*, the performance as a single ritual (*tantra*) is logical;

otherwise, in the absence of a sublation regarding time, since they would be encompassed by distinct injunctions for performance, it would follow that the *śrāddhas* for the solstices (*saṅkrānti*), the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and so forth, must also be performed separately.
Therefore, the performance as a single ritual alone is logical.
For this very reason, "tantra" is mentioned in the previously cited statement, "tattaduttarasātantryāt" (due to the dependence on each subsequent one).
And that [tantra] applies to the ancillaries (*aṅga*), but not to the primary rite (*pradhāna*) as well, because that would result in a contradiction of the number sixteen.
Therefore, a monthly rite (*māsika*) that has been omitted should be performed together with the monthly rite for that specific day by means of *tantra* on the day of another monthly rite.

The annual śrāddha (ābdika), however, should be performed on the new moon day following [the period of impurity] or other occasions when an obstacle such as the impossibility of cooking arises; it must not be done with raw food (āmānnena). Even if one is in a state of ritual impurity (vyāpanna), one should never perform the annual śrāddha with raw food.
This [annual rite] should be performed with cooked food on the new moon day, or during the dark fortnight on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī).
Thus, according to the statement of Kārṣṇājinī;
"spoiled" (*vyāpanna*) means [rendered unfit] by the impossibility of cooking and so forth,
because it occurs in conjunction with the prohibition regarding raw meat (*āma*).
However, one who is unable due to illness or other causes should have it performed on that very day through a son or another representative by means of food;
for it is logical that a substitute for the agent (kartṛ) should conform to the time which is not subject to selection (anupādeya).
As for that which—
When an obstacle arises for the twice-born regarding a *śrāddha*, an *āma-śrāddha* (a rite with raw food) is prescribed;
this applies to obligatory rites such as those on the new moon day, except for those performed monthly or annually.
One should always perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite oneself using cooked food alone;
however, in the absence of cooking vessels, one should fast on that day.
Thus, the statement of Laghu-Hārīta does not prohibit the use of a substitute in general, but rather prohibits a substitute who is not of the same lineage (*asagotra*).
Accordingly, with reference to the rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*), the Brahma-Purāṇa states:
Never should a *śrāddha* be offered by those who are not of the same lineage (*agautra*) to one who is of the same lineage (*sagotra*).

"By those who are not of the same lineage" (*agautraiḥ*) refers to those acting as intermediaries (*dvārabhūtaiḥ*), and not to those who are the actual performers (*sakṛtkartṛbhiḥ*), for otherwise there would be a syntactic inconsistency (*ananvaya*) with the term "to one of the same lineage" (*sagotrāya*).

Consequently, because the annual *śrāddha* (*sāṃvatsarika*) is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *śrāddha* for the deceased (*preta-śrāddha*), and because the prohibition of a non-sagotra substitute applies there as well, the word "himself" (*svayam*) found in the statement of Laghu-Hārīta must, by virtue of being in syntactic agreement (*ekavākyatā*) with that [prohibition], serve as a prohibition against a non-sagotra substitute.
The treatises of Śūlapāṇi and others also explain it in this way.
However, some maintain that the connection is "by cooking oneself.
Here, the term "absence" (abhāva) refers to the absence of the cooking vessel, which indicates the absence of the entire collection of conditions for cooking (pākasāmagrī).

The phrase "one should fast on that day" means that the fasting, which serves as an expiation (prāyaścitta) for the failure to perform the rite at the primary time, must be performed on that very day;
however, the śrāddha ceremony should instead be performed on the eleventh lunar day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇaikādaśī) and other such times.
Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Kārṣṇājini;
furthermore, even when the time for initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites has lapsed, one would incur the consequence of never performing the initiation after having merely performed an expiation.

Therefore, having performed the expiation in the form of fasting on that very day, one must indeed perform the *śrāddha* again on the eleventh lunar day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) or another such occasion.
The Maithilas, however, maintain that fasting alone takes the place of the Śrāddha;
therefore, in the event of inability due to illness or other causes, it should be performed through a son or another proxy.
As for the occurrence of a woman's menses on that very day, the monthly Śrāddha and others should be performed on that same day using food cooked by oneself or others.
As for the statement:
"When the anniversary of death has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, the śrāddha should not be performed then; it should be performed on the fifth day."
This statement, recorded by Hemādri, Mādhava, and others,
is to be explained as referring to a case where the wife of the deceased is in her menses while performing the Śrāddha;
it does not refer to the wife of the performer of the Śrāddha being in her menses.

Hemādri, however, maintains that since a householder has the right to perform the Śrāddha only together with his wife, he lacks the authority to do so during her menstrual period; because the joint entitlement residing in the husband is thereby suspended, the Śrāddha must be performed for her only when that condition has passed. And the statement "on the anniversary of death" (mṛtāhani) is based on this very principle.
As for that which is said:
"Even if his wife has her menses, even if he is staying in a foreign land, or even if he maintains no sacred fire,
one should perform the annual śrāddha with food alone, or with gold, but never with meat."
He says that this statement by Laugākṣi refers to a case where another wife exists who is entitled [to the rite];
but that is not so,
because there is no authoritative evidence for the husband and wife having a joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) in the *śrāddha*.
Nor should it be said that the statement, “For from the taking of the hand [in marriage], there is joint status in all rites,” is the source [of this rule].

This is because it is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of those rites accomplished by the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires where the joint entitlement of both [husband and wife] is already known through other means of knowledge; it does not, like the rules for *pūrta* works and the like, enjoin joint entitlement in the case of the *śrāddha*.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that the *śrāddha* also possesses joint entitlement because it is accomplished by fire.
Even though the qualification [for performing rites] is to be accomplished through fire, it is impossible to assert [such a qualification for her],

because for one whose father and others have died, there is no possibility of qualification for a *śrāddha*— whether for the purpose of avoiding the sin of non-performance on the new moon day (*amāvāsya*) or for the sake of results such as the satisfaction and liberation of the ancestors— since she lacks the status of being one whose father is deceased, which is necessary to define the relationship of "fatherhood" and so forth.
Nor is there any contradiction with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) used in the context of the fire-consecration (*adhāna*).

For from the middle voice, it is understood only that the rites accomplished by the fires produce a fruit for the owner of the fires, and not a fruit for one who is not the owner; it does not follow that they produce a fruit for every possible owner.
When an *iṣṭi* is performed between a husband and wife for the sake of one of them who is afflicted by disease or other ailments, such [a performance] is impossible [if both were required].

Nor should it be argued: "Since the cooking that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha* and the consumption of the middle *piṇḍa* are to be accomplished by the wife, and since the word 'wife' (*patnī*) denotes the owner of the sacrifice, how can her agency be established in the absence of her entitlement?
For, given the impossibility of entitlement according to the aforementioned reasoning, the word 'wife' functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean simply the wife of the sacrificer.

Therefore, since there is no authoritative evidence for the existence of such a qualification [to perform the rite], the Śrāddha for that very day must be performed with food that is not "putrid" (i.e., fresh) even when she is in her menses.
This is the determination regarding obstacles to the Śrāddha.
Now, the times for the Śrāddhas for the deceased (preta-śrāddha).
In that regard, there are two kinds of *preta-śrāddhas*: the "new" (*nava*) and the "mixed with the new" (*navamiśra*).
According to the *Smṛti*: "The *nava-śrāddha* lasts for ten days, while the *navamiśra* lasts for six seasons."
Therefore, the śrāddhas performed during the ten-day interval are designated as "nava" (new).

This naming is for the purpose of their application in penances and other rites, according to the rule: "The cāndrāyaṇa penance is [equivalent to] the nine new śrāddhas. These various types have been described by Bhartṛyajña in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa as cited in the Hemādri.
Listen now to those three things for the purpose of the funeral rite (sañcaya):
one should perform the śrāddha at the very place where death occurred.
Then follows the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; thereafter, at the place where rest was provided on the way, and then at the site of the funeral pyre, the third *śrāddha* is prescribed.
On the fifth, the seventh, likewise on the eighth, the ninth,
and also on the tenth and eleventh— these indeed are the nine śrāddhas.
And here, even that which pertains to the eleventh day is designated as "the ninth.
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
That which is indeed given to a deceased person on the fourth, fifth, ninth, and eleventh days is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Aṅgiras says:
On the first day, the third day, the fifth, the seventh,
as well as the ninth and the eleventh— this is called the ṣaṇnava-śrāddha.
The *Kālādarśa* states that "the ninth and the eleventh" forms a *dvandva* compound.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"O twice-born ones, on the third day, [the rite] should be performed upon the fire used for cremating the deceased."
"At the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), they prescribe the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha for the household," so says Vyāsa—
on the first, seventh, ninth, and eleventh day.
Whatever is indeed given to a living being is called the *nava-śrāddha*.
Thus it is said.
Although these [periods] are of many kinds, they are nonetheless those declared by the elder Vaśiṣṭha:
on the first day, on the third day, on the seventh, and likewise on the ninth.
On the eleventh day and on the fifth day, there are nine *śrāddhas* as well as six.
Thus, these [rites] currently fall within the scope of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
However, Baudhāyana has mentioned only five;
therein it is also stated that if the *navaśrāddha*, which is to be performed on the ninth day, is interrupted due to an obstacle or other cause, it must be performed on the eleventh day.
One should perform a *navaśrāddha* on each of the odd days following death until the ninth;
however, if the ninth is omitted, one should perform it on the eleventh day.
But Kāṇva states that if there is an interruption of any *navaśrāddha*, one must perform the subsequent rites with a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*).
If the *navaśrāddha* or the monthly *māsika* śrāddhas should be omitted,
it is taught that they must be performed in conjunction with the subsequent [śrāddha] of their respective series.
Thus [it is said].
But Śivasvāmin says:
"The followers of the Āśvalāyana school speak of nine *śrāddhas*."
The Āpastambas say there are six, while the Aitareyiṇas state that it is optional.
Thus, there is a settled rule regarding two positions: five for those belonging to the Āśvalāyana branch, and six for the Āpastambas;
furthermore, he states that for the followers of the Aitareya [branch], there is an option between five or six.
The classification according to caste is also stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"For Vaiśyas and kings, there are nine and seven *nava-śrāddhas* respectively, in due order."
But regarding the first and last syllables, the great sages say there are six.
For Vaiśyas there are nine, for kings seven, for Brahmins and Śūdras six; however,
for the purpose of the *nava-śrāddha*, Atri has stated that there is only one on the eleventh day.
In the Kālakāṇḍa section of Hemādri, it is stated:
"One may perform the first Śrāddha on the eleventh day even if impure;
for the performer there is temporary purity, yet he remains impure thereafter."

Thus, in the statement of Śaṅkha, that which is "first" (ādya) is also explained as "new" (nava). In the *Kātyāyana-gṛhya* as well, it is stated "this is not new" (idaṃ nāvam); since the suffix -aṇ is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), "nāvam" means precisely "new" (*nava*).
And although regarding the nine *śrāddhas*:
They diligently perform the nine *śrāddhas* intended for the deceased according to the procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*; never otherwise.

Thus, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, because it occurs prior to the *sapiṇḍana* rite, it takes the form of an *ekoddiṣṭa* offering. Nevertheless, in that case, an even number of Brahmins should be engaged; and one should feed the twice-born at the door of the house for the deceased on the fourth day.
And on the second day, the shaving of the hair should be performed by the relatives.
On the fourth day, the collection of the bones should be performed by all the kinsmen;
they should devoutly employ even-numbered Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas.
On the fifth, the ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day, one should feed an even number of Brahmins; they know that to be the *navaśrāddha*.
Thus it is from the Kūrma Purāṇa. In the Śūlapāṇi, however, the reading is: "One should feed an odd number of Brahmins; that is called the navaśrāddha."
As for what is stated here in the *Brahma Purāṇa* and other texts: "For Brahmins on the fourth day, for kings (Kṣatriyas) on the fifth day,
for those of the Vaiśya caste on the ninth, and for Śūdras after the tenth."
Thus,
on the fourth day, food should indeed be given to the Brahmins by the kinsmen; whatever was dear to him while he lived, that they should diligently offer for him.
On the fourth day— meaning the day of accumulation—
the meaning is that one should give whatever was desired by that deceased person while he was alive. Cows, gold, and wealth should be given according to one's capacity, dedicated to the deceased.
Thus, the collection of duties spoken by Bṛhaspati should be understood in detail from other sources; furthermore,
although the *navaśrāddha* is also prescribed on the eleventh day.

And so it is said: (Aparārka, Āhnika-prakaraṇa, verse 256)—"On the day of death, however, [the rite] should be performed every month for a year," having stated this, [it continues]: "The first [rite] on the eleventh day."

Thus, because Yājñavalkya prescribes the postponement of the first monthly rite—which would otherwise fall on the day of death—to the eleventh day, it follows that the first monthly rite is applicable there.
Nevertheless, upon careful consideration of the subsequent statement, the Mahā-ekoddiṣṭa performed on the eleventh day is indeed distinct from those two. To explain:
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be the "general" (sāmānya);
on that eleventh day, one should give [offerings] to eleven Brahmins.
Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa and the Varāha Purāṇa:
"On the eleventh day, one should diligently perform the Śrāddha for the deceased."
Knowing that "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow," one performs the act of inviting the Brahmins.
And here, the *śrāddha* being prescribed with reference to the deceased is indeed distinct from those two;
for the *navaśrāddha* and the monthly (*māsika*) rites are not at all present to the mind here.

Furthermore, in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, by the passage beginning “On the eleventh day, one should perform [the rite] intending the deceased,” there is an extension of the attributes of the model (*prakṛti*)—namely, the *ekoddiṣṭa* performed on the eleventh day—to the monthly rites as well.
It is seen [in other texts as well]; and also in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Then, on the eleventh day, one should indeed invite eleven twice-born [brahmins]."

Having prescribed the ritual along with its associated duties through such statements as, "But at the end of the *sūtaka* period, a Kṣatriya or others should feed an odd number of twice-born men," [the text continues]:
"By this procedure, one should perform everything month after month."
Thus, having established the *ekoddiṣṭa* as the archetype (*prakṛti*), the monthly rites (*māsika*) and others are designated as its modifications (*vikṛti*).
Bṛhaspati also says:
"That which is offered to a single person according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*..."
It is devoid of the invocation (āvāhana) and the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and is excluded from the rites for the gods (daiva).

Having honored with perfumes and garlands the clothing, ornaments, bed, and so forth, as well as the vehicle and weapons of the deceased father, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha feast.
One should cause various kinds of food and condiments to be prepared,
and according to one's ability, one should likewise bestow gifts such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth.
Thus it is said.

Here too, since the *navaśrāddha* (the first nine-day rite) and the monthly rites (*māsika*) are not present, the *akoddiṣṭa* alone—distinguished by various specific rules—is indeed distinct from those two; so what need is there for further elaboration?

And in that regard, according to the previously cited statement from the *Matsyapurāṇa*, the primary rule is that eleven Brahmins are to be invited at the single place designated for the deceased (*pretasthāna*).

Satyavrata also spoke thus: "Having risen in the morning, one should invite eleven *brāhmaṇas* representing the deceased (*preta*) and, in the afternoon, provide various kinds of foods, snacks, and savory dishes," and so forth.

Then, upon the cessation of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), having thoroughly washed his hands and feet in the morning and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should feed *brāhmaṇas* of such a description according to his capacity—facing north, honored with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and other gifts.
Thus, by the phrase "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) in the Viṣṇu [Purāṇa], many [Brāhmaṇas] are indicated;
however, in the Varāha Purāṇa, because of the reference to a single Brāhmaṇa in various places, the appointment of even a single person is prescribed.
"Just as you have gone to the divine world by the path ordained by Kṛtānta,
O Brahmin, I shall direct you with my mind, which has become like the wind."
"I shall honor him with enjoyments"— thus one should invite the Brahmin;
"one should give the Brahmin bathing and anointing according to the prescribed rule"—
thus one should quickly bring the Brāhmaṇa.
And seeing that a twice-born has arrived, one should perform the rites of welcome.
Thus,
for the purpose of providing shade, an umbrella is given to that brāhmaṇa;
afterwards, one should give a pair of auspicious sandals that touch the feet.
By giving a pair of sandals to a deceased person, one causes them to cross over difficult terrains, such as ground with scorching sand or that covered with great thorns.
Thus it is said.

Even when there is the view that many Brahmins [should be fed], it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara* that the clothing, bedding, and so forth consumed by the pretas should be given to only one virtuous person, while to the others a mere sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given according to one's ability.
Immediately after [the statement] "on the eleventh day," [it says]:
"And there, one should provide a meal for a single high-souled Brāhmaṇa,
as well as clothing, ornaments, a bed, and so forth, along with whatever vehicle the father used."
Having honored them with devotion, one should give cows, houses, seats, and servants;
and one should bestow sacrificial fees upon all of them according to their merit.
The details of such passages should be understood from other sources.
Furthermore, in many of these statements, the mention of the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*) is not intended as an indicator for the days following the period of impurity (*āśauca*).
As it is said: "The śrāddha that is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be the general [śrāddha]."
Indeed, for all the castes, the period of impurity (sūtaka) is distinct for each.
According to this statement of Paiṭhīnasi:
"One should perform the first śrāddha on the eleventh day even while impure;
for the performer there is temporary purity, yet he remains impure thereafter."
And because of this statement of Śaṅkha,
even for Kṣatriyas and others, despite the period of impurity (āśauca), the first *śrāddha* must be performed on the eleventh day from death;
likewise, so it is for those who are impure for one or three days.
Even when purification occurs immediately, the gift must be given on the eleventh day for the deceased;
that very day is prescribed for his śrāddha, the funeral couch, the meal, and other rites.
Thus, according to the statement of Śaṅkha, [the rite] is indeed on the eleventh day;
however, Śūlapāṇi and others [state]: “Now, upon the cessation of impurity,” and likewise:

Based on the statements of the *Viṣṇu* and *Matsya Purāṇas*, "At the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), the Kṣatriyas and others should feed an odd number of twice-born [Brāhmaṇas]," it is said that even for Kṣatriyas and others who have periods of impurity lasting one day or three days, if they perform the rites pertaining to the ten-day period during that interval, the *ekādaśāha-śrāddha* (the eleventh-day rite) must be performed at the conclusion of that [ten-day] period,
and not on the eleventh day itself.
In that view, one must discern what the status of Śaṅkha’s statement— "it should be given even during immediate purification"—
is; for in this position, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the statement of Viṣṇu.
This is because it is logically consistent even with the intention of the Brāhmaṇas;
for in that case, there is merely a restriction, but no indication (lakṣaṇā) of anything whatsoever.

If the word "eleventh day" were used as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) meaning merely the end of the period of impurity, then there would be indication (lakṣaṇā) within the injunction regarding the word "eleventh day."
Nor should it be suspected that this contradicts the statement of Mātsya;
rather, its meaning is as follows, for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of contradiction:

on the eleventh day, a Brāhmaṇa performing those rites should not feed with cooked food, but rather, having set aside at that time enough uncooked rice (āma) sufficient for the required number of Brāhmaṇas, he should cook it at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka) and then feed them.

This being the case, the two-fold injunction—applicable to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others—which is endowed with the two distinct periods of time characterized by the *sūtaka* (impurity) of the eleventh day, becomes meaningful; otherwise, since the performance of the first *śrāddha* common to all castes would be established by the injunction of Viṣṇu alone through that single period of *sūtaka*, the statement of the Matsya Purāṇa would be redundant. Furthermore, the phrase "uneven-numbered twice-born" (*ayujo dvijān*) refers to an odd number, such as nine, seven, thirteen, and so forth.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Nine, seven, or thirteen śrotriyas should be fed."
Atri says:
For the sake of the deceased, one should then feed Brāhmaṇas at the end of the period of impurity;
however, for the purpose of the *navaśrāddha*, one should feed them on the eleventh day.

And this being the case, Hemādri maintains that the feeding of Brahmins prescribed at the end of the period of impurity—following the *navaśrāddha* on the eleventh day—is understood to be a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Furthermore, according to the statement of Pāraskara, “There shall be ten rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) for a Brāhmaṇa,” there are ten, twelve, fifteen, or thirty rice-balls respectively for each caste;
or else, according to the injunction “for all [of them],” there is the alternative view that there are exactly ten rice-balls for everyone.

And for all [castes], on the final day of their respective periods of impurity, the tenth *piṇḍa* is offered; even so, for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, the cessation of the state of being a *preta* occurs only through the *śrāddha* performed on the eleventh day, in conjunction with the tenth *piṇḍa* performed on the final day— this is explained in detail elsewhere.
Śātātapa says:
The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and even the sixteen *śrāddhas* should be performed by one person alone, even among those whose wealth has been divided.
Thus said Gālava:
"If there should be birth-impurity (sūtaka) during the period of mourning (śāva), and likewise if it occurs at the end of the night,"
The nine *śrāddhas* should be offered at the appropriate times according to the prescribed rules.
Thus it is said:
even in the case of *anvārohaṇa* (the widow ascending the funeral pyre), the nine *navaśrāddhas* are performed separately;
all the *navaśrāddhas* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite are performed individually.
The rite of releasing a bull is indeed one alone; in that case, a single cow is given.
Thus it is said;
in some places, having stated "the lamp of armor" (*varmapradīpa*), it is written:
"If, by fate, the *navaśrāddha* has been omitted on the first day."
It should be performed on the third day, or on an odd-numbered day if that is not possible.
Thus it is said.
In that very context, there is this further distinction: namely—
One should not perform the *navaśrāddha* on the Nandā days, on a Saturday, on the fourteenth lunar day, at Tripuṣkara, nor during the Tripāda or Pañcaka constellations.
Thus it is said.
A further distinction was stated by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"One should perform the *navaśrāddha* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with cooked food."
Thus,
the necessity of the nine *śrāddhas* has been stated by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"Without performing the nine *śrāddhas*, one is not released from the state of being a *preta*."
But by obtaining [the fruit] within twelve days, one crosses over evil deeds.
Thus ends the section on the timing for the nine *śrāddhas*. Now follow the timings for the constituent *piṇḍas*.

In that regard, the *Brahma Purāṇa* and other texts state, beginning with “The head [is formed] by the first rice-ball” and ending with “But fullness [is attained] by the tenth,” that the tenth rice-ball must be offered to a Brāhmaṇa on the tenth day; furthermore, it says: “The tenth rice-ball should indeed be given to kings on the twelfth day, and for Vaiśyas, the tenth should likewise be given on the fifteenth.”

"The tenth *piṇḍa* for Śūdras is prescribed when the month is complete. Thus, ten *piṇḍas* are stated for each caste according to the difference in time. However, by Viṣṇu, the number of *piṇḍas* is stated according to the number of days of impurity (*āśauca*): "As long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one *piṇḍa* for the deceased."
Pāraskara also states:
"For a Brāhmaṇa there should be ten rice-balls (piṇḍas); for a Kṣatriya, twelve are prescribed;
for a Vaiśya, fifteen are declared; and for a Śūdra, thirty are proclaimed."
Thus:
"They should offer exactly ten pindas to the deceased belonging to all castes.
This other view regarding the ten pinda rite has also been stated by that same author.
Pracetas also says:
"A funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be given to a Śūdra for eight or nine days;
when the month is complete, one should then conclude the remainder of the piṇḍas."
Thus it has been stated.
In this regard, the following rule has been established: the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) continues for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts; this is the primary position.
The increase to ten piṇḍas alone—such as for kings on the twelfth day and for Vaiśyas on the fifteenth—is the middling [alternative].
Even there, if one is unable, the offering of ten piṇḍas over ten days is the lowest [alternative].
Others, however, say:
In the view of the author of this established rule (*vyavasthākṛt*), regarding the first and subsequent positions concerning Śūdras and others:

until the completion of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) that fill the month, how can there be the procedure for the *ekādaśāha* (eleventh-day) *śrāddha*, and how can the statement of Viṣṇu apply— namely, "For Śūdras, it is ordained on the twelfth day, excluding mantras"?
Thus, the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day and so forth should be considered.
And therefore:
"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), for all castes indeed..."
"Śātātapa has declared that their purification occurs after ten days."

Based on the statement of Ityāṅgirasa, the position that for all [classes] the period of impurity lasts exactly ten days is currently the one most widely prevalent and is consistent with the customs of Kṣatriyas and others. Thus, there is no inconsistency in any of the scriptural statements; for instance, Pāraskara’s statement, “for deceased persons of all castes,” becomes fully justified.
It is established that for a Śūdra as well, the *ekādaśāhika-śrāddha* on the eleventh day and the *dvādaśāhika-sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day are appropriate.
Having stated this, someone named Dharmapradīpa wrote:
"On the first day, or the third, or the fifth, or even the seventh."
Two balls of rice should be offered on each day, and the remaining ones on the tenth day.
And thus,
by the statements of Viṣṇu and others stating "the cessation of impurity," when there is an increase in the period of impurity, the rites must be performed at its conclusion;
however, those texts which prescribe the eleventh day refer to cases where the impurity lasts for ten days.
And as for the claim that there is no contradiction with the methods of giving morsels of food to fill the mouth by this same principle, that is not so;
because it contradicts the statement of Śaṅkha, "Even one who is impure [may perform] the first śrāddha," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the previously stated rule alone is superior.
A specific rule regarding the three-day period of impurity has been stated by Śātātapa:
"Even when the period of impurity is shortened, one should nevertheless offer the ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas)."
Pāraskara:
On the first day, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered by those composed in mind;
on the second day, one should offer four, and likewise perform the collection of the bones.
On the third day, one should give three [gifts] such as clothing and so forth, and likewise wash them.
Thus it is said;
but Dakṣa spoke otherwise:
"On the first day, one funeral cake (piṇḍa), and on the second, four likewise."
In the third [year], one should indeed give five; this is recorded as the rule for the ten piṇḍas.
Thus [it is said].
And regarding one killed in battle and the like, Manu (5.98) states: "And for one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya by weapons raised in combat..."
The sacrifice is completed immediately, and such is the rule regarding impurity.
Thus:
"yajña" means the sacrifice consisting of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth;
"saṃtiṣṭhate" means it comes to completion—that is the meaning.
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"In the case of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), all [offerings] should likewise be given simultaneously."
Now, regarding the time for the *pātheya-śrāddha* (the funeral rite for provisions on the journey):
Śātātapa states:
"One should perform the *śrāddha* for the purpose of going from the world of mortals to the world of the departed (*preta-loka*)."
For that indeed becomes the provision for the journey of a deceased human being.
Thus [it is said].
And here, since it is performed on the first day by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), the first day is to be accepted.

However, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, it is stated: "When the collection [of bones] has been performed, for the deceased who is going from the world of men to the world of the departed (*preta*), one should offer a *pātheya-śrāddha* (provision-journey śrāddha) according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure with raw food (*āma*)."
Therefore, even another day is his time.
Now, regarding the time for the collection of the bones,
Samvarta says:
On the first day, or the third, or the seventh, or even the ninth,
the collection of the bones should be performed by those belonging to that same lineage on that day.
Thus [it is said].
Viṣṇu, however, mentions even the fourth day: “On the fourth day, one should perform the collection of the bones and their casting into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In the Brahmapurāṇa, as recorded in the Divodāsa-nibandha, specific times are also stated according to the social classes (varṇas):
They should perform it on the third day for a Brāhmaṇa, on the fourth for a Kṣatriya,
on the fifth for one born of the Vaiśya caste, and on the tenth day for a Śūdra.
Regarding the specific rule for impurity lasting three days and so forth, it is stated in that very same source:
In the case of a three-day period of impurity, the collection of bones must be performed on the second day;
however, in the case of immediate purification, it must be performed at that very moment—this is the settled rule.

Regarding the cremation with *palāśa* wood for the bones, Śaunaka states: "In the case of cremation with *pālāśa* wood or when the bones are being burned, the collection [of the remains] should take place immediately.
Regarding deaths by leaping into fire (*bhṛgu*) and so forth, a specific rule has been stated by Manu:
"His impurity lasts for three nights, but on the second day, the collection of bones occurs.

As for the presentation by certain moderns that this applies to all times and all castes, that is based on a failure to observe the statement from the *Brahma Purāṇa* and is therefore utterly unreliable.
Furthermore, it should not be said that, under the view of the arrangement set forth in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, the seventh and ninth-day options would be rendered purposeless;
for the *Śrāddhacintāmaṇi* states:
"On the seventh day for the Vaiśya caste, and on the ninth day for one born as a Śūdra."
Because this very reading is respected;
and here, the prohibition regarding weekdays and lunar mansions has also been stated by Yama:
"One should avoid [initiation] on Tuesdays, Sundays, and Saturdays, as well as on pairs of lunar days."
One should avoid the collection of bones under a single-footed asterism, and the collection of bones under a two-footed asterism.
"Especially on the birth asterism of the donor, or on an asterism consisting of three quarters [of a lunar mansion].

Regarding this collection of bones, Aṅgiras states that it should be performed starting from the very day of cremation, whether the rite is for one who maintained the sacred fires (sāgnika) or one who did not (anagnika):
For one who maintained no sacred fire, purification occurs upon the departure [of the breath]; for one who maintained a fire, it occurs through the performance of the funeral rites.
In the case of the collection [of bones], purification follows from the cremation; however, the day of death is determined according to the prescribed rule.
Thus [it is said].
Now follows the time for the offering of water:
Gautama states—"The rite of water-offering is performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days."

Now, if the new moon (*darśa*) occurs during the ten-day period of impurity, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "If the new moon arrives while one is engaged in the ritual procedure of impurity, having completed the water libations and the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*), one should perform only the ritual bath."
The remainder [of the sentence] is "until the completion of the period of impurity.
R̥ṣyaśr̥ṅga says:
"If a new-moon day (darśa) should occur during the period of impurity for members of any caste..."
Gautama says that one should bring the *Pretatantra* to completion.
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"The rites of water and funeral cakes for the deceased should be performed only during the first lunar fortnight;
however, one who performs them during the second lunar fortnight incurs the impurity of death once again."

*Dviraindave* means "in the case of two moons. One moon is waning prior to the new moon (*darśa*), while the other is waxing and will appear after the new moon. However, in the *Kālādarśa*, another statement has been recorded, considering that this same situation occurs subsequently as well.
When there is a double moon (an eclipse), no *tithi* should be assigned for the pacification of a deceased person;
if one were to offer food during a lunar anomaly (*vicanda*), it would bring about the destruction of the donor's lineage.

Thus, regarding parents as well, when there is the occasion for the general performance of the rites such as the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*) on the day of the new moon (*darśa*),
Ślokagautama states:
"If the new moon occurs within the ten-day period [of impurity], one should complete everything therein."
But for the parents, one should offer rice-balls and handfuls of sesame seeds for as long as the period of impurity lasts.
The term "of the parents" (*pitroḥ*) is a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (an elliptical compound consisting of two dissimilar members).
This being the case, as for that which was stated by Gālava: "Even if the new moon day (*darśa*) should arrive during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) of the parents..."
The subsequent tantra should conclude no later than three days from that point.
Thus [it is said]. This is its meaning:

if the completion of the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) is appropriate even when the new moon (*darśa*) occurs during the period of impurity due to a parent, how much more so when it occurs during another period of impurity?

Thus, this is intended to demonstrate that the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttara-tantra*) must necessarily be completed in cases involving *sapiṇḍas* other than the paternal uncle, and not as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) even regarding the father.
Or, let it be a restrictive rule even regarding the father; nevertheless, one should not practice even a duty (*dharma*) that leads away from heaven or is loathed by the world.

By this reasoning, supported by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), the statement of Gālava is set aside by the statement of Gautama, "But [the impurity] for the parents lasts as long as the period of impurity. Thus, even if the *darśa* sacrifice falls during the period of paternal impurity, one should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth for as long as that impurity lasts; however, for others, the completion of the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*) occurs only upon the conclusion of the *darśa*. This is the distinction.

Alternatively, the statement of Gālava concerns the *kṣetraja* son with respect to his biological father (*bījipitṛ*), or adopted sons (*dattaka*) and others with respect to their adoptive parents; whereas the statement of Gautama concerns the legitimate (*aurasa*) son and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) with respect to their own parents. Or else, according to the *Madanapārijāta*, the arrangement for all sons, beginning with the *aurasa*, regarding their own parents, should be understood as depending on whether they resort to the rule for times of distress (*āpad*) or the rule for non-distress (*anāpad*).

In works such as the *Mādhavanirṇaya* and the *Āmata*, it is stated that if the new moon (*darśa*) occurs after three days have passed, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the mother and father may be concluded; however, if the new moon occurs within those three days, even the statement of Gautama applies specifically to that situation.

For those other than the mother and father, if the new moon occurs at any time during the ten-day period, the ritual procedure must indeed be concluded. When the new moon occurs within the ten-day period and the funeral rite (*pretatantra*) has not been commenced prior to the new moon due to negligence, laziness, or similar causes, then its commencement and conclusion are appropriate even after the new moon. At that time—

Furthermore, the fault of performing it on two consecutive new-moon days (*dviraindavata*) is also avoided. Nor should it be argued that, because of the statement "it must be performed on the very first new moon," the commencement [of the vow] is implied to take place even before the new moon by following the [preceding] new moon; for in the phrase "on the very first new moon," the word "must be performed" (*kartavyā*) is not enjoined as a separate injunction. If that were the case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to two distinct objects of injunction: "on the first new moon" and "must be performed."
Therefore, here too, because of the prohibition "twice during the lunar month" (*dviraindava*), it is specifically the state of occurring twice in a single lunar month that is prohibited.

In some places, the completion of the ritual manual (*tantra-samāpti*) occurs even upon the occurrence of a *saṅkrānti* or a *vyatīpāta*, just as in the case of a *darśa*. This statement has been recorded on the grounds that it constitutes a summary (*saṅgraha*). [As it is said: "If the new moon (*darśa*), a solar transit (*saṅkramaṇa*), and an eclipse (*pāta*) should occur within ten days [of one another]..."
"Some maintain that the *uttaratantra* is completed with just that much"; however, this appears to be rejected by the commentators (*nibandhakāra*),

as it seems untenable and because the completion of the *tantra* at the time of a *vyatīpāta*, a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), or an eclipse is not observed even in the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
Now follows the time for the monthly *śrāddhas*, which are well known as consisting of the nine mixed ones (*navamiśra*) and the sixteen [regular] ones.
Regarding these, Āśvalāyana states: "But the nine mixed ones [are performed] during the six seasons.
The meaning of the phrase "during the six seasons" will be explained further on.

And these rites, beginning from the month of death and performed every month for one year, are twelve; together with the *ūnamāsika*, the *traipākṣika*, the *ūnaṣāṇmāsika*, and the *ūnābdika*, they are sixteen. Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
The monthly rites, the first [anniversary], the half-yearly, as well as the three-monthly and the annual— these are the sixteen śrāddhas.
Thus [it is said].

Here, because the "twelve monthly [offerings]" are mentioned separately, the terms *ādyasāṇmāsika* (the first six-monthly) and *ābdika* (annual) refer respectively to the *ūnamāsika* (one-month deficient), *ūnaṣāṇmāsika* (six-month deficient), and *ūnābdika* (year-deficient).
He says:
Gobhila states:

"The *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* [rite] is performed in the sixth month when it is incomplete; the *ūna-māsika* [rite] is likewise when one month is incomplete; the *traipakṣika* [rite] occurs at the end of three fortnights; and similarly, the *ūnābdika* [rite] occurs in the twelfth month when it is incomplete."
Thus:
"within six months" means in the sixth month; "at three fortnights" means in the third fortnight.
The *unābdika* (the annual rite performed before the year is complete) should be performed in the twelfth month that is still incomplete;
the *ūnamāsika* (the monthly rite performed before the month is complete), however, should be performed on the twelfth day or in the month that is still incomplete.
Because it has been stated by that very [author]: "On the twelfth day after death, or on the month, or on the 'deficient month' (ūnamāsa), the *ūnamāsika* [rite] should take place.
Thus, it is said here that the *ūnamāsika* and other rites are to be performed on the deficient month and so forth.
In that regard, when there is an expectation as to how many days less [than the full period] the rites should be performed,
Gālava says:
"Or with three days less, or with two, or likewise with one."
And during the months beginning with the first, one should perform the annual śrāddha and other rites, even if they fall on an inauspicious day.
Thus it is said; and Ślokagautama also states:
"In one, two, or three days less, or even in three hundred minus one [days]."
Gautama states that one should perform the *śrāddha* rites, such as the *ūnābdika* (the annual rite performed before the full year) and others.
Here, "in the *ūna*" means "in the state of being deficient.

By the word "others" (*ādi*), the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* (the six-month rite performed before the completion of six months) and the *ūnādyamāsika* (the monthly rite performed before the completion of the first month) are included.
Jātūkarṇya says: When six months are less than a single day, or even less than three days,
and the year itself [is less than three years], then both [the six-month and the annual periods] shall be observed as six-month rites.
Thus:

"at the six-month [mark]" means at the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* (the deficient six-month anniversary) and the *ūnābdika* (the deficient annual anniversary); "on the day deficient by one day" means on the final day, being short by the completion of one full day.
For this very reason,
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The six-monthly and annual Śrāddhas should both take place on the day preceding [the anniversary]."
The monthly [offerings] should be performed on their own respective day, or even on the twelfth day.
Thus:
*pūrvedyuḥ* means on the day preceding the anniversary of death;
*ṣāṇmāsikābdike* refers to the six-month and annual rites, specifically the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* (six-month minus) and *ūnābdika* (annual minus), according to the *Madanaratna*.
Regarding the time for the three-part rite (*traipakṣika*), Kārṣṇājini says:
"In the case of fewer than [twelve] months, it is performed on an odd day, whether the month itself is deficient or even."
The rites for the three fortnights should be performed during the third fortnight, while the others [the monthly śrāddhas] should be performed on the anniversary days of death.
Thus,
in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"In the sixth month one should perform the six-monthly rite, and in the twelfth month the annual rite."
