The conduct pertaining to the three fortnights occurs immediately after that three-fortnight period.
Thus [it is said].
Kārṣṇājini did not say "in three fortnights," but rather in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa it says, "when three fortnights have elapsed."
Thus it was said; therefore, one should state that there is no contradiction.

Some maintain that the meaning of "vṛtte" is not "having passed," but rather "having begun," in accordance with the locative case used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) as in the phrase "in the third fortnight" (*tripakṣe*).

However, some declare that at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for the deceased in the home on the twelfth day, then on the first day of the month, after three fortnights, and thereafter.

Thus, even in this statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa*, they supply the word "past" (*atīta*) as a supplement after the phrase "in the third fortnight," taking the word "conduct" (*vṛtta*)— as found in the previously cited passage— in its literal sense of "having passed. Vyāsa says:
On the twelfth day, at the three-month mark, at six months, monthly, and on the anniversary year—
these sixteen śrāddhas are remembered by the wise.
This is the meaning:
by the phrase "on the twelfth day," the *ūnamāsika* (monthly rite minus one) performed there is indicated;
by the phrase "in six months," the *ūnaṣāṇmāsika* (six-month rite minus one) is indicated.

The monthly rites (*māsika*) are those performed on the anniversary of death each month, numbering twelve; the annual rite (*ābdika*) and the slightly premature annual rite (*ūnābdika*) are also included.

Regarding these, it is said that while the second and subsequent monthly rites should be performed on the anniversary of death in the second, third, and following months, the first monthly rite must be performed on the eleventh day.
Yājñavalkya (Ācārādhyāya, Śrāddhaprakaraṇa, verse 256): "On the anniversary of the day of death, however, the rite should be performed every month for a year."
And likewise, every year on the eleventh day from the start, [the rite should be performed].
"Vatsaram" means until the completion of the year; the accusative case is used according to the rule "kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge" (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

Regarding this, some say: taking the first anniversary tithi as the starting point, and measuring up to the preceding tithi of the subsequent anniversary tithi by means of the duration of a lunar month consisting of a collection of thirty tithis, then for one who died on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the performance of the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* (six-monthly) and *ūna-ābdika* (annual) rites would take place respectively on the fourth day of the following bright fortnight;

and according to the view that there is a reduction of one day [for each], or a reduction of three days, they would take place on the third day and the first day [of the respective bright fortnights].
That is hollow;

for there is the previously cited statement of Yājñavalkya, "But [the rites] should be performed on the day of death," and the statement of Kārṣṇājini, "But the others on the days of death," as well as [the rule], "The monthly [rites] on their own respective day."
And because of the previously cited statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "The monthly and six-monthly śrāddhas should take place on the very day preceding [the anniversary].
Therefore, for one who died on the fifth lunar day, the monthly śrāddha occurs on the next fifth day, while the six-monthly, less-than-six-monthly, and so forth, occur on the fourth;
however, according to the view that the period is reduced by three days, they occur on the second day.
Therefore, it is stated in the Kālādarśa:
"The monthly rites and even those that are deficient [should be performed] on the twenty-eighth day."

According to Mādhava, the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* (the six-month rite performed before completion) and the *ūnābdika* (the annual rite performed before completion) are to be performed on the day preceding the anniversary of death; that is, the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* occurring at seven months should be performed on the day before the seventh month from the date of death, and the *ūnābdika* should be performed on the day before the first anniversary of the second year from the date of death.
Herein follows a clear analysis of the timing for the purpose of dispelling the confusion of the ignorant:
by the etymological derivation *māse bhavam māsikam* ("that which occurs in a month is *māsika*"), [the term refers to rites occurring within the respective periods].
Whether by the etymology "that which occurs when a month has passed" (*māse 'tīte*), or by the etymology stated by Hemādri as "that which relates to a month" (*māsa-sambandhi*),
or by the etymology "that which exists at the beginning of a month" (*māsādau bhavam*), although the *māsika* [śrāddha] indeed involves its occurrence in that month and its connection to that month;

Or rather, it is possible for [the performance] to have as its locus any particular lunar day within that month— just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice has the spring season as its time, or the Śrāddha has the latter fortnight as its time. Nevertheless, because there is no reason to bypass the first [lunar day], and in accordance with the many Smṛti texts to be cited later, it is determined that the performance must commence at the very beginning of the month.

Those statements, however, refer to the monthly [rites], while others refer to "on one's own day" (the anniversary), as in "on the days of death" and "on the day of death, it should be performed. This is also stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
On the twelfth day, at the end of the month, after three fortnights,
and thereafter every month for as long as a year, the rites should be performed by the twice-born.
After that, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should be performed in due order;
once the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed, the Pārvaṇa rite is prescribed once again.
From that time forward, having been liberated from the state of a preta, he attained the status of a pitṛ;
Vyāghrapāda likewise [performed the rites] on the eleventh day, in the fourth month, and every month for a year.
And likewise, every year on the anniversary of death, one should perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Thus,
this being the case, the first-month rite is performed on the eleventh day,
and the "less-than-month" rite is performed on the twelfth day or within the month.
The second-month anniversary rite (*dvitīyamāsika*) is performed on the first lunar day of death of the second month;

the third-month anniversary rite (*tṛtīyamāsika*) is performed on the first lunar day of death of the third month. Therefore, for one who died on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the second-month rite is performed on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, and [the third-month rite] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.

The third monthly [śrāddha] occurs in this manner; likewise for the subsequent months, having understood each respective month, one performs the twelfth monthly śrāddha on the first lunar day of the month of Phālguna, which is the fifth lunar day (pañcamī). Then, the *ūnābdika* (the annual śrāddha performed before the full year) falls on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.

However, when following the view of Kātyāyana—that "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* takes place once the full year has elapsed"—then on that very same day, because the sequence of the *ūnābdika* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is fixed, the *ūnābdika* [is performed].
Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkṛti* [on the fifth day], if one follows the school of Āśvalāyana— according to which "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs at the end of the year"—

then it should be understood that after performing the *ūnābdika* (the annual rite for the deficient period) on the fourth day of the preceding day, one performs the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, which is the first anniversary (*mṛtatithi*) of the second year, and performs the *ābdika* (annual rite) on that very same occasion.
In reality, however, there are not two positions;
for even in the statement of Kātyāyana, it is possible to explain that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* takes place on the second day once the year is complete.
Furthermore, in the Viśvadarśa, it is explicitly stated in clear terms that the monthly offerings (*māsika*) are to be performed at the time of the anniversary of the initial death.

Regarding what was stated concerning the months: that which is performed on the eleventh day among the eleven days of death, that which is performed in the *nyūnābda* (the year minus one), half of that, and furthermore, that which is performed on the twelfth day or the third fortnight by others.
Thus it is said.

Among these, the first monthly rite (māsika), which is due on the anniversary of death, is prescribed as being deferred to the eleventh day by the scriptural injunction: “The first [is performed] on the eleventh day.
Consequently, it is deferred and performed on the eleventh day.
Thus, on that eleventh day, there are three śrāddhas: the Navaśrāddha, the final one, the first monthly rite, and an independent Ekoddiṣṭa.

It is also stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: "When an independent *ekoddiṣṭa* is being performed, for those who desire the accomplishment of the performance of others through a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), there is [this option]; however, in the case of performing them separately, the independent *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed first.

And thus, [the sequence is]: the first monthly, the *ūnamāsika*, the tri-monthly, the third monthly, the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth monthly, the *ūnābdika*, and so forth.
One should offer the sixteen *śrāddhas* on the lunar days (*tithi*s), as established by the *sūtras* cited by Hemādri; thus, the sequence of *śrāddhas* is also logically consistent.
Otherwise, the status of the monthly rites as following their respective months, and the status of the *traipakṣika* (forty-fifth day) rite as following the second month, would not be possible.
By this, that which was stated by Śūlapāṇi—that the etymological derivation of the designation is simply "that which occurs in a month" (*māse bhavam*)—is refuted.

Nor does this result in the occurrence of the monthly rite (*māsika*) on the anniversary of death for every first day of the lunar month, because it is intended that the lunar month extends from the day of death until the next day of death. Furthermore, the ablative case in "from the day of death" (*mṛtatitheḥ*) functions as a limit; therefore, only the subsequent day of death constitutes the meaning of the term "preceding month. Consequently, the claim that the first monthly rite occurs specifically on the second day of death is refuted.
Because it contradicts the cited sūtra.

If it is argued that—on account of the statement, "And likewise every year"—one should take the first anniversary lunar day and proceed with even the first annual rite just as with the monthly rites, we reply:
True, provided there were a scriptural injunction for this case similar to that for the monthly rites, such as, "The first [annual rite] on the eleventh day."

On the contrary, because it arises on the anniversary of death (*amṛtatithi*) at the beginning of his second year, there is no attainment [of the first anniversary] at all; thus, that which is performed at the start of the second year is called the *ābdika* (annual rite), whereas that performed at the start of the third year is called the *pratyābdika* (subsequent annual rite).
For this very reason, it has been said:
In the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, the sequence is stated as follows: "The *ābdika* [śrāddha] is performed at the beginning of the second year, and the *pratyābdika* at the beginning of the third year.
However, in the *Nirṇayāmṛta*:
One should feed a Brāhmaṇa at the beginning, or otherwise, one should offer oblations into the fire;
then one should feed the Brāhmaṇa again, for there should be a double repetition.
Thus, the first annual śrāddha (ādyābdika) is prescribed to be performed on the eleventh day; furthermore,
if an intercalary month occurs, an additional monthly śrāddha must be performed.
Then there are seventeen [verses], according to the statement of Laugākṣi: "The first [set] should be performed in the eleventh [month]; if [the month] is additional, there should be an addition."
One should give a water-pot for a year, or even well-stored food;
even when the year has increased [in length], one should offer the monthly oblation every month.
And because of the traditional teaching of the Kauthumas:
"Indeed, when there is an excess of a year, there are thirteen months;
therefore, one should not perform the Śrāddha in the thirteenth [month], for it does not stand [as a valid time]."

Thus, because the prohibition of the *māsika* [monthly śrāddha] for one who has been dead for thirteen months is heard in the words of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, some maintain that there is an option regarding the *māsika* even in the case of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*).

However, in reality, since it has been established that this refers to optional (*kāmya*) śrāddhas specifically prescribed for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), an increase in the number of *māsika* rites is indeed appropriate.

As for the enumeration of the sixteen śrāddhas in a different manner in works such as the *Hemādri*, and the description of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites as being included within those sixteen śrāddhas—[this is not the primary view].
For instance, it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"For men who have abandoned their bodies, the sixteen *śrāddha* rites must always be performed."
And likewise in the fourth and fifth, as well as in the ninth and eleventh.

Then, for twelve months, the ancestral rites (śrāddha) should be performed by the faithful according to the number twelve; according to the sacred tradition, one should satisfy the Brahmins there with those offerings.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa as well: "The Śrāddha for the collection of bones, the tri-pakṣa [rite], the monthly rites,
and likewise on the two empty lunar days (riktā)— these are the sixteen Śrāddhas for the deceased."
Thus;
"and on the two empty lunar days" means on the sixth and twelfth months, each being deficient by one day.
Jātūkarṇya says:
The twelve monthly rites, the first six-month rite,
and likewise the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa— these constitute the sixteen śrāddhas.

The first [memorial rite] is that of the eleventh day; the two half-yearly rites are the "less-than-half-yearly" (ūna-ṣāṇmāsika) and the other is the "less-than-yearly" (ūnābdika). One belongs to the first six-month period, while the other belongs to the subsequent six-month period.
In this regard, the assertion that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is included within the sixteen *śrāddhas* appears inconsistent, as it contradicts the statements of many *smṛtis*.
For instance, there is the statement of Laugākṣi: "Having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
Likewise,
according to the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "One should perform the sixteen śrāddhas prior to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa."

Furthermore, because of the statement of Gobhila, "One should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite without having first performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*," the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites are distinct from the sixteen *śrāddhas*. Therefore,

it should be understood that in the scriptural texts (*smṛti-vākyas*), the mention of their inclusion [within the sixteen] is intended to show that they serve the purpose of terminating the state of being a *preta*.

By this, the previously mentioned conformity with the number of monthly rites and the practice of the learned (śiṣṭa) are upheld. However, for those who follow a different calculation, the arrangement should be understood as depending on the difference between Vedic branches (śākhā) or geographical regions (deśa).
Furthermore, even for Kṣatriyas and others, this first Śrāddha must be performed on the eleventh day itself, even if impurity (āśauca) still persists.
Paiṭhīnasi said:
"The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all;
however, the period of impurity (sūtaka) for the four castes is distinct for each."
Thus says Śaṅkha as well:
"One who is impure may perform the first śrāddha on the eleventh day."
The agent's purity is only momentary; he remains impure once again.
Thus,
even regarding immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) and other such cases, the first *śrāddha* must be performed on the eleventh day itself by all classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
And so it is said:
That very same [day]: "Even when immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) applies, the offering must be given on the eleventh day for the deceased;
that same day is prescribed for his śrāddha, the funeral bed, the seat, and so forth."
Thus,
the term "immediate purity" (*sadyaḥśauca*) is an elliptical expression for both one-day and three-day periods of impurity.

If the cremation of a person who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) takes place on a day other than the day of death, one should perform the *navaśrāddha*, the eleventh-day rite (*ekādaśāhika*), and the rite at the end of the third fortnight (*traipakṣika*), beginning from the day of cremation.
However, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), whether he maintains a single fire or is without any fire, [the calculation] begins from the day of death;
but for both types [of those who have maintained the fires], it is from the day after that [death].
Thus he says:
Kātyāyana says:
For one who maintains the sacred fires, the Śrāddha should be performed on the eleventh day after the cremation;
however, one should always perform the obligatory (dhruva) rites on the anniversary of the day of death.
Thus:
"Fixed" (*dhruvāṇi*) is the designation for those [offerings] subsequent to the three-month period.
Any śrāddha offered after the three months shall take place on the very day of death.
However, one should cause the cremation of a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires to take place below [the village].
And because of the statement of Jātūkarṇya:
"For one who possesses fire"— meaning one who maintains many fires—
it should be performed immediately upon death for one whose connection with the fires has ceased.
Impurity shall last until after the cremation for one whose ritual was performed according to the Vaitānika rules.
Thus, because this is consistent with the statement of Śaṅkha, Marīci states the primary and secondary alternatives for the monthly rites:
"The primary śrāddha is performed month after month; in the event of incapacity, it is performed every season."
Or one may perform them over twelve days, or even all twelve on a single day.
Thus:
the *māsika* śrāddha is the primary rule, performed on the anniversary of death every month.
In the event of inability—that is, when one is incapable of performing the śrāddha every month—it is performed every season (*ṛtu*).
Since neither the lunar nor the solar *ṛtu* (season) is possible here, the meaning of that [text] is that the subsequent *śrāddha* for two months must be performed in the following month.
This is the sense:

having bypassed the anniversary date (*mṛtitithi*) in the previous month, both the overdue *śrāddha* and the timely *śrāddha* for the anniversary date in the subsequent month are to be performed there.
In some cases, all three [offerings] are performed together; for example, on the eleventh day, having first completed the initial offering and performed the *ūnamāsika* at its proper time,
one then performs the second monthly offering and the *traipakṣika* (three-fortnightly) offering together with the third monthly offering.
The fourth [month] together with the fourth,
the sixth together with the fifth,
and the deficient sixth-month [period] together with the seventh.

The eighth [year] is combined with the ninth, the tenth with the eleventh, and the twelfth with the *ūnābdika* (intercalary year); this was previously stated as well: "But the sixth plus nine is mixed."
The second alternative is that this very same meaning applies to that [text] as well.
Alternatively, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the phrase "by twelve days" (*dvādaśāhena*) signifies completion (*apavarga*) over twelve days;
thus, the rites pertaining to the twelve-month period should be performed until those days have been completed.
In that regard, on the day following the period of impurity—the eleventh day—the first [offering] is performed;
then, on the day following that, the second, which is the "unādi" offering;
and then, on the day following that, the third, which is the "traipākṣika" offering.
Then, during the three days following that, the fourth, fifth, and sixth [rites] were performed in succession;
then on the next day, the seventh and the half-yearly (*ūnaṣāṇmāsika*) rite;
and then on the subsequent days, the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh.

Then, on the following day, having performed the twelve monthly *śrāddhas*—including the *māsika* for the twelfth month—over the course of twelve days, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed on the day thereafter. However, in the *Śrāddhacintāmaṇi*, it is stated that beginning from the twelfth day, one performs the twelve monthly *śrāddhas* over twelve days, and then the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed on the subsequent day; this is the third alternative.

Alternatively, the fourth option is that one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the very same day— on the eleventh day or the twelfth day— after having performed all twelve monthly rites (*māsika*) on that single day;
"twelve" here means the twelve [monthly rites] and also the sixteen [rites including the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*].
Kaṇva:
Whatever *navaśrāddha* or monthly (*māsika*) rites may have been omitted, it is taught that each of those should be performed according to the subsequent regular schedule.
Thus [spoke] Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has arrived, if an obstacle should arise..."
In another month, on that same lunar day, one should perform whatever rite was previously interrupted.
"In the *Kālādarśa*, it is stated that one should perform the monthly rite for the deceased whose anniversary has been missed during the month following that one;
here, by the use of the word 'ca' (and), there is an inclusion of that specific monthly rite.
In the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, it is stated that one should perform the missed monthly rite for that [specific] month."

However, if there is an interruption of the monthly rites due to impurity (āśauca) and so forth, then—following the secondary rule (anukalpa)—the rite should be performed at the end of the period of impurity, on the anniversary of the date of death in the following month, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, or even on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight.
And it is said in the *Kālanirṇaya*:
"But when the procedure for the monthly rite is defiled by impurity, the time limit for that impurity expires [and the rite is postponed]."
"Or the day after [the death], the new moon day, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, or even the white [fortnight]— these are declared here as secondary alternatives (anukalpa)," and so forth.

These sixteen *śrāddhas*, which are to be performed before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony at the end of twelve days and so on within the first year, must be brought forward and performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
"Having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana*," according to the statement of Laugākṣi; therefore,
one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

And because of this statement of Paiṭhīnasi: even those rites performed by anticipation before the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa must be performed again after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa at their respective proper times. Thus he says:
Aṅgiras:
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (*udakuṃbha*) must also be given for that year.
Thus it is said; and Gālava also states:
"For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before a year [has passed]..."
Gautama states that one should perform a double repetition of the sixteen [verses].
Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini states the specific rule: "In whatever year prior to the first anniversary the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed..."
Beyond that, there shall be the performance of the monthly rites according to their respective times.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning of this is as follows:

among the sixteen [śrāddhas], those two or three which were performed at their respective times—once the *sapiṇḍana* has arrived—one should perform again only those remaining ones that were previously postponed and performed [out of order], and not others.
The meaning is that other [rites] were performed at their respective proper times.

However, regarding rites such as marriage that have arrived, even if they were performed by being drawn forward (apākṛṣya) before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, Kātyāyana states that they must not be performed again after the attainment of intelligence (*buddhi*).
Having completed the ritual for increasing vitality, one should not perform the monthly rites;
otherwise, death would occur before its time and would not be averted.
Thus,
if one does not perform the monthly rites immediately after the annual *vṛddhi* ceremony, then the death would not be "unworn" (fresh);
otherwise, it would become a fresh death— this is the meaning.
A twice-born performer of the rite may perform the remaining *preta-śrāddhas* as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, even by postponing them, and then perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha.
Thus says Śāṭhyāyani:
"But when an occasion for prosperity (vṛddhi) or the like occurs after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, even the monthly (anumāsika) offerings must be brought forward;
this applies even to those already performed by being brought forward prior to the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa."
Furthermore, they are withdrawn because of the prohibition of further increase.
Thus it is stated by Kārṣṇājini.
Therefore, the postponement [of the Śrāddha] both before and after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa is established.
Now, one might object:
The funeral rites for the deceased and the sixteen *śrāddha* offerings must be performed at their proper times; otherwise, one is not liberated from that [debt].
If it is argued that, according to the statement of Hārīta, the postponement [of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*] is not established, that is true;

however, there is no postponement when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed at the end of the year. But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before the year, by what could the postponement be prevented? Therefore, having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed even prior to the completion of the year.
This is the procedure for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*). When one performs the *preta-śrāddhas* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform them according to the rules for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

However, when one performs them after that, then, just as one performs the annual (*ābdika*) *śrāddha*—whether it be by the *pārvaṇa* or *ekoddiṣṭa* method—one should likewise perform the monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddhas*.
One who performs the sixteen śrāddhas prior to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should perform all of them according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa.
After the sapindikarana rite,
whenever one performs [the annual rites], one should perform those [rites] for each year in the same manner as one would perform them annually.
Thus says Vijñāneśvara based on the traditional legal texts (*smṛti*).
Likewise, for the duration of one year, every day a water-pot containing enough food for a meal should be offered, dedicated to the deceased.
As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
And a water-pot, accompanied by various kinds of food and edibles, should be given for as long as a year, O best of men,
preceded by sesame seeds and water.
Thus,
in the *Smṛtisamuccaya* of Hemādri:
"From the eleventh day onwards, a water-pot filled with water and food [should be offered]."
It should be given day by day by the sons for as long as a year lasts.
Thus, Pāraskara has stated that even the offering of the *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) here is optional: "Day by day, one should give food to this Brāhmaṇa and a water-pot; some also offer a *piṇḍa*.
The meaning is: "to this deceased person," that is, with reference to him.
Yājñavalkya states that [the offering] should be given even when the piṇḍīkaraṇa rite is performed before the [prescribed time]: (Ācārādhyāya, Śrāddhaprakaraṇa, verse 255).
For one whose *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs before the completion of a year,
a twice-born man should likewise offer this [water] along with a water-pot for the duration of that year.
Thus,
as in the case of the monthly rites (*māsika*) following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is no mention here of the word "preta" (departed spirit).
From this very statement, it is understood that there is no reduction of the water-pot offering (*udakumbha*).

As for the statement from the Skanda Purāṇa cited in the Gobhila-Śrāddhakalpa-bhāṣya: "Having determined the number according to one's own capacity, food should be given to the Brāhmaṇas for the annual śrāddha, or whatever may serve as its substitute."
O dear one, even if men have performed hundreds of ancestral rites (śrāddhas), if they fail to give a water-pot, they remain poor and miserable,
wandering in the ocean of worldly existence.
"Therefore, even for a *preta*, a water-pot (*udakumbha*) should be offered after [the annual rite] has been deferred"—

this statement regarding the deferral of the water-pot does not intend to permit such deferral because it contradicts the words of Yājñavalkya; rather, it refers to cases where one is unable to provide the daily offering of a water-pot and food.
The meaning is that as many [gifts] as possible should be given on even a single day, or at some time during the course of a year; for such is the observed practice.
In this regard, although in some cases the water-jar is accompanied by food, and in other cases the food is accompanied by the water-jar, [the rule remains the same].
Nevertheless, without intending to emphasize the subordinate or primary status of the elements, one should perform the renunciation separately, as in "this food" and "this vessel.

In this regard, the definition of *śrāddha* stated by Vijñāneśvara is that it is the renunciation of food or a substance serving as its substitute with faith for the sake of the deceased; and that stated by the Kalpataru is that *śrāddha* is the renunciation of a substance directed toward the ancestors, culminating in the acceptance by a Brāhmaṇa.
The definition of *śrāddha* stated by Śūlapāṇi is that it is the offering of oblations (*havis*) while designating the ancestors and others by means of words ending in the dative case;
even so, because the offering of food and water-pots is also covered by this definition of *śrāddha*, it is indeed of the nature of *śrāddha*.
As for the fact that Śūlapāṇi has declared this to be a *nitya-śrāddha* (obligatory daily *śrāddha*)—
"That which is performed day after day is called nitya (obligatory)," because the definition of *nitya-śrāddha* stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* applies here as well— this is not correct.

For it is by stating that "that which is enjoined day after day is called nitya" that what is understood to be enjoined for the duration of one's life, without specifying a particular limit of days, is *nitya*.

In the case of the injunction, "One should perform the Śrāddha every day," there arises the perception of its obligatory nature because it is enjoined by such a mandate; however, this is not the case here [in the present context].
Otherwise, even if it were performed on only a few days—

"Even during the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, one should perform the Śrāddha day after day"— because of this [statement], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the Śrāddha performed in the latter fortnight (āparapakṣika) becomes a mandatory (nitya) Śrāddha.
Therefore, the *ūnamāsika*, *ūnaṣāṇmāsika*, and *ūnābdika* Śrāddhas should not be performed on the Nandā and other such lunar days.
Gārgya says: On the Nandā tithi, on a Friday, on the fourteenth day, or at Tripuṣkara,
a householder should not perform the *ūna-śrāddha*, for fear of the loss of sons and wealth.
Marīci also says: "In Dvipuṣkara, on the Nandās, on the day of Sinīvālī, on the day of Bhṛgu (Friday),
on the fourteenth lunar day, and in Kṛttikā during Tripuṣkara— these are not deficient [in merit]."
Thus:
*tripuṣkara* occurs when there is a conjunction of the three *puṣkara* asterisms, the three *pāna* asterisms, the *bhadrā* lunar day, and any one of the days of Jupiter, Mars, or the Sun.
When there is a conjunction of two [of these], it is *dvipuṣkara*.
In the *Ratnamālā*: "If an odd-numbered lunar mansion coincides with an auspicious lunar day (bhadrātithi) on any day whatsoever during the week of Jupiter, the Sun, or Mars..."
This very thing, known as the "Triple Puṣkara," has been proclaimed by the sages.
Thus:

if the lunar day is auspicious (Bhadrā) and possesses three quarters while being conjoined with Mars, Jupiter, and the Sun, then it is the Tripuṣkara yoga; if it is conjoined with two of them, it is the Dvipuṣkara yoga.
Thus:

when there is a conjunction of the second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days (tithis) known as *bhadra*; the Punarvasu, Uttarā-phālgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, and Pūrvā-bhādrapadā nakṣatras; and the planets the Sun, Mars, and Saturn—this is called *tripuṣkara*. When there is a conjunction of two such sets, it is called *dvipuṣkara*.
The Nandā days are the first, sixth, and eleventh [lunar days].
The rest is well known.
Thus is the determination of the times for the monthly rites.
Now, regarding the times prescribed and prohibited for funeral rites, Gārgya says:
"In the case of the direct consecration of a corpse, one should not purify the day at all."
If the rite of re-consecration (punaḥsaṃskāra) is performed during a period of impurity (āśauca), [the following applies].
The day for purification in that case should indeed be according to what is possible;
however, once the period of impurity has ceased, the deceased is then consecrated again.
If more than a year has passed, one should perform the rites for the deceased after purifying the day; among those times, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is the most excellent.
One should also avoid the dark fortnight and, therein, the day of loss (dinakṣaya).
Regarding the śrāddha for the deceased, Gārgya says:
"On a Nandā [tithi], on a Saturday, on the fourteenth [lunar day], and on a Tripuṣkara [day]."
In that case, a householder should not perform a śrāddha, because of the depletion of his sons and wealth.
Marīci said:
On the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), on Nandā, on Sinīvālī, on a Saturday,
on the fourteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, and under the asterism Kṛttikā— these constitute the Tripuṣkara.
"One should not perform the *śrāddha*," this is the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*). Regarding the very rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*), it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
One should not perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion in which a man was born;
nor, O Bhārata, should it be done under the two Bhādrapadas, nor under the Āgneya (Kṛttikā).
One should avoid all cruel [signs], as well as those that are adverse;
one should diligently avoid whatever has been declared in the science of astrology.
The ellipsis is "are said to be avoided.
As for the "terrible" ones:
the terrible [nakṣatra] is Aśleṣā (coraga), Raudra is Ārdrā, and Aindra is Svātī, as well as Nairṛta [Kṛttikā].
Thus they have been described.
Gratyari is Pañcamatārā. Jyotiḥ is Parāśara.

The performance of funeral rites for humans is not recommended during the Sādhāraṇa, Dhruva, or Ugra yogas, nor under the asterism Maitra (Anurādhā), nor in any way during Tripuṣkara or the mansion of Yama (Bharaṇī).
The common [nakṣatras] are Kṛttikā and Viśākhā.
The fixed [nakṣatras] are the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī.
The fierce [nakṣatras] are the three Pūrvas, Bharaṇī, and Maghā.
Maitra is Anurādhā;
Yamaladhiṣṇya is Dhaniṣṭhā;
[and] Kaśyapa—
Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Aśleṣā, and the first three quarters of Mūla are extremely unfavorable for rites concerning the deceased, as is the pentad beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: One should avoid performing rites for the deceased when the Moon is in the fourth, eighth, or twelfth house, as well as during Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, and Parigha yogas.
Likewise, on the day of Saturn during the *viṣṭi* yoga,
specifically on the thirteenth lunar day, and also during the three birth asterisms (*janmatārā*).
The three birth-stars are the first, the tenth, and the twenty-first [lunar days].
On a Nandā tithi, on a Friday, and on the thirteenth lunar day— on these three "births"—
one should not perform a Śrāddha ceremony, due to the destruction of sons, wife, and wealth.
And prohibitions such as these do not apply to anything other than rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*).
Even among the *śrāddhas* for the deceased, they do not apply to those performed at optional times;
however, they do apply to those performed at their own prescribed time when no other occasion is available.
Regarding this, Gobhila says: "On the Nandā tithis, on Fridays, on the fourteenth lunar day, and during the three births [of the moon],
the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is forbidden starting from the eleventh day."
Vaijavāpa says:

If, by chance, funeral rites for a deceased person fall on a day of solar transit (saṅkrānti), the beginning of a Yuga or a Manvantara, or on a New Moon (darśa), one need not examine the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and other such factors.
Thus end the prescribed and prohibited times for the rites for the deceased. Now follows the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
In that regard, if both the sacrificer and the deceased have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the end of one year is the primary [time].
Or it refers to the period preceding the manifestation of growth;
and thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
O bull of the Bharatas, a sacrificer who maintains no sacred fire should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a deceased person who was not an *āhitāgni* once the full year has elapsed.
Likewise, Pulastya also says:

"One who maintains no sacred fires (niragni) shall, according to dharma, perform the offering of the funeral cakes (sahapiṇḍatva) for his father and mother when the full year has elapsed, or on whatever day an auspicious rite (vṛddhi) occurs."

For here, time is restricted on the basis of the performer’s lack of sacred fires (niragnitva) as the intended object; this is because that [time] alone is enjoined as an auxiliary to the ritual action. As for the statement of those learned in the Nyāya that "the action is enjoined in relation to time, not time in relation to the action," that is intended to mean that [time] is not something to be adopted (anupādeya), and not that it is not an injunction (avidheya).
For if that were the case, time itself would not be an auxiliary (aṅga), because it is not being enjoined;
indeed, that which is not enjoined cannot be an auxiliary.
Here, the word "pūrṇe" means on the day following the completion of the year.
And thus Uśanas says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father is performed on the anniversary of his death during the annual rite;
however, upon the occurrence of events such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), this may take place even before the year has elapsed."
Also in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father is established as taking place after one year;
however, if there is to be a future *vṛddhi* (prosperity) rite, one should perform it even before that."

As for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi— that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs at the end of the year— even there, the word "end" (*ante*) refers specifically to the seventh month, and not to the end of ten months, because such a usage would lack denotative power (like the expression "the cloth at the end of the ten") and would contradict the previously cited scriptural statements.

Furthermore, regarding the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, which states that the *ūnābdika* (the annual rite for the deficient year) occurs on the penultimate day of the twelfth month, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the following day, and the first annual rite (*prathamābdika*) on the day after that, which is the actual anniversary of death— this is also incorrect.
This [view] is to be disregarded because it contradicts the statement: “on the anniversary of death during the rainy season.

Such being the case, having performed the *sapiṇḍana* at midday with the *ekoddiṣṭa* as the primary rite, or having performed the *sapiṇḍana* in the afternoon with the *pārvaṇa* as the primary rite, one should perform the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) śrāddha in the afternoon itself when possible, or during the late afternoon (*sāyāhna*), which constitutes a secondary period (*gauṇakāla*).
The rite must be performed, but there is no omission of it.

However, some say that on the anniversary of death, when the *sapiṇḍana* is performed, there is indeed an omission of the annual (*ābdika*) rite because its primary time has passed; furthermore, since the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha* is not completed without the consumption of the remaining food, it is improper to commence another *śrāddha*.
That is not so;

for it is not the case that performance during the secondary time (gauṇakāla) is prohibited, but rather that for one who is not entitled [to perform] at the primary time (mukhyakāla), [performance is prohibited] even at the secondary time.
And in the present context, there is nothing whatsoever that establishes a lack of entitlement at the primary time.
As for the claim that because the ritual action cannot be completed without consuming the remainder, one must not begin another ritual action— that is not so;
for the preliminary application (prayoga) is fully concluded by the dismissal (visarjana) itself.

And after that, when food has been obtained through desire, for one who expects the performance [of the rite], there is a restriction regarding the remainder; however, eating the remainder is not an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*.

Or rather, it is like the celibacy (*brahmacarya*) observed during the night; it is an integral part that lies outside the actual performance (*prayoga*), and because it must necessarily be performed as part of the annual rite (*pratyābdika*), it is so designated.

There is nothing inconsistent in the fact that what is prescribed [for the annual śrāddha] can be performed on a single day together with the remaining meal of the annual śrāddha (sābdika-śrāddha) by means of a single ritual procedure (tantra), just like the simultaneous performance of the remaining meals of several annual rites occurring by the force of fate.
"Vṛddhi" means prosperity or an auspicious occasion.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the auspicious ceremony.
Thus it is stated by Laghu-Hārīta.
Gobbila also says, "on whatever day an increase occurs," or "on whatever day there may be an increase.
Here, the term *vṛddhy-ahaḥ* (the day of increase) refers to a day distinct from the one immediately preceding.
Otherwise, there would be the contingency of performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that very same day,
and that is contradictory;
for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs at midday, whereas the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* occurs in the morning.
And it is clearly stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"The *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for the father is established as taking place after one year has elapsed."
If an increase is expected to come, one should have it performed even before that time.
And this is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for any ritual action whatsoever that serves as a cause for a *nāndī* [rite].
Thus says Śāṭhyāyani:
A twice-born performer of the rite may perform all the *śrāddhas* for deceased ancestors, as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, even by postponement; however, he must not postpone the *nāndīmukha*.
Thus,

some maintain that this reduction [of the number of ancestors] is to be understood as being due to the impossibility of performing the *nāndī-śrāddha*— since, without the *sapiṇḍana*, the status of being a paternal ancestor (*pitṛ*) worthy of the *pārvaṇa* rite has not been attained for the father and others— and not as something explicitly stated in the scriptures.
Others, however, argue that there is no need for a reason regarding a matter not yet perceived.
For in the case of a reduction [of the number of offerings], it is not the possibility of a deity that serves as the motive, but rather the injunction itself.
In the absence of a deity, however, it is more logical that the ritual action simply be omitted, just as it is for one whose father is still living.
If the postponement were due solely to the requirements of the deities, it would follow that postponement could also occur for the sake of performing *tīrtha-śrāddha* and other such rites;
therefore, the postponement occurs only by virtue of the specific scriptural injunction.

Furthermore, in the case of those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), even when a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) is present, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the maternal grandfather might—due to the requirement of the *pārvaṇa* rite—have to be performed for the maternal uncle who lacks the sacred fires, or else the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the maternal uncle might have to be performed at a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) due to the presence of the daughter’s son.
Furthermore, this is because it would result in the redundancy of the separate statement, "neither the *pārvaṇa* nor the *abhyudaya* [rites].
Moreover, the *abhyudaya* rite is mandatory (*nitya*) and not merely optional (*kāmya*),
since it can be performed separately even when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is not deferred.
Laghuhārīta states the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed by one without a sacred fire (*niragni*) for a deceased person who had a sacred fire (*sāgni*):
"O Hero, when [the performer] is without a sacred fire..."
At that time, the householder should perform it; if the deceased possessed the sacred fires, his *sapiṇḍana* should indeed take place at the end of three fortnights.
The householder is the performer.
Sumantu also says:
"If the deceased was one who maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), but the performer is without such fires..."
The sapindikarana rite should be performed then, on the third fortnight.

And here, in the statement "The *sapiṇḍana* [rite] indeed [occurs] in the third fortnight," the locative sense of the third fortnight is expressed by the hearing of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*).
Nor can it be argued that although the locative is used, it is a locative absolute (*satisaptamī*).
And thus, it should be stated that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs on a lunar day (*tithi*) of the same type as the deceased’s anniversary, just like the monthly and annual *śrāddha* rites; for,

according to the maxim “the case-ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than the case-ending used as a qualifier (*upapada-vibhakti*),” the locative of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) is stronger than the locative of time, and by the force of the suffix expressing completion (*pūraṇa-artha-pratyaya*), the second interpretation alone is obtained.
Nor should it be argued that in the statement of Gobhila, “In a full year, six months, three fortnights,

or on the day when prosperity occurs,” the word “full” (pūrṇe) must be supplied to both the six-month and three-fortnight periods just as it is to the year, and therefore only the day following those periods is intended to be taken.

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence, in the case of the statement, "Having performed the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices for a month, they proceed with the Upasad rites," the phrase "the month is full" does not apply here as it does there [to the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa], because it cannot be attached to either six months or three fortnights.
Therefore, the completed third [fortnight] serves as the locus [for the rite].

Although Hemādri states that "the month is full" in all three views, he asserts—based on the natural sense of the locative case—that the locus is specifically the day of the completion of the third fortnight, and not the day following it.
Regarding the performer being possessed of the sacred fires,
Sumantu says:
"O King, the sacrificer is one who possesses the fires."
The deceased shall remain a *preta* without fire;
on the twelfth day, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed by the sons.
Kātyāyana states:
Having performed the rites for the eleventh day,
a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for his mother and father before the new moon, according to the prescribed rule.
Thus, although it is stated here that "before the new moon," the rite must be performed precisely at the time prescribed by Baudhāyana and others— namely, "on the eleventh or twelfth day"— because,
since it is possible to do so without subverting that [prescribed time], subversion is improper, and because it would otherwise entail the undesirable consequence of postulating an independent time.
Hemādri, however, states that this is an independent alternative time period,
as it is said:
"But that new moon which occurs on the tenth day from the anniversary of death..."
On that [anniversary], the son who maintains the sacred fires should indeed perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
Thus, the statement of Jābāli refers to the tenth day counting from the day of death;
in this way, the eleventh day is indicated.
And when [the new moon] occurs...

If it occurs after twenty-two days have passed, then after the period of impurity has ended, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas* during the twelve days that follow, and on the thirteenth day, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed. Regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, [it is said]: "Just as with the monthly rites, having performed the *śrāddha* for twelve days, one should perform it on the thirteenth day."
Thus it is stated by Viṣṇu.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the purpose (*artha*) or objective of the monthly rites (*māsika*) is the cessation of the state of being a *preta*; the *śrāddha* is that which effects this.
The singular number is used here to express a collective sense (*gaṇābhiprāya*).
Among these, the monthly, three-fortnightly, and six-monthly rites should be performed on the first, second, sixth, twelfth, and so forth days, because the day stands in the place of the month.
For this very reason, it is stated further on: "If an intercalary month should occur within the year, then one day [is added] for the purpose of the monthly rite."

"He should increase [the period]"—thus it was stated by that very [author], as well as "twelve days" or "thirteen days," beginning precisely from the day following the impurity (*āśauca*), because of the statement of Jāvāla: "beyond the ten nights.
Here, the mention of "ten nights" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the respective periods of impurity.

Therefore, even for one who has traveled abroad with his sacred fires or whose fires have been extinguished, an advancement [of the śrāddha] must be performed in accordance with the requirements of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*.
And so it is said in the *Hemādri*, by Prajāpati:

A son who has not yet performed the *sapiṇḍana* rite and does not maintain the sacred fire should not perform the *pitṛyajña*; by performing neither the *pārvaṇa* nor the *abhyudaya* rites, he does not obtain their fruit.
This is because the *pārvaṇa* has been described as being concomitant with the *abhyudaya* (prosperity) that must necessarily be performed;
and because, by the inclusion of the term "prior to the *darśa*" (*arvāk darśāt*), the *pārvaṇa* is understood here just like the *pitṛyajña* connected with the *darśa*.
Furthermore, even according to the view in which the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is caused by the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, this rite must be performed for the mother just as it is for the father.
She has attained oneness with her husband in respect of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the lineage (*gotra*), and the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
therefore, the wife shares the lineage of her husband's ancestors.
It is the settled conclusion in the sacred laws that after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, all those who receive what is offered to the ancestors become sharers of the entire inheritance.
Thus, according to the statements of Yajñapārśva and Baudhāyana, she shares in a portion of the ancestral *piṇḍa*;
nor should it be argued that this would result in her becoming the intended recipient (*uddeśya*) of the offering,
for she attains a state of single form once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed.
By this statement, even though she is not specifically designated as being accompanied by her co-wife, it is stated that she partakes in a portion of the husband's *piṇḍa*;

otherwise, if she were to perform the *sapiṇḍana* with her maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), she would not be an enjoyer of the *piṇḍa* of the maternal grandfather. For there is no authoritative evidence for the designation of maternal grandfathers as being "accompanied by their daughters."

Therefore, after the period of impurity has passed, the performer who maintains the sacred fires (agnihotrī) should perform the monthly śrāddhas on the twelfth days; then, on the thirteenth day from the date of death—or on the twelfth or even the eleventh day if the new moon (darśa) falls on those dates—he should perform the sapindikarana on that very occasion. And if, through negligence, it is not performed then, it should be performed at the times prescribed for the three-fortnightly periods and so forth.
And likewise, Gobhila says:
"That which was not performed out of negligence during the periods of twelve days and so forth,"
One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite during the subsequent periods.
And this [procedure] applies only to one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*),

because for such a person, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and others are the primary rites, while the subsequent ones are prescribed as secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*); it does not apply to one who is without the sacred fires (*niragnika*),
because for him, the end-of-year sacrifice (*varṣānta*) alone is the primary rite.
And there is no time prescribed subsequent to that.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"On the twelfth day, or the sixth, or after three fortnights, or after three months..."
Or even in the eleventh month, when an auspicious occasion has arrived.
In this context, the word "month" (*māsa*) is connected with the phrase "or in the sixth.

Thus says Baudhāyana: "Now, when a year has elapsed, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed—either in the third fortnight, in the third month, in the sixth, or in the eleventh; or else on the twelfth day."

In this case as well, since the status of being the locus [of the rite] is established by the reasoning previously stated, the explanation offered by some that it occurs "in the past sixth month" must have its source sought elsewhere.
Paiṭhīnasi states another time:
At the end of the year, there is a dismissal; some say this refers to the ninth month.
Viṣṇu also states: "Just as with the monthly rites, having performed the Śrāddha for twelve days, one should perform it on the thirteenth day."
Vyāghra states the excellence of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) by way of general principle:
"Because of the infinity of family duties, because of the decay of men's lifespan,
and because of the instability of the body, the twelve-day rite is praised."
"Family duties" (*kuladharmāṇām*) refers to family customs performed at fixed times, such as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and the performance of rites like the tonsure (*cūḍā*).
"Instability" (*asthiti*) consists in the possibility of abandoning one's country due to royal oppression and the like, or the incapacity to perform the rite due to illness and so forth.
"Excellence" (*prāśastya*) means that even if performed at that [specific] time rather than the primary time, the cessation of the state of being a *preta* occurs through this very act.

Regarding the term *dvādaśāha*: based on the etymology "the twelfth day" (*dvādaśam ahaḥ*), it refers to the twelfth day, and that is indeed calculated starting from the day of death. Śūlapāṇi maintains that the *dvādaśāha*—meaning the aggregate of twelve days—is the time for the postponement of the sixteen *śrāddhas*, and that this [twelfth day] is of the nature of an *abhyudaya* (an auspicious occasion).

Now, one might ask: how can this be considered praiseworthy? For the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is intended for the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor), and performing it merely on the twelfth day does not by itself effect that attainment of *pitṛtva*.
For it is said in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"When the sapindikarana has been performed, after the lapse of one year, a man [attains the status of a Pitṛ]."
Having abandoned the body of a preta, one attains a body for enjoyment.
Thus it is said;
and also in the Agni Purāṇa: "If for anyone the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should take place before a year has passed..."
O King, it should be known that even for him, the state of being a preta lasts for one year.

Thus, if it is asked: "Since the state of being a *preta* (ghost) ceases only at the end of the year even if the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed previously, how can this [performance] be considered commendable?"—the answer is that these two statements have the following purpose: unless the sixteen *śrāddhas* have been performed, one does not attain the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor) even if the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed.

Because of the syntactic unity with the statement, "One should not perform the tonsure ceremony without having offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*," it is also implied by this very text that the sixteen *śrāddhas* may be deferred.

Otherwise, if there were no postponement of the sixteen *śrāddhas*, and consequently no cessation of the state of being a *preta* (ghost) evidenced by them, how could even the performed *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha* be purposeful?

[Objection: But surely, once the *sapiṇḍana* has been performed after postponing the sixteen *śrāddhas*, since the cessation of the state of being a *preta* has already occurred, the monthly *māsika* and *udakumbha-śrāddhas* should not take place again.
[Reply: True.
If—
for someone whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* takes place before the end of a year—
the monthly rites and the water-pot offering (*udakumbha*) must also be performed by him for the duration of that year.
Otherwise, the statement of Laugākṣi would be contradicted;
therefore, by that very statement, there is a return [to the status of a living relative].

However, some maintain that even when the *sapiṇḍana* rite is performed prematurely without the occasion for an increase in lineage (*vṛddhi*), the cessation of the state of being a *preta* occurs precisely at the end of the year.
However, when the *sapiṇḍana* rite is postponed for the sake of a prosperity-rite (*vṛddhi*), the cessation of the state of being a *preta* occurs immediately thereafter, without any interval.
For this very reason, having stated the postponement of the *sapiṇḍana* by the rule "in the case of a prosperity-rite before a year has passed," Śātātapa says:
Therefore, from that point onward, the offering of separate funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is not prescribed here for any of the deceased who have been summoned by means of mantras.
Having crossed over from the state of being a preta here, they have reached the company of the ancestors.
Thus it is said:

"Alternatively, if by chance the performance of the *vāśavatyā* occurs at a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) and thereafter an occasion for a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* (an auspicious rite) should arise, then upon reaching that time for the *vṛddhi*, the liberation from the state of being a *preta* occurs; for that [secondary time] is equal to the time at the end of the year," so they say.
In this regard, the following occurs to the mind:
how is it that this [period] is equivalent to the end of a year?

If it is because the *sapiṇḍana*—which, like the twelve-day rite of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), is primary and has the fruit of terminating the state of being a *preta*—is prescribed here; then [the answer follows].
At that time, the status of being "prescribed" (vihitatva) exists for the secondary [time] as well.

Moreover, the primary time is not the motivator by its own nature; otherwise, even in the absence of the *sapiṇḍana* rite at the end of the year, the cessation of the state of being a *preta* would necessarily occur. Therefore, it must be stated that only the *sapiṇḍana* performed at the primary time is what brings about the cessation of the state of being a *preta*.

This being the case, since it is untenable for that which is prescribed to be purposeless, let it be granted that the performance [of the rite] at the prescribed time alone is what removes the state of being a *preta*; enough with insisting on its being the "primary" time.
Therefore, it is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* itself, accompanied by the sixteen *śrāddhas*, that removes the state of being a *preta*, not its performance at the primary time.

However, some maintain that for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), all times are primary; thus, the *sapiṇḍana* performed at the twelfth month and other such times removes the state of being a *preta*, just like when it is performed preceded by a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
And those are the times:
therein, first, according to the Caturviṃśatimata—
"The Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa [should be performed] when the year is complete, or even on an auspicious occasion (abhyudaya)."
According to the opinion of some, however, it should be performed on the twelfth day, or likewise on the eleventh.
Thus [it is said].

However, some maintain that this [text] summarizes the primary times common to all [rites], but does not establish the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*) and so forth for one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*);
otherwise, it would also establish the time at the end of the year for one who maintains the fires (*sāgni*).

And thus, they say that by such statements as "the new moon which occurs before," the [texts] merely enjoin those very times already established for various [persons], and do not have the basis of a previously unheard scripture (*apūrva-śruti*).
In the *Parāśara-mādhavīya*, the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* states:
"The sacrificer who is without sacred fires (*anagnimān*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
O bull among the Bharatas, for one who has died without having established the sacred fires, [the rite is performed] when a full year has passed.
On the twelfth day, or the sixth, or after three fortnights, or after three months,
or even on the eleventh day of the month, or upon the arrival of some auspicious occasion.
Thus;
and all these are primary [options].
Among them, the twelve-day rite is most excellent.
Because of statements such as "due to infinity" (*ānantya*),
Mādhava holds that there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on one's desire;
others, however, maintain that the end of the year is the primary [time], while the eleventh month proximate to it is secondary.
In this way, others are more remote, being inferior as previously described.
And when the sixteen śrāddhas are brought forward for the purpose of the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, they should be performed on a lunar day (tithi) of the same type as the day of death,
because even a single [day] provides the primary time.
But in the event of impossibility, [the rites] should be performed on the very day of the *sapiṇḍana* because of the proximity of the occasion;
or else, if there is an interval of time, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas* on the twelfth day, according to the previously cited statement of Viṣṇu.
For Śūdras, however, the *sapiṇḍana* rite occurs on the twelfth day itself.
And so says Viṣṇu: "For Śūdras, indeed, [the rite] is on the twelfth day, excluding the mantras."

Nor should it be argued that because Kātyāyana has prescribed, "For all castes, the *sapiṇḍana* occurs at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*)," and since for a Śūdra there is a month-long period of impurity, the tenth individual *piṇḍa* is ordained for him at the end of that *sūtaka*, how then can the *sapiṇḍana* of a Śūdra take place on the twelfth day? *Note:* The argument addresses a perceived contradiction between the general rule for all castes and the specific duration of impurity for a Śūdra. The response implies that the rule regarding the timing of *sapiṇḍana* is not absolute for Śūdras, as other authorities (such as Viṣṇu) prescribe it for them on the twelfth day regardless of the length of their *sūtaka*. Thus, the citation from Kātyāyana does not preclude the practice of performing the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day for a Śūdra.

There is no fault in performing [the rite] either by relying on the position that "for all castes, the period of impurity (sūtaka) lasts ten days," or by accepting the cessation of impurity through the force of the scriptural injunction— just as in the rule for the eleventh day— in accordance with the Darśa-śrāddha of a virtuous Śūdra, or even while still in the midst of the impurity, because of the direct statement of the text.

In reality, the term "twelfth day" (*dvādaśāha*) does not refer to the period starting from the day of death, but rather to the performance of the twelve monthly *śrāddhas* after the final day of the impurity period (*sūtaka*), following the custom of the twice-born; thus, the *sapiṇḍana* rite should be performed on the twelfth day itself, and not on the thirteenth day as is the case for the twice-born.
For this very reason, it is stated therein: "If there is an intercalary month (adhikamāsa), then [the śrāddha] is on the thirteenth day.
By this, the claim that any increase in śrāddha occasions is not an increase in the number of days is also refuted.
However, there is a specific distinction regarding a son who resides in another country.
Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"In the case of sons who have gone to another country, what should be done?
Upon hearing [of their death], shaving [the head] must be performed, and for ten days, water with sesame seeds [should be offered]."
Then, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the eleventh day;
[regarding] the lapse of time until the end of the year, another period is mentioned in the *Mādhavīya*, where Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
If the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha has not been performed at the prescribed time,
one should perform it under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Hasta, Rohiṇī, or Anurādhā.

And this should also be understood to apply when, due to the influence of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and other factors, an increase [of days] occurs such that even though another prescribed time is not available.
Thus ends the section on the time for the *sapiṇḍana* rite. Now follows the determination of the lunar day (*tithi*) for general *śrāddha* ceremonies.
The *śrāddha* is of three kinds: *pārvaṇa*, *ekoddiṣṭa*, and *daivika*. Regarding this, Kaṇva states:
"That *śrāddha* which is performed with reference to a single person is proclaimed as *ekoddiṣṭa*."
Indeed, that which is performed with reference to three ancestors is known as the pārvaṇa by the sages.
Pāraskara states: "That which is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika* (divine).
One should perform that with effort on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions, following the procedure for the daily *śrāddha*."

In that regard, if the lunar day (tithi) on which the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha is prescribed should span two days, then it should be performed on whichever day— either the preceding or the following— one the Pārvaṇa rite occupies the afternoon (aparāhṇa).
For whatever the time of a ritual action may be, the lunar day must occupy that specific time.
One should perform one's duties by means of that [knowledge]; neither decrease nor increase is a cause for concern.
Thus, from the words of Yājñavalkya:
"That lunar day which extends through midday shall be the one for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite;
that lunar day which extends through the afternoon shall be the one for the *pārvaṇa* rite."
And because of the statement of Gautama:
"When [the tithi] on the previous day extends into the afternoon, then that very [previous] one is to be accepted.
Thus says Manu:
The ancestors attend to that [time] at which the sun sets;
for the afternoon was assigned by the Self-born Creator himself to the ancestors.
The meaning is that the afternoon in which the sun sets is recommended for rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*).
Thus says Hārīta:
"The afternoon belongs to the ancestors; it is that which follows after the afternoon."
She should be accepted for the ancestral rites, but not one who follows after those previously deceased.

"Astānuyāyinī" means "following until sunset. Thus, the meaning is that for rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitṛkārya), that [tithi] which extends into the afternoon and follows until sunset is to be accepted.
However, when it does not extend into the afternoon on either of two days, then the earlier one alone is to be accepted.
And likewise, Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya states:
"For rites pertaining to the gods, the lunar day (tithi) on which the sun has risen should be known [as the one to be observed]."
For rites dedicated to the ancestors, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be known as the one for performance.
In the *Śivarahasya* and the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"Generally, those desiring divine rewards should fast on the concluding part of the lunar day;
for the root [of the rite] is said by the great sages to be the ancestral [part], for the sake of satisfying the ancestors."
In the Māradvīpa Purāṇa: "The wise know that the end of the lunar day (tithi), called the 'divine' (surākhya), is indeed to be observed as the fast;
whereas the beginning of the lunar day, called the 'ancestral' (pitrya), is declared by those learned in the scriptures and experts in time."
In rites for the ancestors (pitrya), a lunar day touched at the time of sunset is called "full";
in that case, the lunar day associated with sunrise is not to be accepted, for in rites for the gods (daiva), the lunar day is that which begins at sunrise.
Gobhila states: "That [lunar day] which extends into the evening (sāyāhna) is prescribed for the Pārvaṇa rite.
And this extension into the evening occurs only when [the lunar day] is not less than three muhūrtas in duration.
Vaudhāyana also says:
"When the sun has risen, that is the time for rites to the gods; when the sun has set, it is for rites to the ancestors.
That lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas during the day or three [muhūrtas] at night is the one prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors."
When the sun has risen, the two muhūrtas—that is, the period of two muhūrtas—is *daivata*, meaning suitable for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva-karma*).

When the sun has set, or when it has begun to set, the three muhūrtas prior to its setting are *pitrya*, meaning suitable for rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya-karma*). Therefore, the meaning is that the lunar day (*tithi*) existing during those periods is to be accepted for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).

When there is an unequal overlap with a portion of the afternoon on both days, the day possessing the greater duration of that overlap should be taken, according to the maxim: "Even a minute distinction determines the decision. When there is an equal overlap with a portion of the afternoon on both days—occurring due to the increase, decrease, or equality of the lunar day (tithi) that serves as the constituent part of the Śrāddha—and a doubt arises as to which day the Pārvaṇa rite should be performed:
Kharva, Darpa, and Hiṃsā—these are the three characteristics of the lunar days (tithis).
Of these, Sarva and Darpa are to be honored as the latter [part of the day], while Hiṃsā belongs to the preceding time.
Thus ends the determination regarding the tiger-skin [tithis].
A *kharva* tithi is one that is equal;
a *darpa* tithi is one that possesses increase (*vṛddhi*).

Violence (*hiṃsā*), waning (*kṣaya*), and that which possesses these [two]—this is the threefold definition of the lunar day (*tithi*), the essential nature of the lunar day. Here, it is stated that qualities such as "entirety" (*sarvatva*) and so forth pertain to the lunar day to be accepted; for it is specified that when the [preceding] new moon (*kharva*) and full moon (*darpa*) are subsequent, and violence (*hiṃsā*) is prior, they are to be accepted.
And this pervasion of equal time and a single portion occurs in this manner through the increase, decrease, or equality of the lunar day to be accepted at the time when night and day are equal.

When the preceding lunar day (tithi) measures twenty ghaṭīs and the succeeding lunar day measures twenty-two ghaṭīs, then on both days there is an equal extent of four ghaṭīs covering a portion of the afternoon; furthermore,
the tithi to be observed increases by two ghaṭīs.

And when the preceding lunar day (tithi) measures twenty-two ghaṭīs and the succeeding lunar day measures twenty ghaṭīs, even then there is an equal overlap of one part of the afternoon consisting of two ghaṭīs, and the lunar day is diminished by those two ghaṭīs.

And when the preceding and succeeding lunar days on the preceding and succeeding days each measure twenty-one ghaṭīs, even then there is an equal overlap of one part of the afternoon measuring three ghaṭīs, and the lunar day—
It attains equality.
In this regard, between increase and equality, the latter is to be accepted; in the case of decrease, the former.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha].
Regarding the time for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, Hārīta says:
"The *āmaśrāddha* is in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is at midday,
the *pārvaṇa* is in the afternoon, and that performed on account of prosperity is in the morning."

Vyāsa states the time for commencing [the rite]: "One who is self-restrained should commence the Ekoddiṣṭa either during the first part of the Kutapa period, or near the time of the sun's turning back (āvartana), at that very same time."

Ślokagautama states the time for its completion: "A wise man, knowing the rules, having commenced the Śrāddha during the Kutapa period, should perform it until the Rauhiṇa; adhering to the ritual injunction, he must not let the Rauhiṇa pass."
And thus, since the two muhūrtas known as Kutapa and Rohiṇī constitute the time for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, the determination [of the proper day] is made solely by the extent of their overlap.
Here too, regarding the two positions—that the lunar day (tithi) overlaps with midday on the previous day alone, or that it overlaps with midday on the following day alone—it is said:
"Whether the lunar day that overlaps with midday is the earlier one or the later one..."
In that [lunar day], offerings should be given to the ancestors; neither decrease nor increase [of the moon] is a cause for concern.
This is the determination based on the statement of Baudhāyana:
when [the tithi] spans both days at midday, or when it does not touch either day at all, the performance should take place on the previous day alone.
Regarding rites for the gods, the lunar day on which the sun rises should be known as the one to be observed.
For rites dedicated to the ancestors, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be known as the one for performance.
This is established by the statement of Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya and other previously cited passages from the Śivarahasya, the Saura Purāṇa, and so forth.
When the [tithi] occupies only a portion of both days equally, the determination is made as before according to the *kharva* and other rules.
However, when it occupies a portion of one day more than the other, the determination is made on the basis of its greater extent.
The time for the *daivika* śrāddha is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The *daivika* śrāddha is performed in the forenoon, while the *pārvaṇa* is performed in the afternoon."
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed at midday, while that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) is performed in the morning.
Regarding the forenoon:
"The forenoon is indeed prior to midday, and the afternoon is that which follows";
thus it has been stated.
In that regard also:
"A superior twice-born man should not perform a śrāddha at the time of dawn;
however, for occasional (naimittika) śrāddhas, no restriction regarding the time is prescribed."

From this statement of Śiva and Rāghava cited by Mādhava, since the morning time is prohibited for *śrāddhas* other than the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* prescribed for the morning, the time for the *daivika-śrāddha* is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) excluding that [morning]. The determination [of the specific time] within that period is as previously stated.

However, the distinction is this: when, due to [the length of the day being caused by] increase or decrease, the occupation of the ritual time (*karmakāla*) is equal on both days, then only the latter [day] should be taken.
When the sun has risen for rites to the gods, and when it has set for rites to the ancestors,
that lunar day (tithi) which lasts for two muhūrtas during the three periods of the day is the one prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

This is because of the statement of Baudhāyana, and because the passage concerning the "dwarf" (kharva) and others refers to śrāddhas for ancestors other than these [specific cases]. Thus concludes the determination of the lunar days for general śrāddhas.
Now, the characteristics of the afternoon and other periods are described in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The period prior to the turning [of the sun] is the forenoon, and that which follows it is the afternoon."

Thus, in the word *āvartanāt*, the prefix *ā-* must be elided (*praśleṣa*). "Turning point" (*āvartana*) refers to the middle of the day; therefore, the meaning is that the preceding portion up to the turning point is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), and the subsequent portion beyond that limit is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
Intending this very distinction, Manu said (A. 3, Śloka 278):
"And just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,"
Likewise, for one who observes the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the afternoon is superior to the forenoon.
Thus [it is said].

Here, by taking the two equal halves of the month—the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) and the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa)—as an illustration, the two parts of the day consisting of the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa) and afternoon (aparāhṇa), which take the form of the first half and the second half, are understood.
In the Śruti, three parts of the day divided into three—namely the forenoon, midday (madhyandina), and afternoon—are assigned specific functions.
