"The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors; therefore, one gives in the afternoon"—in this passage, since the connection of the forenoon with the gods and midday with humans, which is stated for the purpose of praising the enjoined afternoon, is not known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), two injunctions are inferred: "one gives to the gods in the forenoon" and "one gives to humans at midday."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The first five muhūrtas after sunrise are declared to be the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa); that which follows is the midday (madhyāhna)."
After that, the afternoon is said to consist of five muhūrtas.
Śātātapa also says: "Therefore, during the forenoon of that day, the gods partake of food;
at midday, humans; and in the afternoon, the ancestors."
Gobhila states the fourfold division as follows:
"The forenoon lasts for one and a half *praharas*, the midday likewise for one *prahara*;
the afternoon extends until the third [watch], and the evening is thereafter."

Thus says the Śatapatha Śruti, illustrating the fivefold division: "The sun indeed is all the seasons. When it rises, that is spring; when it is the time for milking [the cows], that is summer; when it is midday, that is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, that is autumn; and when it sets, that is winter."
A single portion of a day consisting of fifteen muhūrtas is measured at three muhūrtas;
thus, there are five such portions known as morning (prātaḥ), forenoon (saṅgava), midday (madhyāhna), afternoon (sāyāhna), and late afternoon (aparāhṇa).
Vyāsa also says:
The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration;
midday should consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise the same.
"The three-muhūrta period of evening is excluded from all [ritual] duties.
Thus, a fifteenfold division is stated in the *Grhabhāsakhaṇḍa*.
"The moments (muhūrta) of the day are always to be known as fifteen.
This means that whether the day is measured by thirty ghaṭīs or is shorter or longer, the muhūrtas are always exactly fifteen.
The names of the muhūrtas in sequence are:
Raudra, Śveta, Maitra, and Sārabhaṭa is likewise remembered;
then Sāvitra, Vaiśvadeva, Gāndharva, and Kutapa.
Rohiṇa, Tilaka, Vibhava, Nikṛti,
Śambara, and Vijaya— these are remembered as the fifteen varieties.
Thus, the eightfold divisions and so forth have not been described here because such conventional usage does not exist for them.
Now, the measurements of these portions of the day are being determined.

In that regard, the *prātaḥ* (forenoon) and *saṅgava* (mid-morning) periods each measure exactly three *muhūrtas*. However, as for the *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon), it measures seven and a half *muhūrtas* when divided into two parts, five *muhūrtas* when divided into three parts,
and one and a half *praharas* when divided into four parts.
Thus, the forenoon is of three kinds:
when divided into three parts, it measures five *muhūrtas*; when divided into four parts, it measures one *prahara*; and when divided into five parts, it measures three *muhūrtas*.
Likewise, the afternoon is of two kinds when divided into two parts, measuring seven and a half *muhūrtas*.
The afternoon is of four kinds: it is measured at five muhūrtas when divided into three parts, at half a prahara when divided into four parts, and at three muhūrtas when divided into five parts.
In the fourfold division of the day, the evening (sāyāhna) is measured by one *prahara*; in the fivefold division, it is measured by three *muhūrtas*. Thus, there are two types of evening.

These divisions, beginning with the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), are to be understood according to their specific application in various rites or as they may be available, just like the choice between barley and rice.

Alternatively, since statements such as “the forenoon [ends] at the *āvartana*” establish that a period of time consisting of three and a half *muhūrtas* constitutes the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), it would follow that a smaller measure of time— such as one and a half *praharas* contained within that [larger period]— would also be considered the forenoon by virtue of being included therein.

To avoid the resulting redundancy of statements such as “the forenoon is one and a half *praharas*,” there must exist a gradation of relative degrees among the various measures of the forenoon, from the larger to the smaller, in comparison to one another.
Hemādri states that it should be so calculated. Now, regarding the time of Kutapa,
the Skanda Purāṇa and the Vāyu Purāṇa state:
The time when the Sun, the lord of rays, shines with his full intensity upon the earth is known as *kutapa*;
what is given at that time yields great fruit.
*kuṃ* = the earth;
*gopatiḥ* = the sun;
*gobhiḥ* = by means of rays.
The meaning is that because the sun situated in the middle of the sky causes the entire earth to heat up, the time characterized by that is denoted by the word *kutapa*.
And that is the eighth *muhūrta* of the day.
As it has been said:
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The time after the seventh Muhūrta and before the ninth Muhūrta is known as Kutapa; what is given to the ancestors during that time becomes inexhaustible."
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"A Brāhmaṇa, a blanket, cows, silver, fire, guests,
sesame seeds, darbha grass, and midday— these nine are remembered as 'impure' (kupāḥ)."
Also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Midday, a sword-vessel, as well as a Nepalese blanket,
silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth."
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because these eight cause torment (santāpa) to it, they are therefore renowned as "kutapa."
Thus ends the section on the *kutapa*.
Now follows the time for the *śrāddha* ceremony;
therein, it is first defined by way of its prohibitions.

Manu (A. 3, Śloka 280): One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
Thus,
here by the word "sandhyā" (twilight)— the twilight preceding sunrise is intended to be three *ghaṭikās*.
The evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā) indeed consists of three ghaṭikās after the sun has set.
Thus, the *sandhyā* defined by convention is not accepted;
rather, it is the primary one, consisting of the time suitable for perceiving the solar disc.
This is because the conventional definition is already established through the very prohibition of [the conventional] night.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"The evening consists of three muhūrtas; one should not perform a śrāddha at that time.
Baudhāyana says:

When the fourth watch (prahara) has arrived, one should not perform a śrāddha there; and these [prohibitions] are not optional, because that would lead to the contingency of optionality (vikalpa). Nor can the avoidance of optionality be established here as it is in the case of the rule: "One who is initiated does not give."
Since both the injunction and the prohibition have distinct objects by virtue of being intended for the *śrāddha* rite according to the context,
these [prohibitions] are indeed exclusions (*paryudāsa*).

As for what was stated here by Śūlapāṇi and others— that exclusions are not accepted out of fear of optionality (*vikalpa*) because there is no equality of strength between an injunction and a prohibition due to their being general and particular respectively— that is incorrect, as such an optionality does not even arise.
"But [it is] because of the simplicity of having a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
That [argument], however, is prompted by ignorance of the authoritative sources (*ākara*).

Otherwise, there would also follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of an option (*vikalpa*) even in the case of the statement: "One does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice" (*na tau paśau karoti*).
Therefore, it is by the very method stated above that these are exclusions (*paryudāsa*).

And regarding their status as exclusions, Śūlapāṇi maintains that they are supplementary to the injunction for the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), meaning they apply to the new moon day other than the night and so forth.
That is incorrect.

Since the parts of the night and so forth are components of the *sāvana* day and lack the status of being components of the lunar *tithi* denoted by the term "new moon" (*amāvāsyā*), such an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would otherwise be untenable. Therefore, the exclusion applies specifically to those portions of the *sāvana* day other than the night and so on; thus, the exclusion functions precisely through the restriction of the *sāvana* day.
Nor can it be argued that because there is no injunction regarding the *sāvana* day, how could this be an exclusion as a supplement to it?

This is because the injunctions regarding the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such times serve to prescribe the *sāvana* day; for since it is impossible to perform a ritual without a full day and night (*ahorātra*), those injunctions likewise refer to the day-and-night period.

Just as the scriptural mention of spring and so forth as the occasion (*nimitta*) for a rite refers to a living person—since performance is impossible for one who is not alive—it ultimately pertains to a living being delimited by the season of spring and so on.
For this very reason, in the ritual declaration (*saṅkalpa*) beginning with "Today," the learned (*śiṣṭas*) mention the solar day (*sāvana-dina*) as the locus of the rite.
Furthermore, even in the Purāṇas, the ritual declaration stating, "Having reached today, the eighth day of the birth [of Kṛṣṇa]," indicates the injunction regarding the solar day.
Therefore, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) occurs precisely through the restriction to the solar day.

If it is objected: "Since even an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) depends upon the prior occurrence of that which is to be excluded, and since in all *śrāddhas* specific times such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) or afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) are fixed—such that there is no possibility of [the performance occurring] at night and so forth—how can these be considered exclusions? [The answer is: First, the exclusion of the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*) and its vicinity refers to *vṛddhi-śrāddhas* other than those occasioned by the birth of a son, which are prescribed for the morning.
Furthermore, even "nearby" here refers to a mere moment, according to the statement of Śātātapa: "at the moment of sunrise.
Moreover, the exclusions regarding the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsandhyā*) and its vicinity, such as the late afternoon (*sāyāhna*), pertain specifically to the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha.
Likewise, for the śrāddha, the afternoon is preferred over the forenoon.

Because of such statements as "in the third part of the day," which prescribe that time beginning from the afternoon— comprising the divisions of two or three parts of the day up to the end of the night—

as well as the fourth watch, the *sāyāhna*, the eighth part of the day, and the final *muhūrta*, their status as times to be avoided should be understood according to their relative degree of intensity.
However, the exclusion of the night applies to the domain of *śrāddhas* performed on specific occasions such as eclipses, the birth of a son, and so forth— as stated in the verse:
"At the sight of Rāhu [an eclipse], at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṅkrānti*), at marriages, at the end of a year, and at prosperity-rites (*vṛddhi*)."
And in the case of optional vows (kāmyavrata), one should perform bathing, giving, and other such rites at night.

Because [the performance] at night is established by such statements of Devala and others, some maintain that since a prohibition—even one occurring within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *darśa* sacrifice—cannot be accommodated within that very context, it must be displaced (*utkarṣa*). Others, however, argue that because the injunction and the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) have equal force as they both concern the same subject matter, such as the taking of food, a dilemma (*vikalpa*) would arise; therefore, the exclusion of the night applies specifically to the *tīrtha-śrāddha*.

For that [act], which by its original nature (*prakṛti*) applies to the afternoon, is indeed established as occurring even at night due to the general application resulting from the direct sequence of the occasion (*nimitta*), since it is set aside by the directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) immediate sequence; however, unlike the case of the "taking up" (*grahaṇa*) and so forth, there is no injunction specifically predicated with reference to that [night]. Therefore, because there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) arising in that regard, that very [act] is the object of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the night.

As for the statement— "Whether out of season or in season, one should perform the *tīrtha-śrāddha* and libations"— even that, because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), is intended to indicate that even the secondary times such as morning and evening, which are obtained by exclusion from other scriptural injunctions (such as the prohibition of the night), possess a degree of primacy; it does not, however, [mean that they are equal to the primary time].

Others say that even at night it should be performed, as that is the primary injunction. However, others maintain that since it is possible for the context to remain uncontradicted, it is improper to contradict it; thus, if during the performance of the *śrāddha* in its original form (the *prakṛti*), the sun should set due to some divine or human obstacle before the rite is completed, then—because the rite has already been commenced—the completion of it at night would follow, and therefore "not at night" (*naktaṃ*) [as a prohibition] does not apply.
The injunction “one should perform the *śrāddha*” is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary specification).
Accordingly, having set aside what has already been partially performed, the rite must be completed by the sacrificer on the following day; furthermore, he himself should eat only after that.
For this very reason, they say that the *Āpastamba-sūtra* passage, “Or [the rite may be resumed] when it has begun until its completion,” is in accordance with the commentaries of the students.

In reality, however, the injunctions regarding the afternoon and so forth do not serve as restrictive rules (niyama), but rather for the purpose of indicating excellence. As it is said: "The ancestral rite (śrāddha) which is proclaimed for the new moon is celebrated as the pārvaṇa;
therein, an offering in the afternoon is highly commended for the ancestors."
This is because it is understood exactly so from the statements of Śātātapa and others.
And since those times are not fixed, when all times would otherwise be applicable, the exclusion of the night is appropriate.

Therefore, it is established that for occasional (*anaimittika*) *śrāddhas*, the time consists of even a single *muhūrta* occurring within the interval between them—excluding the night, the two twilights (*sandhyā*), and the morning and evening periods immediately preceding and following them.
Even within that [period], the five muhūrtas beginning with Kutapa are highly recommended for the Pārvaṇa rite;
from the Kutapa onwards, the four muhūrtas,
or even the five muhūrtas, are desired as the abode of the Svadhā offering.
Thus ends the statement of Śātātapa.
And for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, midday is recommended;
and in this context, that consists of only two muhūrtas, namely Kutapa and Rohiṇī, excluding Gāndharva.
Having commenced the Śrāddha during the Kutapa period, a wise man should perform it until the Rauhina period;
one who knows the ritual procedure, adhering to the rule, must not let the Rauhina period pass.
Thus, according to the statement of Gautama:
"Even though the evening [time] is prohibited, when its own time has passed, one should perform [the rite] before night; that is the limit."
Because of this re-enactment by the words of Vyāsa, [the time] is secondary (*gauṇa*).
Even therein, among the first, second, and third *muhūrta*s, there is a gradation of being secondary, more secondary, and most secondary.

Furthermore, because of the prohibition regarding the final *muhūrta* of the eighth part of the day, it is not the case that [the time] is prescribed in every respect, as is the case with the times of night and morning.
Because there is no further injunction regarding the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣ�ṭa* rites for those two [times] as there is for the evening;
nor should it be argued that, since the first muhūrta is specifically prohibited, the remaining portion of that time is understood to be permitted as a secondary (gauṇa) option—
because by implication, that [remaining portion] has already been stated to pertain to the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.

The time of *saṅgava* is neither prohibited nor praised. Alternatively, let it be that the scriptural mentions of midday, morning, and so forth in the context of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and other rites serve the purpose of restriction (*niyama*); whereas the mention of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) in the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, according to the previously cited statements, serves solely to indicate its superior excellence (*prāśastyātiśaya*).
Therefore, the exclusion of night and other such times is logical.
And here, although the Pārvaṇa rite takes place in the afternoon, its commencement must be at the Kutapa hour itself:
"The muhūrtas of the day are always known to be fifteen;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called Kutapa."
Since the sun always becomes mild at midday,
an undertaking begun then is distinguished by yielding infinite fruit.
Thus, according to the Matsya Purāṇa;
nor is this statement restricted to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite alone,
for if it were so restricted, the mention of "the commencement" (*prārambha*) would result in being redundant.
Furthermore, regarding this modified form of the *pārvaṇa* rite, a rule is recorded by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"A wise man should perform the *śrāddha* in the forenoon of the bright fortnight;
however, in the afternoon of the dark fortnight, he must not let the time of Rohiṇī pass."
Thus it is said.
However, this statement has been cited by Śūlapāṇi and others as being from the Vāyu Purāṇa.

For this statement establishes that for all rituals—such as those related to the *yugas*, *manvantaras*, and annual ceremonies (*sāṃvatsarika*)—pertaining to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the time is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), while for those pertaining to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the time is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
It does not enjoin [the morning time],
because in one case there would be the consequence of subverting the afternoon and so forth, and in the other case [the morning] is already established by default.

Nor should it be argued that the portion belonging to the dark fortnight is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), while the injunction of the morning for the portion of the bright fortnight occurs precisely by subverting the afternoon obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Since it is improper for that [time] to be established as valid when it can be established without contradiction,

it is proven by this statement that the time for commencing the rite is determined according to different positions: namely, the earlier part of the *kutapa* included within the forenoon divided in two ways, and the later part included within such an afternoon.
By this very [statement], he establishes the meaning already proven by the scriptural injunction regarding the beginnings of the Yugas:
"The wise know that there are two white and two black beginnings of the Yugas;
the white ones are to be taken in the forenoon, and the black ones in the afternoon."
Thus has the statement from another Smṛti been explained.
Others, however, explain these very statements exactly as they are heard.
Such, then, is the time for the Pārvaṇa and Ekoddiṣṭa rites.

However, in the case of the *devaśrāddha* and similar rites, the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is to be adopted, according to such scriptural injunctions as: "The *daivika* śrāddha is performed in the forenoon.
And the *devaśrāddha*—that śrāddha which is directed toward the gods—is called *daivika*.
This was stated by Viśvāmitra in such passages as these.
Here, by the word "forenoon" (pūrvāhṇa), the *saṅgava* period is intended;
for there is no obstacle to the prohibition regarding the morning time (*prātaḥ-kāla*) applying here as well.

Thus, regarding the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) performed in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇe*), the same rule applies here as well: "One should perform the *āmaśrāddha* on that lunar day (*tithi*) which remains for three *muhūrtas* after the morning time, or even if the lunar day lasts for only two *muhūrtas*."
Thus, according to the statement of Vyāghrapāda,
this rule for the forenoon (*pūrvāhna*) procedure in an *āma-śrāddha* applies only to an *āma-śrāddha* performed by the twice-born (*dvijāti*), and not even to an *āma-śrāddha* performed by a Śūdra;
for while raw food (*āma*) is not mandatory when the performance occurs on a day [of the fortnight] with the twice-born as the performers, it is [mandatory] in the performance by a Śūdra.

Because [the time] is fixed in both cases, there would arise the contradiction of a mandatory rule being joined with a non-mandatory one (nityānitya-saṃyoga-virodha) if the rule for the forenoon were applied.
And thus:
"That which is declared as the *kutapa* occurring after midday..."
There too, even with mere raw food, he gave sustenance to the ancestors.
Hemādri maintains that, on this basis, the statement of Śātātapa would also possess its proper scope;
however, that is not correct,
for there is a contradiction with an obligatory connection (*nityasaṃyoga*), according to the principle of the section concerning the *phalacamasa* (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 3.5.18).
Or it might be [established] by the principle of the section on *saṃsthā* (A.

8, Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 4). It is not the first case, because the time such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) lacks the status of being a property of substances such as *āmāśaka*, unlike the pressing (*abhiṣava*) and other such acts.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) is distinct from the *annaśrāddha* (funeral rite with cooked food).

As for the scriptural statement, if it were inclusive, then let it prescribe another time-period chosen as the forenoon for all *āmaśrāddhas*; however, there is no specific distinction regarding the *āmaśrāddha* of a Śūdra.
Therefore, even that Śūdra must perform the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) specifically in the forenoon.
Thus, based on the statement, “The [rite] caused by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) is in the morning,” the *nāndīśrāddha*—with the exception of the birth of a son—must be performed in the morning.
However, in the case of the birth of a son, due to the inherent nature of the occasion, the time immediately following [the birth] itself is primary.
And here, the morning time is divided into five parts, because in other [traditional] systems there is no division of the morning;
as for the occasional use of the word "morning" even for the first portions of days divided into three or four parts, that is said to be figurative in the *Parvanirṇaya*.
Thus concludes the section on the time for the Śrāddha.
Now, regarding the times when the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) is prohibited:
on this point, Pulastya states—
"The śrāddha [should be performed] during the two solstices (ayana) and likewise during the two equinoxes (viṣuvat)."
And on all the beginnings of the Yugas, except for the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa).
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"And [the śrāddha] should be performed on the *saṅkrāntis*, with the exception of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*).

Regarding this, Hemādri states that since the *ayanādi* (solstices and so forth) are already included by the very mention of *saṅkrānti*, the separate mention of them is for the purpose of indicating an excess of merit (or a greater degree of fault in omission).
Others, however, say that the prohibition is based on what is attained through error;
in reality, however, the validity of the prohibition arises from the difference between sages.
This was stated by Vācaspati:

From that time forward, one should perform the *tri-piṇḍa* śrāddha on the occasion of the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṅkrānti*), during eclipses and other festival days (*parvan*), and the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the anniversary of death.

Based on this statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa*, a *śrāddha* with three rice-balls (*tripiṇḍa*) should be performed even at the time of the *saṅkrānti* and other such occasions. Nor is there any inconsistency in the aforementioned prohibition, for if that [prohibition] is well-founded, it can be explained as being optional (*vikalpa*). This is not so, because the term "three rice-balls" (*tripiṇḍa*) refers specifically to the *pārvaṇa* rite.
Otherwise, if three were enjoined by way of restating the *piṇḍas*, there would be the undesirable consequence of interrupting the flow of the injunction.
Nor can it be argued that the word "three *piṇḍas*" enjoins the *piṇḍas* alone, while the number three is a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*);

for in your view, since the prohibitory statement lacks a basis, enjoining again the primary subsidiary act consisting of the offering of *piṇḍas* would result in its being treated as a prior [independent] rite.

On the other hand, if the offering of the *piṇḍas* were considered the primary element, since that would already be established by the term *śrāddha* itself, a further injunction would result in the exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the other primary element, which consists in the feeding of Brahmins.
Nor should it be argued that the injunction for the offering of *piṇḍas* exists merely to establish the optional nature [of the rite] by accepting that the prohibition has a valid basis (*samūla*).

Since it is appropriate for the three-fold formula (*tripiṇḍapada*)—being a restatement of the *pārvaṇa* rite as established by its very nature—to function as a subordinate element of the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, it is improper to resort to either a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) or an option (*vikalpa*).
Having cited a verse from the *Matsyapurāṇa* in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"And when a learned man (*śrotriya*), a knower of the Vedas who has maintained the sacred fires (*agnicit*), comes to one's house..."
Thus,
concerning the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada conjoined with the Maghā constellation,
the Devīpurāṇa states:
In that regard as well, a great worship should be performed for the ancestors and the deities;
however, the eldest son should avoid the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) there.
Pūjā is characterized by the śrāddha rite;
the Maghā constellation is the deity of the ancestors. Thus says Bṛhat-Parāśara.
One should not perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) under the *Bharaṇī* asterism;
for this is a prohibition against the giving of rice-balls in a *śrāddha* specifically connected to *Bharaṇī*.
This is because even that [asterism], when included within the *Mahālaya* period, possesses the status of being a time for *śrāddha*.
The Bharaṇī [nakṣatra] during the fortnight of the ancestors is proclaimed to be most significant;
he by whom a Śrāddha is performed on this day becomes one who has performed a Śrāddha at Gayā.
Thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
Likewise, in another *Smṛti*:
"During the *gaṇḍa*, *vaidhṛti*, and *pāta* yogas, the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) must be abandoned by those desiring sons."
In this case as well, the prohibition applies specifically to the *śrāddha* rites occasioned by those respective [times]. As for those [verses] which state:
"On Sundays, on Tuesdays, on the thirteenth lunar day, on the *nandā* tithis, on Saturdays, and under the *maghā* nakṣatra..."
One should not perform the offering of funeral cakes, bathing with clay, or the libation of sesame seeds.
Likewise—

such statements as "on the Nanda, Aśva, Kāma, Vyāra, Bhṛgu, Agni, Pitṛ, and Kāla lunar days," cited in the *Prayogapārijāta*, apply to the single-day (*sakṛt*) and other options prescribed for the latter fortnight of the Mahālaya.
On the thirteenth lunar day falling on a Saturday during the three births of Nandā,
and under the asterisms of Revatī and Maghā, one should not perform the rites of the dark fortnight.

Some maintain that these and similar statements prohibiting *śrāddha* should be interpreted as prohibitions against *śrāddha* performed on those specific [days], since they form a single syntactical unit with them.

However, in reality, because *śrāddha* is prescribed for specific lunar days (*tithi*) and weekdays (*vāra*), the prohibition of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) applies only to the *śrāddha* occasioned by those [specific times].
For this very reason, they recite:

Whatever defect is indeed proclaimed as being caused by the lunar day (tithi) and the weekday (vāra), that applies only to the śrāddha performed on account of those [specific factors], and never to any other śrāddha.
Thus, in the Smṛtiratnāvalī:
"When a son is born, during a Vyatīpāta yoga, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun..."
One should perform the śrāddha with diligence, even if it is without the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
And thus:
"When an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurs while the sun is in Capricorn,
the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at the Gaṅgā is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds."
Thus, the statement from the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa cited by Hemādri refers specifically to the occasion of an eclipse occurring during the Gaṅgā. Kārṣṇājini states:
"In the cases of marriage, vows, and tonsure ceremonies, [the period of impurity lasts] for a year, half a year, and half of that [respectively]."
One should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), bathing with clay, or the libation of sesame seeds (tarpaṇa).
Likewise, in other cases involving mere prosperity,
the eminent teachers such as Garga and others have prescribed the exclusion of the offering of funeral cakes for ritualists for one month.
And this [rule] applies even to the sapinda relatives;
likewise, Jyotihparāśara states:
When a marriage has been performed, the sapinda relatives should indeed avoid [participating in] the offering of funeral cakes for twelve months;
however, in the case of the investiture of the sacred thread, they should avoid it for six months.
The exception to this is stated in that very same work:
"In the Mahālaya rite, in the Gayā Śrāddha, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
and likewise in the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for any mortal whatsoever."
"Even one who has performed the marriage ceremony should always perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Now, is it not the case that in the aforementioned statements there is no possibility of a prohibition against the giving of the rice-balls?
Is this a prohibition (pratiṣedha) or an exclusion (paryudāsa)?
Not the first [alternative],

because if the offering of a ball of rice (piṇḍadāna) established by the scripture were prohibited, it would result in an option (vikalpa), similar to the rule "one does not perform [the rite] for a sacrificial animal.
Nor the second.
This is because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the various injunctions for those specific *śrāddhas*.

For here, while several *śrāddhas* are mentioned within a single sentence, the prohibition of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) cannot be said to have been recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of each of those respective *śrāddhas*.

Consequently, just as in the case of the statement “one does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice” (*na tau paśau karoti*), where an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is impossible due to the absence of proximity to the injunctions for the subsidiary parts (*aṅga-vidhi*), so too here, because of the absence of proximity to the injunctions for those various *śrāddhas* prescribed in other Smṛtis, [an exclusion is likewise impossible].
If it is asked, "How then can there be a cessation of the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for those śrāddhas that are [merely] excluded?"—the answer is: no. For it is said:
"The śrāddha on the two solstices (*ayana*), and likewise on the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."

In such sentences, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is not excluded by way of a *paryudāsa* (prohibitive exclusion) with reference to the *śrāddha* rites prescribed in other Smṛtis—by which the aforementioned fault might arise—but rather, the performance of a previously unestablished rite is enjoined.
Furthermore, because this is from a different Smṛti, the enjoining of what has already been enjoined does not constitute a fault.

Therefore, since the phrase "except for the offering of rice-balls" can be construed as a single syntactical unit with the specific *śrāddha* injunctions prescribed in its own sentence, it is logical that it functions as a *paryudāsa*, and thus the cessation of the offering of rice-balls is indeed justified.

Thus ends the time for the prohibition of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*). [This work was composed by] the son of Śrī Paraśurāma Miśra, grandson of Śrī Haṃsapāṇḍita, and great-grandson of Śrī Vīrasiṃhadeva—who was commissioned by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāparudradeva, whose lotus feet were illuminated by the clusters of rays from the crest-jewels of the entire circle of vassal kings; and who was the son of the illustrious Mahārāja Madhukarasāha, and the sun that caused the blooming of the white lotus-heart of the earth encircled by the four oceans.

In the *Samayaprakāśa*, a section of the work titled *Vīramitrodaya* composed by the illustrious Mitramiśra— the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the entire ocean of knowledge, a lion to the great elephant of worldly poverty, and the life-breath of learned men— herein concludes the determination of the times for *Śrāddha*.
Now follow the miscellaneous times.
In that regard, the time for the Vaiśākha bath is as follows:
having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu,
and likewise on the fifteenth, O Hero!
Or indeed at the sun's entry into Aries.
Having obtained the permission of the Brāhmaṇas and having worshipped Madhusūdana, one should perform the vow of the Vaiśākha bath preceded by the formal declaration of intent (saṅkalpa).
Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"And regarding Kārttika— beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, a human being [should observe the vow]."
"One should perform the morning bath"— thus it is stated in the Viṣṇurahasya:
"On the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, being composed in mind..."
One should bathe with supreme devotion throughout the entire month of Kārttika.
Thus it is stated in the Āditya Purāṇa: "And this [should be performed] before sunrise;
he who, devoted to celibacy, [bathes] at Bindu-tīrtha in the month of Kārttika..."
He will bathe before the sun has risen; how can there be fear for one born from the Sun?
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. Also, Viṣṇu says regarding Māgha:
"A man should be one who bathes in the morning during the months of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries."
According to the Brāhma [Purāṇa]:
One should begin on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa,
and complete it on the twelfth day or the full moon of the bright fortnight.
Viṣṇu says:
One should perform the ritual bath beginning either on the new moon day or the full moon day;
and this [should be done] when the sun has risen.
This is because of the statement in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "When the sun has slightly risen.
But according to the *Bāhu* [Purāṇa]:
"O Lord, beginning from the dawn (aruṇodaya) until the end of the morning time."
The merit of those who perform the Māgha bath is established there in due order.
Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the auspicious lunar days beginning with the first day (pratipad):
among them, the first day is described in the *Padma-purāṇa*:
O mighty-armed one, in ancient times, the first day of the month of Caitra was meritorious;
on that day, the best of men who, having seen the Tapanam [sacred site], performs an ablution—
O King, for him there is no misfortune whatsoever, nor mental anxieties, nor physical ailments. [His] son is right there—
these three lunar days were previously mentioned, O joy of the Kurus.
In the month of Kārttika, or Āśvayuja, or likewise in Caitra, O King.
Thus:
"these" refers to the previously mentioned steps;
thus [is] the step.
Now, the second [verse] from the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the month of Āśvina, the meritorious second lunar day belonging to the bright fortnight [is sacred]."
A gift bestowed upon her is said to yield infinite fruit.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"And on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika, there is the ritual worship."
Thus ends the second [section].
Now begins the third; concerning the month of Caitra, it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
On the third day, one should worship the Goddess together with Śaṅkara with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the damana plant adorned with fine garlands.
The third lunar day of the bright fortnight occurring in the month of Vaiśākha should be known as yielding infinite fruit for rites such as ritual bathing and giving gifts.

In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the third lunar day, balls of flour mixed with jaggery (guḍāpūpa) and milk-rice (pāyasa) should be given for the satisfaction of Vāmadeva."
O King, on the third lunar day of the month of Māgha, the gift of jaggery and salt brings auspicious merit to both women and men.
Thus ends the third [verse].
Now, the fourth: in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa—
O King, Śivā, Śāntā, and Sukhā are considered the three kinds of the fourth [tithi]. Among these,
the bright (śukla) fourth tithi in the month of Bhādrapada is honored by the worlds as Śivā.
O Lord of the Earth, that fourth lunar day which falls in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha should always be known as the bestower of peace; it indeed always brings about tranquility.
When the day of Mars falls on the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, it should be known as "Sukhadā" (the giver of happiness), for it is celebrated as the "Sukhānāmā" (named Sukhā).
Thus ends the fourth [verse]. Now, the fifth: in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa—
Then, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the fair-faced Śrī,
by the command of Keśava, descended from the world of Viṣṇu to the human realm.
Therefore, one should worship her there; Lakṣmī does not abandon him who does so.
Likewise: "The meritorious Pañcamī of the month of Bhādrapada is called Nāgapañcamī."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The bright fifth day of Mārgaśīrṣa and that which falls in Śrāvaṇa are meritorious;
through bathing and giving gifts, they yield great fruit and bestow the world of the Nāgas."
Now, the sixth [verse]: In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*—
"O bull of the Bharatas, this which is the sixth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada..."
All acts such as bathing and giving charity performed on this day are said to be inexhaustible.
Likewise:
"O bull among the Bharatas, on this sixth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada,
whoever worships the son of Gaṅgā residing in the southern region,"
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise:
"That sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is dear to Hari."
"That is known as the Great Sixth"—
thus concludes the section on the sixth [day].
Now, the seventh.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O Lord of Gaṇas, that seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada is renowned as Aparājitā, which destroys even the greatest of sins."
But that which falls on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, O Hero, is declared to be auspicious and the bringer of all joy.
In her, one enjoys the fruits of rites such as bathing and giving as inexhaustible;
likewise:
"Nandā is the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the bestower of bliss."
That lunar day is called Jayantī; it destroys even the greatest of sins.
Viṣṇu states: "The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse. Thus ends the section on the seventh day.
The eighth lunar days (*aṣṭamī*)—namely, the *jayantī*, the *aṣṭakā*, and the *durgāṣṭamī*—have been described in their respective places.
Thus concludes the discussion of the eighth lunar day.
Now, the ninth lunar day (*navamī*).
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina..."
O Lord of Men, a gift given on that [day] becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one who is composed should bathe, give gifts, and pay homage; he obtains inexhaustible fruit.
Thus ends the ninth [day]. Now, the tenth:
the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha is remembered as the mouth of the year.
One should perform a ritual bath in it, and especially offer gifts.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one who performs vows and other rites on that day obtains their desired fruit."
The eleventh and the twelfth [lunar days].
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"One should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights."
He who worships Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day shall partake in infinite fruit.
Now, the thirteenth [day]:
in the Skanda Purāṇa—it is said that the thirteenth day of Caitra is meritorious; on that day, the fruit is tenfold.
Now, regarding the fourteenth day:
in the *Skanda Purāṇa*—
the bright fourteenth day of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada.
For that [gift] during the dark fortnight of Māgha indeed yields great fruit.
Thus ends the fourteenth [day].
Now, regarding the full moon day (paurṇamāsī),
it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:

"The full moon days of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha yield great fruit. Now, the auspicious lunar days (tithis) according to the influence of the constellations (nakṣatras), weekdays (vāra), and so forth, are described.
The third lunar day (tṛtīyā) that is specifically conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism,
if it is obtained when further joined with Mercury (Budha), is especially distinguished.
In that [day], bathing, fasting, and so forth, shall yield infinite fruit.
Regarding the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* states: "Due to its conjunction with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, it is remembered as equal to Kurukṣetra."
Especially when the third lunar day is conjoined with Mercury, it is particularly significant.
Yama states:
"If the fourth lunar day falls on a Saturday in conjunction with the Bharaṇī asterism..."
Then, by worshipping the god Yama, one is liberated from all sins.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"If Sunday should fall on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, that seventh day is named Vijayā; what is given there yields great fruit."
Likewise:
"On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, the constellation consisting of five stars"—
this is to be connected with the word "meritorious" (puṇya) which will be mentioned later.

Rauhiṇī, Āśleṣā, Hasta, Puṣya, and Maghā are well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) as having five stars each. Furthermore, when the sun enters [a new sign] on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, that seventh day becomes "Mahājayā," for it is dear to the Sun.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, and the worship of the ancestors and gods—
all these are said to be multiplied ten millionfold, according to the word of Bhāskara.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The seventh lunar day (Saptamī) joined with the asterism Revatī and the Sun is of great fruit.
In the Mahābhārata:
When the eighth day of the bright fortnight is full and conjoined with the Moon’s son (Mercury), those who observe the religious vow on that day shall not have their prosperity impaired.
The son of the Moon is Saumya.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa:
"In the month of Pauṣa, the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight on a Wednesday is Mahābhadra, which yields great fruit."
Thus, in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, when [it falls] in the month of Pauṣa..."
On the eighth day, the constellation presided over by Yama arises; it is meritorious and is called Raudra in the world.
Then that [day] is known as the highly meritorious Jayantī Aṣṭamī;
Yamadaivata is Bharaṇī.
Its ferocity arises from its being presided over by a cruel deity. As stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "If the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha should coincide with a Tuesday..."
This lunar day, conjoined with the asterism Hasta, should be known as the remover of all sins.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight under the Puṣya asterism is most meritorious and destroys all sins.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, when the lunar mansion is Punarvasu, that day is known by the name Vijayā; it is the most excellent of all lunar days.
He who gives a *prastha* of sesame seeds for the duration of a year,
and another who is devoted to fasting— these two produce an equal result.
Having propitiated Govinda, the Lord of the lords of the worlds, in that [place],...
One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the month of Caitra, when conjoined with the constellation Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), yields great fruit."
In Vaiśākha, it is joined with Hastā; in Jyeṣṭha, it is conjoined with Svāti; likewise in Āṣāḍha, it is with Jyeṣṭhā; and in the month of Vaiṣṇava (Śrāvaṇa), it is endowed with Mūla.
The month of Śrāvaṇa is sacred to Viṣṇu; likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, the twelfth day joined with the asterism Śravaṇa is meritorious,
as is the twelfth day in Āśvina joined with the asterism Ārdrā.
In Kārttika, it is joined with Revatī; in Saumya (Mārgaśīrṣa), it is joined with Kṛttikā—Saumya being Mārgaśīrṣa;
in Pauṣa, it is joined with Mṛgaśiras; and in Māgha, it is conjoined with Āditya (Punarvasu).
In the month of Phālguna, the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is supremely purifying.
"Bathing, giving gifts, and fasting performed under these [lunar days] conjoined with the constellations [are meritorious].
When the full moon of Māgha has passed, it is joined with the constellation Śravaṇa.
That twelfth day which falls in the dark fortnight is called Tilavaiṣṇavī.
Likewise:
when the moon is situated in Mūla in the month of Māgha,
on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, one should observe a fast with the senses subdued.
By consuming only sesame seeds on the twelfth lunar day, one is liberated from sins.
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
"If the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra falls on a Tuesday..."
Furthermore, one shall not become a Piśāca again by bathing and eating at the Gaṅgā.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, when it falls on a Tuesday and the moon is in the Citrā constellation,
Sthāṇu, being worshipped on that day, will certainly grant the city of Śiva.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Likewise, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight falling on a Tuesday, there is the libation to the ancestors.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
On all full moon days, and especially when they coincide with the Maghā asterism,
it is taught that the fruit of gifts given here is tenfold.
That full moon day is called "Mahatī" (Great) when it is joined with the full moon and Jupiter.
In the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra):
"In whichever direction the Moon and Jupiter are seen together,
that full moon day is declared to be 'Mahatī' (the Great) within the year."
In that [state], it is proclaimed that acts such as giving and fasting become inexhaustible.
Likewise:
when the moon and Jupiter are in the lunar mansion called Māsa, and the sun is fifteen [degrees] from that, it is the full moon on a Thursday;
indeed, that lunar day is called "Mahat."
Thus: at Harikṣetra, at the Gaṅgā, at the ocean, and likewise at Naimiṣa,
bathing, giving gifts, and performing śrāddha on the Mahāśabda lunar day yield infinite merit.
Thus:

when Jupiter and the Moon are in the asterism of Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), and likewise the Sun is in the asterism of Prajāpati (Pūrvaphalgunī) on the full moon day, that should be known as the one celebrated as Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"When the lunar mansion of Kṛttikā (Āgneya) should ever occur on the full moon day of Kārttika,
that lunar day is to be known as 'Great' (Mahatī), and it is most excellent for bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites."
Whenever the constellation of Yama (Bharaṇī) occurs on that lunar day at any time,
that lunar day is proclaimed by the sages to be exceedingly meritorious.
O lord of men, when the lunar mansion is Prājāpatya (Rohiṇī) during that month, it is called Mahākārttikī; it is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
On Monday, Sunday, or Thursday— on these three days of the week,
O Brahmā— and on these three constellations, it was proclaimed by Brahmā himself.
O King, for one who has bathed there, the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice shall accrue;
likewise, their gifts and libations to the ancestors become inexhaustible.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The Mahākārttikī is meritorious when the moon is in conjunction with the Kṛttikās;
and when the moon is in conjunction with Maghā and Āśleṣā, it is called Mahāmāghī."
In the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra): "When Saturn is situated in Aries, Jupiter and the Moon are in Leo,
and the Sun is in the asterism called Śravaṇa, that is remembered as Mahāmāghī."
Śātātapa says:
When the day of the new moon coincides with the day of Mars,
one obtains the merit of a thousand cows merely by bathing in the Ganges.
In the Mahābhārata: "When it coincides with the moon, Mars, Jupiter, and likewise the sun,
that sacred ford named Puṣkara is superior to a hundred solar eclipses."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"When the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is conjoined with the asterisms of Anurādhā or Viśākhā,
the host of ancestors then attains satisfaction for eight years through the śrāddha."
In some places, however, the reading is "the *viśākhā* and *svāti* constellations.
When the new moon occurs under the *puṣya*, *raudra* (ārdrā), or *punarvasu* constellations,
the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.

For one desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors, [this] is difficult even for the gods to obtain on the lunar mansions of Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), Ajaikapāt (Śatabhiṣaj), and Pitṛs (Maghā), as well as on that of Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) and Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā).
O King, if the fifth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Māgha ever coincides with the Vāruṇa asterism (Śatabhiṣaj),
that is the supreme time for the ancestors; indeed, it is not obtained by those of little merit.
Vyāsa says:
If the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, conjoined with the Vāruṇa yoga,
can be obtained on the Gaṅgā, it is equal to a hundred solar eclipses.
When that [asterism] is conjoined with Saturday, it is known as Mahāvāruṇī;
if Śatabhiṣā occurs on a Saturday conjoined with an auspicious yoga,
it is renowned as Mahāmahā, which shall uplift thirty million lineages.
The Ardhodaya is described in the Mahābhārata:
"If [the moon] is conjoined with Amāvāsyā, Ārdrā, Bhauma (Mars), and Śravaṇa during the months of Puṣya or Māgha,
that is to be known as Ardhodaya, equal to ten million solar eclipses."
In some places, however, the reading is "kiñcidūno mahodayaḥ" (slightly less than a great success).
It is said: "This yoga is auspicious only during the day, but never at night."

Regarding Kapila-ṣaṣṭhī in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The sixth lunar day in the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), when conjoined with the asterism Rohiṇī and the conjunctions of the Moon, Rāhu, and Mars, is proclaimed as 'Kapilā' by those who know the Purāṇas."
There, one should worship the Sun with vows, fasts, and observances;
and by giving a tawny cow to an eminent brahmin, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice.

In the *Purāṇasamuccaya*, however, it is said: "When the moon is in the constellation Hasta during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, on a Saturday, a Tuesday, and under the asterism Rohiṇī— that sixth lunar day is known as Kapilā."
Thus it is said;
and here, Bhādrapada is intended as the month ending with the new moon (darśānta). On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of that very month, Rohiṇī occurs.
And when this is complete, it is at that very moment meritorious.
As it has been said:
"But when there is a conjunction of these four, it is designated as such by the supreme seeker."
And "the sun in the hand" is for the purpose of indicating an excellence of results.
Śaṅkha says: "The new moon day [is auspicious] with the Moon, and the seventh [lunar day] together with the Sun."
The fourth [tithi] is with the son of the Earth (Mars), and the eighth with Wednesday (Budha).
Four lunar days are as meritorious as the time of an eclipse and the like;
here, it is said that all acts such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation become inexhaustible.
Śātātapa states: When the fourth or fourteenth lunar day falls on a Tuesday,
it is as meritorious as the new moon (kuhū) falling on a Monday.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
If the Puṣya asterism occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight,
or on the twelfth day, it is traditionally held to effect the destruction of all sins without exception.
Vyāsa says:
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, the fourth or the fourteenth day is meritorious when it falls on a Tuesday, just as the new moon (Kuhū) is on a Monday.
Thus [ends the section on] auspicious lunar days joined with constellations, weekdays, and so forth. Now,
the things to be avoided at night.
One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor especially a gift;
however, one may perform occasional baths and gifts even during the nights.
Thus end the things to be avoided at night. Now, the times for avoiding the frequenting of crossroads:
at midday, at midnight, after having eaten a *śrāddha* meal, or after eating meat.
And during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
Thus ends the section on the times to avoid crossroads. Now, the specific lunar days (tithis) to be avoided.
In that regard, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight when the Sun is in Leo, one must not look at the moon.
Mārkaṇḍeya states: "On the fourth day of the bright fortnight when the Sun is in Leo, [one should avoid] looking at the moon."
One might falsely accuse him; therefore, one should not look at him at that time.
Thus [it is said]:
with the exception of the sixth day,
one should avoid oil for anointing on the sixth day.

And so it is said in the *Ratnamālā*: "Sages declare that for men, applying oil on the sixth lunar days, shaving on the eighth, and sexual intercourse with women on the fourteenth— when the digits [of the moon] have vanished— lead to the destruction of one's lifespan."
Thus [it is said].
Now, the things to be avoided on the seventh lunar day:
regarding that, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa—
On the seventh day, a man should not touch oil, nor should he wear blue clothing;
he should neither bathe with *āmalaka* fruits nor engage in quarreling.
On the seventh lunar day, one should certainly not eat from a copper vessel.
Budha says: Eating neem, oil, sesame-seed offerings, collyrium,
not eating on the seventh lunar day, and eating from a copper vessel— [these are forbidden].
Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the days to be avoided on the eighth lunar day,
Vyāsa states:
On the sixth, eighth, new moon, and the fourteenth day of both fortnights, sin is present; likewise in oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.
Some authorities maintain that on these lunar days, in their respective order, there are prohibitions:
oil on the sixth day is detrimental to longevity; likewise, meat on the eighth;
sensual enjoyment on the fourteenth; and shaving on the new moon day.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), one might think that there is no fault in doing so on other days; however, that is not correct, because Manu has prohibited oil and other such things on other days as well, stating: "The fifteenth day [is forbidden] for eating meat, and the fourteenth day for anointing with oil."

Furthermore, in the prohibition of "oil" (*taila*) in all cases, it is specifically sesame oil that is prohibited, because the word *taila* has its primary denotation (*śakti*) there alone; however, when there is a general prohibition of "anointing with oil" (*abhyaṅga*), it is indeed a prohibition of any unctuous substance (*sneha*).
Since the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) possesses the nature of a festival (parvan), all prohibitions associated with such occasions apply there. Its status as a festival is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
The fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon— these, O king of kings, are the sacred festival days (parvan), as is the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti).
Having stated these [days] in that very same [text]:
"The man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these parvan days..."
A man who consumes feces and urine goes to hell.

Thus, Vaudhāyana prescribes a prohibition based on the lunar festivals (parvan): "On the festival days one should not take [food], nor should one eat meat; for on the festival days there are Rākṣasas, Piśācas, adulterers, and women with loose morals."
Manu says: On the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, the full moon, and during the sun's transit (saṅkrānti),
one should avoid oil, meat, and tooth-sticks for women.
On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, a wise man should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and shaving.
Hārīta says:
Misfortune (Alakṣmī) has always made her abode in the Śleṣmātaka tree;
she constantly dwells in the female organ, in meat, in razors, in oil, and on the sacred festival days (parvan).
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"He who cuts down creepers while the moon is situated in the constellation Viśākhā,
or who causes their leaves to fall, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."
"Vīrutsaṃsthe" means situated in a tree;
and being situated in a tree means remaining there for three muhūrtas and a fourth [muhūrta].
"The sun should remain for three muhūrtas; it should remain in water for three muhūrtas."
One should dwell among cows for three muhūrtas, and for three muhūrtas at a tree.
Thus says the Smṛti. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The evening twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), the food of another, and likewise sesame flour..."
On the new moon day, one should not engage in sexual intercourse or eating at night.

The meaning is "having reached the new moon day" (amāvāsyām). However, in reality, *amāvāsyām* is in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). [The etymology is: she who dwells (*vasati*) in her (*asyām*), or she who is the dwelling (*vāsī*); preceded by *amā*, it is also called *amā*.
Thus, the lunar day of Kṛṣṇapañcadaśī is said to be ninefold.
Thus, according to the *Kośa*:
"One should cut green *kuśa* grasses, as well as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), from the *nāma* [side]."
And this prohibition applies except for the sake of rites dedicated to the gods (daiva) and the ancestors (pitrya).
Thus, Kātyāyana, having stated the prohibition against cutting darbha grass on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), said:
Or one may collect [the grass] for the purpose of offerings to the ancestors, gods, and recitation;
likewise, in the Smṛti of Kātyāyana: "In the month of Nabhasya, on the new moon day, fresh darbha grass is prescribed to be taken."
Those Darbha grasses that have not lost their potency may be employed again and again.
Thus:
on the day of the new moon, a twice-born man should gather kuśa grass, vegetables, flowers, and grass for the sake of cattle, for the purpose of the gods and the ancestors.
And from the statement cited in the *Dīpikā*: "In the compendium of Smṛtis:
'The evening twilight prayer, food from another, eating again, and sexual intercourse...'"
One should avoid oil, meat, and substances ground on a stone on the new moon day.
Mārkaṇḍeya says:
On all new-moon days (amāvāsyā), one should not wear new clothing. Thus ends the section on things to be avoided on sacred festival days (parvan).
Now, regarding the specific times to be avoided,
the Skanda Purāṇa states: "A human skull, entrails, nails, skin, and likewise sesame seeds..."
One should avoid these [foods] regularly on the eighth day and other such occasions.
The head is the coconut;
the skull is the bottle gourd;
the intestine is the long patola.
Nakha means *niṣpāva* (flat beans) and *carmauma-sūrya*;
*tila* means *vṛntāka* (eggplant).
Hemādri states that this is known as the *bṛhatī-prasiddhi*.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"On the day of a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), on the fifteenth (*pañcadaśī*), on the twelfth (*dvādaśī*), and on the day of a *śrāddha*..."
One should not wring out one's garment, nor indeed should one be harmed even by a razor.
In Hemādri, however, the reading in the fourth quarter is "budhyate kareṇāpi hi" (it is perceived even by the hand). Vyāsa states:
"One should not touch raw oil, nor should one cut down trees and the like."
And at the beginning of a lunar fortnight, on Sundays, on the sixth lunar day, and likewise on the Riktā days.
In this context, the prohibition of oil is for the purpose of prohibiting more [substances], since there is a general prohibition of oil.
Bṛhaspati says:
"On the new moon, during the sun's passage into a zodiac sign (saṅkrānti), and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days..."
A man shall be born in the womb of a caṇḍāla by consuming oil, women, and meat.
In the Purāṇa, in the first half [of the work], it is said: "On the new moon, the full moon, the saṅkrānti, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days."
The latter half is the same as that [verse].
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"One should not perform an oil massage on the Nandā days, nor a haircut on the Riktā days, nor eat meat on the Jayā days."
A woman should be avoided when the lunar mansions are *pūrṇā*; one should undertake all activities when they are *bhadra*.

One should not perform an oil massage on Sunday nor on Tuesday; one should avoid milk on Friday and meat on Tuesday; one should not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman on Wednesday; on all other days, one may always practice all these things.
Oil and milk should be avoided under the asterisms Citrā, Hasta, and Śravaṇa, as well as on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) and under Viśākhā;
meat should be avoided under Mūla, Mṛgaśiras, the two Bhādrapadas, Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the three Uttarās; and sexual intercourse with women should be avoided under the same asterisms.
Yama says: Likewise, on the eighth days of the dark fortnights, on the fourteenth day, and on the new moon day,
one should avoid oil massage, shaving, and sexual union with women.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "A wise man should not take clay or water at night, nor cow-dung, nor cow-urine, during the evening twilight (pradoṣa)."
And this prohibition applies to rites other than those for purification and the like, since the taking of earth is prescribed for them.
Māṇḍavya says:
[The taking of earth is forbidden] during Vedic study, piercing [the ear], birth-rites, the first feeding of solid food, journeys, and the worship of images.
When Jupiter is situated in the house of the Sun, no marriage ceremony should be performed.
The abode of the Sun is the zodiac sign of Leo;
and this is on the northern side of the Narmadā, not the southern.
And so it is said:
In the science of astrology (Jyotiḥśāstra):
When Jupiter is in Leo, marriage is not desired in the Leo-lagna as far as the northern bank of the Godāvarī and as far as the southern bank of the Bhāgīrathī;
this same defect applies even when the Sun is in Aries.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Upon the death of a great guru (mahāguru), one should not perform bathing, great gifts, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors during the first year."
Desired bathing refers to bathing with flowers and the like.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* it is said:
"While Viṣṇu is asleep, all auspicious and other ritual acts are suspended."
The performance of marriage, the binding of vows, and other rites such as the tonsure ceremony and initiation.
Sacrifices, the entry into a new home, the consecration of deities and kings,
and whatever other meritorious rites there may be— none of these would take place while the Lord of the World is asleep.
Thus says Manu:
"One should avoid these four actions during the twilight (sandhyā)."
Food, sexual intercourse, sleep, and study as the fourth.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, sleep, ritual action, Vedic study, as well as giving and receiving gifts during the time of the twilights (saṃdhyā).
From eating [at an improper time], disease arises; from sexual intercourse, a fierce fetus is conceived;
from sleeping [during the day], one becomes unfortunate; and in this case, even religious action is fruitless.
The student goes to hell, and the donor does not obtain the fruit thereof;
one becomes sinful by accepting [such a gift], therefore one should avoid the twilight [period].
Likewise, the Smṛti in the Hemādri states:
"One should never, under any circumstances, perform a gift at night;
for the Rākṣasas seize it, and therefore it brings fear to the giver."
Especially at midnight, a virtuous deed does not lead to well-being;
therefore, a wise person should avoid the middle of the night for acts such as giving.
An exception to this has been stated by Devala:

"One should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at night during an eclipse, at the passage of the sun into a new sign (saṅkrānti), at weddings, during times of calamity, on occasions of prosperity, and during optional vows."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"In the cases of eclipses, weddings, transits [of the sun], journeys, calamities, and childbirth, giving is to be known as occasional (naimittika); that is permitted even at night."
Likewise:
"These gifts are recommended at a sacrifice, a wedding, a journey, or when reading a book; likewise, they are recommended at night or in a temple."
Likewise, in the Hemādri:
"The Aśvattha tree and the ocean should be honored, but never touched;
one should touch the former on a Wednesday and the latter on the full moon."
Koṇa is Saturn (Śanaiścara). Regarding the prohibition of oil massage, it was stated by Sumantu:
"Oil massage should not be performed on Sunday, nor on Tuesday, nor during a solar transit (saṅkrānti), nor during the Vaidhṛti yoga, nor on the Viṣṭi karana, nor on the sixth lunar day."
On the festival days and on the eighth day, that [observance] is not desired; it is desired only on the day of the Sun's son (Saturday), excluding those [days] previously mentioned.
Yogiyājñavalkya states: "He who, out of delusion, applies oil for anointing on the Pratipadā, the sixth lunar day, the new moon (Kuhū), or a Riktā tithi, is deprived of four things."
On the fifth, the fourteenth, and the seventh [lunar days], on the sun's transit (saṅkrānti),
and on the twelfth, seventh, and sixth [lunar days], one should avoid contact with oil.
One should not perform an oil massage on the thirteenth, the third, the first, or the ninth lunar days; however, one may do so on the other days except for the ninth.
And as it is said:
"The fifth, the tenth, the third, the thirteenth, the eleventh, and the second— these [days] of both fortnights [are sacred]."
Whoever indulges in affection here through acts such as anointing and touching shall experience an increase in four things: wealth, progeny, strength, and longevity.
Thus, according to Garga, the mention of certain [days] refers specifically to oil cooked with those [substances];
this applies even when the days of the week such as Sunday and Friday, as well as the prohibited lunar dates (*tithis*), are involved.
Whether one has bathed or not bathed, cooked oil does not become defiled.
Thus, according to some, this is based on the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
Others, however, hold that the prohibition concerns oil obtained through desire (*rāgaprāpta*);
and thus, when a prohibition against all oil would otherwise apply, cooking [with it] is here provided as an exception (*pratiprasava*).
And when an oil massage is prescribed, even raw [oil] is indeed to be used; this is the summary.
Yama also says:
"Ghee, mustard oil, and whatever oil is scented with flowers..."
There is no fault in constantly using cooked oils for bathing and anointing the body.
Kātyāyana also says: "An auspicious bath performed on occasions of prosperity, festivals, and celebrations, when combined with even a small amount of oil, is superior to one taken at midday."
Thus,
regarding the time for the prohibition of meat, the Nandipurāṇa states:
"If indeed one should always avoid meat on the fourteenth day..."
A man whose mind is set on attaining heaven should avoid [the practice] during the primary solstice.
The fourth, the eighth, the twelfth, the fourteenth,
as well as the fifteenth, and the six "mouths" (aśītimukha) [of the lunar month], are to be avoided.
Furthermore, at the transition of the sun, at the equinoxes, and during the rainy season,
a mortal who abstains from meat goes to heaven for three days.
Likewise, one should avoid eating meat during the month of Āśvayuja;
by doing so, a person shall obtain the merit accumulated over many months.
By renouncing the consumption of meat, a person becomes pure in mind;
that man who completely avoids meat during the month of Kārttika [attains this purity].
One obtains the merit of a year by abstaining from meat;

however, in the *Kālanirṇayadīpikā*, instead of the reading "yadi nāma caturdaśyām" (if indeed on the fourteenth day), the reading is "yadi nāma ca śarvaryām" (if indeed during the night). Thus end the specific prohibitions regarding time.

Now, regarding the duties to be performed on the lunar festival days (parvan): Viṣṇu states—on the festival days, one must certainly perform oblations with sesame seeds, remain adorned, and thus be a follower of right conduct.
Manu (4.150) says:
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations on the festival days (parvan).
"Sāvitra" refers to those having Savitṛ as their deity.
In this case, the ritual substance (dravya) is unbroken grains (akṣata).
"One who desires peace should, being pure, offer oblations with unbroken rice grains while reciting the Gāyatrī," according to the Smṛti.
Kātyāyana says:
Sleeping on the ground is prescribed on the full moon and new moon days;
this rule applies even to one who has not maintained the sacred fires, and it is prescribed after the fire-rituals have been performed.
"One who has not maintained the [Śrauta] fires" means one who possesses the Smārta fire.
Āpastamba states: "By day the sun protects beings;
by night the moon. Therefore, on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), one should especially desire protection for oneself."
"By means of the vow pertaining to Prajāpati and by the period of celibacy, Sūrya and Candramas dwell this night together with his wife.
"By the vow pertaining to Prajāpati" means by being free from approaching a woman other than one's own wife.
Thus it is said:
On the new moon day of the month of Nabhas, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed;
that darbha grass, being of undiminished potency, may be used again and again.
Thus end the duties to be performed on the festival days (parvan). Now follow the characteristics of the various Yugas.
Regarding this, Aupakāyana says:
Revelation, purity, and conduct vary from time to time;
diverse dharmas prevail among human beings in age after age.

The means of valid cognition, such as the Vedas, and conduct, such as ritual purity, differ according to each time-period and each age. With the first half of this verse, the difference in the rituals—such as the *agnihotra*—denoted by the term "conduct" for each age is stated; and because of that very difference in those rituals, the difference in the means of valid cognition, such as the Vedas, which establish them is also stated. He states the reason for that difference in rituals with the second half of the verse, beginning with "nānādharmāḥ" (various duties).

The qualities [of the age] are health and so forth; as it was stated by Manu (A. 1, Śl. 83–84): "They were free from disease, accomplished in all their aims, and possessed a lifespan of four hundred years."
However, in the Kṛta, Tretā, and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
The lifespan declared for mortals in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to each successive age.
Thus it is said;
likewise, in the Araṇyaka Parvan, during the encounter with Hanumān, after citing the dharmas of the Kṛta age and others, it is stated:
"With one foot alone, O Kaunteya..."
Dharma remains established in the Kali Yuga;
having reached the Tāmasa age, Keśava becomes dark-complexioned.
The practices prescribed by the Vedas cease, as do the performance of dharma-sacrifices;
likewise, calamities, diseases, lethargy, faults such as anger,
and other afflictions, mental anxieties, and even the fear of hunger prevail.
Thus, this is the meaning:

for the twice-born, whose powers of the organs of knowledge and action diminish day by day due to the inherent nature of the age (yuga), [the performance of] rites such as the Agnihotra is accompanied only by a few constituent parts.

The intention is this: due to negligence, laziness, and so forth, because of the loss of various constituent parts, those [Vedic texts] which do not recognize [the identity] in its true nature appear as if they were different; thus, there arises an appearance of difference even in the Śruti and other sources that expound that [identity].
However, there is no real, ontological difference between the Śruti and the like, nor among the ritual acts themselves. It is by this very method that statements of this kind are to be understood.
Manu also says (A. 1, Ślokas 85–86):
"The duties in the Kṛta age are of one kind; in the Tretā, knowledge is said to be the primary one;
and in the Kali age, they are different for men, according to the decline of the ages."
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone is supreme.
*Austerity* (*tapas*) refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such practices. As it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
That which consists of the emaciation of the body through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such methods prescribed in the Vedas is called "tapas" by the wise.
Thus;
"supreme" means the primary [principle].
In the Mahābhārata:
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is best;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is paramount; and in the Kali age, charity alone is the highest path.
Likewise:
"In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā, knowledge is best;
in the Dvāpara, they say sacrifice alone [is best]; but in the Kali age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are supreme]."
Bṛhaspati says:

In the Kṛta age, austerity is the dharma; in the Tretā age, knowledge is established; in the Dvāpara, sacrifice is proclaimed; and in the Tiṣya (Kali) age, charity, compassion, and self-restraint [are the dharma].
Tiṣya is Kali. In the Śiva Purāṇa:
"Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta Yuga; in the Tretā Yuga, the worship of the Liṅga."
In the Dvāpara age, there is the study of scripture; in the Tiṣya age, the glorification of Mahādeva.
Likewise:
"Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age, and likewise sacrifice in the Tretā;
worship of the Liṅga in the Dvāpara, and the chanting of Śaṅkara’s praises in the Kali age."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Supreme knowledge [prevails] in the Kṛta age, and after that in the Tretā;
likewise, sacrifice in the Dvāpara, but in the Kali age, however, it is ritual installation."

Parāśara states the authoritative sources that prevail predominantly in the Kṛta and other ages: "In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu are authoritative; in the Tretā age, those of Gautama are considered so."
In the Dvāpara age, the codes of Śaṅkha and Likhita were remembered; in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are remembered.

Regarding the statement that "in the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme," and so forth, he states the reason for this: "In the Kṛta age, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā age, they have taken refuge in the flesh."
In the Dvāpara age they abide in blood, and in the Kali age they abide in food and other such things.
Prāṇa is a specific type of wind endowed with the fivefold functions beginning with inhalation (prāṇana);
bound by the thread of karma within bodies composed of bone, flesh, and so forth, it remains situated within the bones and other parts through the power of the [karmic] age.

He states that the prohibition of those statements which do not serve as a direct means for engagement or withdrawal, but rather explain the nature of the ages (*yuga*) and so forth, results in a specific conclusion—
namely, that very [text]:
"In each age, whatever duties exist, and in each place, whatever twice-born ones (*dvija*) there may be..."
One should not speak ill of them, for those twice-born ones are indeed like the [current] age itself.

The phrase "of them" (*teṣām*) is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that, having recognized all defects such as desire, anger, greed, and so forth to be produced by time, one should not censure anyone.
But if this is so—
In the Kali age, righteousness is indeed conquered by unrighteousness, and truth by falsehood; kings are overcome by spies, and men by women.
Regarding the irreproachability of living beings who follow the *yuga-dharma* (the duties of the age) as indicated by such statements:
"Practice righteousness, speak the truth;
there is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood."
For truth is the foundation of dharma; therefore, one should not violate the truth.

If it be argued that scriptural texts of the Śruti and Smṛti which concern injunctions and prohibitions— such as those cited above— would thereby be rendered invalid, we say no. For those who, having considered their own respective capacities in accordance with the particular age (yuga), perform the obligatory and occasional rites either by the primary method or by a secondary substitute,
and who avoid what is prohibited, and who perform penances for sins committed through negligence, or even those who are utterly incapable [of performing rites], there is no blame.
Thus, the fact that others are censurable is established as a matter of reality;
yet even though this is so, one should not personally disclose the faults of even those who are censurable—this is the intended meaning of the statement that "one should not practice their censure.
Bṛhaspati says:
In the Kṛta age, that which constitutes a year's worth of dharma occurs there in the Tretā age in three seasons;
in the Dvāpara, it occurs in three fortnights, and in the Kali age, it occurs in a single day.
