In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "The dharma that lasts for a year in the Tretā age is recorded as lasting for a month in the Dvāpara age;
by practicing it according to one's ability, a wise person may attain its fruit in a single day during the Kali age."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"That which [is accomplished] in ten years during the Kṛta age, in one year during the Tretā,
and in one month during the Dvāpara, is accomplished in a single day and night during the Kali."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the Kṛta age, the god is Brahmā; in the Tretā, the Lord is Ravi (the Sun);
in the Dvāpara, the Lord is Viṣṇu; and in the Kali age, the god is Maheśvara."
In the Kṛta age, the subtle Nārāyaṇa is worshipped in his pure form;
in the Tretā age, he is worshipped in the form of sacrifice; and in the Dvāpara age, by means of the Pāñcarātra.
In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "Keśava is worshipped according to various rituals in the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages,
assuming diverse colors, names, and forms."
In the Kṛta age, he was white, four-armed, with matted hair, clad in bark garments,
wearing a black antelope skin as a sacred thread, and carrying a variegated staff and water-pot.
At that time, humans were peaceful, free from enmity, friendly, and impartial;
they worshipped the Divine through austerity, tranquility, and self-restraint.
Vaikuṇṭha, who has the color of a swan, the excellent Lord of Yoga, the stainless one, the Sovereign, the Puruṣa, the unattached one— He is celebrated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).

In the Tretā age, he is red in color, four-armed, and wears three girdles; he has golden hair, embodies the three Vedas, and is characterized by the sacrificial ladle (sruk), the dipping-spoon (sruva), and other such implements.
Then those most righteous men, exponents of the Veda, worship that Lord Hari— who embodies all the gods— with the threefold knowledge.
Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pṛśnigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama, Vṛṣākapi, Jayanta, and Urugāya— thus he is proclaimed.
In the Dvāpara age, the Blessed One is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, bearing his own weapons,
and distinguished by the Śrīvatsa and other such marks.
O Great King, mortals who desire to know the Supreme worship that Puruṣa, characterized as the Great King, according to both the Vedas and the Tantras, O Ruler.
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, Pradyumna and Aniruddha.
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the seer, the primordial person, the great-souled one; to the Lord of the universe, the universe itself, whose self is all beings.
Thus, in the Dvāpara age, they praise the Lord of the Earth as the Lord of the World.
Listen now to how, even in the Kali age, [one may worship] by means of the rites of various tantras:
[one should meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, endowed with a dark complexion, together with his limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants.
For the wise indeed worship with sacrifices consisting primarily of congregational chanting;
thus does the Blessed One manifest according to the age by those who abide in that age.
"O King, Hari, the lord of all blessings, is worshipped by men," as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara should be resorted to in the Kṛta age, likewise Naimiṣa in the Tretā;
Kurukṣetra in the Dvāpara, but in the Kali age one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā.
Vāmadeva said:
"In the Kṛta age all sacred fords are supreme; in the Tretā age, Puṣkara is the best; in the Dvāpara age, Kurukṣetra; but in the Kali age, the Gaṅgā is distinguished as the most excellent."
Thus end the various duties of the different ages.
Now, regarding the things to be avoided in the different ages, Śātātapa says:
One should abandon the country in the Kṛta Yuga, leave the village in the Tretā Yuga,
the family in the Dvāpara Yuga, but in the Kali Yuga, one should abandon the doer himself.
In the Kṛta age, one falls by mere conversation; in the Tretā, by touch;
in the Dvāpara, by taking food; and in the Kali, by the performance of the act itself.
Thus end the things to be avoided in the various yugas. Now, the characteristics of the Kali Yuga,
as stated in the Mahābhārata:
Whoever worships Śaṅkara even once at a single time with this mantra, "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya," is liberated from all sins.
Even if he has reached every possible state or is joined with all manner of sins,
that man in the Kali age who [utters] "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya" is indeed liberated.
Even a salutation offered with deceit to the wielder of the trident brings about the destruction of the multitude of defects of saṃsāra in the Kali age.
Likewise:
"O best of sages, he who always worships him with faith—
whether in a linga or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even in a consecrated image— according to the prescribed ritual,"
Having completely conquered the defects of the age, he rejoices in the world of Rudra.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "In the Kali age, Rudra is Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita."
He of transformed form manifests for the sake of the establishment of the Dharma.
Those wise ones who serve Śaṅkara by any means whatsoever,
having utterly conquered the defects of the Kali age, proceed to the supreme state.
Vyāsa says: What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the name of Keśava.
In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa:
"The noble ones, who recognize virtues and partake of the essence, celebrate the Kali age,
for in it every personal goal is attained through mere chanting."
By the chanting of the names of Hari— that is, by chanting the names of the Supreme Lord—
there is indeed no gain higher than this for embodied beings wandering here in this world;
for through it one attains supreme peace, and the cycle of worldly existence perishes.
In the *Agnipurāṇa*:
"O Sage, in this terrible age of darkness (Tāmasa Yuga), which is devoid of sacrifices and gods, there is nothing that brings greater welfare to men than the propitiation of Viṣṇu."
O King, in the Kali age, one should perform worship of Vāsudeva;

for the fruit that was obtained by worshipping Hari with devotion according to the prescribed rites for a hundred years in the Kṛta age, O monarch, is obtained in the Kali age in a single day and night.
Likewise:
Those men who constantly worship Hari, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age and the remover of all sins, they too are to be revered just as Hari is.
In the Kali age, a man who knows the Dharma attains an exceedingly high degree of merit with very little effort; therefore, I am pleased with the Kali age.
O Brahmins, in this blessed Kali age, great fruit is obtained with little effort.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"In the Kali age, kings desiring to attain the heavenly world must construct cities filled with the abodes of the deities."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"One should resort to the Gaṅgā alone, especially at Prayāga;
for nothing else is able to destroy the extremely difficult-to-remedy impurity produced by the Kali age."
From the *Skanda-purāṇa* and the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*: "If a man desires the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation through an easy means,
the wise one should resort to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) alone in the Kali age, and especially to the Gaṅgā."
In Kāśī, the Gaṅgā flows northward and my Liṅga is Viśveśvara;
both grant liberation when the conflagration of the Kali age arrives.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"The great sages have declared that, in the Kali age, the worship of the Gaṅgā alone is the supreme and swift means for men to attain the highest Brahman."
In the *Kāmikasaṃhitā*:
"The perfection of Vedic mantras does not occur for one devoid of purity;
without mantras, wisdoms do not succeed, yet purity is difficult to attain."
In this Kali age, especially, no pure thing is seen;
for in the terrifying Kali Yuga, dharma has been destroyed by darkness.
For the stream of dharma is indeed the Ganges, its continuity unbroken;
otherwise, how could there be a path consisting of dharma in the Kali age without the Gaṅgā?
Better for him to have his head cut off or even to give up his life.
But he who, being capable, does not go to the Gaṅgā in this Kali age, [is lost].
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "In the Kali age, for those of defiled minds, whose souls delight in sinful things,
and who perform rites devoid of scriptural injunctions, there is no destination other than the Gaṅgā."
Indeed, he who desires liberation in the Kali age without resorting to the Gaṅgā is like one born blind who strives here to see the sun.
In this Kali age, the lineage, learning, sacrifices, asceticism, and gifts of one who does not go to the Gaṅgā are all in vain.
Thus end the characteristics of the Kali Yuga. Now, regarding the things to be avoided in the Kali Yuga,
it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Long-term celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),

marriage with a woman from one's own lineage or from the maternal sapinda-lineage, the killing of cows, the human sacrifice, the horse sacrifice, and liquor— these are to be avoided by the twice-born in the Kali age.
Likewise:

"In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a married woman, the inheritance of the eldest brother's share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother's wife, and the use of a water-pot."
Kratu said: "The procreation of sons by means of a brother-in-law is permitted; a daughter once given away is not to be returned.
In the Kali age, the slaughter of a cow at a sacrifice must not be performed, nor is the use of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) allowed."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Oaths, omens, dreams, physiognomy, portents, vows,
and prophecies occur only occasionally in the Kali age."

Therefore, one should not perform that action which can be accomplished merely by obtaining those [essential materials]. Likewise, due to the conventions of those who know the Dharma, other things as well are to be avoided in the Kali age:
the appointment of a brother-in-law for the procreation of offspring upon a widow;
And for one whose womb has been damaged by sand, union with another man occurs through a boon.
Marriage by twice-born men with girls of a different caste, and the killing of murderous aggressors— even those who are the best of the twice-born— by means of righteous warfare;
The inclusion of a twice-born man who has traveled by boat upon the ocean— even if he has been purified—
and the initiation for a sacrificial session (sattra) for all castes, as well as the carrying of the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), [are likewise forbidden].
The Great Departure, the instruction regarding the cow in the Gosava sacrifice,
and the inclusion of the taking of *surā* liquor in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
The licking of the Agnihotra ladle, the consumption of what has been licked, and the entry into the forest-dweller's stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) as prescribed by rule; all these are permitted.
Likewise, the reduction of impurity (aghasaṅkocana) is dependent upon one's conduct and Vedic study;
and there is the prescription of penance for Brahmins that ends with death.
The fault of social association, the expiation for theft and other mortal sins (mahāpātakas),
and the ritual of preparing animals for sacrifice for the sake of gods, guests, and ancestors.

The adoption of sons other than the *datta* and *aurasa* types is permitted for those of the same caste (*savarṇa*), provided they have not been corrupted by association with the wicked, even if they have already been purified.
(*1) There is an alternative reading in the *Nirṇayasindhu* and other works: "by those corrupted by women of the same caste.
When sexual intercourse occurs in a non-vaginal opening, there is the abandonment of the elder’s wife.
Also included are the renunciation of one's own self for the sake of another and the avoidance of even the remnants of food.
The formal resolve (saṅkalpa) accompanied by its ritual rules for the purpose of worshipping the image,
as well as the touching of the limbs [of the deceased], take place after the collection of the bones.
Serving as the slaughterer for Brahmins, selling Soma, eating the food of those who have fasted for six meals, and taking food from one of low-caste occupation; these are [grounds for loss of caste].
Among Śūdras, the food of slaves, cowherds, family friends, and those who till half the field may be eaten by a householder; however, he must avoid visiting their sacred bathing places from afar.
A disciple’s conduct toward the wife of his guru should be practiced as he would toward the guru himself;
likewise, for the best of the twice-born, there is the practice of subsisting in times of distress and the state of not providing for the morrow.

The acceptance of wives from among the twice-born for the sake of progeny, the wandering of Brahmins, and the practice of blowing upon the sacrificial fire with the mouth— all these are for the purpose of the people.
The forcible abduction of a wicked woman is prescribed by rule;
likewise, for an ascetic, the practice of begging alms from all castes is ordained by rule.
When water is newly poured out, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is directed by the preceptor for ten days.
Even for a Śūdra, there is the performance of cooking and other such acts for Brāhmaṇas and others;
likewise, there is death by leaping from a precipice or into fire, as well as the death of the elderly and so forth.
The practice of sipping water (ācamana) by the learned from milk that remains after they have satisfied their thirst;
the determination of punishment for witnesses in disputes between fathers and sons.

And the practice of the ascetic returning home in the evening— these were established at the beginning of the Kali age by the high-souled sages intent on the ultimate truth for the sake of protecting the world.
Actions have been established by the wise according to fixed rules;
and the agreement of the virtuous shall be authoritative, just like the Veda.

In another Purāṇa: "In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a woman already married, the granting of the eldest son's special share, the killing of a cow, approaching a brother's wife, and [carrying] a water-pot."
In the *Nigama* as well: "Unhusked grain, cattle, meat at a *śrāddha*, honey,
and procreation through the husband's brother— these five one should avoid in the Kali age."
Vyāsa said:
When four thousand and four hundred years of the Kali age have passed, then the adoption of the Tretā [dharma] will occur.
And renunciation should not be undertaken by a wise Brāhmaṇa. Devala says:
"As long as the distinction of castes exists, and as long as the Veda continues to prevail..."
One should perform both the Agnihotra sacrifice and renunciation during the Kali Yuga.
Laukāxi says: "The *ardhādhāna* is recorded as the separate establishment of the Śrauta and Smārta fires;
the *sarvādhāna* is their combined establishment, which was practiced in former ages."
Thus end the things to be avoided in the Kali age.
Now, the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*).
In the *Kālottara*:
The conjunction of autumn and spring is prescribed for the ritual procedure of initiation;
in their absence, however, even the rainy season is commended, provided it is not otherwise.
The phrase "the conjunction of autumn and spring" means in both autumn and spring.
Regarding the results for those months, it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "Failure, attainment of land, death, and the destruction of kinsmen."
The increase of lifespan, the destruction of progeny, prosperity, and the accumulation of jewels.

The attainment of auspiciousness, loss of position, gain of intelligence and wealth, and subjugation—these are to be known as the results for those born in Caitra and the subsequent months; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
Regarding the causes, however, the results of the months are stated otherwise:
"The commencement of a mantra in the month preceding Vaiśākha is very difficult to endure;
in Vaiśākha it bestows wealth, but in Jyeṣṭha it becomes a giver of death."
In Āṣāḍha, it is for the attainment of a son; in Śrāvaṇa, it is considered to bestow auspiciousness;
in Bhādrapada, there is a loss of knowledge, and likewise, non-attainment is proclaimed.
In Āśvina there is the accomplishment of all goals; Kārttika bestows the attainment of knowledge;
Mārgaśīrṣa shall be the bringer of auspiciousness; and Pauṣa is the cause of suffering.
In Māgha there is an increase in intelligence, and in Phālguna there is mastery over all.
Thus [it is said].
Here, because the previous statement described Āṣāḍha as yielding undesirable results while this one describes it as having correct results, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, there is a specific distinction.
Initiation during the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit;
initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling in this regard.
The months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Māgha are esteemed as the youngest by the virtuous;
whereas the month of Caitra, as well as Pauṣa and Bhādrapada, are censured.
Initiation is declared to be auspicious even during censured months, as well as during eclipses;
according to the *Kāraṇa*:
"In the month preceding Āṣāḍha, in Āṣāḍha, and in Mārgaśīrṣaka."
The wise one should not perform initiation during other months; he should perform it during [the appropriate] months.
"In the bright fortnight, under an auspicious asterism, and likewise on a favorable day and lunar date.
However, in the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*, it says:
Initiation should not take place except on a festival day, nor during the rainy season, nor in the months of Madhu and Pauṣa;
however, it may always be performed at other times for the sake of purifying both teacher and disciple.
"Indeed, having observed auspicious omens at the beginning of the rainy season...

Thus Hemādri states that even during times forbidden for the commencement of the year and so forth, if favorable omens such as auspicious portents are perceived, the *dakṣiṇā* (the ritual fee) should be performed;
this is stated in the *Agastisaṃhitā*:
"Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, initiation brings all happiness.
This is the specific rule in the *Kālottara*.

"The commencement of initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed by those desiring prosperity during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and by those desiring liberation during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
However, in the Saṃhitā it is said:
The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh,
as well as the thirteenth and the tenth— these are praised as bestowing all desires.
Thus it is said;
and elsewhere as well:
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth, or on a day of the five parvans."
Thus,
in the *Mantrasārasaṅgraha*: "The second, the fifth, and especially the sixth [lunar days]..."
It should be performed on the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Mantraratnāvalī*:
"The fourth, the ninth, the sixth, the eighth, and the fourteenth [lunar days]..."
Except for the full moon day, the remaining days are beneficial for those seeking liberation in their quest for freedom.
In the Hemādri, another Smṛti states:
"The rite of initiation (dīkṣā) is recommended on the seventh, the ninth, the eleventh, as well as the tenth, or the thirteenth lunar day."
In some places, however, the reading is "on the thirteenth or the new moon";
one should examine the white [Venus], the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter according to their merits and demerits.
"One should accept her who is endowed with virtues, but one should avoid her who is devoid of virtues.
Here, *sita* means *śukra* (semen).
The "knower" (jña) is the wise one.

By means of the merits and defects of these [planets]—arising from the conjunction of lunar days and weekdays; appearing as rising, setting, retrogression, or exceeding motion; and existing in the form of positions in the angles (kendras), trines (trikoṇas), the sixth, the eighth, or the twelfth houses at the time of initiation (dīkṣā)—[one should judge].
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
On the fourth, or the eighth, or likewise on the fourteenth,
or on the full moon day, this should always be performed during the bright fortnight by those desiring prosperity.
Those desiring liberation should perform whatever rite they may during the dark fortnight,
except on the days of the lunar intercalations (dinacchidra) and those other lunar days that are traditionally prohibited.
Thus,
there is a specific rule in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"Having carefully considered each respective lunar day (*tithi*), one should initiate those who are devoted to that [deity] on that very day."
Indra said:
"O Nārada, tell me in brief: for whom is which lunar day (tithi) prescribed? Nārada replied:
The full moon day is prescribed for Brahmā; the twelfth day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu);
the fourteenth day is prescribed for Śiva; and the thirteenth day is declared for Vāc.
The second is declared to be Śrī, while the third belongs to Pārvatī;
among the paths of Pārvatī, the eighth and the fourteenth are eternal.
The fourth lunar day is declared for Gaṇanātha, and the seventh for Bhānu;
thus, O Lord of the Gods, the principal lunar days have been defined.
Thus, in the *Ratnāvalī*:
"For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya, Maṅgala, and Sauri."
Thus it is said;
however, in the *Saṃhitā*:
"It should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Friday, Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday."
Thus; "in the white" means during the bright fortnight.
In the *Saṃhitā*—
One should perform the consecration with mantras under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, Hasta, and likewise under Jyeṣṭhā and the three Uttaras.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "The three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Maghā, Mūla, and Revatī."
The fourteenth lunar day, when conjoined with the asterisms Abhijit and Śravaṇa, is a Śiva-yoga.
Regarding the causes: the asterisms of Revatī, Rohiṇī, Āditya (Punarvasu), Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, Sāvitra (Hasta),
Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Vāyavya (Svātī), Aindra (Jyeṣṭhā), and Nairṛta (Mūlā).
O observer of noble vows, the constellations Tiṣya (Puṣya), the three Uttarās, Ārdrā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and the birth-star of the disciple are recommended for the rite of initiation.
Thus:
Pauṣṇa is Revatī;
Āditya is Punarvasu.
Sāvitra is Hasta;
Tvāṣṭra is Citrā;
Vāyavya is Svāti.
Aindra is Jyeṣṭhā;
Nairṛta is Mūla;
Saumya is Mṛgaśīrṣaka.
The "birth asterism of the three [types of] disciples" refers to the tenth, nineteenth, and twenty-ninth asterisms from the disciple's birth asterism.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Puṣya, and Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā)."
Dhaniṣṭhā, Vāyu, Mitra, Agni, Pitrya, Tvāṣṭra, and Nairṛta.
"The hands of Īśa and Viṣṇu are indeed auspicious for initiation.
Thus it is said.
The yogas are also described in the Ratnāvalī:
And the yogas are remembered as Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya,
Śobhana, Sukarmā, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
The most excellent are Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Indra—the sixteen [deities].
All those [other forms] are to be censured; these alone are praised for the sake of liberation.
The first lunar day (pratipad) is with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the fifth is likewise with Kṛttikā;
the sixth is with Pūrvābhādrapadā, and the tenth is likewise with Rohiṇī.
The twelfth lunar day with all the asterisms, and the thirteenth with the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa—
these are known as the "asterism-conjunctions" (nakṣatrayoga), which bring prosperity even to the gods.
"One should especially avoid Śakuni and the others, as well as Viṣṭi.
Thus [it is said] regarding the cause.
The movable signs are considered excellent, while those that are both [movable and fixed] are middling;
and all planets are avoided when situated in the eighth house (the house of death).
When there is mutual compatibility between the teacher and the disciple, it will bring about auspicious results.

In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*: "The purification of the zodiac signs and other divisions, as well as the strength of the ascendant, the Moon, and the Sun, and the determination of their positions according to the *gocara* system, should be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*)."
Indeed, all defects of the ascendant and defects of the planets are destroyed when Venus is mature and situated in the ascendant,
or when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant.
Having carefully examined [the candidate] in this manner and other ways, the preceptor should perform initiation;
however, for one seeking liberation, no restriction of time is prescribed.
Thus,
the wise one should combine the accomplished (siddha) and well-accomplished (susiddha) letters from among the syllables of the mantra;
he should multiply the hostile (vairi) and neutral (udāsīna) letters separately by ten.
One should divide the heap of Siddhas by eight, twelve, and six;
having established it in three places, that which remains as the remainder is indeed declared to be the number of Yāmas.
Having established three [units] here, whatever remains is indeed declared to be the number of watches (yāma).
The remaining month, when situated in the sign of the enemy, is thus proclaimed;
it removes a fifteenth part solely for the sake of knowing the lunar day (tithi).
In that month and at such a watch, one should perform the formal reception of the mantra;
or, having been initiated, one should do so at a lagna determined by the science of astrology.
Thus it is said;
this is what is meant:

having accepted a single square consisting of four compartments within the grid-circle (*koṣṭhacakra*) for the syllables of the mantra to be given, according to the divisions of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *vairin*.

Having separated them, one should combine the letters of the *siddha* and *susiddha* categories among them; then, having multiplied each of the letters of the *sādhya* and *vairi* categories by ten, one should place all these resulting figures separately in three locations and divide the first by eight.
The remainder corresponds to the watch (*yāma*).
When [the total] is thus divided by twelve, the remainder corresponds to the month;
when divided by fifteen, the remainder corresponds to the lunar day (tithi).
On that day, during that specific hour of that month in the bright fortnight, one should impart the mantra.
In the initiation for those seeking liberation (mumukṣu-dīkṣā), the specific rule is that the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is [preferred].
As stated in the Ratnāvalī:
"All those [times] which are censured are praised for the sake of liberation."
In the *Saṃhitā*:
"On a day pure in its five components, during its own rising, when the lunar day and the weekday are auspicious,
when Jupiter and Venus are rising, and when the ascendant is purified by the twelve [houses]."
When Venus is waxing and endowed with strength, and likewise Jupiter;
when there is an auspicious conjunction with the Moon, and [the planet] is in an auspicious varga at an auspicious rising.
"In such passages as these, there is a compendium of all mantras that brings about all happiness.
Likewise, elsewhere:
On the birthday of a disciple, during the transit of the sun, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, on other meritorious conjunctions, and during lunar or solar eclipses.
"Or, at a time favorable to the disciple, purification of the body brings about auspiciousness.
Thus it is said in the Mahākāpila Pañcarātra.

Thus, when the lunar mansion, lunar day, and so forth, as well as the *karaṇa* and *yoga* day are auspicious, the instruction of mantras by the Guru and the practice of sādhana bring about prosperity.
Thus;
the ellipsis is "to be performed by the teacher.
"Sādhana" means the commencement of the practice (*sādhanārambha*).
The word "kāryam" (should be performed) is the ellipsis. Now follows an exception to the previously mentioned time for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
In the *Agastisaṃhitā*:
At the time of a solar eclipse, however, nothing else need be sought;
there is nothing whatsoever equal to the time of a solar eclipse.
"In that regard, whatever is performed there shall all yield infinite fruit.
Thus,
on the solar festival (sūryaparvan), there is no need for the calculation of months, lunar days, weekdays, and so forth.
He gives what is desired and accepted by the teacher among men at that time.
Success in the mantra occurs without effort and with speed;
it should be accomplished with every possible exertion by those desiring the attainment of the mantra.
Thus;
the connection is that at that time, whatever was received from the Guru, that bestows what is desired among men.
As stated in another treatise:

One who is performing a mantra-initiation at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), during an eclipse of the sun or moon, or on the festivals of Tantudāma and Parvan, need not purify the month, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), and so forth.
At another time—
during initiation, consecration, as well as the formal acceptance of mantras,
at the commencement and conclusion of vows, and during the ritual undertaking of substances.
On the full moon day of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of Rāhu (Svarbhānu),
during lunar and solar eclipses, and at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods.
During the conjunctions of planets and lunar mansions, at the equinoxes, during festivals, and at all solstices, the practice [of yoga] grants the accomplishment of all goals.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*: "The well-known lunar days, the sighting of Rāhu, the festivals of the Guru,
and the day of the Pavitraka rite are supreme for the performance of the ritual of initiation."
Thus:
"the well-known" refers to the lunar days (tithis) just mentioned;
as stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:

Initiation should be performed at the times of the equinoxes, the two solstices, on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, during the Damanaka festival, and for the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
Thus it is said;
and elsewhere as well:
"In a holy pilgrimage site, at Kurukṣetra, and in the four seats of the Goddess (devīpīṭha)."
At Prayāga, Śrīgiri, and Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the proper and improper times.
The four seats of the Goddess (devīpīṭha) are known as Uḍḍīyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇāgiri, and Kāmarūpa.
Some say that "Śrīgirau" refers to Śrīparvata;
it is also found elsewhere.

During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the birth of the disciple, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn, and at a time of [the Guru's] compassion—these are required for initiation; however, regarding the constellations and so forth, they are not considered necessary for the initiation.
Thus, it is said in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"Listen now to the specific occasion for initiation even without regard for the lunar day (*tithi*)."
For when the rare opportunity of even a single meeting with true gurus has arisen, [one must seize it].
Having obtained his permission, that great occasion for initiation should be granted—
whether in a village or a forest, in a sacred field, by day or by night.
When the Guru arrives by chance, then initiation should take place;
whenever there is a desire, then initiation occurs in accordance with the Guru’s command.

Neither the lunar day, nor water, nor fire-offerings, nor ritual bathing, nor the practice of recitation are the causes for initiation; rather, the cause is the attainment of a true Guru according to one's own desire.
In this regard, some say that initiation (dīkṣā) should not be performed during a lunar eclipse, as it would result in dullness (jaḍatva).

However, they are to be disregarded because they contradict the numerous statements of the sages, such as: "At a sacred bathing place during a solar or lunar eclipse," "And during eclipses of the moon and sun," "During the seizure of the moon and the sun," and "The sight of Rāhu and the festival of the Guru."
The specific rule for the Viṣṇu-initiation is stated in the Pañcarātra:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, or likewise at the sun's transit (saṅkramaṇa)..."
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, or on the full moon day, O Sage.
Likewise, on the new moon day, the preceptor, having determined the time,
should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) one, two, three, or even nine days prior.
Also in the *Tattvatantrasāgarasaṃhitā*:
"The full moon day is declared for Brahmā; the twelfth day [is sacred] for the Wielder of the Discus."

Thus, it is said that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Viṣṇu should be performed during the times of planetary ingress (*grahaṇa*) and so forth, as well as on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the aforementioned months.
These are the times for initiation. Now follows the time for the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Now, in all rites, one should mutter all the names of Hari.
Likewise:
O King, one who wanders abroad seeking liberation should meditate upon the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the plow, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and likewise the wielder of the sword,
in the directions beginning with the east.
In all worldly affairs, one should always remember with devotion that Person who is unconquered, undecaying, the Lord of all, and the vast Pṛthu.
When crossing water, one should meditate upon the Tortoise, the Boar, or the Fish;
being unwearied, one should mutter the name that is radiant and the generator of fire.
Going toward the front of the battle, he should call to mind the Unconquered One;
he should likewise mutter the names Keśava, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Puṣkarākṣa.
In all afflictions of the eyes, as well as in the preparation of medicinal remedies, one should likewise recite the names Hṛṣīkeśa, Acyuta, and Amṛta.
By recollecting the one whose banner is Garuḍa, a person is released from calamity;
the affliction of fever, diseases of the head, and the potency of poisons are pacified,
as well as the distress caused by planets and constellations, and the dangers posed by gods and in the forests.
In times of obstruction by robbers or enemies, in danger from tigers, lions, and the like,
and likewise in intense darkness, one should chant "Nārasiṃha."
In bad dreams, one should remember Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the bearer of Śrī, the liberator of the elephant, Vāmana, and the one who holds a sword.
When a fire has broken out, one should remember the one who reclines upon the waters;
one seeking victory in battle should remember Balabhadra, and at the commencement of agriculture, one should remember Halāyudha.
O King, one seeking success in trade should glorify Uttaraṇa; for prosperity, one should glorify Śrīśa; for auspiciousness, Viṣṇu; and for all auspicious occasions, one should glorify Maṅgalya.
When all the fires have been extinguished, one should likewise mutter "O Viśokā";
when rising, a man should glorify Viṣṇu, and while asleep, he should glorify Mādhava.
One should remember Govinda during meals, Madhusūdana in all circumstances,
and Nārāyaṇa at all times, even when stumbling while hungry or in similar situations.
In meditation, in the worship of the deity, in the fire-oblation, in prostration, and in circumambulation;
And one should recite the name of Vāsudeva, or among the Yādavas even those not specifically mentioned;
likewise, O King, at the commencement of any undertaking,
one may recite any name according to one's desire.
For all names indeed belong to him, O King;
for they lead to the accomplishment of every purpose for a person.
Therefore, one may certainly call upon the deity by whatever name one desires.
One should recite [the mantra] with devotion in all undertakings.
Thus ends the time for the chanting of Viṣṇu’s names.
Now follows the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (adhāna).
Regarding this, the Śruti says:
"One who has fathered a son and possesses black hair should establish the sacred fires.
This is an indication of a particular stage of life;
if he should have a son born to him, he should say: "I invoke that blessing for you, that auspicious light."
In such passages as these, because the connection [with the verb] is observed, even for one whose son has not yet been born, the *ādhāna* (consecration) must come first.

And thus, it is indicated that the specific age which serves as a qualification for the particular stage of life (*upalakṣya-vayovasthā*) constitutes the time for the *ādhāna*. He states another time:

Baudhāyana says: "The marriage ceremony has been explained; the time for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is according to one's faith from that point onward. One should establish the fires while the father is still living," so says Baudhāyana. Śālāki says: "Whether the father is living or deceased, having obtained a wife, one should establish the fire on the tenth day."

By stating "having obtained a wife," because marriage is valid at all times, it is implied that [the rite may be performed] even during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) and even in the dark fortnight (parvan). Furthermore, regarding the view that [one may marry] while the father is still living, Baudhāyana himself stated that there is no transgression for one who maintains the *aupāsana* fire: "One who maintains the *aupāsana* fire does not become a base Brāhmaṇa. This time-period is common to all three social classes (*traivarṇika*). Now, specific seasons are being distinguished without regard to the particular class.
In this regard, the Vedic revelation (śruti) states: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring,
a Rājanya in summer,
and a Vaiśya in autumn."
Regarding the phrase "the chariot-maker (rathakāra) during the rains":
the rathakāra is not the specific caste mentioned by Yājñavalkya in the verse, "A rathakāra is born from a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother";
rather, it is another synonym for the Saudhanvana.
Āpastamba, however, states: "Spring is for the Brāhmaṇa, summer or winter for the Rājanya, autumn for the Vaiśya, and the rainy season for the Rathakāra.
This is the time for those of the three castes who perform this rite;
the cool season is for all castes."

"Those of the three castes" means those who are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; among these three castes, for those who would perform this work—the work of a chariot-maker—this is the [proper] time.
And thus, a chariot-maker is not a distinct caste, but rather belongs to one of the three [higher] castes.

Regarding the different timing, Baudhāyana says: "Whenever faith (śraddhā) should come upon him, then he should establish the fires; that itself is his success. This [is for] one who is afflicted or for one who is excessively full of faith.
"Afflicted" (ārta) means one who is diseased.

"Exceedingly endowed with faith" means possessing faith to an extraordinary degree. Now, the seasons are specified according to particular desires by Kātyāyana: "Spring for the Brāhmaṇa desiring Vedic luster; summer for the Kṣatriya desiring glory; and the rainy season for the Vaiśya desiring progeny and cattle, and for the Rathakāra."

By this, it is established that for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, there are other times as well for optional rites (*kāmya*). The seasons, such as spring and so forth, are of two kinds; they have been distinguished according to the solar and lunar divisions in the analysis of the seasons.
It has also been stated that the solar months are of two kinds, distinguished as Pisces-Aries, Aries-Taurus, and so forth. Thus,

the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha, along with Māgha and Phālguna combined— based on the previously cited statement, “The Śiśira season belongs to all castes”— it is established that these five months constitute the time for the *ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires) for a Brāhmaṇa.
It is precisely on this basis that the well-known tradition among ritualists (*yājñika*) holds that the five months beginning with Māgha constitute spring.
Now, regarding the lunar days (*tithi*):
on this point, Āpastamba states—"One should begin [the study] on the new moon day or the full moon day."
Likewise, having stated, "One should establish the sacred fires on the full moon day of Phālguna," it is further specified as "two days before" or "one day before";
"two days" means two days [prior],
and "before" means one day prior.

And thus, the meaning is that one should establish the sacred fires on the thirteenth day if the two-day interval (dvyaheti) is the rule, and on the fourteenth day if the one-day interval (ekāheti) is the rule.
Baudhāyana says: "That new moon which occurs after the full moon of Vaiśākha coincides with Rohiṇī once every year; on that [day] one should establish the fires."
Āśvalāyana states: "One should establish the sacred fires on the full-moon day in spring.

Satyāṣāḍha, however, begins with "one should establish [the fires]" and continues: "On the new moon, the full moon, during the waxing fortnight, or under an auspicious lunar mansion—at this time, where three [factors] coincide, that is the collection [of requirements].
In case of conflict, the season and the lunar mansion take precedence."
The "meritorious lunar mansions" (*puṇyanakṣatra*) are the fourteen *nakṣatras* beginning with Kṛttikā, according to the Vedic revelation: "Kṛttikā is the first," and so forth.

However, in the Vājasaneyaka, it is stated—preceded by a deprecation of the *nakṣatras*—"One should establish the sacred fires on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyā*); therefore, the [lunar] festival (*parvan*) is more highly esteemed.
Now, regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*):
on this matter, Kātyāyana says—"Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, the two Phalgunīs, Hasta, and Citrā are for one desiring gain. Baudhāyana says—"Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, the two Phalgunīs, and Citrā."

Āśvalāyana says: "The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) may be performed under the Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, the two Phalgunīs, Viśākhā, or the two Uttaraproṣṭhapadas—under any one of these.
Āpastamba, however, states: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires under the Kṛttikās; he becomes preeminent and possessed of great luster. Yet, his fire will be a burner of his house."
By establishing the fires under Rohiṇī, one attains all forms of growth.
One who desires spiritual luster or the performance of sacrifice, or one who was previously auspicious but has become more wicked, should establish the fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa or Punarvasu.
One who desires [specific results] should [establish them] under the two Pūrva-phalgunīs.
"May my subjects be desirous of giving"—this is for the first two [rites]. For one who desires, "May I be a bestower of fruit," it is for the latter two.

This is the reverse of the former case. Furthermore, having performed the first two, one becomes worse off; having performed the latter two, one becomes superior in power. In the hand [of the sacrificer], it is as follows.

He who desires, "May I be distinguished," [should sacrifice] under Citrā; a kṣatriya who has rivals [should sacrifice] under Viśākhā; one desiring progeny under Anurādhā; one desiring prosperity under the Uttaraproṣṭhapadas;
and one desiring firm standing under the same Uttaraproṣṭhapadas. Some authorities prescribe all these rites as being obligatory (nitya).
This is the meaning.

*Mukhya* means *śreṣṭha* (preeminent). *Kalvān* refers to those who grow or ascend, such as elephants and the like. *Purābhadra* refers to the fruit of *pūrvā-phalgunī* [occurring] in *uttarā-phalgunī*.

The fruit of Uttarā-phalgunī [is to be understood] as occurring under Pūrvā-phalgunī; here, even though not intended, an undesirable result arises by the inherent power of the thing itself, as in the case of the rule: "He who should threaten a Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is stated in the Garga-saṃhitā:

The Brahmins and other castes should perform the primary installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) under the asterisms presided over by Puṣya, Agni, the three Uttarās, Āditya, Pūṣan, Jyeṣṭhā, Citrā, and Kṛttikā, and specifically during the spring, summer, or the end of the hot season.
Pauṣṇa is Revatī;
Ka is Brahmā, and Rohiṇī has him as its deity;
"ādya" refers to the first installation (of the sacred fires).

Because the word "first" (ādyam) is used here, there is no requirement for specific seasons or lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) in cases such as re-consecration (*punarādhāna*). It has been stated by Āpastamba that even in the case of a first *soma* sacrifice following the consecration (*somapūrvīdhāna*), there is no regard for season or lunar mansion: "One intending to sacrifice with the *soma* need not observe the season nor the lunar mansion."

He who desires to perform the Soma sacrifice itself before all other rites, such as the Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, need not heed nor pay attention to the season (*ṛtu*) or the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); however, he must certainly observe the *parvan* (the junction day). Thus says Dhūrtasvāmin: "In the case of the option of a single initiation (*ekadīkṣā*) for the establishment of the Soma-fire (*somādhāna*), it occurs only on a *parvan*, because the establishment of the Soma-fire requires the *parvan* and not on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) or similar dates."
Rudradatta, however, has stated that the mention of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is for the sake of illustration and thus there is no regard for the [specific] lunar day (*parvan*).
Here, this is to be considered:
does this statement imply a sublation of the time for the Soma sacrifice in general, or a sublation of the time for the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) alone?

Not the first [alternative], for it is appropriate that only the time of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) be set aside on account of the context, and not the *soma*, since that is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).

Furthermore, Āpastamba has not mentioned lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) in connection with the *soma*, such that one could claim a setting aside based merely on their being present in the mind in some way.
Not the second [alternative] either.

This being the case, the statement in this passage regarding the disregard for the season with respect to the Brāhmaṇa would be purposeless, because even when the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is performed at the time of the *soma*, spring is nonetheless unavoidable.
Nor can it be argued that at that time spring is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the *soma* alone, and not a subsidiary element of the *ādhāna*.
Because that [time] is common [to all rites];
for time assists solely by way of being a locus (adhikaraṇa),
and when it exists, how could it not be an auxiliary (aṅga)?

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the Soma sacrifice should belong to a Brāhmaṇa because of his preeminence," it was stated in the section concerning the pregnant woman (*antarāgarbhiṇī*)— specifically in the passage "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma"— that the time for the Soma sacrifice, which consists in its occurring after the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), is set aside by the connection of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) and the Soma sacrifice within a single day.

By the same principle, here too, when the fire-installation is performed at another time while disregarding spring, [it is done so] for the sake of establishing the connection between the Soma sacrifice and the fire-installation within a single day.
The season for the Soma sacrifice is indeed sublated; therefore, it is not a sublation of the time for the Soma alone, nor a sublation of the time for the consecration (dīkṣā) alone.
Consequently, [your] statement is purposeless.
To this, we reply:
True, it is not that only the time of one is sublated;
rather, the time for both the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is sublated.
In that regard, the spring season—which is a constituent part of both—is sublated.
The lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), however, is indeed merely a subsidiary element of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires).

For this very reason, Bhāradvāja stated that one should establish the fires "as soon as the sacrifice approaches him," thereby showing disregard for the lunar mansion and other such factors; this is not at all inconsistent, as it refers to one who possesses the intention to perform a sacrifice.

It has been stated by the Teacher [Āpastamba] that the entire northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is a time for the *ādhāna*; this was mentioned by Keśavasvāmin in his commentary on the Baudhāyana-sūtra.

Although the *jyotiḥśāstra* prescribes the *lagna* (ascendant) and so forth for the *ādhāna*, it must nevertheless be adopted; for even though it belongs to the *smārta* tradition, it is enjoined specifically with reference to the *ādhāna*, and since it cannot be established otherwise, it must necessarily be integrated [into the ritual].
Others, however, maintain that because this [prescription] is *smārta*, its integration applies only to the *smārta* *ādhāna* and not to the *śrauta* *ādhāna*.
Furthermore, this [consecration] should not be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) and so forth, nor when Jupiter (*guru*) or Venus (*śukra*) are in retrogression (*mauḍhya*).
This concludes the section on the time for the *ādhāna* (establishment of the sacred fires).
Now follows the time for the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* (the established animal sacrifice).

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya (1.125) states: "The Soma sacrifice should be performed every year, as well as the animal sacrifice at each solstice; likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed."
Thus:
"pratyayanam" means "for every solstice" (ayanam ayanam prati); that is to say, for both the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) and the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
Although the solstice is common to its entirety, the rite must be performed on the very day the solstice begins.
This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Āpastamba: "At the mouth of the return, at the mouth of the return.
"Return" (āvṛtti) means the turning back of the sun from its northern limit (Capricorn) or its southern limit (Cancer); the "mouth" (mukha) of that [return] means its first day.
Having introduced the established animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), Āpastamba states regarding the timing: "One should sacrifice every year, or every six months, according to some;
or at the change of seasons, or when there is good pasture."
The word "when a year has been completed" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Therefore, some commentators state that the meaning is "on the day of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) in the following year.
However, others [say]:

According to the grammatical rule, "The case-ending denoting the agent (kāraka-vibhakti) is stronger than the case-ending denoting a locative adjunct (upapada-vibhakti)," the year itself is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). When the question arises as to *when* within that [year], two points in time are indicated: one is "at the turning of the seasons" (*ṛtuvyāvṛttau*), and the other is "in the good season" (*suvayasaḥ*).
Regarding "at the turning of the seasons," the meaning is: on whichever day during the course of the year there is a change of season.
*Suyavase* means "in that which has excellent grass (*suyavasa*), namely *arjuna* grass, during the rains"—this is the meaning.

According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, there is an alternative view that [the rites are performed] at the transition of seasons; specifically, at each seasonal transition, thus six times in a year. Furthermore, "*suyavasa*" is an independent alternative from the view of the year itself.
And there is yet another alternative view: "every six months."
The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that "six months" should be understood as the completion of six months starting from the day of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration).
However, according to the view of some, they connect this "six-month" option with the phrase "at the commencement of the repetition.
Thus, in the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra, one position is that [the rite should be performed] every year on the day of the *ādhāna*.
The second [view] is that it occurs every six months from the day of conception;
the third is that it occurs at the change of each season within the year.
The fourth [view] is that it is only during the rainy season within the year;
thus, there are five times known as the "entrances of recurrence.
However, according to the opinion of some, in the view that it should be done every year, it may be performed in any season whatsoever.
Another [teacher] says "suyavase" (in good pasture);
and according to the view that it occurs every six months, it is the third [period], characterized by a reversal of direction.
And in this case, regarding the fixed number of days, there is no restriction as to the lunar festival (parvan).
In the alternative view, that very restriction [is maintained] because of the statement "if one praises.
Kātyāyana also mentions two times: "The animal sacrifice (paśvijyā) is performed every year in the rainy season, or at the beginning and end of the year.

Baudhāyana mentions another time, stating: "Having commenced with the injunction 'one should sacrifice with the animal offering,' [he says] 'either after performing the New Moon oblation (āmāvāsya-havis) or under a [specific] lunar mansion (nakṣatra)."
"Having sacrificed with the new-moon oblation" refers to the day on which the sacrifice is to be performed;
others, however, say it is the full [moon] in the bright fortnight.
"Under a lunar mansion" means under the fourteen auspicious constellations mentioned in the Taittirīya branch, beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Viśākhā.
Alternatively, it is called a *nakṣatra* because the moon does not wane (*na kṣīyate*) in it; thus, it means the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

According to this view, since the performance of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices begins on the full-moon day, no other ritual may be commenced from the start of the Pūrṇamāsa until the Darśa, in accordance with the rule that "one who is engaged in a ritual must not commence another ritual."

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, by examining the statement contained within the explanatory passage (arthavāda), “If one does not sacrifice with an animal for a year,” states that the sixth time [for the animal sacrifice] is that it should be performed on any parvan day during the year following the day of the fire-installation (ādhāna). Furthermore,
this animal sacrifice is obligatory (nitya), because of the hearing of the repetitive expression (vīpsā) in the words “year after year” and “at each [new] moon.”
Furthermore, because the expiation for failing to perform this [rite] will be stated later as prescribed by Manu and others.
Thus ends the section on the time for animal sacrifices. Now, the time for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is determined.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya has stated that "the Cāturmāsyas must indeed be performed" (*cāturmāsyāni caiva hi*).
The word "must be performed" (*kartavyāni*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

In this context, the term *cāturmāsya* is the collective name for the group of sacrifices consisting of the Vaiśvadeva, Varuṇapraghāsa, Sākamedha, and Śunāsīrīya, just as the term *rājasūya* is used for its constituent rites.
And these are of three kinds: those involving lifelong practice, those involving a year-long practice, and those involving a twelve-day practice.
Some maintain that [the rites] are completed at the time of the conclusion of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Among those, even those involving a year-long application (*saṃvatsara-prayoga*) are of two kinds: by way of the *ṛtukuyājika* ritual procedure and by way of the *cāturmāsyayājika* ritual procedure.

Regarding the distinctions among these ritual applications (*prayoga*), the authoritative evidence is to be understood solely from the specific injunctions for their respective times that will be mentioned later.

In that regard, it has been stated that all these applications are to be performed subsequent to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, by means of the injunction: "Having sacrificed with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*s... (*darśapaurṇamāsābhyāmiṣṭvā*).
Now, the specific times for the annual and other such ritual applications are being analyzed.
Regarding the annual application, Āpastamba has stated the time for the Vaiśvadeva and subsequent rites according to the model of the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyājika*):
"It is known that one sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva in spring, with the Varuṇapraghāsas in the rainy season, and with the Sākamedhas in autumn."
In these three seasonal festivals (*parvan*), the time is prescribed as fixed.

However, regarding the *Śunāsīrīya*, it appears that only the winter season (*śiśira*) should be accepted, in accordance with the designation of the *ṛtuyāja* offerings. Even in this case, the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is indeed required.

Since the validity of that [time] stated by the words of Bhāradvāja—“during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight”—is established without contradiction even though there exist many optional times, it is improper to assume a contradiction;

for the same time is prescribed both in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and in the lifelong performance (*yāvajjīvaprayoga*), as in: "He who sacrifices every four months is a performer of the Cāturmāsya."
Regarding that, he states the rule: one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on the full moon of Phālguna or Caitra;
then, after four months, one should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsas on the full moon of Āṣāḍha or Śrāvaṇa;
then, after another four months, having commenced on the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should sacrifice for two days with the Sākamedhas.
Then, after two days, three days, four days, half a month, a month, or four months, [the sacrifice is performed] with the Śunāsīrīya offerings.

In this regard, when the commencement is on the full moon day of Phālguna, it takes place on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, and so forth; and when it is on the full moon day of Caitra, it takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.

The distinction between this position and that of the Ṛtuyājin is this: in the case of the Ṛtuyājin, it is possible to perform the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice at the first parvan of the rainy season after having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva rites at the end of spring;
whereas in the case of the Cāturmāsyayājin, there is a rule that they must be performed every four months.
Baudhāyana and Bhāradvāja state that the ritual procedure lasts for twelve days.

Regarding this, Bhāradvāja says: one intending to perform the sacrifice for twelve days [should begin] on the first day (pratipad) with the Vaiśvānara-Pārjanya offerings; on the second day, with the Vaiśvadeva; having ceased on either the third or the fourth day, he performs the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings on the fifth day; having ceased on either the sixth or the seventh day, [he performs them] on the eighth day.

Or, having concluded with the Sākamedha offerings on the ninth, tenth, or eleventh day, one performs the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice on the twelfth and the animal sacrifice on the thirteenth; for it is known that "the twelve nights are indeed a counterpart of the year; thus one sacrifices for the sake of the year itself. Regarding the statement "the animal sacrifice on the thirteenth," this should be understood as applying to the alternative view where the ritual concludes with the animal sacrifice.

In this context, the words "second" and so forth refer to the second lunar day (tithi) and the rest, as is clear from the opening statement regarding the first day (*pratipad*). And it has been stated by Baudhāyana:

"One should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya offerings even on the twelfth day; having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva on the first [lunar day], one sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsas on the fourth; with the Sākamedhas on the eighth and the ninth; and with the Śunāsīrīya on the twelfth—it is thus understood that a person should sacrifice."

A different time has also been stated by Baudhāyana: "Some say the performance should take place under a [specific] lunar mansion; one should perform it during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day.
According to this view, the commencement occurs under an auspicious lunar mansion during the waxing fortnight.
The author of the Bhāṣya holds that "the commencement at a [favorable] lunar mansion" is a qualification of this [rite], such as occurring during the northern course of the sun and so forth.
However, in the view that the performance lasts for one's entire life, the commencement follows the very procedure of the Cāturmāsya sacrificer.
Regarding the second year, a specific rule has been stated by Baudhāyana:

How indeed is the subsequent performance (*anuprayoga*) of the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, which are to be performed for as long as one lives, carried out? On the full moon day of either Phālguna or Caitra, having performed the *Śunāsīrīya* sacrifice, one should fast for the *Vaiśvadeva*. Having sacrificed with the *Vaiśvadeva*, one should then perform the *Paurṇamāsa* and *Vaimṛdha* sacrifices. Now, if one should sacrifice with an *Iṣṭi*, an animal sacrifice, or the Soma sacrifice, how is it in that case?

"One should perform [the sacrifice]"—having thus drawn back [the rule], for this position it is said: "The man should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrīya; he should sacrifice with one of these [three]; then he should fast for the Vaiśvadeva;
having sacrificed with the Vaiśvadeva, he should sacrifice with the Full-moon and Vaimṛdha offerings.
Now, they also report this as the position of Baudhāyana: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices should indeed be performed throughout one's entire life."
The *anuprayoga* is the second performance.
In this regard, when the commencement was made in Phālgunī of the previous year, then [the second performance] is in Phālgunī; and when the commencement was made in Caitrī, then it is in Caitrī.
Now, if it is said "with an *iṣṭi*," meaning that if an *iṣṭi* or similar rite is performed for the sake of concluding the performance, then this is the sequence.

By the statement "if" (*ced*), because of the unity of purpose from the commencement until the completion of the lifelong practice (*yāvajjīva-prayoga*), the animal sacrifices and so forth are understood to be optional (*pākṣika*).
Furthermore, by the statement beginning with "Now this is the view of Baudhāyana," it should be understood that even the lifelong practice is optional.
Baudhāyana also mentions another time [for the performance]:
"According to the performance," says Aupamanyava.
"According to the performance" means that for as long as it takes to complete the performance, one should perform [the recitation] continuously during the forenoon and so forth;
according to this view, the commencement occurs only during the northern course of the sun and under an auspicious lunar mansion.
Rudradatta and others do not accept this view;

for by the phrase "according to the performance," it is not the prescription of the time for the Cāturmāsya sacrifices that is intended, but rather a restriction on the period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), meaning that the observance of the vow lasts only as long as the day of the performance.
And this is clearly understood from the context of the opening statement itself.

And so says the Sūtra: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices should be performed throughout one's life, with the pairing [of rites] occurring at intervals; however, in the very first year, one should observe the vow. Regarding this, Śālāki said: "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices are indeed annual, for they involve the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)."
"According to the ritual application," says Aupamanyava.
The meaning of this is as follows:
according to the view of Baudhāyana, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must be performed for the duration of one's life, including the *antar-yajña* and the *mithuna*.
And it is said that the practice of the barley-vow (*yavavrata*) lasts for the first year;
however, according to the opinion of Śālīkī, this rule applies only to rites lasting one year and not to those lasting a lifetime.
According to the opinion of Upamanyu, the practice of the vow occurs on the very day of the performance.

Others, however, say: "Let it not be according to the [usual] application; rather, let there be continuous performance. Nevertheless, because of the statement of Bhāradvāja—"All [the rites] during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight"—there is the performance of all [the rites] joined together. Furthermore, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices pertaining to this world have been described by Śāṅkhāyana.
Now, regarding the time for the Soma sacrifice:
on this point there is a Vedic revelation (śruti), "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring";
and Yājñavalkya also states, "The Soma [sacrifice] is performed every year."

It has been stated that this [Soma sacrifice] must also be performed after the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), based on the scriptural injunction: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma.

This is the general rule; however, in the case of the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) followed by the Soma sacrifice, it is performed even prior to the Darśapūrṇamāsa because of its performance at that time.

Āśvalāyana also states, "Even before the Soma [sacrifice] by means of one alone," thereby indicating that the performance of the Soma sacrifice is to take place even prior to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Furthermore, this [Soma sacrifice] is to be performed on a festival day (*parvan*) even in spring, according to the injunction, "If one should sacrifice. Baudhāyana also mentions another time:

"Having sacrificed with the new-moon oblation, [one may sacrifice] under a lunar mansion," the meaning of which has been explained in the determination of the time for the animal sacrifice. Thus ends the section on the time for the Soma sacrifice.
When the moon of his face rises, the glorious ocean of the gift-giving of the Lion among Heroes— which dispels the darkness of the wretchedness of those who seek his aid— increases at every moment.
In this treatise composed by the learned Mitra Miśra at the command of the King, the fourth chapter, which is devoted to the exposition of the *samaya*, has reached its completion.

Thus, in the work composed by the illustrious Mitramiśra—the son of Paraśurāma Miśra, who was the son of Śrī Haṃsapāṇḍita; who was commissioned by the illustrious Vīrasiṃhadeva, the sun that causes to blossom the lotus-heart of the earth bounded by the four oceans, the grandson of the illustrious Mahārāja Madhukara Sāha, and the son of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāparudra, whose lotus-feet were honored by the clusters of rays from the crest-jewels of the entire circle of subordinate chieftains; and who was the foremost among those who have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of all sciences, a lion to the great elephant of world-wide poverty, and the life-sustenance of learned men.
The Samayaprakāśa, within the treatise titled Vīramitrodaya, is completed.
May there be auspiciousness!
